Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: The Jūnzǐ says:
Learning must never cease.
Blue dye is taken from the indigo plant,
yet it is bluer than the indigo;
ice is made from water,
yet it is colder than the water.
Wood as straight as a plumb line,
if steamed and bent to make a wheel,
its curve will fit the compass;
even if it dries in the sun again,
it will not straighten out,
because the bending has made it so.
Thus, wood becomes straight when applied to the plumb line,
and metal becomes sharp when applied to the whetstone.
The Jūnzǐ learns broadly
and examines himself daily;
thus his wisdom becomes enlightened
and his actions will be without error.
Therefore, without climbing a high mountain,
one does not know the height of heaven;
without looking into a deep ravine,
one does not know the thickness of the earth;
without hearing the bequeathed words of the Xiānwáng,
one does not know the greatness of learning.
The children of Gān, Yuè, Yí, and Mò
make the same sounds at birth,
but grow up with different customs,
because education makes them so.
The Shī says:
"O you Jūnzǐ,
do not constantly rest in ease.
Quietly attend to your positions,
loving what is upright and correct.
The spirits will hear you
and grant you great fortune."
No spirit is greater than being transformed by the Dào;
no fortune is more lasting than being free from calamity.
I once spent the whole day in thought,
but it was not as good as what is learned in a moment;
I once stood on tiptoe to look far off,
but it was not as good as the broad view from high ground.
When you wave from high ground,
your arm is not any longer,
yet you can be seen from further away;
when you call out with the wind,
your voice is not any louder,
yet you can be heard more clearly.
One who uses a carriage and horses
does not have faster feet,
yet can reach a thousand lǐ;
one who uses a boat and oars
is not necessarily able to swim,
yet can cross rivers and seas.
The Jūnzǐ is not born different;
he is simply good at making use of external things.
In the south there is a bird
named the Méngjiū,
which makes its nest of feathers,
weaving it together with hair,
and tying it to the tip of a reed.
When the wind comes, the reed breaks,
the eggs are smashed, and the young birds die.
It is not that the nest was not well-made;
it is because of what it was tied to.
In the west there is a plant
named the Shègān,
its stem is only four inches long,
yet it grows on top of high mountains
and overlooks a chasm of a hundred rèn;
it is not that the plant's stem is long,
it is because of where it stands.
When fleabane grows among hemp,
it stands straight without support;
when white sand is mixed with black mud,
it becomes black as well.
The root of the Lánhuái is the zhǐ perfume.
If it is soaked in foul water,
the Jūnzǐ will not go near it,
and common people will not wear it.
It is not that its essence is not beautiful;
it is because of what it was soaked in.
Therefore, when the Jūnzǐ dwells,
he must choose his neighborhood;
when he travels, he must associate with scholars;
this is how he guards against depravity
and draws near to what is balanced and upright.
When things of various kinds arise,
they must have a starting point.
When honor or disgrace comes,
it must reflect one's virtue.
Rotting meat produces worms,
and drying fish produce maggots.
If one is negligent and forgets himself,
then calamity and disaster arise.
What is stiff invites snapping;
what is soft invites binding.
When evil and filth are in oneself,
resentment is what builds up.
If firewood is laid out uniformly,
fire will move toward the dry pieces;
if the ground is level,
water will move toward the damp spots.
Plants and trees grow in clusters,
birds and beasts live in groups;
all things follow their own kind.
Thus, when a target is set up,
the bow and arrow will arrive;
when the forest trees are lush,
the axe will arrive;
when a tree provides shade,
the birds will rest there;
when vinegar turns sour,
the gnats will gather there.
Therefore, words can bring calamity,
and actions can invite disgrace;
the Jūnzǐ must be careful where he takes his stand!
Accumulate earth to form a mountain,
and wind and rain will arise from it;
accumulate water to form a deep pool,
and dragons will be born in it;
accumulate goodness to form virtue,
and divine clarity will be naturally attained;
the mind of a Shèngrén is thus complete.
Therefore, without accumulating single steps,
one cannot reach a thousand lǐ;
without accumulating small streams,
one cannot form rivers and seas.
Even a Qiíjì in one leap
cannot cover ten paces;
an old nag in ten days of pulling
achieves success by not giving up.
If you start carving and then stop,
even rotten wood will not break;
if you carve and do not stop,
even metal and stone can be engraved.
The earthworm has no sharpness of claws or teeth,
nor the strength of muscles or bones,
yet it eats the dust above,
and drinks from the yellow springs below,
because its mind is focused on one thing.
The crab has six legs and two claws,
yet without the burrows of snakes or eels
it has no place to lodge,
because its mind is restless.
Therefore, one who lacks hidden will
lacks brilliant understanding;
one who lacks quiet dedication to his tasks
lacks illustrious achievements.
One who walks at a crossroads will not arrive;
one who serves two masters will not be accepted.
The eyes cannot look at two things and see clearly;
the ears cannot hear two things and understand distinctly.
The Téngshé has no feet yet flies;
the Wúshǔ has five skills yet is at its wits' end.
The Shī says:
"The Shījiū is in the mulberry tree;
its young are seven.
The virtuous Jūnzǐ
is uniform in his demeanor.
Uniform in his demeanor,
his heart is as if bound."
Thus, the Jūnzǐ is bound to the One.
In the past, Hù Bā played the sè,
and the swimming fish came out to listen;
Bó Yá played the qín,
and the six horses looked up from their fodder.
Therefore, no sound is so small that it is not heard,
and no action is so hidden that it is not manifested.
When jade is in the mountain, the plants and trees are lush;
when pearls are born in the abyss, the banks do not dry up.
Is it not because of the accumulation of goodness?
How could it not be heard of?
Where does learning begin?
Where does it end?
I say:
In its method, it begins with reciting the classics
and ends with reading the Lǐ;
in its purpose, it begins with becoming a Shì
and ends with becoming a Shèngrén.
Truly accumulate effort for a long time and you will enter into it;
learning only stops when death comes.
Thus, the method of learning has an end,
but its purpose must not be abandoned for a moment.
To do it is to be human;
to abandon it is to be a beast.
Therefore, the Shū is the record of government affairs;
the Shī is the resting place of balanced sounds;
the Lǐ is the great division of the laws
and the guiding principle of all categories of things.
Therefore, learning reaches its culmination in the *Lǐ* and then rests.
This is called the peak of Way and Virtue.
The reverence and refinement of the *Lǐ*,
the balance and harmony of the *Yuè*,
the breadth of the *Shī* and *Shū*,
the subtleties of the *Chūnqiū*—
everything between Heaven and Earth is fully contained within them.
The learning of the *Jūnzǐ*:
it enters through the ears,
becomes fixed in the heart,
spreads through the four limbs,
and manifests in movement and stillness.
The slightest word,
the smallest movement,
each can serve as a model.
The learning of the petty man:
it enters through the ears,
and comes out through the mouth.
Between the mouth and the ears
is only four inches;
how could that be enough to beautify a seven-foot body!
Scholars of antiquity studied for themselves;
scholars of today study for others.
The learning of the *Jūnzǐ*
is used to beautify his person;
the learning of the petty man
is used as gifts like poultry and calves.
Therefore, to tell without being asked is called being overbearing;
to tell two things when asked one is called being wordy.
To be overbearing
or wordy is wrong;
the *Jūnzǐ* is like an echo.
In learning, nothing is more convenient than being close to the right person.
The *Lǐ* and *Yuè* provide standards but do not explain them;
the *Shī* and *Shū* record ancient matters but are not immediate;
the *Chūnqiū* is concise and not quickly understood.
If one follows the practices of such a person
and the explanations of a *Jūnzǐ*,
then one will be honored and comprehensive,
encompassing all the world.
Thus it is said:
In learning, nothing is more convenient than being close to the right person.
Of the paths to learning, none is faster than loving such a person,
and exalting ritual comes next.
If above one cannot love such a person,
and below one cannot exalt ritual,
then one will merely study miscellaneous records
and follow the *Shī* and *Shū*;
then throughout one's life and to the end of one's years,
one will not escape being a narrow-minded scholar.
If one wishes to trace the Former Kings to their source
and make Benevolence and Righteousness one's foundation,
then Ritual is the correct warp and woof, the path and track.
It is like grabbing a fur coat by the collar:
bend five fingers and give it a shake,
and the hairs that fall into place are countless.
If one does not follow the laws of Ritual
but tries to do it through the *Shī* and *Shū* alone,
it is like trying to measure a river with a finger,
pounding millet with a spear,
or eating from a pot with an awl;
one cannot succeed.
Therefore, if one exalts Ritual,
even if not yet enlightened,
one is a man of standards;
if one does not exalt Ritual,
even if one is observant and eloquent,
one is a fragmented scholar.
If someone asks about crude matters,
do not answer him;
if someone speaks of crude matters,
do not question him;
if someone explains crude matters,
do not listen to him;
if someone has a contentious spirit,
do not debate with him.
Therefore, one must arrive by way of the Path
before one is received;
if it is not the Path, then avoid it.
Therefore, when ritual is respectful,
only then can one discuss the methods of the Path;
when speech is agreeable,
only then can one discuss the principles of the Path;
when the countenance is compliant,
only then can one discuss the ultimate goal of the Path.
To speak when it is not yet appropriate to speak
is called being overbearing;
to not speak when it is appropriate to speak
is called being secretive;
to speak without observing the countenance
is called being blind.
Thus the *Jūnzǐ* is not overbearing, not secretive, and not blind;
he is cautious regarding his person.
The *Shī* says:
"Neither overbearing nor lax,
the Son of Heaven bestows his favor."
This is what it refers to.
If out of a hundred shots one misses once,
it is not enough to be called an expert archer;
if in a thousand-mile journey one fails to complete the last half-step,
it is not enough to be called an expert charioteer;
if relationships and categories are not understood,
and Benevolence and Righteousness are not unified,
it is not enough to be called an expert scholar.
Learning
is indeed learning to unify these.
Departing from this once,
entering into it once,
one is a man of the streets and alleys.
If one's good qualities are few
and bad qualities are many,
one is a *Jié*, a *Zhòu*, or a *Dàozhí*.
To perfect it and exhaust it completely,
only then is one a scholar.
The *Jūnzǐ* knows that what is not complete and not pure is not sufficient to be beautiful.
Therefore, he recites and enumerates to link them,
contemplates and seeks to understand them,
acts as the right kind of person to dwell in them,
and eliminates what is harmful to maintain and nourish them.
He makes his eyes desire to see nothing that is not this,
his ears desire to hear nothing that is not this,
his mouth desire to speak nothing that is not this,
and his heart desire to think of nothing that is not this.
When he reaches the ultimate point,
he loves it.
His eyes love it more than the five colors,
his ears love it more than the five sounds,
his mouth loves it more than the five flavors,
and his heart finds it more beneficial than possessing the world.
Therefore, power and profit cannot subvert him,
the masses cannot shift him,
and the whole world cannot shake him.
He lives by this,
he dies by this;
this is called virtuous constancy.
With virtuous constancy, one can then be steadfast;
with steadfastness, one can then respond;
being steadfast and able to respond,
this is what is called a complete man.
Heaven shows its brilliance,
Earth shows its glory,
and the *Jūnzǐ* values his completeness.
Seeing what is good,
one must be respectful and certainly preserve it in oneself;
seeing what is not good,
one must be apprehensive and certainly examine oneself.
If good is within oneself,
one must be resolute and certainly love it;
if what is not good is within oneself,
one must be distressed and certainly hate it.
Therefore, one who criticizes me and is correct
is my teacher;
one who affirms me and is correct
is my friend;
one who flatters me
is my thief.
Thus the *Jūnzǐ* exalts his teacher and is close to his friends,
so as to utterly hate his thieves.
Loving what is good without satiation,
accepting admonition and being able to take warning—
even if one desired not to progress,
how could that be possible!
The petty man is the opposite:
he is extremely chaotic
yet hates it when others criticize him;
he is extremely unworthy
yet desires others to consider him worthy;
his heart is like a tiger or wolf,
his conduct is like that of a beast,
and yet he hates it when others treat him as a thief.
He is close to flatterers,
distant from those who admonish him,
regards cultivation and correction as a joke,
and considers ultimate loyalty as thievery;
even if he desired not to perish,
how could that be possible!
The *Shī* says:
"Chattering and slandering,
this is indeed most lamentable.
If a plan is good,
they all oppose it;
if a plan is not good,
they all follow it."
This is what it refers to.
As for the standard of comprehensive goodness,
if used to regulate one's *qì* and nourish life,
one will follow after *Péng Zǔ*;
if used to cultivate the person and strengthen oneself,
then one's name will match *Yáo* and *Yǔ*.
Suiting prosperous times,
beneficial when dwelling in poverty—
ritual and trustworthiness are these.
Whenever employing one's vital energy, will, and intellect,
if one follows Lǐ, then there will be order and success;
if one does not follow Lǐ, then there will be disorder, arrogance, and laziness.
In eating and drinking, clothing, and dwelling, in movement and stillness,
if one follows Lǐ, there will be harmony and moderation;
if one does not follow Lǐ, there will be conflict, pitfalls, and illness.
In appearance, attitude, advancing and retreating, and manner of walking,
if one follows Lǐ, there will be elegance;
if one does not follow Lǐ, there will be coarseness, obstinacy, and perversion, making one common and boorish.
Therefore, without Lǐ, a person cannot live;
without Lǐ, an undertaking cannot succeed;
without Lǐ, a state cannot be at peace.
The Shī says:
"Rituals and ceremonies follow the measure;
laughter and speech are perfectly appropriate."
This is what is meant.
To lead others with goodness is called "teaching";
to harmonize with others with goodness is called "compliance."
To lead others with what is not good is called "flattery";
to harmonize with others with what is not good is called "sycophancy."
To affirm what is right and deny what is wrong is called wisdom;
to deny what is right and affirm what is wrong is called folly.
To injure the good is called slander;
to harm the good is called villainy.
To call right "right" and
wrong "wrong"
is called uprightness.
To steal goods is called theft;
to conceal one's actions is called deception;
to speak glibly is called falsehood.
To have no fixed principle in what one takes or leaves is called inconstancy;
to protect profit and abandon righteousness is called the ultimate villainy.
To hear much is called erudition;
to hear little is called shallowness;
To see much is called cultivation;
to see little is called crudeness.
To be slow to advance is called indecision;
to be easy to forget is called leakiness.
To be few but well-ordered is called governed;
to be many but chaotic is called wasted.
As for the techniques of regulating vital energy and nourishing the heart:
If the vital energy is hard and strong,
then soften it with harmony.
If the intellect and thoughts become too deep,
then unify them with simplicity and goodness.
If one is courageous, bold, fierce, and perverse,
then assist them with the way of compliance.
If one is quick and clever,
then moderate them with movement and stillness.
If one is narrow and petty,
then broaden them with vastness.
If one is low and damp, heavy and slow, or greedy for profit,
then lift them with high aspirations.
If one is common, mediocre, and scattered,
then constrain them with teachers and friends.
If one is negligent, frivolous, and self-abandoning,
then illuminate them with the threat of disaster.
If one is simple, sincere, and upright,
then harmonize them with Lǐ and music,
and connect them through reflection.
Of all techniques for regulating vital energy and nourishing the heart,
none is more direct than following Lǐ,
none is more essential than finding a teacher,
and none is more divine than unifying one's focus.
This is what is called the technique of regulating vital energy and nourishing the heart.
If the will is cultivated, then one looks down upon wealth and status;
if the Way and righteousness are valued, then one holds kings and dukes lightly;
if one reflects within, then external things become light.
The Zhuàn says:
"The Jūnzǐ makes things his servants;
the petty person is made a servant by things."
This is what is meant.
If the body is labored but the heart is at peace,
do it;
if the profit is little but the righteousness is much,
do it.
To serve a chaotic ruler and find success
is not as good as serving a destitute ruler and being in accord with the Way.
Thus, a good farmer does not stop plowing because of flood or drought;
a good merchant does not stop trading because of losses;
the Shìjūnzǐ does not neglect the Way because of poverty.
If the body is respectful and the heart is loyal and trustworthy,
if one's methods follow Lǐ and righteousness and one's feelings are for loving others,
though one travels across the world
and is hard-pressed among the Sìyí,
there is no one who will not value them.
In matters of labor and hardship, they strive to be first;
in matters of abundance and joy, they are able to yield;
they are upright, sincere, and faithful,
careful in their duties and detailed.
Though such a person travels across the world
and is hard-pressed among the Sìyí,
there is no one who will not trust them.
If the body is arrogant and obstinate
and the heart is full of power and deception,
if one's methods follow Shùn and Mò
and one's essence is mixed and foul,
though one travels across the world
and reaches every corner of the land,
there is no one who will not despise them.
In matters of labor and hardship, they shrink away and escape;
in matters of abundance and joy, they are glib and opportunistic without integrity,
perverse and without sincerity,
calculating their duties without diligence.
Though such a person travels across the world
and reaches every corner of the land,
there is no one who will not abandon them.
Walking with a cautious and reverent air
is not because of mud or puddles;
walking with a bowed head
is not because of an impending blow;
looking sideways and then looking down
is not because of fear.
Rather, the Shì wishes to cultivate his own person alone,
so as not to offend the common people of the day.
The horse Jì can travel a thousand lǐ in one day;
a slow horse in ten days of pulling
can also reach the same distance.
But if one attempts to exhaust the inexhaustible
or pursue the infinite,
then though one breaks their bones and snaps their sinews,
one will never reach it to the end of their life.
If there is a point to stop at,
then even if a thousand lǐ is far,
it is only a matter of being slow or fast, first or last;
why should they not be able to reach one another?
Does the person who does not understand the path of walking
intend to exhaust the inexhaustible
and pursue the infinite?
Or does he also have a point to stop at?
Investigations into "Hardness and Whiteness," "Sameness and Difference," or "Having Thickness or No Thickness,"
are not without discernment;
however, the Jūnzǐ does not debate them
because he stops himself.
Eccentric and strange conduct
is not without difficulty;
however, the Jūnzǐ does not practice it
because he stops himself.
Thus, learning may be called slow;
if the goal stays there and waits for me,
and I walk toward it,
then it is only a matter of being slow or fast, first or last;
why should it be impossible for all to arrive together?
Therefore, if one takes even half-steps without stopping,
a lame turtle can travel a thousand lǐ;
if one piles up earth without ceasing,
a high mountain will be completed.
Stop the source
and open the channels,
and even the Jiāng and Hé rivers can be dried up.
If one moves forward one step and retreats one step,
or goes one way to the left and another to the right,
even six Jì horses will not arrive.
The difference between the talents and natures of people
is surely not as great as that between a lame turtle and six Jì horses!
Yet the lame turtle arrives
while the six Jì horses do not;
there is no other reason for this
than that one does the work
while the other does not.
Although the Way is near,
if one does not walk, one will not arrive;
although the matter is small,
if one does not do it, it will not be completed.
For a person who has many idle days,
their progress beyond others will not be far.
One who loves the laws and acts upon them
is a Shì;
one who is firm in will and embodies them
is a Jūnzǐ;
one who is clear and bright without exhaustion
is a Shèngrén.
If a person has no law,
they will be aimless;
if they have laws but no will to understand their meaning,
they will be narrow-minded;
if they rely on the laws
and further deepen their understanding of their categories,
then they will be warm and gracious.
Lǐ is that by which one corrects the self;
the teacher is that by which one corrects Lǐ.
Without Lǐ, how can one correct the self?
Without a teacher, how can I know that Lǐ is correct?
If Lǐ dictates it and one acts accordingly,
then one's emotions are at peace with Lǐ.
If the teacher says it and one speaks accordingly,
then one's knowledge is like that of the teacher.
When emotions are at peace with Lǐ
and knowledge is like that of the teacher,
then one is a Shèngrén.
Therefore, to reject ritual
is to be without law;
to reject a teacher
is to be without a teacher.
To not follow a teacher or the ritual
but to be fond of following one's own way
is comparable to the blind distinguishing colors
or the deaf distinguishing sounds;
apart from chaos and recklessness, one does nothing.
Therefore, learning
means to take ritual as one's law.
As for the teacher, he uses his own person as a standard model
and values being at peace with himself.
The *Shī* says:
"Neither knowing nor being conscious,
one follows the laws of the Lord-on-High."
This is what it refers to.
One who is upright, sincere, and compliant with elders
may be called a good youth;
if one adds to this a love for learning and being humble and quick,
then one has no equal and no superior
and can become a *Jūnzǐ*.
One who is lazy, cowardly, and afraid of work,
lacking a sense of shame and being greedy for food and drink,
may be called a bad youth;
if one adds to this being reckless, fierce, and non-compliant,
being perilously malicious and disrespectful to elders,
then one may be called an inauspicious youth,
and even if one falls into execution, it is fitting.
Respect the elderly, and the strong will turn to you;
do not bring distress to the destitute, and those who are successful will gather around you;
act in the shadows and give without seeking recompense,
and the worthy and unworthy will be treated as one.
If a person has these three conducts,
even if they have great faults,
will Heaven not be favorable to them?
The *Jūnzǐ*’s pursuit of profit is negligible,
his distancing from harm is early,
his avoidance of disgrace is fearful,
and his practice of the Way and principles is courageous.
The *Jūnzǐ* remains broad in will even when poor,
and remains respectful in carriage even when rich and noble;
when at leisure and ease, his vital breath and blood do not become lazy;
when weary with labor, his appearance does not wither;
when angry, he does not go too far in punishing,
and when joyful, he does not go too far in rewarding.
The *Jūnzǐ* remains broad in will when poor
because he exalts benevolence;
he remains respectful in carriage when rich and noble
because he curbs his power;
he is not lazy when at ease
because he selects principles;
he does not wither when weary
because he loves refinement.
He does not punish excessively in anger
nor reward excessively in joy
because the law overcomes personal feelings.
The *Shū* says:
"Do not act out of personal preference,
follow the Way of the King;
do not act out of personal dislike,
follow the Path of the King."
This means that the *Jūnzǐ* is able to let public righteousness overcome private desires.
In action, the *Jūnzǐ* does not value what is merely difficult;
in speech, he does not value what is merely subtle;
in reputation, he does not value what is merely widespread;
he values only what is appropriate.
Thus, embracing a stone and leaping into a river
is a difficult action to perform,
and *Shēntú Dí* was capable of it;
yet the *Jūnzǐ* does not value it
because it does not fall within ritual and righteousness.
"Mountains and abysses are level,"
"Heaven and Earth are comparable,"
"*Qí* and *Qín* are joined together,"
"what enters the ear
comes out the mouth,"
"hooks have whiskers,"
"eggs have feathers"—
these are arguments difficult to maintain,
and *Huì Shī* and *Dèng Xī* were capable of them;
yet the *Jūnzǐ* does not value them
because they do not fall within ritual and righteousness.
The chanting of the lips of *Dào Zhí*,
his fame was like the sun and moon,
transmitted along with *Yǔ* and *Shùn* without ceasing;
yet the *Jūnzǐ* does not value it
because it does not fall within ritual and righteousness.
Therefore it is said:
In action, the *Jūnzǐ* does not value what is merely difficult;
in speech, he does not value what is merely subtle;
in reputation, he does not value what is merely attained;
he values only what is appropriate.
The *Shī* says:
"The things are there,
only when the time is right."
This is what it refers to.
The *Jūnzǐ* is easy to be in harmony with but difficult to be familiar with;
he is easy to fill with awe but difficult to coerce;
he fears disaster but does not avoid dying for righteousness;
he desires profit but does not do what is wrong;
he is close with friends but does not form cliques;
his speech is eloquent but not confusing.
Vast and grand, he is distinct from the world.
When the *Jūnzǐ* is capable, he is good;
when he is not capable, he is also good.
When the *Xiǎorén* is capable, he is ugly;
when he is not capable, he is also ugly.
When the *Jūnzǐ* is capable,
he is broad-minded, easy, and upright to guide others;
when he is not capable,
he is respectful, cautious, and retiring to serve others with awe.
When the *Xiǎorén* is capable, he is arrogant, perverted, and contrary to overbear others;
when he is not capable, he is envious, resentful, and slanderous to subvert others.
Therefore it is said:
When a *Jūnzǐ* is capable, people find it an honor to learn from him;
when he is not capable, people take pleasure in informing him.
When a *Xiǎorén* is capable, people find it base to learn from him;
when he is not capable, people feel ashamed to inform him.
This is the distinction between the *Jūnzǐ* and the *Xiǎorén*.
The *Jūnzǐ* is broad-minded but not negligent;
he is scrupulous but does not cut others;
he is eloquent but does not engage in petty disputes;
he is observant but not extreme;
he stands upright but does not try to overpower others;
he is firm and strong but not violent;
he is gentle and compliant but does not drift away;
he is respectful and cautious yet accommodating.
This is called the utmost refinement.
The *Shī* says:
"A mild and respectful person
is indeed the foundation of virtue."
This is what it refers to.
The *Jūnzǐ* honors the virtue of others
and spreads their beauty;
this is not flattery.
He is righteous and points directly
to point out the faults of others;
this is not slander or fault-finding.
He speaks of his own brilliance and beauty,
likening himself to *Yǔ* and *Shùn*,
and matching himself with Heaven and Earth;
this is not boasting or extravagance.
He bends or extends according to the times,
being as flexible as reeds or rushes;
this is not cowardice.
He is firm, strong, fierce, and resolute,
and there is nothing he does not make known;
this is not arrogance or violence.
He responds to changes through righteousness,
because he knows what is appropriate in bending and straightening.
The *Shī* says:
"To the left, to the left,
the *Jūnzǐ* handles it appropriately;
to the right, to the right,
the *Jūnzǐ* possesses it."
This means that the *Jūnzǐ* can bend or extend and respond to changes through righteousness.
The *Jūnzǐ* and the *Xiǎorén* are opposites.
When the *Jūnzǐ*'s mind is broad, he respects Heaven and follows the Way;
when his mind is careful, he fears righteousness and practices restraint.
When he is wise, he is enlightened, thorough, and categorizes things;
when he is simple, he is upright, sincere, and follows the law.
When he is employed, he is respectful and knows when to stop;
when he is excluded, he is respectful and self-regulating.
When joyful, he is harmonious and orderly;
when sorrowful, he is quiet and orderly.
When successful, he is refined and enlightened;
when in distress, he is frugal and detailed.
The *Xiǎorén* is not like this.
When his mind is broad, he is negligent and violent;
when his mind is careful, he is licentious and subversive.
When he is wise, he is a thief and deceptive;
when he is simple, he is poisonous, malicious, and chaotic.
When he is employed, he is pleased and arrogant;
when he is excluded, he is resentful and dangerous.
When joyful, he is frivolous and flighty;
when sorrowful, he is discouraged and terrified.
When successful, he is arrogant and biased;
when in distress, he is abandoned and slovenly.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"The *Jūnzǐ* advances in both,
the *Xiǎorén* fails in both."
This is what it refers to.
The Jūnzǐ governs order;
he does not govern disorder.
What does this mean?
It means:
Ritual and Righteousness are what is called order;
the absence of Ritual and Righteousness is what is called disorder.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ
is one who governs Ritual and Righteousness,
not one who governs the absence of Ritual and Righteousness.
In that case, will a state in disorder not be governed?
The answer is:
To govern a state in disorder
does not mean to take that disorder and govern it;
it means to remove disorder and cover it with order.
To cultivate a person who is corrupt
does not mean to take that corruption and cultivate it;
it means to remove corruption and replace it with cultivation.
Thus, one removes disorder rather than governing disorder;
one removes corruption rather than cultivating corruption.
The term "governing"
is like saying the Jūnzǐ acts for order and not for disorder,
acts for cultivation and not for corruption.
When a Jūnzǐ makes his arguments clear, those who are like him will join him;
when he makes his speech good, those of his kind will respond.
Thus, when a horse neighs, other horses respond;
this is not because of knowledge,
but because their natural disposition is so.
Thus, one who has just bathed shakes out his clothes;
one who has just washed his hair brushes off his hat;
this is human nature.
Who could take their own purity
and accept the filth of others?
In nourishing the heart, nothing is better for the Jūnzǐ than Chéng;
once Chéng is brought to its height, there is nothing else to do,
except to guard Rén
and to practice Yì.
If one guards Rén with a sincere heart, it will become manifest;
if manifest, it will become divine;
if divine, it can transform others.
If one practices Yì with a sincere heart, it will become orderly;
if orderly, it will become clear;
if clear, it can change things.
Transformation and change arising in turn
is called Heavenly Virtue.
Heaven does not speak, yet people acknowledge its height;
Earth does not speak, yet people acknowledge its thickness;
the four seasons do not speak, yet the common people rely on their cycles.
These have constancy
because they have reached their ultimate Chéng.
When a Jūnzǐ reaches ultimate virtue,
he is understood even in silence,
he is loved before he bestows anything,
and he is majestic without anger.
This is following the mandate
and being Shèn Qí Dú.
Regarding the Way of goodness:
without Chéng, one cannot be singular;
without being singular, one cannot be manifest;
if one is not manifest, then even if it arises in the heart,
is seen in the expression,
and is spoken in words,
the people still will not follow;
even if they follow, they will surely doubt.
Heaven and Earth are great,
yet without Chéng, they could not transform the myriad things.
The Sage is wise,
yet without Chéng, he could not transform the myriad people.
Father and son are close,
yet without Chéng, they become estranged.
The ruler is exalted,
yet without Chéng, he becomes base.
Chéng
is what the Jūnzǐ guards
and is the foundation of government.
Only by where one dwells do things of that kind arrive.
Grasp it and you obtain it;
let it go and you lose it.
If you grasp and obtain it, it becomes easy;
if it is easy, you act with singularity;
if you act with singularity and do not let go,
then you will succeed;
when you have succeeded and your talents are fully utilized,
continuing to advance without returning to the beginning,
then you are transformed.
A Jūnzǐ's position is exalted but his will is humble;
his heart is cautious but his Way is great.
What he hears and sees is nearby,
but what he perceives is far-reaching.
Why is this?
It is because of the technique he employs.
Thus, the feelings of a thousand or ten thousand people
are the same as the feelings of one person.
The beginning of Heaven and Earth
is found in today.
The Way of the hundred kings
is found in the Hòu Wáng.
The Jūnzǐ examines the Way of the Hòu Wáng
and discusses it in relation to the hundred kings of old,
as if aligning threads and debating.
He extends the lineage of Ritual and Righteousness,
distinguishes the divisions between right and wrong,
grasps the essentials of the world,
and governs the masses within the seas
as if managing one person.
Therefore, the technique he grasps is more concise,
while the matters he handles are greater.
A five-inch square
can measure all the squares in the world.
Thus, the Jūnzǐ does not descend from his halls,
yet the conditions of all within the seas are gathered there;
this is because of the technique he employs.
There are Tōng Shì,
there are Gōng Shì,
there are Zhí Shì,
there are Què Shì,
and there are Xiǎo Rén.
Above, he can honor the ruler;
below, he can love the people.
When things arrive, he responds;
when matters arise, he distinguishes them.
Such a person can be called a Tōng Shì.
He does not form factions below to obscure the ruler,
nor does he agree with those above to harm those below.
When disputes arise within,
he does not let private interests damage the situation.
Such a person can be called a Gōng Shì.
Even if the ruler does not know his strengths,
he does not use them to defy the ruler;
even if the ruler does not know his weaknesses,
he does not use them to obtain rewards.
He does not disguise his strengths or weaknesses,
and exerts himself according to his true nature.
Such a person can be called a Zhí Shì.
In ordinary speech, he is always trustworthy;
in ordinary conduct, he is always cautious.
He fears the law and follows custom,
and dares not rely on what he alone thinks is right.
Such a person can be called a Què Shì.
His speech has no constant trust,
his conduct has no constant integrity.
Wherever profit lies,
there is nowhere he will not lean.
Such a person can be called a Xiǎo Rén.
Public-mindedness produces clarity;
partiality produces darkness.
Uprightness and scrupulousness produce comprehensiveness;
deceit and hypocrisy produce blockage.
Chéng and trust produce divinity;
boasting and falsehood produce confusion.
These six productions
are what the Jūnzǐ is cautious about,
and they are how Yǔ and Jié were distinguished.
The scale for desires, aversions, choosing, and rejecting:
When one sees what is desirable,
one must consider before and after what might be detestable about it.
When one sees what is profitable,
one must consider before and after what might be harmful about it.
Weigh them together,
calculate them maturely,
and then decide upon one's desires, aversions, choosing, and rejecting.
In this way, one will usually not fall into great pitfalls.
The common affliction of people
is being harmed by partiality.
Seeing what is desirable,
they do not consider what might be detestable;
seeing what is profitable,
they do not regard what might be harmful.
Therefore, when they move they surely fall;
when they act they surely suffer disgrace.
This is the affliction of being harmed by partiality.
What people detest,
I also detest.
As for those who are wealthy and noble,
they are invariably haughty toward them;
as for those who are poor and lowly,
they seek to be gentle toward them.
This is not the feeling of a Rén person;
it is the work of a villain seeking to steal fame in a dark age;
there is no greater danger.
Thus it is said:
Stealing fame is not as good as stealing goods.
Tián Zhòng and Shǐ Qiū were not as good as common thieves.
Arrogance and dissipation
are a person's calamity;
respect and frugality
are what keep the five weapons away.
Though there may be the piercing of halberds and spears,
they are not as advantageous as respect and frugality.
Therefore, speaking kind words to others
is warmer than cloth and silk;
harming others with words
is deeper than spears and halberds.
Therefore, even on a vast land,
one may not find a place to tread.
It is not that the land is unstable;
it is that one with endangered feet has nowhere to tread.
It all depends on one's speech.
On a great road, one yields;
on a small path, one is in danger.
Even if one wishes not to be careful,
it is as if one cannot help but be so.
Those who perish from momentary pleasure are driven by anger;
those who are ruined by meticulousness are driven by aggressiveness;
those who become impoverished despite broad knowledge are driven by slander;
those who become more turbid the more they try to be pure are driven by their mouths;
those who become thinner the more they are fed are driven by their social associations;
those who are eloquent but unconvincing are driven by contentiousness;
those who stand upright but are not recognized are driven by the desire to surpass others;
those who are incorruptible but not valued are driven by being sharp and harmful;
those who are brave but not feared are driven by greed;
those who are trustworthy but not respected are driven by the love for acting arbitrarily:
these are the pursuits of the petty person
and what the Jūnzǐ does not do.
Those who fight
are those who forget their own persons,
forget their parents,
and forget their lord.
To act on a moment's anger
and lose the body of a lifetime,
yet still do it—
this is forgetting one's person.
To have one's household immediately ruined
and relatives not escape punishment and execution,
yet still do it—
this is forgetting one's parents.
To do what the lord and superiors detest
and what the penal laws strictly forbid,
yet still do it—
this is forgetting one's lord.
Grievingly forgetting one's person,
internally forgetting one's parents,
and upwardly forgetting one's lord—
this is what the penal laws do not pardon
and what the sage kings do not tolerate.
A suckling pig does not provoke a tiger;
a suckling dog does not wander far;
they do not forget their parents.
As for humans,
grievingly forgetting their persons,
internally forgetting their parents,
and upwardly forgetting their lord—
then such people
are even inferior to dogs and pigs.
All those who fight
must believe themselves to be right
and others to be wrong.
If oneself is truly right
and the other is truly wrong,
then oneself is a Jūnzǐ
and the other is a petty person.
To use a Jūnzǐ and a petty person to harm one another,
grievingly forgetting one's person,
internally forgetting one's parents,
and upwardly forgetting one's lord—
is this not an extreme error!
Such a person
is what is called "using the halberd of Húfù to poke ox dung."
Is this to be considered wise?
Then there is no greater folly.
Is this to be considered beneficial?
Then there is no greater harm.
Is this to be considered honorable?
Then there is no greater disgrace.
Is this to be considered secure?
Then there is no greater danger.
Why is it that humans have fights?
If I wish to attribute it to madness, confusion, or illness,
that is not possible,
for the sage kings also punish it.
If I wish to attribute it to birds, rats, or beasts?
That is not possible, for their forms are human,
and their likes and dislikes are mostly the same.
Why is it that humans
have fights?
I find it very shameful!
There is the courage of dogs and pigs;
there is the courage of merchants and thieves;
there is the courage of the petty person;
there is the courage of the Shìjūnzǐ.
Fighting over food and drink,
having no sense of shame,
not knowing right from wrong,
not avoiding death or injury,
not fearing the many or the strong,
covetously seeing only food and drink—
this is the courage of dogs and pigs.
Doing things for profit,
fighting over goods and wealth,
having no deference or yielding,
bold yet perverse,
fierce, greedy, and contrary,
covetously seeing only profit—
this is the courage of merchants and thieves.
Disregarding death and being violent—
this is the courage of the petty person.
Where righteousness lies,
not swaying for power,
not considering personal profit,
even if the whole state is offered, not changing one's view,
valuing death yet holding to righteousness without flinching—
this is the courage of the Shìjūnzǐ.
The Tiáo and the Cān
are fish that swim at the surface.
When cast upon the sand and longing for water,
it is too late.
Being caught in trouble and then wishing to be careful
is of no use.
One who knows himself does not resent others;
one who knows destiny does not resent Heaven.
One who resents others reaches an impasse;
one who resents Heaven has no resolve.
Failing in oneself
yet seeking it in others—
is this not perverse!
The great distinction between honor and disgrace,
and the constant patterns of safety, danger, benefit, and harm:
placing righteousness first and profit second is honor;
placing profit first and righteousness second is disgrace.
The honored often find success;
the disgraced often reach an impasse.
The successful often control others;
the impassed are often controlled by others.
This is the great distinction between honor and disgrace.
The talented and sincere always enjoy safety and benefit;
the reckless and fierce always encounter danger and harm.
The safe and benefited are often happy and at ease;
those in danger and harm are often worried and in peril.
The happy and easy often live long lives;
the worried and imperiled often die young.
This is the constant pattern of safety, danger, benefit, and harm.
When Heaven produced the masses of people,
there were means by which things were obtained.
When the will is perfectly cultivated,
virtuous conduct is perfectly thick,
and wisdom and deliberation are perfectly clear—
this is how the Tiānzǐ obtains the world.
When administrative orders are lawful,
actions are timely,
and judgments are impartial;
upwardly being able to follow the commands of the Tiānzǐ,
and downwardly being able to protect the common people—
this is how the Zhūhóu obtain their states.
When resolve and conduct are cultivated,
one's official duties are well-managed;
upwardly being able to follow superiors,
and downwardly being able to maintain one's post—
this is how the Shìdàfū obtain their fields and towns.
Following the laws, measures, punishments, and registers without knowing their meaning,
carefully guarding their technical details,
and cautiously not daring to subtract or add to them;
passed down from father to son
to serve the kings and dukes—
therefore, though the Sāndài have perished,
the laws of governance still remain;
this is how the Guānrén and all the clerks obtain their salaries and ranks.
Being filial, fraternal, honest, and sincere, laboring diligently and vigorously to attend to one's tasks without daring to be lazy or arrogant—
this is how the Shùrén obtain warm clothes and full stomachs,
live long lives,
and avoid punishment and execution.
Adorning deviant theories,
embellishing treacherous words,
doing eccentric things,
being deceitful and boastful,
raiding and stealing,
being reckless, fierce, arrogant, and violent,
to steal a living and toss about in the midst of a chaotic world—this is how the treacherous obtain danger, disgrace, death, and punishment.
Their planning is not deep,
their choices are not careful,
and their decisions on what to take or leave are crude and negligent—this is why they are in danger.
Talent, nature, knowledge, and ability
are the same for the Jūnzǐ and the petty person.
Liking honor and hating disgrace,
liking profit and hating harm—
these are the same for the Jūnzǐ and the petty person;
but the way they seek them is different.
As for the petty man,
he is quick to act deceitfully yet wants others to believe him;
he is quick to act fraudulently yet wants others to be close to him;
and he has the conduct of beasts yet wants others to think well of him.
His deliberations are difficult to understand,
his actions are difficult to find security in,
and his position is difficult to establish.
If he succeeds, he will certainly not obtain what he likes,
and will certainly encounter what he dislikes.
Therefore, as for the jūnzǐ,
he is trustworthy,
and yet also wants others to believe him;
he is loyal,
and yet also wants others to be close to him;
he is cultivated, upright, orderly, and discerning,
and yet also wants others to think well of him.
His deliberations are easy to understand,
his actions are easy to find security in,
and his position is easy to establish.
If he succeeds, he will certainly obtain what he likes,
and will certainly not encounter what he dislikes.
For this reason, if he is in straits, he is not hidden;
if he is successful, he is greatly illustrious;
and even when his body dies, his name becomes all the more clear.
Among petty men, there are none who do not crane their necks and stand on tiptoe, wishing and saying:
“His wisdom, deliberations, talent, and nature
are inherently superior to those of other men.”
They do not know that he is fundamentally no different from themselves;
rather, the jūnzǐ’s applications and arrangements are appropriate,
while the petty man’s applications and arrangements are erroneous.
Therefore, if one closely examines the knowledge and ability of the petty man,
it is sufficient to know that he has more than enough
to do what the jūnzǐ does.
To use an analogy, the people of Yuè are at ease in Yuè,
the people of Chǔ are at ease in Chǔ,
and the jūnzǐ is at ease in refinement.
This is not because their knowledge, ability, talent, or nature are inherently so;
it is because the regulations of their applications, arrangements, habits, and customs differ.
Benevolence, righteousness, and virtuous conduct
are the methods for constant security,
and yet they are not necessarily without danger;
corruption, negligence, violence, and theft
are the methods for constant danger,
and yet they are not necessarily without security.
Therefore, the jūnzǐ follows the constant way,
while the petty man follows the deviant way.
All people have certain things in common:
when hungry, they desire to eat;
when cold, they desire to be warm;
when weary, they desire to rest;
they like profit and dislike harm.
These are things that people possess from birth;
they are so without depending on anything,
and are what Yǔ and Jié both shared.
The eyes distinguish between white and black, the beautiful and the ugly;
the ears distinguish between tones and sounds, the clear and the turbid;
the mouth distinguishes between sour, salty, sweet, and bitter;
the nose distinguishes between the fragrant and the rank;
and the body, skin, and pores distinguish between cold and heat, pain and itching.
These are also things that people constantly possess from birth;
they are so without depending on anything,
and are what Yǔ and Jié both shared.
One can become a Yáo or a Yǔ,
or one can become a Jié or a Zhí;
one can become a craftsman,
or one can become a farmer or merchant.
These depend only on the accumulation of circumstances, applications, arrangements, habits, and customs.
This is also something that people possess from birth;
it is so without depending on anything,
and is what Yǔ
and Jié both shared.
If one becomes a Yáo or a Yǔ, one will always have security and honor;
if one becomes a Jié or a Zhí, one will always have danger and disgrace.
If one becomes a Yáo or a Yǔ, one will always have joy and ease;
if one becomes a craftsman, farmer, or merchant, one will always have toil and labor.
Yet human effort strives for this
and rarely strives for that,
why is this?
I say:
It is because of ignorance.
As for Yáo and Yǔ,
they were not born complete.
They arose from transformative circumstances,
reached perfection through continuous effort and cultivation,
and only after exhaustive effort were they fully prepared.
At birth, people are inherently petty men;
without a teacher and without models, they see nothing but profit.
At birth, people are inherently petty men,
and if they also encounter a chaotic age
and obtain chaotic customs,
then this is adding pettiness to pettiness
and obtaining chaos through chaos.
Unless a jūnzǐ obtains the power to oversee them,
then there is no way to open their minds or lead them in.
Now, how can the mouth and belly of a person
know ritual and righteousness?
How can they know deference and yielding?
How can they know integrity, a sense of shame, and the accumulation of boundaries?
They only chirp and chew,
and clamor only to be filled.
If a person has no teacher and no models,
then his heart is solely focused on his mouth and belly.
Suppose a person from birth had never seen grass-fed or grain-fed meats, or fine rice and millet,
but had only seen beans, pulse, dregs, and chaff,
then he would consider the ultimate satisfaction to be found in these.
If suddenly someone were to arrive resplendently holding grass-fed and grain-fed meats,
then he would look at them in amazement and say:
“What strange thing is this?”
But if he smells it and finds it fragrant to his nose,
tastes it and finds it sweet to his mouth,
and eats it and finds it agreeable to his body,
then there is none who would not discard the former and take the latter.
Now, consider the Way of the Former Kings,
the guiding principles of benevolence and righteousness,
used to live together in community,
to support and nourish one another,
to protect and adorn one another,
and to make one another secure and stable.
Compared with the way of Jié and Zhí,
the distance between them
is surely like the distance between grass-fed and grain-fed meats and fine grains versus dregs and chaff!
Yet human effort strives for this
and rarely strives for that,
why is this?
I say:
It is because of ignorance.
Ignorance
is the common affliction of the world,
and the greatest disaster and harm to humanity.
Therefore it is said:
“The benevolent man loves to instruct and show others.”
If one instructs them and shows them,
guides them and makes them quick, leads them and focuses them,
then those who are blocked will suddenly find passage,
those who are ignorant will suddenly become broad-minded,
and those who are foolish will suddenly become wise.
If this were not the case,
then what benefit would there be in Tāng and Wǔ being on the throne?
And what loss would there be in Jié and Zhòu being on the throne?
When Tāng and Wǔ exist,
the world follows them and is well-ordered;
when Jié and Zhòu exist,
the world follows them and is in chaos.
That things are like this,
is it not because human emotions
can indeed be like the former
or can be like the latter?
It is the nature of human emotions
to desire grass-fed and grain-fed meats for food,
embroidered patterns for clothing,
and carriages and horses for travel;
they also desire the wealth of surplus goods and accumulations.
Yet, though they toil through their whole lives and for generations, they do not know what is sufficient;
such is the nature of human emotions.
Now, when people are alive,
they may know how to raise chickens, dogs, and swine,
and also how to raise cattle and sheep,
and yet for their own food they dare not have wine or meat.
They may have a surplus of coins and currency,
and possess granaries and cellars,
and yet for their own clothing they dare not have silk.
Even the constrained have stores in baskets and chests,
and yet for travel they dare not have carriages or horses.
Why is this?
It is not that they do not desire these things;
rather, they take long-term thought for the future
and fear having nothing to sustain them.
Consequently, they economize on expenditures and restrain their desires,
gathering and storing in order to sustain themselves.
This taking of long-term thought for oneself and looking to the future—
is it not truly excellent!
Now, those who live carelessly and possess shallow wisdom
do not even know this.
They eat too extravagantly,
without regard for their future,
and suddenly they are exhausted and in dire straits.
This is why they cannot avoid freezing and hunger,
and why they end up carrying begging bowls and sacks, becoming emaciated corpses in the ditches.
How much more, then, is this true of the Way of the Former Kings,
the guiding principles of benevolence and righteousness,
the *Shī*,
the *Shū*, the *Lǐ*, and the *Yuè*! These are indeed the great deliberations for the world,
which for all the living people of the world
take long-term thought for the future and protect ten thousand generations.
Their influence is long-lasting,
their benevolence is profound,
and their achievements are magnificent and far-reaching.
Unless one is a jūnzǐ who follows them and matures through cultivation,
none can understand them.
Therefore it is said:
A short rope cannot be used to draw water from a deep well;
one whose wisdom is not subtle cannot be part of the words of the Sages.
The distinctions of the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè*
are certainly not things that a mediocre person knows.
Therefore it is said:
By unifying them, they can be repeated;
by possessing them, they can last long;
by broadening them, they can become communicative;
by considering them, they can provide peace;
by examining them closely, they become even more likeable.
If used to govern the emotions, it is beneficial;
if used to make a name, it is glorious;
if used in a group, it brings harmony;
if used in solitude, it is sufficient
joy. Is this not their intent?
To be as noble as the Son of Heaven
and as wealthy as possessing the whole world
is what is commonly desired in human nature.
However, if one follows people's desires,
then power cannot contain them
and resources cannot satisfy them.
Therefore, the former kings accordingly established the systems of ritual and righteousness to create distinctions,
making ranks for the noble and the lowly,
differences between the elder and the younger,
and distinctions between the wise and the foolish, the capable and the incapable.
They made all people carry out their duties
and each obtain what is appropriate for them,
and then they made the quantity and quality of grain and salary correspond to this.
This is the way for a group to live in harmony and unity.
Therefore, when a humane person is in power,
the farmers use their full strength in the fields,
the merchants use their full discernment in wealth,
the various craftsmen use their full skill in tools and vessels,
and from the scholar-officials up to the Dukes and Marquises,
none fail to use their benevolence, generosity, wisdom, and ability to fulfill their official duties.
This is called the "Greatest Equality."
Thus, some receive the emoluments of the whole world
and do not consider it too much,
and some are gatekeepers, hostel keepers,
gate guards, or night watchmen
and do not consider it too little.
Therefore it is said:
"Uneven yet orderly,
bent yet compliant,
different yet unified."
This is called the human order.
The *Shī* says:
"Receiving small tributes and large tributes,
they became a shield for the subordinate states."
This is what is meant.
Physiognomizing people
did not exist among the ancients;
scholars do not speak of it.
In ancient times, there was Gūbù Zǐqīng;
in the current age, Liáng has Táng Jǔ.
They physiognomize a person's shape, features, and complexion
to know their fortune, misfortune, disaster, or omen,
and the common people praise them.
But among the ancients, this did not exist;
scholars do not speak of it.
Therefore, physiognomizing the form is not as good as evaluating the mind;
evaluating the mind is not as good as choosing the method.
Form does not overcome the mind;
the mind does not overcome the method.
If the method is upright and the mind is compliant,
then even if the physical form is ugly, if the mind and method are good,
it does not hinder one from being a *Jūnzǐ*;
even if the physical form is beautiful, if the mind and method are evil,
it does not prevent one from being a petty person.
To be a *Jūnzǐ* is called "auspicious";
to be a petty person is called "ominous."
Therefore, height, size,
and the beauty or ugliness of the physical form
are not matters of fortune or misfortune.
Among the ancients, this did not exist;
scholars do not speak of it.
Dì Yáo was tall,
Dì Shùn was short;
Wén Wáng was tall,
Zhōu Gōng was short;
Zhòngní was tall,
Zǐgōng was short.
Long ago, Wèi Líng Gōng had a minister named Gōngsūn Lǚ.
He was seven feet tall,
his face was three feet long,
his forehead was only three inches wide,
with nose, eyes, and ears all present,
and his name moved the world.
Sūnshū Áo of Chǔ
was a rustic man from Qīsī;
he was bald and his left side was long,
and he was shorter than the crossbar of a carriage,
yet he made Chǔ a hegemon.
Shè Gōng Zǐ Gāo
was tiny, short, and emaciated,
walking as if he could not support his own clothes. Yet
during the rebellion of Bái Gōng,
when Lìngyǐn Zǐxī
and Sīmǎ Zǐqī
both died,
Shè Gōng Zǐ Gāo entered and occupied Chǔ,
executed Bái Gōng,
and stabilized the state of Chǔ
as easily as turning over his hand.
His benevolence, righteousness, and achievements are praised by later generations.
Therefore, the scholar does not measure length,
does not gauge size,
and does not weigh lightness or heaviness;
he simply focuses his will on the mind.
Height, size,
and the beauty or ugliness of the physical form—
why should they be discussed?
Moreover, Xú Yǎn Wáng's appearance was such that
his eyes could look at a horse;
Zhòngní's appearance was such that
his face was like a ghost mask;
Zhōu Gōng's appearance was such that
his body was like a withered tree;
Gāoyáo's appearance was such that
his complexion was like a peeled melon;
Hóngyāo's appearance was such that
no skin was visible on his face;
Fù Yuè's appearance was such that
his body was like a finned fish;
Yī Yǐn's appearance was such that
he had no beard or eyebrows;
Yǔ was lame and Tāng was partially paralyzed;
Yáo and Shùn both had double pupils.
Should followers evaluate will and intent
and compare literature and learning?
Or should they simply distinguish height
and beauty from ugliness
and deceive and look down on others?
Of old, Jié and Zhòu were tall, huge, and handsome,
heroes of the world,
with muscles and strength so robust
that they could rival a hundred men.
Yet their bodies perished and their states were destroyed,
and they became the great disgrace of the world;
when later generations speak of evil,
they must cite them.
This was not the fault of their appearance,
but because their learning was not broad
and their reasoning was base.
Nowadays, the chaotic rulers of the common world
and the clever youths of the villages
are all beautiful and seductive,
wearing strange clothes and feminine ornaments,
with a disposition and attitude like that of women.
Among women, none fail to wish to have them as husbands;
among young maidens, none fail to wish to have them as suitors;
those who would abandon their families to run away with them
arise shoulder to shoulder.
However, an average ruler would be ashamed to have them as ministers,
an average father would be ashamed to have them as sons,
an average elder brother would be ashamed to have them as younger brothers,
and an average person would be ashamed to have them as friends.
Soon they are bound by the authorities
and executed in the great market;
none fail to cry to heaven and weep,
bitterly lamenting their present
and regretting their beginning.
This is not the fault of their appearance,
but because their learning was not broad
(and) their reasoning was base.
Therefore,
whom should a follower follow?
A person has three misfortunes:
being young but refusing to serve the elder,
being lowly but refusing to serve the noble,
and being unworthy but refusing to serve the worthy.
These are a person's three misfortunes.
A person has three ways to reach a dead end:
being a superior but unable to love inferiors,
being an inferior but liking to criticize superiors—
this is a person's first dead end.
Being submissive in person
but slandering behind their back—
this is a person's second dead end.
When wisdom and conduct are shallow and meager,
yet the distance between right and wrong is vast,
if a humane person cannot promote them
and a wise man cannot clarify them—
this is a person's third dead end.
If a person has these several behaviors,
then being a superior, they will surely be endangered,
and being an inferior, they will surely be destroyed.
The *Shī* says:
"The falling snow is heavy,
but it soon melts in the warmth.
None are willing to follow the path,
and so they repeatedly act with arrogance."
This is what is meant.
Why is it that man is man?
It is said:
Because he possesses distinctions.
When hungry he desires to eat,
when cold he desires warmth,
when weary he desires rest,
and he likes benefit while hating harm—
these are things that man is born with;
they are so without waiting for anything;
they are what Yǔ and Jié shared in common.
However, that which makes man man
is not merely that he has two legs and no fur,
but that he possesses distinctions.
Now, the xīngxīng has a human-like form and laugh,
and it also has two legs and fur,
yet the Jūnzǐ sips its broth
and eats its meat.
Therefore, that which makes man man
is not merely his two legs and lack of fur,
but his possession of distinctions.
Birds and beasts have fathers and sons
but no kinship of father and son;
they have males and females but no distinction between men and women.
Thus, in the Way of Man, there is nothing without distinction.
Of distinctions, none are greater than social divisions;
of social divisions, none are greater than ritual propriety;
of ritual propriety, none are greater than the Sage Kings.
There have been a hundred Sage Kings;
which one should I take as a model? (
Therefore) it is said:
Cultural forms, when ancient, are extinguished;
rhythmic structures, when ancient, are severed;
the officials who maintain the laws and numbers,
once rituals reach their limit, are stripped of their duties.
Therefore it is said:
If one wishes to observe the traces of the Sage Kings,
then look to those that are most brilliant;
the Latter Kings are they.
Those Latter Kings
are the lords of all under Heaven.
To set aside the Latter Kings and speak of high antiquity
is like setting aside one's own lord
and serving the lord of another.
Therefore it is said:
If you wish to observe a thousand years,
then count today;
if you wish to know hundreds of millions,
then examine one or two;
if you wish to know the ages of high antiquity,
then examine the Way of Zhōu;
if you wish to know the Way of Zhōu,
then examine its people and the Jūnzǐ whom they value.
Therefore it is said:
Use the near to know the far;
use the one to know the ten thousand;
use the subtle to know the manifest.
This is what it means.
Pretentious men say:
“Ancient and modern times have different conditions;
the ways by which order and chaos are brought about are different.”
And the masses are deluded by this.
Those masses
are foolish and lack explanation,
narrow and without standards.
Even what they see before them
can still be a source of deception,
how much more so the traditions of a thousand generations!
Pretentious men
can be misled and deceived even regarding what is between the gate and the courtyard,
how much more so regarding what happened a thousand generations ago!
Why is it that a Sage cannot be deceived?
It is said:
The Sage
is one who measures things by himself.
Therefore, he uses humans to measure humans,
emotions to measure emotions,
categories to measure categories,
arguments to measure achievements,
and the Way to observe the whole;
past and present are one.
Categories do not conflict;
though time be long, the principle remains the same.
Thus, he faces what is crooked and evil without becoming lost,
and observes a confusion of things without being deluded,
measuring them by this standard.
Beyond the Wǔdì, there are no recorded men;
it is not that there were no worthy men,
but because of the great length of time.
Among the Wǔdì, there are no recorded policies;
it is not that there were no good policies,
but because of the great length of time.
Yǔ and Tāng have recorded policies, but they are not as clear as those of Zhōu;
it is not that they did not have good policies,
but because of the great length of time.
As traditions age, they become more sketchy;
as they are more recent, they become more detailed.
When sketchy, one cites the major points;
when detailed, one cites the minor ones.
The foolish hear the sketchy points and do not know the details;
they hear the minor points and do not know the major ones.
This is why cultural forms, when ancient, are extinguished,
and rhythmic structures, when ancient, are severed.
All speech that does not agree with the Former Kings,
or does not follow ritual and righteousness,
is called treacherous speech;
even if it is eloquent,
the Jūnzǐ will not listen.
One who models himself on the Former Kings,
follows ritual and righteousness,
and associates with scholars,
but yet does not like to speak
or does not delight in speech,
must not be a sincere gentleman.
Therefore, regarding what is good, the Jūnzǐ
aims his will to love it,
practices it with ease,
and delights in speaking of it.
Thus, the Jūnzǐ must engage in discourse.
No one among men fails to like speaking of what they consider good,
and the Jūnzǐ does so even more.
Therefore, to present someone with speech
is weightier than gold, stone, pearls, or jade;
to display speech to someone
is more beautiful than embroidered patterns;
to hear someone's speech
is more joyful than bells, drums, lutes, or zithers.
Thus, the Jūnzǐ never tires of speech.
The vulgar man is the opposite;
he likes the substance but does not care for the refinement,
and thus to the end of his life he does not escape being low, filthy, menial, and vulgar.
Therefore, the Yì says:
“Tying up the sack; no blame, no praise.”
This refers to the rotten scholar.
In all persuasion, the difficulty
lies in using the extremely lofty to meet the extremely low,
and using extreme order to engage with extreme chaos.
One cannot approach directly;
to cite distant examples risks the error of misunderstanding;
to cite near examples risks the error of being common.
One who is good at this operates in the space between;
they must cite distant examples without misunderstanding
and cite near examples without being common,
shifting with the times,
rising and falling with the world,
whether slow or urgent, expanding or contracting,
bending and yielding as if the press and the straightening frame were applied to oneself,
following the intended meaning in every curve,
yet without snapping or being damaged.
Thus, the Jūnzǐ measures himself with a plumb line
but engages with others as if using a steering oar.
Measuring himself with a plumb line,
he is sufficient to be a standard for all under Heaven.
Engaging others with a steering oar,
he is able to be tolerant
and rely on the masses to achieve the great affairs of the world.
Thus, the Jūnzǐ is worthy but can tolerate the failed,
wise but can tolerate the foolish,
broad but can tolerate the shallow,
and pure but can tolerate the mixed;
this is called the comprehensive technique.
The Shī says:
“The region of Xú having been unified,
it was the achievement of the Son of Heaven.”
This is what it means.
The technique of discourse and persuasion:
approach it with dignity and gravity,
handle it with uprightness and sincerity,
maintain it with firmness and strength,
use analogies and comparisons to illustrate it,
use distinctions to clarify it,
and deliver it with joy and fragrance,
treasuring it,
valuing it,
taking responsibility for it,
and treating it as divine.
If done like this, then persuasion will always be accepted.
Even if one does not persuade people,
no one will not value him;
this is called being able to value what is worthy of being valued.
The Zhuàn says:
“Only the Jūnzǐ is able to value what is worthy of being valued.”
This is what it means.
The Jūnzǐ must engage in discourse.
No one among men fails to like speaking of what they consider good,
and the Jūnzǐ does so even more.
Thus, the petty man's discourse is dangerous,
while the Jūnzǐ's discourse is humane.
If speech does not hit the mark of humaneness,
then speaking is not as good as silence,
and eloquence is not as good as being tongue-tied.
If speech hits the mark of humaneness,
then those who like to speak are superior,
and those who do not like to speak are inferior.
Therefore, humane speech is great indeed.
That which originates from above and is used to guide those below
consists of government decrees;
that which originates from below and is used to show loyalty to those above
consists of providing counsel and remediation.
Therefore, the conduct of benevolence by the *jūnzǐ* is never weary.
His will delights in it,
his conduct is at peace with it,
and he finds joy in speaking of it;
therefore, it is said that the *jūnzǐ* must be eloquent.
Minor eloquence is not as good as seeing the first inklings;
seeing the first inklings is not as good as seeing the fundamental roles.
If minor eloquence is discriminating,
if the first inklings are clear,
and if fundamental roles are orderly,
then the distinctions between the sage, the scholar, and the *jūnzǐ* are complete.
There is the eloquence of the petty man,
the eloquence of the scholar-nobleman,
and the eloquence of the sage:
He does not deliberate in advance,
nor does he plan early,
yet his utterances are appropriate,
they form a refined pattern and are of the proper category;
in his various dwellings and movements,
his response to changes is inexhaustible—
this is the eloquence of the sage.
He deliberates in advance,
plans early,
and even his momentary speech is worth listening to;
it is refined yet reaches reality,
broad yet aligned with the correct—
this is the eloquence of the scholar-nobleman.
If you listen to his words, his phrasing is eloquent but lacks a unifying principle; if you employ him, he is full of deceit and achieves no results.
Above, he is not sufficient to follow a brilliant king;
below, he is not sufficient to harmonize and unify the common people.
Nevertheless, regarding the use of his tongue
in chatter and responses, he has a certain rhythm,
enough to be considered among the extraordinary or the haughty—
this is what is called a hero among wicked men.
When a sage-king arises,
such a person is the first to be executed.
Then thieves and robbers come next.
Thieves and robbers might change their ways,
but this kind of person cannot change.
In the present age,
there are those who embellish heterodox theories,
refine wicked speech,
in order to throw the world into chaos,
and deceive and delude the ignorant masses.
Using deceitful, grand, or trivial ways, they cause the world to be so muddled that it knows not where right and wrong or order and chaos reside—
such people exist.
They indulge their emotions and nature,
are content with wild arrogance,
and behave like beasts,
being insufficient to join with refined culture or connect with good governance.
Nevertheless, they maintain their views with some basis,
and their words are formed with some logic,
enough to deceive and delude the ignorant masses—
these are Tā Xiāo and Wèi Móu.
They suppress their emotions and nature,
acting in peculiar and extreme ways,
taking it as lofty simply to be different from others,
being insufficient to unite the masses
or clarify the great social distinctions.
Nevertheless, they maintain their views with some basis,
and their words are formed with some logic,
enough to deceive and delude the ignorant masses—
these are Chén Zhòng and Shǐ Qiū.
They do not know how to unify the world or establish the standards for the state;
they elevate utility
and overemphasize extreme frugality,
while slighting social ranks and grades,
being not even sufficient to accommodate differences
or determine the distinctions between ruler and subject.
Nevertheless, they maintain their views with some basis,
and their words are formed with some logic,
enough to deceive and delude the ignorant masses—
these are Mò Dí and Sòng Xián.
They honor laws yet have no true law;
they do not follow tradition but love to innovate.
Above, they seek to be heard by superiors;
below, they seek to follow the common customs.
All day they speak in what seems like refined canons,
but if one turns back to examine them,
they are scattered and have no ultimate destination;
they cannot be used to manage the state or fix social distinctions.
Nevertheless, they maintain their views with some basis,
and their words are formed with some logic,
enough to deceive and delude the ignorant masses—
these are Shèn Dào and Tián Pián.
They do not model themselves after the Former Kings
and do not consider ritual and rightness as correct;
rather, they love to cultivate strange theories
and play with curious phrases,
being very discriminating but not focused on what is urgent,
eloquent but useless,
and engaging in much activity but achieving little success.
They cannot be used as the guiding principles for governance.
Nevertheless, they maintain their views with some basis,
and their words are formed with some logic,
enough to deceive and delude the ignorant masses—
these are Huì Shī and Dèng Xī.
They broadly model themselves after the Former Kings but do not understand their unifying principle;
nonetheless, their talents are abundant and their ambitions are great,
and their learning is varied and wide.
They examine the past and create theories
which they call the "Five Elements,"
which are very eccentric and lack proper categorization,
obscure and lacking explanation,
and cryptic and lacking clarification.
They polish their phrasing
and treat it with reverence,
saying,
"These are truly the words of the former noblemen."
Zǐsī initiated it,
Mèng Kē harmonized with it.
The narrow-minded and ignorant scholars of the world clamorously do not know what is wrong with it,
so they receive and transmit it,
believing that Zhòngní and Zǐyóu were particularly esteemed by later generations because of this—
this is the crime of Zǐsī and Mèng Kē.
As for summarizing methods and strategies,
aligning words and deeds,
unifying all categories,
and gathering the heroes and outstanding talents of the world
to inform them of high antiquity,
and teaching them the utmost compliance—
within the private rooms
or upon the woven mats,
the refined culture of the sage-kings is fully present in an integrated manner,
and the customs of a peaceful age arise brilliantly;
then the six theories cannot enter,
and the twelve masters cannot draw near.
Although they have not even enough land to stand a needle,
kings and dukes cannot compete with them for fame.
If they held the position of a single grand master,
then one ruler could not maintain them alone,
and one state could not accommodate them alone.
Their fame spreads even more among the feudal lords,
none of whom would not wish to have them as ministers—
these are sages who did not obtain power,
such as Zhòngní and Zǐgōng.
Unifying the world,
regulating the myriad things,
nurturing the people,
and benefiting the world as a whole,
so that all within the connected regions follow and submit—
the six theories would immediately cease,
and the twelve masters would be transformed.
These are the sages who obtained power,
such as Shùn and Yǔ.
Now, as for the benevolent man,
what should he strive for?
Above, he models himself after the systems of Shùn and Yǔ;
below, he models himself after the righteousness of Zhòngní and Zǐgōng,
striving to put an end to the theories of the twelve masters.
In this way, the harms of the world are removed,
the work of the benevolent man is finished,
and the traces of the sage-kings become manifest.
To believe what is believable is trustworthiness;
to doubt what is doubtful is also trustworthiness.
To honor the worthy is benevolence;
to despise the unworthy is also benevolence.
To speak when appropriate is wisdom;
to be silent when appropriate
is also wisdom.
Therefore, knowing when to be silent stems from knowing when to speak.
Thus, one who speaks much yet stays within proper categories
is a sage;
one who speaks little yet remains within the law
is a *jūnzǐ*;
one who speaks much or little without law
and is drifting and indulgent,
even if eloquent,
is a petty man.
Therefore, to exert effort on what does not serve the people's needs
is called "wicked deeds";
to exert one's intellect without following the model of the Former Kings
is called "wicked mind";
to use eloquent debate and analogies,
and to be quick and clever in speech
without complying with ritual and righteousness,
is called "wicked theories."
These three wicked things
are what the sage-kings prohibited.
Being knowledgeable but treacherous,
being predatory but uncanny,
practicing deception with skill,
being useless but eloquent,
being pedantic about matters that are not urgent—
these are the great calamities of governance.
Acting perversely but with stubbornness,
embellishing wrongs to make them seem attractive,
indulging in wickedness to make it appear glossy,
