using eloquent speech that is contrary to right principles—
these were the great prohibitions of antiquity.
Being knowledgeable but without law,
being brave but without fear of consequences,
being observant and eloquent but holding biased views,
being excessive and grand in one’s expenditures,
being fond of wickedness and gathering a following,
being swift in the pursuit of profit but becoming lost,
carrying a stone and falling into a pit—
such a person is abandoned by the world.
To win the hearts of all people under Heaven:
those of high and noble status
do not use it to be arrogant toward others;
those of intelligence and sagely wisdom
do not use it to exhaust others;
those of quickness and versatility
do not use it to surpass others;
those of fortitude and bravery
do not use it to harm others.
If one does not know, then ask;
if one lacks ability, then learn;
even if capable, one must yield—
only then is it considered virtue.
When meeting a ruler, cultivate the duties of a minister.
When in the village, cultivate the duties of elder and younger.
When meeting an elder, cultivate the duties of a son or younger brother.
When meeting a friend, cultivate the duties of ritual, courtesy, and yielding.
When meeting those of low status or the young,
then cultivate the duties of instruction, guidance, and tolerance.
There is none they do not love,
none they do not respect,
and they do not contend with anyone,
being as expansive as Heaven and Earth enveloping the myriad things.
If one acts like this,
then the worthy will honor them
and the unworthy will feel close to them.
If one acts like this
and there are still those who do not submit,
then they may be called monstrous and cunning people;
even if they are among one’s own sons or brothers,
it is appropriate for punishment to reach them.
The *Shī* says:
"It was not that the High Lord was untimely,
but that Yīn did not follow the old ways.
Although there are no veteran statesmen,
there are still the statutes and laws.
Why is this not heard?
The Great Mandate has thus tilted."
This is what it refers to.
What was called an "official-scholar" in ancient times
was one who was sincere and solid,
one who unified the community,
one who delighted in wealth and status,
one who delighted in sharing and distributing,
one who distanced themselves from crimes and faults,
one who applied themselves to the principles of affairs,
and one who was ashamed of being wealthy alone.
What is called an "official-scholar" today
is one who is stained and filthy,
one who is predatory and chaotic,
one who is arrogant and unrestrained,
one who is greedy for profit,
one who is confrontational and offensive,
and one who lacks ritual and righteousness and only craves power and influence.
What was called a "retired-scholar" in ancient times
was one whose virtue was abundant,
one who could be tranquil,
one who cultivated correctness,
one who understood destiny,
and one who made the right manifest.
What is called a "retired-scholar" today
is one who has no ability but claims to have it,
one who has no knowledge but claims to have it,
one whose heart is insatiable for profit
but feigns a lack of desire,
one whose conduct is hypocritical, treacherous, and foul
but loudly proclaims high-mindedness and sincerity,
who treats eccentricity as a standard
and who acts in a peculiar and critical manner.
What a noble man can and cannot do:
A gentleman can make himself worthy of honor,
but cannot ensure that others will honor him;
he can make himself trustworthy,
but cannot ensure that others will trust him;
he can make himself useful,
but cannot ensure that others will employ him.
Therefore, the gentleman is ashamed of not being cultivated,
but is not ashamed of being slandered;
he is ashamed of not being trustworthy,
but is not ashamed of not being trusted;
he is ashamed of lacking ability,
but is not ashamed of not being employed.
Thus, he is not enticed by praise,
not intimidated by slander,
follows the Way in his actions,
remains upright in his person,
and is not swayed by external things;
this is called being a true gentleman.
The *Shī* says:
"Mild and respectful people
are the foundation of virtue."
This is what it refers to.
The appearance of a noble man:
His cap is high,
his robes are ample,
his demeanor is fine,
dignified,
robust,
auspicious,
unhurried,
expansive,
broad,
clear,
and vast—this is the appearance of a father or elder brother.
His cap is high,
his robes are ample,
his demeanor is sincere,
reserved,
reliant,
helpful,
upright,
attentive,
deep,
diligent,
and focused—this is the appearance of a son or younger brother.
I will tell you of the distorted appearance of a false scholar:
His cap is tilted,
his hat strings are loose,
his demeanor is sloppy;
acting heavy,
jumping about,
being silent,
staring blankly,
looking anxious,
appearing exhausted,
and wide-eyed;
in the midst of wine, food, music, and women,
he is dazed
and dim-sighted;
in the midst of ritual and etiquette,
he is hurried
and critical;
in the midst of labor and affairs,
he is lazy
and detached;
stealing ease and deceptive,
without a sense of honor or shame, and enduring insults—this is the distortion of a scholar.
Wearing a cap sloppily,
speaking in a deceptive manner,
walking like Yǔ and hurrying like Shùn—
these are the base Ru of the house of Zǐ Zhāng.
Straightening their robes and caps,
standardizing their facial expressions,
and remaining silent all day long—these are the base Ru of the house of Zǐ Xià.
Stealing ease and fearing work,
lacking a sense of honor or shame and being fond of eating and drinking,
while always saying, "A gentleman certainly does not use physical strength"—
these are the base Ru of the house of Zǐ Yóu.
That gentleman, however, is not like this;
he is leisurely but not lazy,
hardworking but not disrespectful,
following the source while responding to changes,
and correctly handling all matters according to their propriety.
Acting like this, he is then a sage.
Among the followers of Zhòng Ní,
even a five-foot-tall boy
would feel ashamed to speak of the Wǔ Bà.
Why is this?
The answer is:
Indeed,
they are truly shameful to mention.
Qí Huán was the greatest of the Wǔ Bà,
yet in his past actions, he killed his brother to contend for the state;
in his private conduct, seven of his sisters remained unmarried;
within the palace gates,
he indulged in pleasure and extravagance,
such that even the resources of the state of Qí were insufficient to support him;
in external affairs, he deceived Zhū and attacked Jǔ,
annexing thirty-five states.
His actions and conduct were thus so treacherous, filthy, and excessive.
How could he be worthy of mention within the gates of a great gentleman!
If one acts like this and does not perish,
but instead becomes a hegemon, why is that?
I say:
Alas! Qí Huán Gōng possessed the great integrity of the world;
who could have caused him to perish?
Calmly he saw that Guǎn Zhòng's ability was sufficient to be entrusted with the state;
this is the greatest wisdom in the world.
He settled his anger and
forgot his enmity,
then established him as Zhòng Fù;
this is the greatest decisiveness in the world.
Having established him as Zhòng Fù,
none of the noble relatives dared to be jealous of him;
he gave him the positions of Gāo and Guó,
and none of the ministers at court dared to hate him;
he gave him three hundred administrative districts,
and none of the wealthy people dared to oppose him.
Noble and base, old and young,
in an orderly manner,
all followed Huán Gōng in honoring and respecting him;
this is the great integrity of the world.
If a feudal lord has one aspect of integrity such as this,
then none can destroy him;
Huán Gōng combined several such aspects of integrity and possessed them all;
how could he possibly perish?
His hegemony
was indeed fitting!
It was not luck;
it was inevitable logic.
However, within the gate of Zhòng Ní,
even a five-foot-tall young lad
would be ashamed to speak of the Wǔ Bà;
why is this?
I say:
Indeed.
They did not balance government and education,
they did not attain the highest excellence,
they did not perfect culture and principles,
and they did not win over the hearts of the people.
They oriented themselves toward strategy,
scrutinized labor and leisure,
were careful with accumulation and storage, and prepared for combat,
and thus were able to overthrow their enemies.
They won through a heart of deception.
They used yielding to disguise contention,
relied on benevolence while pursuing profit;
they were the heroes among petty men;
how could they be worthy of being mentioned within the gates of the great gentlemen?
Those who are True Kings are not like that.
They attain worthiness and can thus save the unworthy;
they attain strength and can thus be lenient toward the weak;
in battle, they could certainly endanger the enemy yet are ashamed to fight them;
majestic and refined,
they manifest this to the world,
and violent states will naturally be transformed;
if there are those who are calamitous and perverse,
only then do they punish them.
Therefore, the punishments of Sage Kings are extremely rare.
Wén Wáng punished four,
Wǔ Wáng punished two,
Zhōu Gōng completed the task,
and by the time of Chéng Wáng,
there were no more punishments.
Therefore, how could the Way not be practiced?
Wén Wáng possessed a mere hundred li of land,
yet the world was unified;
Jié and Zhòu cast it away;
though they were steeped in the power of possessing the world,
they could not even live out their lives as common men.
Therefore, if one uses it well,
a state of a hundred li is sufficient to stand independent;
if one does not use it well,
then Chǔ, with its six thousand li, becomes a servant to its enemies.
Therefore, if a ruler does not strive to attain the Way
but only to broaden his power,
that is the very reason he is in danger.
The technique for maintaining favor and occupying a position
throughout one's life without ever being tired of:
If the ruler honors and ennobles him,
then he should be respectful and modest;
if the ruler trusts and loves him,
then he should be cautious and humble;
if the ruler grants him sole responsibility,
then he should be scrupulous and thorough;
if the ruler is comfortable with his proximity,
then he should be careful in his associations and not deviant;
if the ruler distances himself from him,
then he should remain whole and unified and not turn his back;
if the ruler demotes him,
then he should be apprehensive but not resentful.
Being noble but not boastful,
being trusted but not forgetting to remain humble,
holding heavy responsibility but not daring to be arbitrary,
when wealth and profit come,
he considers it good but does not reach for it;
he must fulfill the duty of declining and yielding
before accepting.
When fortunate events arrive, he is harmonious and orderly;
when calamitous events arrive, he is quiet and orderly;
when wealthy, his generosity is broad;
when poor, his spending is frugal;
he can be noble or base,
he can be wealthy or poor,
he can be killed but cannot be made to act wickedly.
This is the technique for maintaining favor and occupying a position without being tired of.
Even in a state of poverty or solitary living,
he also takes this as his model;
such a person is called an auspicious man.
The Shī says:
"He loves this one man,
responding to him with obedient virtue.
Forever thinking with filial piety,
brightly he continues the service."
This is what it refers to.
The technique for seeking to handle great importance well and
manage great affairs,
while enjoying exclusive favor in a state of ten thousand chariots
without having future troubles:
There is nothing better than liking to share with others,
supporting the worthy and bestowing widely,
and removing resentment without harming others.
If one is capable of the task,
then one should carefully practice this Way.
If one is not capable of the task
and fears losing favor,
then there is nothing better than sharing early,
promoting the worthy and yielding to the capable,
and peacefully following behind them.
In this way,
if one has favor, it will certainly lead to glory;
if one loses favor, one will certainly be without blame;
this is the treasure of one who serves a ruler
and the technique that ensures no future troubles.
Thus, when one who understands military affairs takes action,
when full, he considers insufficiency;
when on level ground, he considers danger;
when secure, he considers peril;
he doubles his precautions in every detail,
yet still fears failure;
therefore, in a hundred actions, he never falls into a trap.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"One who is skillful yet loves rules
will surely be temperate;
one who is brave yet loves to share with others
will surely be victorious;
one who is wise yet loves to be humble
will surely be worthy."
This is what it refers to.
The foolish person does the opposite.
Occupying a position of weight and monopolizing power,
he loves to handle matters alone and is jealous of the worthy and capable;
he suppresses those with merit and pushes aside those with faults;
his will is arrogant and full, and he makes light of old resentments;
because of stinginess, he does not practice generosity;
he flatters those above to gain weight,
and grabs power from below to harm people.
Even if he wishes not to be in danger,
can he avoid it?
If his position is noble, it will certainly be precarious;
if his responsibility is heavy, he will certainly be cast aside;
if he monopolizes favor, he will certainly be disgraced;
this can be expected in a moment,
it can be done in the time it takes to cook a meal.
With such conduct,
those who would trip him up are many,
and those who would support him are few.
The technique of conduct for the world:
if used to serve a ruler, one will certainly succeed;
if used to practice benevolence, one will certainly become a sage;
establish what is supreme and do not be of two minds.
Then use respect and reverence to lead,
use loyalty and trustworthiness to unify,
use caution and prudence to act,
and use uprightness and sincerity to maintain it;
when exhausted or in difficulty, apply effort to reassert and emphasize it.
Even if the ruler does not recognize it,
have no heart of resentment or hatred;
even if your merit is very great,
have no look of boasting about your virtue;
ask for little, achieve much,
and be tireless in love and respect.
If you act like this, then things will always be smooth.
To serve a ruler with this will lead to success;
to practice benevolence with this will lead to sagehood;
this is called the technique of conduct for the world.
The young serving the old,
the lowly serving the noble,
and the unworthy serving the worthy—
this is the universal principle of the world.
There are those
whose position is not above others,
yet who feel ashamed to be below others;
this is the mind of a wicked person.
If the will does not escape the wicked mind,
and the conduct does not escape the wicked path,
yet one seeks the name of a Jūnzǐ or a Shèng Rén,
to use a comparison,
it is like lying on one's face to lick the sky,
or pulling on the feet of someone who has hanged themselves to save them;
such theories will surely never be effective,
and the more they strive, the further they will be from their goal.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ bends when the time is to bend,
and stretches when the time is to stretch.
The effectiveness of the Dà Rú:
When Wǔ Wáng passed away
and Chéng Wáng was young,
Zhōu Gōng shielded Chéng Wáng and succeeded Wǔ Wáng
to hold the world together for the Zhōu,
fearing that the world would turn against the Zhōu.
He occupied the position of the Tiān Zǐ,
decided the judgments of the world,
and acted with such composure as if it were naturally his own,
yet the world did not call him greedy.
He executed Guǎn Shú
and emptied the state of Yīn,
yet the world did not call him cruel.
He collectively governed the world
and established seventy-one states,
of which fifty-three were held by members of the Jī clan,
yet the world did not call him partial.
He taught and guided Chéng Wáng,
making him understand the Way,
and was able to uphold the legacy of Wén and Wǔ.
When Zhōu Gōng returned to the land of Zhōu
and returned the records of authority to Chéng Wáng,
the world did not stop serving the Zhōu,
and yet Zhōu Gōng faced north and paid court to him.
As for the Tiān Zǐ,
the position cannot be held by the young,
nor can it be performed by a temporary proxy.
If one is capable, the world turns to them;
if one is not capable, the world leaves them.
Therefore, Zhōu Gōng shielded Chéng Wáng and succeeded Wǔ Wáng
to hold the world together for the Zhōu,
fearing that the world would depart from the Zhōu.
When Chéng Wáng was capped
and became an adult,
Zhōu Gōng returned to the land of Zhōu
and returned the records of authority to him,
making clear the duty of not extinguishing the line of the ruler.
Zhōu Gōng no longer possessed the world, though he previously had;
now that he did not have it,
it was not an act of usurpation.
Chéng Wáng previously did not have the world,
but now he had it;
this was not an act of seizure.
It was simply the proper measure of changing circumstances and the sequence of order.
Thus, for a branch line to substitute for the main ruler is not a transgression;
for a younger brother to execute an elder brother is not violence;
for ruler and minister to exchange places is not disobedience.
Relying on the harmony of the world,
he brought to fruition the work of Wén and Wǔ,
and clarified the duty between branch and main lines.
Though there were indeed changes and shifts,
the world remained satisfied and united.
No one but a Shèng Rén could have done this;
this is what is called the effectiveness of the Dà Rú.
Qín Zhāo Wáng asked Sūn Qīng Zǐ,
“Are Rú of no benefit to a ruler's state?”
Sūn Qīng Zǐ said,
“Rú take the Xiān Wáng as their model,
exalt ritual and rightness,
and are diligent as ministers and sons to highly honor those above them.
If a ruler employs them,
then their position in the court is appropriate;
if they are not employed,
they retire to be ranked among the common people and are sincere,
surely becoming obedient subjects.
Although impoverished, freezing, and starving,
they will never use wicked ways out of greed.
Even without a patch of land to place a needle,
they are clear about the great duty of maintaining the state altars;
they may cry out and find no one to respond,
yet they are well-versed in the management of all things
and the principles for nourishing the common people.
When in a position above others,
they have the talent of kings and dukes;
when they are below others,
they are ministers of the state
and treasures of the ruler.
Although hidden in poor alleys and leaky houses,
everyone honors them; they are honored because
the Way truly resides in them.
When Zhòng Ní was about to become the Sīkòu in Lǔ,
the Shěn Yóu clan did not dare to water their sheep in the morning;
the Gōng Shèn clan sent away their wives;
the Shèn Kuì clan moved across the border;
those who sold cattle and horses in Lǔ did not inflate their prices
but surely corrected them beforehand to wait for him.
When he lived in the Què Dǎng,
none of the youth in the hamlet failed to share their portions;
those with parents took more,
as they were transformed by filial piety and brotherly respect.
Rú in the court create beautiful government;
in lower positions, they create beautiful customs.
This is how Rú act when they are below others.”
The King said,
“Then what are they like when they are above others?”
Sūn Qīng said,
“When they are above others,
they are vast and grand:
their will is settled within,
rituals are cultivated in the court,
laws and measures are rectified in the offices,
and loyalty, trust, love, and benefit are manifested among those below.
To perform one unrighteous act
or kill one innocent person
to gain the world,
they would not do it.
This is how the Jūnzǐ's righteousness and trust are known to the people;
it spreads through the Four Seas,
and the world responds to them with a great clamor of joy.
Why is this?
It is because their noble name is bright and the world is well-governed.
Therefore, those near sing their praises and rejoice in them,
and those far off stumble over themselves to hasten toward them.
Within the Four Seas, it is like one family;
all who are reachable follow and submit.
This is what is called being a teacher of men.
The Shī says,
‘From the west and from the east,
from the south and from the north,
no one thinks of not submitting.’
This is what it refers to.
Since their being below others is like that,
and their being above others is like this,
how can it be said they are of no benefit to a ruler's state?”
Zhāo Wáng said,
“Excellent.”
The Way of the Xiān Wáng
is the pinnacle of benevolence;
they follow the Middle Way and act upon it.
What is meant by the Middle Way?
It is said:
ritual and rightness are it.
The Way
is not the Way of Heaven,
nor the Way of Earth;
it is that by which people find their path
and which the Jūnzǐ follows as the Way.
What the Jūnzǐ calls ‘worthy’
does not mean being able to do everything that everyone else can do;
what the Jūnzǐ calls ‘wise’
does not mean being able to know everything that everyone else knows;
what the Jūnzǐ calls ‘skilled in debate’
does not mean being able to debate everything that everyone else debates;
what the Jūnzǐ calls ‘discerning’
does not mean being able to discern everything that everyone else discerns:
there is a point where they stop.
In assessing high and low land,
looking at whether soil is barren or fertile,
and ordering the five kinds of crops,
the Jūnzǐ is not as good as the farmer.
In circulating goods and wealth,
judging quality,
and distinguishing between expensive and cheap,
the Jūnzǐ is not as good as the merchant.
In setting up compasses and squares,
laying out the ink-line,
and making tools convenient and ready,
the Jūnzǐ is not as good as the artisan.
In not caring about right and wrong
or the reality of whether things are so or not,
using words to promote or suppress others,
or to shame and embarrass them,
the Jūnzǐ is not as good as Huì Shī or Dèng Xī.
But as for evaluating virtue and determining rank,
measuring ability and assigning office,
making sure both the worthy and the unworthy find their proper place,
and that the capable and the incapable each find their proper office,
ensuring all things obtain their suitability,
and that all events find their proper response,
so that Shèn and Mò cannot advance their talk,
and Huì Shī and Dèng Xī dare not sneak in their discernment—
when words must match principle
and actions must match the needs of the time,
this is what the Jūnzǐ excels at.
In all matters of action,
those that are beneficial to governance
are established;
those that are of no benefit to order
are abolished.
This is what is called moderate action.
In all knowledge and discourse,
that which is beneficial to order
is practiced;
that which is of no benefit to order
is set aside.
This is what is called moderate discourse.
When actions and conduct miss the mark of moderation,
it is called wicked action;
when knowledge and discourse miss the mark of moderation,
it is called a wicked way.
Wicked actions and wicked ways
are what a well-governed age rejects
and what a chaotic age follows and obeys.
As for the mutual transformation of the full and the empty,
or the separation of "hardness and whiteness" and "sameness and difference"—
these are things that even sharp ears cannot hear,
clear eyes cannot see,
and eloquent debaters cannot express.
Even with the wisdom of a *shèngrén*,
one could not count them on one's fingers.
Not knowing them does not prevent one from being a *jūnzǐ*,
and knowing them does not lessen one's being a *xiǎorén*.
If craftsmen do not know them,
it does not prevent them from being skillful;
if a *jūnzǐ* does not know them,
it does not prevent him from being a good governor.
If kings and dukes love such things, they throw the laws into chaos;
if the common people love them, they throw their work into chaos.
Yet those who are wild, confused, stupid, and crude
begin to lead their followers,
debate their theories,
and clarify their analogies and citations.
They grow old and raise children in this,
yet they do not know it is loathsome.
This is called supreme stupidity,
which is not even as good as the fame gained from judging fighting cocks and dogs.
The *Shī* says:
"Were you a ghost or a *yù*,
you could not be caught.
But with your thick-skinned face and features,
people's view of you is endless.
I have composed this good song
to probe your perversity."
This refers to such people.
I wish to go from lowly to noble,
from ignorant to wise,
and from poor to rich—
is it possible?
The answer is:
It is only through learning.
As for those who learn,
if they put it into practice,
they are called *shì*;
if they are sincere and devoted to it,
they are *jūnzǐ*;
if they fully understand it,
they are *shèngrén*.
Above, one becomes a *shèngrén*;
below, one becomes a *shì* or a *jūnzǐ*.
Who can stop me!
Formerly, one was a muddled person of the streets;
suddenly, one stands equal to *Yáo* and *Yǔ*.
Is this not going from lowly to noble!
Formerly, one was confused by the distinction between a door and a room,
and was muddled and unable to decide;
suddenly, one traces the origins of benevolence and righteousness,
distinguishes right from wrong,
turns the world around in the palm of one's hand,
and distinguishes white from black.
Is this not going from ignorant to wise!
Formerly, one was a *xūmí*,
and suddenly the great instruments for governing the world are all here in one's possession—
is this not going from poor to rich!
Now, suppose there is a person here
who diligently stores treasures worth a thousand *yì*;
even if they beg for food as they walk,
people will call them rich.
As for those treasures,
they cannot be worn as clothes,
they cannot be eaten as food,
and they cannot be sold quickly.
Yet people call such a person rich;
why is this?
Is it not because the instruments of great wealth are truly there?
Such a person is indeed a *yúyú* rich man;
is this not going from poor to rich!
Therefore, a *jūnzǐ* is noble without rank,
rich without a salary,
trusted without speaking,
majestic without anger,
honored while living in poverty,
and joyful while living alone.
Is it not that the essences of being most honored, most rich, most significant, and most dignified are all accumulated here!
Therefore it is said:
A noble reputation cannot be gained through cliques and contention;
it cannot be possessed through boasting and lies;
it cannot be coerced through power and weight;
one must be sincere in this and only then will it come.
Contending for it leads to loss;
yielding for it leads to its arrival.
Following the path leads to accumulation;
boasting and lies lead to emptiness.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* strives to cultivate his inner self
and yields to others on the outside;
he strives to accumulate virtue in his person
and conducts himself with compliance.
In this way,
his noble reputation will rise like the sun and moon,
and the world will respond to him like thunder and lightning.
Therefore it is said:
The *jūnzǐ* is hidden yet manifest,
subtle yet brilliant,
and wins through yielding.
The *Shī* says:
"The crane cries in the nine marshes,
and its voice is heard in the heavens."
This is what it means.
The vulgar man is the opposite of this.
The more he forms cliques, the less he is praised;
the more he contends meanly, the more his name is disgraced;
he toils and labors to seek peace and profit,
but his person becomes increasingly endangered.
The *Shī* says:
"The people are not good;
they resent one another in every quarter.
They receive rank without yielding,
until they reach their own ruin."
This is what it means.
Therefore, to be small but try to serve the great
is like having little strength but taking on a heavy burden;
there is no destination but to be crushed and broken.
To be unworthy oneself but to slander the worthy
is like being a hunchback who loves to climb high places;
the people pointing at the top of one's head will only be more numerous.
Therefore, a brilliant ruler measures virtue to determine rank,
which is how he prevents disorder;
a loyal minister is sincere in his ability before he dares to accept office,
which is how he avoids exhaustion.
When positions are not disordered above
and abilities are not exhausted below,
this is the pinnacle of orderly governance.
The *Shī* says:
"Orderly and peaceful are those on the left and right,
and they are all led to follow."
This speaks of the interactions between those above and below not being in disorder.
Taking following the customs to be good,
taking wealth and goods to be treasures,
and taking the nourishment of life as one's ultimate way—
this is the virtue of the common people.
Executing the law with great firmness
and not allowing private desires to disorder what one has heard—
in this case,
one can be called a sturdy scholar.
Executing the law with great firmness,
liking to cultivate and correct what one has heard
to bridge and decorate one's nature and emotions—
his words are mostly appropriate
but not yet fully enlightened;
his actions are mostly appropriate
but not yet fully at ease;
his thoughts and deliberations are mostly appropriate
but not yet fully comprehensive or meticulous;
above, he can magnify what he honors,
and below, he can open the way for those not as good as himself—
in this case,
one can be called a sincere and generous *jūnzǐ*.
Cultivating the laws of the *Bǎi Wáng*
as clearly as distinguishing white from black;
responding to the changes of the present age
as easily as counting one and two;
grasping the essential points of ritual and being at ease with them
as if they were one's own four limbs;
the skill of establishing merit by seizing the opportune time
as if commanding the four seasons;
the excellence of being fair, upright, and harmonizing the people
so that a multitude of millions are unified as one person—
in this case,
one can be called a *shèngrén*.
Orderly and well-regulated he is;
grave and dignified, he is able to respect himself;
firm and resolute, he has a beginning and an end;
serene and satisfied, he can endure for long;
joyful and happy, he holds to the Way without peril;
bright and brilliant, he uses his wisdom with clarity;
cultivated and grand, he uses the conduct of systematic categories;
tranquil and composed, he possesses refinement;
cheerful and harmonious, he rejoices in the goodness of others;
apprehensive and concerned, he fears that others may be improper;
(then he may be called a Shèngrén).
This Way of his issues from Oneness.
What is meant by Oneness?
It is said:
Grasping the spiritual and being firm.
What is meant by spiritual?
It is said:
The perfection of goodness and the comprehensive grasp of order are called spiritual.
What is meant by firm? It is said: That which nothing among the myriad things is sufficient to overthrow is called firm.
Spirit and firmness are what define a Shèngrén.
As for the Shèngrén,
he is the conduit of the Way.
The Way of all under heaven is channeled through this;
the Way of the hundred kings is unified by this;
therefore the Way of the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè* returns to this.
The *Shī* speaks of this—it is its intent;
the *Shū* speaks of this—it is its affairs;
the *Lǐ* speaks of this—it is its conduct;
the *Yuè* speaks of this—it is its harmony;
the *Chūnqiū* speaks of this—it is its subtlety.
Therefore, the reason why the *Fēng* does not go to excess
is that this is taken to regulate it;
the reason why the *Xiǎoyǎ* is minor
is that this is taken to ornament it;
the reason why the *Dàyǎ* is major
is that this is taken to glorify it;
the reason why the *Sòng* is the ultimate
is that this is taken to permeate it:
the Way of all under heaven is complete in this.
Those who turn toward this are good;
those who turn away from this perish.
Turning toward this and not being good,
or turning away from this and not perishing—
from antiquity to the present,
such a thing has never occurred.
A guest once said:
"Kǒngzǐ said:
'How magnificent was Zhōugōng!
His person was noble yet he grew more respectful;
his family was wealthy yet he grew more frugal;
he defeated the enemy yet grew more cautious.'"
To this it is answered:
"This is likely not the conduct of Zhōugōng,
nor the words of Kǒngzǐ.
When Wǔwáng died
and Chéngwáng was young,
Zhōugōng shielded Chéngwáng and succeeded Wǔwáng,
assuming the registry of the Son of Heaven,
sitting with his back to the screen,
while the feudal lords scurried below the hall.
At that time,
to whom would he be respectful?
He jointly regulated the world and established seventy-one states,
of which fifty-three were occupied by those of the Jī surname alone.
Among the descendants of Zhōu,
provided they were not insane or deluded,
none failed to become illustrious feudal lords of the world.
Who could call Zhōugōng frugal?
When Wǔwáng executed Zhòu,
the day he marched forth was a day of military taboos;
he faced east to meet the Tàisuì star;
reaching the Fàn River, it overflowed;
reaching Huái, the road broke;
reaching Gòngtóu, the mountain collapsed.
Huòshū was terrified and said:
'We have been out for three days and five calamities have arrived;
is this not unfavorable?'
Zhōugōng said:
'Bǐgān was disemboweled and Jīzǐ was imprisoned;
Fēilián and Èlái controlled the government;
how could there be anything unfavorable?'
He then selected horses and advanced,
eating breakfast at Qī,
lodging at Bǎiquán for the night,
and at dawn reaching the wilds of Mùzhīyě.
He beat the drums and Zhòu's soldiers switched sides;
he then took advantage of the Yīn people to execute Zhòu.
For those who did the killing were not the Zhōu people,
but the Yīn people themselves.
Thus there was no capture of heads or prisoners,
nor rewards for braving danger.
Returning, he set aside the three armors,
laid down the five weapons,
united the world,
and established music.
Whereupon the *Wǔ* and *Xiàng* dances arose while the *Sháo* and *Hù* music fell into disuse.
Within the four seas,
none failed to change their hearts and minds to be transformed and follow him.
Thus the outer gates were not closed,
and he strode across the world without boundaries.
At that time,
against whom would he be cautious?"
Zàofù
was the best charioteer in the world,
but without a carriage and horses, he would have no way to show his ability.
Yì
was the best archer in the world,
but without a bow and arrows, he would have no way to show his skill.
A Dàrú
is one who is good at harmonizing and unifying the world,
but without a territory of a hundred *lǐ*,
he would have no way to show his achievement.
If the carriage is sturdy and the horses are chosen
but one cannot reach the far distance
or cover a thousand *lǐ* in a day, then it is not Zàofù.
If the bow is tuned and the arrows are straight
but one cannot shoot far and hit the minute,
then it is not Yì.
If one uses a territory of a hundred *lǐ*
but cannot harmonize and unify the world
and control the violent,
then it is not a Dàrú.
That Dàrú,
though he may be hidden in a poor alley or a leaky house,
without enough land to stick an awl,
kings and dukes cannot compete with his fame.
If he holds the position of a Grand Officer,
then a single ruler cannot keep him alone,
and a single state cannot contain him alone.
His name is established among the feudal lords,
none of whom would not wish to have him as a minister. Using a territory of a hundred *lǐ*,
a state of a thousand *lǐ* cannot compete for victory with him.
He lashes the violent states,
unifies the world,
and none can overthrow him.
This is the evidence of a Dàrú.
His words have systematic order;
his conduct has ritual propriety;
his undertakings lead to no regrets;
his handling of danger and response to change are perfectly appropriate;
shifting with the times,
and adapting to the world;
through a thousand actions and ten thousand changes,
his Way remains one.
This is the verification of a Dàrú.
When he is in poverty, the Súrú laugh at him;
when he is successful, heroes are transformed by him,
the mean and petty flee from him,
heterodox doctrines fear him,
and the masses feel ashamed before him.
In success, he unifies the world;
in poverty, he stands alone with a noble name.
Heaven cannot cause him to die;
Earth cannot bury him;
the eras of Jié or Zhí cannot defile him.
None but a Dàrú can stand so firm;
Zhòngní and Zǐgōng were such as these.
Therefore there are Súrén,
there are Súrú,
there are Yǎrú,
and there are Dàrú.
Those who do not study,
have no sense of justice,
and take wealth and profit as the highest pursuit—
these are the Súrén.
Wearing loose robes and broad belts,
and high Jiěguǒ caps,
they sketchily follow the Former Kings while sufficing for the arts of a chaotic age.
They engage in erroneous studies and miscellaneous actions,
not knowing how to model themselves on the Latter Kings to unify systems,
and not knowing how to exalt ritual and righteousness while giving less weight to the *Shī* and *Shū*.
Their dress and conduct are already identical to the worldly and vulgar,
yet they do not know to detest it.
Their speech and discussions are already no different from those of Mòzǐ,
yet their intelligence cannot distinguish this.
They call upon the Former Kings to deceive the foolish and seek food and clothing.
Gaining enough stores to fill their mouths,
they are smug and self-satisfied.
They follow their masters,
serve their flatterers,
and behave like honored guests,
cringing like lifelong slaves and not daring to have any other ambition—
these are the Súrú.
Modeling themselves on the Latter Kings,
unifying systems,
exalting ritual and righteousness while giving less weight to the *Shī* and *Shū*—
their words and actions already have a great standard,
yet their intelligence cannot equalize that which laws and teachings do not reach.
Where hearing and seeing have not reached,
then knowledge cannot categorize.
To say you know what you know
and to say you do not know what you do not know,
internally not falsely slandering
the outside
and externally not deceiving
what is inside,
thereby honoring the worthy and fearing the law while not daring to be indolent or arrogant—
this is a *Yǎrú*.
Modeling after the *Xiānwáng*,
unifying *Lǐ* and *Yì*,
standardizing the systems,
using the shallow to grasp the profound,
using the ancient to grasp the present,
using the one to grasp the myriad,
provided they are of the category of *Rén* and *Yì*,
even if they are among birds and beasts,
it is like distinguishing white from black.
As for strange objects and transformations,
things never before heard
and never before seen,
if they suddenly arise from one quarter,
he takes the guiding principles and categories to respond to them
without any hesitation or shame.
He applies the law to measure them,
and they match as perfectly as two halves of a tally—
this is a *Dàrú*.
Therefore, if a ruler employs a *Súrén*,
then a state of ten thousand chariots will perish;
if he employs a *Súrú*,
then a state of ten thousand chariots will survive;
if he employs a *Yǎrú*,
then a state of one thousand chariots will be secure;
if he employs a *Dàrú*,
then even a territory of one hundred *lǐ*
will endure; and after three years,
the world will become one,
and the *Zhūhóu* will become his ministers.
If he employs such a man in a state of ten thousand chariots,
then actions and arrangements will be settled,
and in a single morning he will become a *Bà*.
Not hearing is not as good as hearing;
hearing is not as good as seeing;
seeing is not as good as knowing;
knowing is not as good as practicing.
Learning reaches its end only when it is practiced.
Practicing it
is clarity;
clarity constitutes a *Shèngrén*.
As for the *Shèngrén*,
he takes *Rén* and *Yì* as his root,
handles right and wrong appropriately,
aligns his words and actions
without the slightest error.
There is no other way;
it ends in practicing it.
Therefore, to hear of something but not see it,
though one be broad, one will surely be in error.
To see it but not know it,
though one remembers, one will surely be deluded.
To know it but not practice it,
though one be diligent, one will surely be in difficulty.
Without hearing and without seeing,
then even if one happens to be correct,
it is not *Rén*;
such a path, in a hundred attempts, will result in a hundred failures.
Thus, if a person has no *Shī* and no *Fǎ*
and yet is knowledgeable, he will surely be a thief.
If he is brave, he will surely be a brigand.
If he is capable, he will surely cause chaos.
If he is observant, he will surely be eccentric.
If he is argumentative, he will surely be absurd.
If a person has a *Shī* and a *Fǎ*
and is knowledgeable, he quickly achieves understanding.
If he is brave, he quickly achieves authority.
If he is capable, he quickly achieves success.
If he is observant, he quickly achieves thoroughness.
If he is argumentative, he quickly achieves sound discourse.
Therefore, having a *Shī* and *Fǎ*
is a person's greatest treasure;
lacking a *Shī* and *Fǎ*
is a person's greatest calamity.
If a person lacks *Shī* and *Fǎ*,
then he prioritizes nature;
if he has *Shī* and *Fǎ*,
then he prioritizes accumulation.
As for *Shī* and *Fǎ*,
they are what is obtained through accumulation,
not what is received from nature.
Nature is insufficient to stand alone and bring order.
As for nature,
it is what I cannot create,
yet it can be transformed.
As for accumulation,
it is not what I originally possess,
yet it can be created.
Arranging choices and practicing customs
are the means by which nature is transformed.
Concentrating on the one without being divided
is the means by which accumulation is accomplished.
Practice and custom shift the will;
remaining at ease for a long time shifts one's substance.
Concentrating on the one without being divided,
one then communicates with the divine and bright
and forms a triad with Heaven and Earth.
Thus, accumulating earth makes a mountain,
accumulating water makes a sea,
and the accumulation of mornings and evenings is called a year.
The ultimate height is called Heaven,
the ultimate depth is called Earth,
and the six directions within the universe are called the ultimate limits.
For the common people on the road,
accumulating goodness until it is complete and exhaustive
makes one a *Shèngrén*.
He seeks it and then gets it;
he works at it and then succeeds;
he accumulates it and then becomes high;
he exhausts it and then becomes a sage.
Therefore, as for the *Shèngrén*,
he is the result of what a person accumulates.
A person accumulates weeding and plowing to become a farmer,
accumulates carving and shaving to become an artisan,
accumulates the exchange of goods to become a merchant,
and accumulates *Lǐ* and *Yì* to become a *Jūnzǐ*.
Among the sons of artisans,
none fail to carry on the work,
and the people of the capitals and states are comfortably accustomed to their professions.
Living in *Chǔ*, one becomes like the people of *Chǔ*;
living in *Yuè*, one becomes like the people of *Yuè*;
living in *Xià*, one becomes like the people of *Xià*.
This is not natural instinct,
but is caused by accumulated influence.
Therefore, if a person knows to be careful in arranging choices,
cautious in customs,
and great in accumulated influence,
then he becomes a *Jūnzǐ*.
If he gives rein to his passions and nature and is insufficient in inquiry and learning,
then he becomes a *Xiǎorén*.
To be a *Jūnzǐ* is to be constantly at peace and honored;
to be a *Xiǎorén* is to be constantly in danger and disgraced.
Among all people, there are none who do not desire peace and honor and hate danger and disgrace.
Therefore, only the *Jūnzǐ* is able to obtain what he likes,
while the *Xiǎorén* daily meets what he hates.
The *Shī* says:
"Only this good man
does not seek or follow [bad ways];
only that cruel-hearted one
looks back and returns to them.
The people's greed for chaos
would rather be a bitter poison."
This refers to this.
Regarding the categories of people:
If one's will cannot avoid being crooked and private
and yet one hopes that others regard oneself as public-minded;
if one's conduct cannot avoid being filthy and stained
and yet one hopes that others regard oneself as refined;
if one is extremely foolish and ignorant
and yet one hopes that others regard oneself as wise—
this is the *Zhòngrén*.
If the will restrains privacy,
then one can be public-minded.
If conduct restrains the passions and nature,
then one can be refined.
If one is knowledgeable and fond of questioning,
then one can be talented.
Being public-minded, refined, and talented,
one can be called a *Xiǎorú*.
If the will is at peace with being public-minded,
conduct is at peace with being refined,
and knowledge penetrates the guiding categories—
such a one can be called a *Dàrú*.
A *Dàrú*
is one of the *Sāngōng* to the *Tiānzǐ*.
A *Xiǎorú*
is one of the *Zhūhóu*, *Dàfū*, or *Shì*.
The *Zhòngrén*
are the artisans, farmers, and merchants.
*Lǐ* is the ruler's standard of measurement for the various ministers;
through it, human relations are exhausted.
The *Jūnzǐ*’s speech has its domain,
his conduct has its defenses and markers,
and his Way has a single priority.
In speaking of the pursuit of Way and Virtue,
he does not descend below security and survival;
in speaking of the pursuit of will and intent,
he does not descend below the *Shì*;
in speaking of the pursuit of Way and Virtue,
he is not of two minds regarding the *Hòuwáng*.
To take a way that goes beyond the Sāndài is called dissolute;
to follow laws other than those of the Latter Kings is called unrefined.
Whether raising or lowering,
whether diminishing or making things subjects,
one does not go beyond this;
this is how the Jūnzǐ gives free rein to his will and purpose within the bounds of the halls and courts.
Therefore, when the Zhūhóu ask about governing,
if it does not concern security and survival,
then one does not inform them;
when a common man asks about learning,
if it does not concern becoming a Shì,
then one does not teach him;
as for the theories of the Hundred Schools,
if they do not reach the standards of the Former Kings,
then one does not listen to them.
This is what is meant by the Jūnzǐ having boundaries for his speech
and landmarks for his conduct.
May I ask about governing?
The answer is:
Raise up the worthy and capable without waiting for their turn in sequence;
dismiss the incompetent and incapable without waiting a moment;
execute the chief criminals without waiting for instruction;
and transform the mediocre and mixed masses without waiting for government measures.
When social status is not yet determined,
there are the Zhāomù orders.
Even if they are the descendants of kings, dukes, or Shì Dàfū,
if they cannot adhere to ritual and righteousness,
then they are relegated to the status of commoners.
Even if they are the descendants of commoners,
if they accumulate cultural learning,
rectify their personal conduct,
and can adhere to ritual and righteousness,
then they are promoted to the rank of Qīngxiàng or Shì Dàfū.
Therefore, those who use wicked speech,
wicked theories,
wicked deeds,
or wicked abilities,
and those people who are evasive, rebellious, and unstable,
should be assigned duties and taught,
waited upon and observed,
encouraged with rewards,
and deterred with punishments.
If they are content in their duties, they are maintained;
if they are not content in their duties, they are cast out.
As for those with the five disabilities,
the superior shall take them in and nourish them,
employ them according to their talents,
and have officials provide them with clothing and food,
covering them all without omission.
Those whose talents and conduct oppose the times shall be put to death without pardon.
This is called the Virtue of Heaven;
this is the governance of a King.
The major distinctions in hearing government matters are:
those who come with good are treated with ritual;
those who come with what is not good are treated with punishment.
When these two are distinguished,
the worthy and the unworthy are not mixed,
and right and wrong are not confused.
When the worthy and the unworthy are not mixed,
then heroes and outstanding men arrive;
when right and wrong are not confused,
then the state is well-ordered.
If it is like this,
one's reputation will be heard daily,
the world will desire to follow,
commands will be carried out and prohibitions observed,
and then the work of a King is complete.
In all hearing of matters,
if one is majestic and fierce
and does not like to guide people,
then subordinates will be fearful and not close,
secretive and not exhaustive.
If it is like this,
then great matters are in danger of being neglected,
and small matters are in danger of being recklessly pursued.
If one is harmonious, conciliatory, and communicative,
and likes to guide people
but has no point of firmness or cessation,
then wicked speech will arrive together,
and deceptive theories will rise like spearheads.
If it is like this,
then hearing great matters becomes burdensome,
and this again harms them.
Therefore, to have laws but not discuss them
means those things to which the law does not reach will surely be neglected;
to have duties but not communicate them
means those things which duties do not cover will surely fall away.
Therefore, have laws and discuss them,
have duties and communicate them,
have no hidden plots,
and no omitted good,
so that the hundred affairs have no errors;
none but a Jūnzǐ can do this.
Therefore, impartiality
is the balance for hearing;
harmony and moderation
are the marking-line for hearing.
Where there are laws, act according to the law;
where there are no laws, act by analogy;
this is the exhaustion of hearing.
Partiality and lack of constant principles
are the perversion of hearing.
Thus, instances of having good laws yet having disorder
have occurred;
but instances of having a Jūnzǐ yet having disorder,
from antiquity to today,
have never been heard of.
The Tradition says:
"Order arises from the Jūnzǐ,
and disorder arises from the Xiǎorén."
This is what it means.
If distribution is equal, there is no partiality;
if power is equal, there is no unity;
if the masses are all equal, they cannot be employed.
There is Heaven and there is Earth,
and there is a difference between above and below.
When the Enlightened Kings first established themselves,
they had regulations for residing in the state.
Indeed, two of high rank cannot serve each other,
and two of low rank cannot command each other;
this is the natural order.
If power and status are equal
and desires and dislikes are the same,
and if goods cannot satisfy them, then they must struggle;
struggle leads to disorder,
and disorder leads to exhaustion.
The Former Kings detested such disorder,
therefore they established ritual and righteousness to distinguish them,
causing there to be gradations of poverty and wealth, nobility and lowliness,
sufficient for them to oversee and encompass one another;
this is the root of nourishing the world.
The Shū says:
"Only through inequality is there equality."
This is what it means.
If the horses are startled by the carriage,
then the Jūnzǐ is not at ease in the carriage;
if the commoners are startled by the government,
then the Jūnzǐ is not at ease in his position.
If the horses are startled by the carriage,
then nothing is better than calming them;
if the commoners are startled by the government,
then nothing is better than showing them kindness.
Select the worthy and good,
promote the earnest and respectful,
encourage filial piety and fraternal duty,
take in the orphaned and widowed,
and assist the poor and destitute;
if it is like this,
then the commoners will be at ease with the government.
When the commoners are at ease with the government,
only then is the Jūnzǐ at ease in his position.
The Tradition says:
"The ruler is the boat;
the commoners are the water.
The water can carry the boat;
the water can overturn the boat."
This is what it means.
Therefore, he who rules others,
if he desires security, then nothing is better than making governance fair and loving the people;
if he desires glory, then nothing is better than exalting ritual and respecting the Shì;
if he desires to establish merit and fame, then nothing is better than valuing the worthy and employing the capable;
—these are the great principles for one who rules others.
When these three principles are correct,
then all other things will be correct;
if these three principles are not correct,
then even if other things are partially correct,
it will still be of no benefit.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If the great principles are right
and the minor principles are right,
he is a superior ruler.
If the great principles are right
but the minor principles are wrong—departing in one instance
and returning in another—
he is a mediocre ruler.
If the great principles are wrong,
then even if the minor principles are right,
I have no need to observe the rest of him."
Chéng Hóu and Sì Gōng were rulers who focused on accumulation and calculation;
they did not reach the level of winning over the people.
Zhèng Zǐchǎn was one who won over the people,
but he did not reach the level of practicing true governance.
Guǎn Zhòng was one who practiced governance,
but he did not reach the level of cultivating ritual.
Therefore, he who cultivates ritual becomes a King;
he who practices governance becomes strong;
he who wins over the people becomes secure;
and he who focuses on accumulation perishes.
Therefore, a true king makes the people wealthy;
a hegemon makes the knights wealthy;
a state that merely survives makes its high officials wealthy;
a state destined to perish fills its baskets and trunks,
and makes its treasuries and storehouses full.
Once the baskets and trunks are rich,
and the treasuries and storehouses are full,
while the common people are impoverished,
this is called "overflowing at the top and leaking at the bottom."
At home, it cannot be defended;
abroad, it cannot wage war;
then downfall and destruction can be expected in no time.
Therefore, if one accumulates wealth while perishing,
the enemy obtains it and becomes strong.
Excessive taxation and accumulation
are the way to summon invaders, fatten the enemy, ruin the state, and endanger one's person.
Thus, an enlightened ruler does not follow this path.
A true king wins over the people;
a hegemon wins over allies;
one who relies on strength seizes land.
He who wins over the people makes the feudal lords his subjects;
he who wins over allies becomes friends with the feudal lords;
he who seizes land becomes an enemy to the feudal lords.
He who makes the feudal lords his subjects is a true king;
he who is a friend to the feudal lords is a hegemon;
he who is an enemy to the feudal lords is in peril.
One who uses strength:
while others defend their cities,
and others go out to battle,
if I defeat them through force,
then the injury to the other's people must be extreme.
When the injury to their people is extreme,
then their people's hatred for me must be extreme.
When their people's hatred for me is extreme,
they will daily desire to fight against me.
While others defend their cities,
and others go out to battle,
if I defeat them through force,
then the injury to my own people must also be extreme.
When the injury to my people is extreme,
then my people's hatred for me must be extreme.
When my people's hatred for me is extreme,
they will daily desire not to fight for me.
When the other's people daily desire to fight me,
and my own people daily desire not to fight for me,
this is why the strong paradoxically becomes weak.
Land is gained while the people depart;
burdens increase while achievements diminish;
though the things to be defended increase,
the means by which to defend them decrease;
this is why the great state paradoxically is carved away.
The feudal lords all harbor mutual resentment
and do not forget their enemy;
they watch for a gap in the powerful state's defenses,
and take advantage of its exhaustion.
When they perceive the powerful state's exhaustion,
this is the time of peril for the powerful. One who knows the Way of Strength does not strive for raw power;
he plans using the royal mandate
to keep his strength whole,
and to concentrate his virtue.
If his strength is whole, the feudal lords cannot weaken him;
if his virtue is concentrated, the feudal lords cannot diminish him.
If the world lacks a true king or hegemon as leader,
he will always be victorious.
This is one who knows the Way of Strength.
The hegemon is not like this.
He opens up the wild fields,
fills the granaries and storehouses,
makes ready the equipment and supplies,
and carefully recruits, selects, and reviews men of talent and skill.
Then he uses rewards and commendations to encourage them,
and strict punishments to correct them.
He preserves those states facing ruin and continues those whose lines are severed,
protects the weak and restrains the violent.
Having no heart for annexation,
the feudal lords will feel close to him.
He cultivates the way of befriending equals,
and treats the feudal lords with respect;
then the feudal lords will be pleased with him.
The reason they feel close to him
is that he does not annex them;
if a desire for annexation is seen,
then the feudal lords will distance themselves.
The reason they are pleased with him
is that he treats them as equals;
if a desire to make them subjects is seen,
then the feudal lords will drift away.
Therefore, by making clear his conduct of non-annexation,
and being faithful to the way of befriending equals,
if the world lacks a true king or hegemon as leader,
he will always be victorious.
This is one who knows the Way of the Hegemon.
Mǐn Wáng was ruined by the five states;
Huán Gōng was coerced by Lǔ Zhuāng;
for no other reason than
they did not follow the proper way yet planned with royal ambitions.
A true king is not like this.
His benevolence is supreme in the world;
his righteousness is supreme in the world;
his majesty is supreme in the world.
Because his benevolence is supreme,
none in the world fail to feel close to him.
Because his righteousness is supreme,
none in the world fail to honor him.
Because his majesty is supreme,
none in the world dare to oppose him.
With an unopposable majesty
supporting the way of winning people's submission,
he conquers without fighting,
gains without attacking,
and the world submits without wearying his armor or weapons.
This is one who knows the Way of the King.
One who knows these three instruments
may become a king if he wishes,
a hegemon if he wishes,
or strong if he wishes.
The King's Men:
They adorn their movements with ritual and righteousness,
they hear and decide cases based on categories,
their clarity reaches even the finest tip of a hair,
and their actions in response to change are inexhaustible.
This is called "having a source."
These are the King's Men.
The King's Institutions:
His Way does not go beyond the *Sān Dài*;
his laws do not diverge from those of the *Hòu Wáng*.
A Way that goes beyond the *Sān Dài* is called "extravagant";
laws that diverge from the *Hòu Wáng* are called "unrefined."
Clothing has its regulations;
palaces and houses have their measures;
the number of retainers is fixed;
mourning, sacrifices, implements, and vessels all have their appropriate grades.
As for music—then all sounds that are not elegant are abolished;
as for colors—then all patterns that are not of the ancient style are ended;
as for implements—
then all vessels that are not of the ancient fashion are destroyed.
This is called "restoring antiquity."
These are the King's Institutions.
The King's Judgments:
None without virtue are honored;
none without ability are given office;
none without merit are rewarded;
none without guilt are punished.
In the court, there are no positions gained by luck;
among the people, there is no survival by luck.
He honors the worthy and employs the capable,
yet does not neglect the hierarchy of ranks.
He distinguishes the sincere and restrains the aggressive,
yet his punishments do not exceed what is proper.
The common people clearly understand that if they do good in their homes,
they will receive rewards at the court;
and if they do evil in private,
they will suffer punishment in public.
This is called "fixed judgment."
These are the King's Judgments.
The King's Law:
He grades taxes, manages affairs, and regulates all things,
in order to nourish the myriad people.
For the fields, the tax is one-tenth;
at barriers and markets, there is inspection but no toll;
in the mountains, forests, marshes, and weirs,
there are seasonal prohibitions and openings but no taxes;
he assesses the land to determine the grade of taxation,
and arranges the tribute according to the distance of the roads.
He facilitates the flow of goods, wealth, and grain
so that there is no stagnation,
allowing them to be mutually transferred and redistributed.
Within the four seas, it is like one family.
Therefore, those nearby do not hide their talents,
and those far away do not resent their toil.
There is no remote or secluded state
that does not hasten to serve him and find peace and joy in it.
This is called "the teacher of men."
This is the King's Law.
From the Northern Sea come swift horses and barking dogs,
yet *Zhōngguó* obtains and raises them for use.
From the Southern Sea come feathers, ivory, hides, copper ores, and cinnabar,
yet *Zhōngguó* obtains and treats them as resources.
From the Eastern Sea come purple cloth, fine linen, fish, and salt,
yet *Zhōngguó* obtains them for clothing and food.
From the Western Sea come leather and patterned yak-tails,
yet *Zhōngguó* obtains and employs them.
Thus, those of the marshes have an abundance of wood,
those of the mountains have an abundance of fish,
farmers have enough tools without carving or smelting,
and craftsmen and merchants have enough grain without plowing the fields.
Though tigers and leopards are fierce,
the gentleman skins them and uses their pelts.
Therefore, what Heaven covers,
what Earth supports,
all fulfill their beauty
and achieve their utility;
above, they adorn the worthy and good,
and below, they nourish the common people and make them peaceful and happy.
This is what is called Dà Shén.
The *Shī* says:
“Heaven created the high mountain;
Tàiwáng opened it up.
He developed it;
Wénwáng made it peaceful.”
This is what it means.
Using categories to manage complexity,
using the One to manage the myriad,
the beginning becomes the end,
and the end becomes the beginning,
like a ring without an end;
if one abandons this, the world falls into decay.
Heaven and Earth
are the beginning of life;
Lǐ Yì
is the beginning of order;
the Jūnzǐ
is the beginning of Lǐ Yì.
Acting upon them,
penetrating them,
accumulating them,
and coming to love them—
this is the [beginning of] the Jūnzǐ.
Therefore, Heaven and Earth give birth to the Jūnzǐ,
and the Jūnzǐ brings order to Heaven and Earth.
The Jūnzǐ
is the triad with Heaven and Earth,
the summation of the myriad things,
and the father and mother of the people.
Without the Jūnzǐ,
Heaven and Earth would not be ordered,
Lǐ Yì would have no unifying system,
above there would be no ruler or teacher,
and below there would be no father and son
or husband and wife; this is called Supreme Chaos.
Ruler and minister, father and son, brother and brother, husband and wife—
the beginning becomes the end,
and the end becomes the beginning;
they share the same principle with Heaven and Earth,
and the same endurance with ten thousand generations;
this is called the Dà Běn.
Therefore, mourning rites and sacrifices, court audiences and diplomatic visits, (and military expeditions) are one;
nobility and meanness, killing and sparing, giving and taking are one;

the ruler acting as a ruler, the minister as a minister, the father as a father, the son as a son, the elder brother as an elder brother, the younger brother as a younger brother are one; and the farmer acting as a farmer, the scholar as a scholar, the artisan as an artisan, and the merchant as a merchant are one.
Water and fire have vital energy but no life;
grasses and trees have life but no awareness;
birds and beasts have awareness but no righteousness;
humans have vital energy, life, and awareness,
and also have righteousness;
therefore, they are the most noble in the world.
Their strength is not equal to that of an ox,
their running is not equal to that of a horse,
yet the ox and horse are used by them.
Why is this?
It is said:
Humans can form groups,
while they cannot form groups.
How can humans form groups?
It is said:
Through distinctions.
How can distinctions be carried out?
It is said:
Through righteousness.
Therefore, when righteousness is used to make distinctions, there is harmony;
when there is harmony, there is unity;
when there is unity, there is much strength;
when there is much strength, there is power;
when there is power, one overcomes things.
Thus, palatial houses can be obtained for dwelling.
Therefore, ordering the four seasons,
managing the myriad things,
and collectively benefiting the world—
there is no other reason for this
than obtaining it through distinctions and righteousness.
Therefore, human life cannot be without groups.
If there are groups without distinctions, there is conflict;
if there is conflict, there is chaos;
if there is chaos, there is separation;
if there is separation, there is weakness;
if there is weakness, one cannot overcome things.
Thus, palatial houses cannot be obtained for dwelling.
This is what is meant by saying one must not for a single moment abandon Lǐ Yì.
Being able to serve one’s parents is called filial piety;
being able to serve one’s elder brother is called brotherly respect;
being able to serve one’s superior is called obedience;
being able to employ subordinates is called being a ruler.
A ruler
is one who is good at forming groups.
When the way of the group is appropriate,
the myriad things all obtain their proper place,
the six domestic animals all obtain their growth,
and all living things obtain their natural lifespan.
Therefore, when nourishment and growth follow the seasons,
the six domestic animals thrive;
when killing and life follow the seasons,
grasses and trees multiply;
when government orders follow the seasons,
the common people are unified
and the worthy and good are submissive.
The regulations of the Shèngzhǔ:
When grasses and trees are in their flowering and fruiting period,
axes and saws do not enter the mountain forests,
so as not to cut short their lives
or end their growth.
When soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, fish, turtles, loaches, and eels are spawning,
nets, baskets, and poison do not enter the marshes,
so as not to cut short their lives
or end their growth.
Spring plowing, summer weeding, autumn harvesting, and winter storing—
when these four do not miss their timing,
the five grains are never exhausted
and the common people have surplus food.
Ponds, pools, streams, and marshes—
when the seasonal prohibitions are strictly observed,
fish and turtles are abundant
and the common people have surplus resources.
Felling and nourishing do not miss their timing,
so the mountain forests are not denuded
and the common people have surplus timber.
The management of the Shèngwáng:
Above, it observes Heaven;
below, it establishes itself on Earth;
it fills the space between Heaven and Earth
and is applied over the myriad things.
It is subtle yet bright,
short yet long,
narrow yet wide;
its spiritual brilliance is vast and great, yet reaches the most essential.
Thus it is said:
“He who is one with the One and thereby becomes a man”
is called a Shèngrén.
Ordering the offices:
The Zǎijué knows the number of guests, sacrifices, banquets, and sacrificial animals.
The Sītú knows the number of clans, city walls, and ritual vessels.
The Sīmǎ knows the number of troops, armor, weapons, and horses.
Repairing laws and mandates,
examining the *Shī* and *Shāng*,
banning licentious sounds,
and making adjustments according to the seasons
to ensure that barbarian customs and corrupt tones do not disturb the elegant music—
this is the duty of the Dàshī.
Repairing dikes and bridges,
clearing canals and ditches,
draining floodwaters,
securing water storage,
and opening or closing them according to the seasons—
so that even in years of failure, floods, or droughts,
the people have fields to weed and harvest—
this is the duty of the Sīkōng.
Assessing heights and depths,
inspecting fertile and barren soil,
ordering the five kinds of seeds,
overseeing agricultural labor,
and being careful with storage,
making adjustments according to the seasons
to ensure that farmers are simple and hardworking,
this is the duty of the Zhítián.
Managing fire regulations,
nourishing mountain forests, marshes, grasses, trees, fish, turtles, and various raw materials,
and prohibiting or allowing their use according to the seasons,
to ensure the state has sufficient resources
and wealth is not exhausted—
this is the duty of the Yúshī.
Harmonizing the neighborhoods and villages,
settling residences and dwellings,
nourishing the six domestic animals,
interplanting crops,
encouraging transformation through education,
and promoting filial piety and brotherly respect,
making adjustments according to the seasons
to ensure that the common people obey mandates
and live peacefully in their villages—
this is the duty of the Xiāngshī.
Evaluating the various artisans,
examining seasonal tasks,
distinguishing between fine and poor quality,
valuing completeness and utility,
and facilitating preparation for use,
so that carvings and patterns do not dare to be privately produced in homes—
this is the duty of the Gōngshī.
Observing the Yīnyáng,
divining by the omens in the atmosphere,
drilling tortoise shells and laying out hexagrams,
presiding over the five types of divination for exorcism and selection,
and knowing the good and bad fortune, the auspicious and the ominous—
this is the duty of the yǔwū and the bǒjí.
Repairing levies and tolls,
clearing the roads,
watching for thieves and bandits,
standardizing regulations for lodgings,
and maintaining these according to the seasons,
so that traveling merchants are secure and wealth and goods circulate—
these are the duties of the Controller of Markets.
Restraining the impulsive and prohibiting the violent,
guarding against excess and eliminating evil,
punishing with the five penalties,
so that the fierce and violent are transformed
and villainy and depravity do not arise—
these are the duties of the Sīkòu.
Rooting government and education,
rectifying laws and standards,
hearing all sides and periodically auditing them,
measuring their achievements and labor,
deliberating on their rewards and honors,
and maintaining these according to the seasons,
so that the various officials exert themselves to the
utmost and the common people are not negligent—
these are the duties of the Zhǒngzǎi.
Discoursing on ritual and music,
rectifying personal conduct,
broadening education and transformation,
beautifying customs and habits,
and covering all under one harmonious standard—
these are the duties of the Bìgōng.
Perfecting Way and Virtue,
achieving the utmost height,
bringing refinement and order to the peak,
unifying all under Heaven,
and moving even the smallest detail,
so that there is none under Heaven who does not follow and submit in harmony—
these are the duties of the Tiānwáng.
Therefore, if government affairs are in disorder,
it is the fault of the Zhǒngzǎi;
if the state loses its proper customs,
it is the error of the Bìgōng;
if all under Heaven is not unified
and the regional lords rebel against the common customs,
then the Tiānwáng is not the right person for the role.
When all these aspects are fully prepared, one rules as a King;
when they are prepared in certain ways, one rules as a Hegemon;
when they are prepared in some ways, one survives;
and when they are prepared in no way, one perishes.
For one who employs a state of ten thousand chariots,
the means by which power and strength are established,
the means by which reputation becomes beautiful,
the means by which enemies are made to submit,
and the means by which the state's safety or danger and its goodness or badness are determined—
the control over these lies within oneself;
it does not lie with others.
Whether one becomes a King or Hegemon, remains secure and survives, or faces danger and destruction,
the control over these lies with oneself;
it does not lie with others.
Now, if one's power and strength are not sufficient to threaten neighboring enemies,
and one's reputation is not sufficient to be prominent throughout all under Heaven,
then the state cannot yet stand independent.
How could it ever avoid being burdened by others?
If all under Heaven is coerced by a violent state,
and one is forced into a faction against one's will,
even if one daily acts and moves alongside a Jié,
it does not prevent one from becoming a Yáo.
This is not where merit and fame are achieved,
nor is it what determines survival or destruction, safety or danger.
Where merit and fame are achieved
and where survival or destruction, safety or danger are determined,
it must surely lie in the place of joyful abundance and sincere devotion.
Truly, if one makes one's state the kind of place where a King resides, one will be a King;
if one makes one's state the kind of place of danger and destruction, one will face danger and destruction.
In days of prosperity,
if one remains neutral,
showing no partiality
toward the affairs of alliances or rivalries,
calmly keeping the troops still and unmoving,
while watching the violent states grapple with each other.
One should stabilize government and education,
be careful with regulations and rhythms,
and sharpen the spirit of the common people.
When these things are done,
then one's military will be the strongest in all under Heaven.
If one cultivates benevolence and righteousness,
upholds the lofty and high,
rectifies laws and standards,
selects the worthy and good,
and nurtures the common people,
when these things are done,
then one's reputation will be the most beautiful in all under Heaven.
Authority is made weighty,
the military is made strong,
and reputation is made beautiful.
Even Yáo and Shùn, who unified all under Heaven,
could not add even a hair's breadth to this.
Therefore, when people of schemes and subversion retreat,
then worthy, good, wise, and sage-like scholars will naturally come forward.
When punishments and government are fair,
the common people are in harmony,
and the state's customs are regulated,
then the military will be strong, the cities secure,
and enemy states will naturally submit.
By attending to fundamental tasks,
accumulating wealth and goods,
and never allowing for
idleness or waste, this ensures that all ministers and common people act according to the regulations;
then wealth and goods will accumulate,
and the state will naturally become wealthy.
When these three things are embodied, all under Heaven will submit,
and the rulers of violent states will naturally be unable to use their armies.
Why is this?
Because they have no one to join them.
Those who would join them
would have to be their own people,
but their people would be as happy to be close to me as they are to their parents,
and would love me as if I were as fragrant as the Iris and Orchid.
When they look back at their own superiors, it is as if looking at the pain of burning or branding,
or at a mortal enemy.
This is human nature;
even for a Jié
or a Zhí, how could anyone be willing to do what they hate
and harm what they love? Their people have already been taken from them.
Thus, among the people of old,
there were those who took all under Heaven starting from a single state;
it was not that they went out and did it by force,
but that they cultivated government in their own place,
and there was no one under Heaven who did not desire them.
In this way, they could punish the violent and prohibit the fierce.
Therefore, when Zhōugōng campaigned in the south, the northern states complained,
saying,
"Why does he not come to us alone?"
When he campaigned in the east, the western states complained,
saying,
"Why are we left for last?"
Who could possibly fight against such a person?
One who comfortably brings their state to this condition will be a King.
In days of prosperity,
if one peacefully stills the military and rests the people,
shows compassion and love for the common people,
opens up the fields and wilderness,
fills the granaries and storehouses,
prepares tools and equipment,
and carefully recruits, selects, and reviews men of talent and skill;
then gradually uses rewards and honors to lead them,
uses strict punishments to guard them,
and chooses scholars who understand affairs
to lead and coordinate them;
thus, they will calmly accumulate and maintain resources
so that the supply of materials is sufficient.
As for weapons and armor,
the enemy will daily expose them to damage and breakage in the open fields,
while I will refine them,
maintain them,
and store them away in the treasuries and armories.
As for wealth, goods, and grain,
the enemy will daily waste and scatter them in the wilds,
while I will accumulate and gather them in the granaries.
As for men of talent and skill, loyal assistants, and brave and strong warriors,
the enemy will daily exhaust and wear them down against their foes,
while I will attract them,
review them together,
and sharpen their skills at the court.
In this way,
the enemy daily accumulates wear and tear,
while I daily accumulate wholeness;
they daily accumulate poverty,
while I daily accumulate wealth;
they daily accumulate exhaustion,
while I daily accumulate ease.
As for the relationship between ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
they will be harsh and daily become more alienated and resentful,
while we will be sincere and daily become closer and more affectionate;
in this way, I wait for their collapse.
One who comfortably brings their state to this condition will be a Hegemon.
If in one’s personal conduct one follows common customs,
in one’s actions one follows common precedents,
in promotion or demotion one raises up common scholars,
and in one's manner of dealing with the common people below one uses common leniency and kindness—
one who acts like this will remain secure and survive.
If in one’s personal conduct one is frivolous and careless,
in one’s actions one is suspicious and inconsistent,
in promotion or demotion one raises up the fawning and slick,
and in one's manner of dealing with the people and common people below one is fond of seizing and expropriating—
one who acts like this is in danger.
If in one’s personal conduct one is arrogant and violent,
in one’s actions one is subversive,
in promotion or demotion one raises up the devious, treacherous, and deceitful,
and in one's manner of dealing with the people and common people below
one is fond of demanding their life's effort
while being negligent of their merits;
and if one is fond of excessive taxation
while forgetting the fundamental duties—
one who acts like this will face destruction.
These five categories
must be chosen with care;
they are the instruments for being a *Wáng*, a *Bà*, for safety and survival, for peril and danger, or for ruin and destruction.
Those who choose well control others;
those who do not choose well are controlled by others.
Those who choose well will become a *Wáng*;
those who do not choose well will perish.
The difference between a *Wáng* and one who perishes,
or between controlling others and being controlled by others,
is a vast distance indeed.
The myriad things share the same universe but have different bodies;
they have no inherent appropriateness but are useful to man—
this is a matter of natural law.
