Human beings live together in society;
they have the same requirements but different ways of seeking them;
they have the same desires but different degrees of understanding—
this is the nature of their birth.
That everyone has things they approve of
is the same for the wise and the foolish;
where they differ in what they approve of
is where the wise and the foolish are distinguished.
If their power were equal but their knowledge different,
if they could act for private gain without disaster,
and indulge their desires without limit,
then the hearts of the people would be stirred and could not be persuaded to order.
In such a case,
the wise would not be able to govern;
if the wise are unable to govern,
then achievements and reputation will not be established;
if achievements and reputation are not established,
then the masses will not be organized;
if the masses are not organized,
then the relationship between ruler and minister will not be established.
Without a ruler to control the ministers,
and without a superior to control the subordinates,
the world will suffer harm from the indulgence of desires.
Desires and dislikes are directed at the same objects;
desires are many, but objects are few;
when they are few, there will inevitably be strife.
Therefore, the products of the hundred crafts
are used to support a single individual.
Yet an individual cannot master every craft,
nor can one person fulfill every office.
If people live apart and do not rely on one another, they will be impoverished;
if they live together but have no social distinctions, they will fight.
Poverty is a hardship;
strife is a calamity.
To save against hardship and eliminate calamity,
there is nothing better than clarifying social distinctions to organize the group.
If the strong threaten the weak,
the clever intimidate the foolish,
the subordinates disobey their superiors,
and the young insult the old,
while government is not conducted according to virtue;
then the old and weak will have the worry of losing their support,
and the strong will face the calamity of conflict and strife.
Labor is what people dislike,
and profit is what they like;
if there are no distinctions in occupations,
then people will have the hardship of performing tasks
and the calamity of fighting over rewards.
Regarding the union of male and female
and the distinction between husband and wife:
if marriage proposals and the taking of a wife,
or the sending and receiving of the bride, are without ritual propriety;
then people will have the worry of losing their proper union
and the calamity of fighting over sexual beauty.
Therefore, the wise established distinctions for them.
The way to make a state sufficient is
to moderate expenditures, enrich the people,
and be good at storing the surplus.
Moderate expenditures through ritual propriety;
enrich the people through government policy.
When the people are enriched,
there will be much surplus.
If you enrich the people, they will become wealthy;
if the people are wealthy, the fields will be fertile and well-tilled;
if the fields are fertile and well-tilled, the harvest will increase a hundredfold.
The superiors take from them according to the law,
and those below moderate their use according to ritual propriety.
The surplus will be like hills and mountains;
occasionally it must even be burned
because there is nowhere to store it.
Why then should a *Jūnzǐ* worry about a lack of surplus?
Therefore, if one understands how to moderate expenditures and enrich the people,
then one will surely have the reputation of being humane, righteous, sagely, and good,
and will also possess accumulations as rich and thick as hills and mountains.
There is no other reason for this
than it being born from moderating expenditures and enriching the people.
If one does not understand how to moderate expenditures and enrich the people, then the people will be poor;
if the people are poor, the fields will be barren and weed-grown;
if the fields are barren and weed-grown, the harvest will not even reach half the usual amount.
Though the superiors may be fond of taking and seizing,
they will still obtain very little;
and if they moderate expenditures without ritual propriety,
they will surely have a reputation for greed and fraud,
and will possess the reality of emptiness and exhaustion.
There is no other reason for this
than not understanding how to moderate expenditures and enrich the people.
The *Kānggào* says:
"Great as the covering of Heaven,
if such virtue enriches your person,
you shall not be cast out from the royal court." This is what it means.
As for ritual:
there are grades for the noble and the base,
distinctions between the old and the young,
and appropriate matches for the poor and the rich, the light and the heavy.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* wears the vermillion dragon robes and ceremonial cap;
the *Zhūhóu* wear the dark dragon robes and ceremonial cap;
the *Dàfū* wear the lower ceremonial cap;
and the *Shì* wear the skin-cap garment.
Virtue must match the position;
the position must match the stipend;
the stipend must match the expenditures.
From the *Shì* upward, they must be regulated by ritual and music;
as for the masses and common people, they must be controlled by laws and regulations.
Measure the land to establish states;
calculate benefits to nurture the people;
gauge human strength to assign tasks.
Ensure the people are capable of their tasks;
ensure tasks produce benefits;
ensure benefits are sufficient to sustain the people.
Make it so that clothing, food, and all requirements balance income and expenses;
and always store the surplus at the proper time—
this is called "appropriate numbering."
Thus, from the *Tiānzǐ* down to the commoners,
in matters great or small, many or few,
this principle is extended.
Therefore it is said:
"In the court there are no positions held by luck;
among the people there is no life sustained by luck."
This is what it means.
Lighten the taxes on fields and wilds;
equalize the levies at borders and markets;
reduce the number of merchants;
rarely call for corvée labor;
and do not take away the farmers' seasons.
In this way, the state will be wealthy.
This is called enriching the people through government policy.
In human life, one cannot live without a group;
if there is a group but no social distinctions, there will be strife;
if there is strife, there will be chaos;
if there is chaos, there will be poverty.
Therefore, the lack of social distinctions
is the greatest harm to man;
having social distinctions
is the fundamental benefit to the world;
and the ruler of men
is the pivot for managing these distinctions.
Therefore, to beautify him
is to beautify the foundation of the world;
to secure him
is to secure the foundation of the world;
to honor him
is to honor the foundation of the world.
In ancient times, the former *Wáng* divided the people and distinguished them by grades,
and thus made some things beautiful
and others ugly,
some thick
and others thin,
some at leisure and ease,
and others at hard labor—
not specifically to indulge in excessive or extravagant displays of sound,
but to clarify the patterns of benevolence
and to facilitate the compliance with benevolence.
Thus they created carvings, engravings, embroidered patterns, and ornaments,
making them sufficient to distinguish the noble from the base and nothing more,
without seeking after mere appearance;
they created bells, drums, flutes, lithophones, zithers, and reed organs,
making them sufficient to distinguish auspicious from inauspicious occasions and to harmonize joy and peace and nothing more,
without seeking after anything else;
they created palaces, halls, terraces, and towers,
making them sufficient to avoid heat and dampness,
to cultivate virtue, and to distinguish ranks and nothing more,
without seeking after anything beyond that.
The *Shī* says:
"Carved and polished is its pattern;
like gold and jade is its substance.
Diligent is our *Wáng*,
giving order to the four quarters."
This is what it means.
As for having layered colors for clothing,
layered flavors for food,
layered wealth and goods to manage,
and uniting the world to rule over it—
this was not specifically to indulge in excess.
It was certainly to unify the world,
govern the myriad transformations,
utilize the myriad things,
and nourish the myriad people.
For one who would comprehensively control the world,
there is nothing better than the goodness of a humane man!
Thus his wisdom and deliberation are sufficient to govern it;
his benevolence and generosity are sufficient to bring peace to it;
his virtuous reputation is sufficient to transform it,
If they obtain it, there is order;
if they lose it, there is chaos.
The common people truly rely on his wisdom;
therefore, they lead one another to labor for him to ensure his leisure
and to nourish his wisdom.
They truly admire his generosity;
therefore, they face death and ruin to protect and save him
and to nourish his generosity.
They truly admire his virtue;
therefore, they provide carvings, engravings, embroidered robes, and patterns to adorn him
and to nourish his virtue.
Therefore, when a benevolent person is in a high position,
the common people value him like a *Dì*,
love him like their father and mother,
and will face death and ruin for him without hesitation,
for no other reason than this:
what he affirms is truly beautiful,
what he obtains is truly great,
and the benefits he provides are truly many.
The *Shī* says:
"I carry my load, I push my barrow;
I drive my carriage, I lead my ox.
My journey is completed;
can I not finally return home?"
This is what it refers to.
Thus it is said:
"The *Jūnzǐ* works through virtue,
while the *Xiǎorén* works through strength."
Strength
is the servant of virtue.
The strength of the common people
depends on him before it achieves results;
the gathering of the common people
depends on him before it achieves harmony;
the wealth of the common people
depends on him before it is accumulated;
the status of the common people
depends on him before it is secure;
the longevity of the common people
depends on him before it is extended.
Fathers and sons cannot but be close,
brothers cannot but be compliant,
and men and women cannot but be joyful.
The young are raised,
and the old are cared for.
Thus it is said:
"Heaven and Earth produce them,
and the *Shèngrén* completes them."
This is what it refers to.
The present age is not so:
they impose heavy taxes on currency
to seize their wealth,
heavy taxes on the fields
to seize their food,
and harsh tolls at passes and markets
to hinder their business.
It does not end there;
there are entrapments, deceptions,
intrigues, and subversions
to overthrow one another
and exhaust the people.
The common people clearly know their corruption, violence, and chaos,
and that they are on the brink of great ruin.
Consequently, some subjects assassinate their lords,
some subordinates kill their superiors,
they betray their cities,
abandon their integrity,
and will not die for their cause.
There is no other reason:
the ruler brought this upon himself.
The *Shī* says:
"No word goes unreciprocated,
no virtue goes unrewarded."
This is what it refers to.
The way to fully provide for the world lies in clarifying social distinctions.
Leveling the land and marking the boundaries,
weeding the grass and planting grain,
and using plenty of manure to fertilize the fields—
these are the affairs of the farmers and the commoners.
Observing the seasons and employing the people's labor,
advancing the work and increasing achievements,
harmonizing the common people,
and ensuring they are not indolent—
these are the affairs of the generals and commanders.
Ensuring high lands do not suffer drought,
low lands do not flood,
cold and heat are balanced,
and the five grains ripen in their proper season—
these are the affairs of Heaven and Earth.
As for universally protecting them,
universally loving them,
and universally regulating them
so that even in years of failure, flood, or drought,
the common people suffer no hunger or cold—
these are the affairs of the *Shèngjūn* and the *Xiánxiàng*.
*Mòzǐ*'s words clearly show he worries the world lacks enough.
Insufficiency is not a universal affliction of the world;
it is merely *Mòzǐ*'s private worry and excessive planning.
Now, when this earth produces the five grains,
if people manage it well,
then one mu yields several *pén* of grain,
with two harvests in one year.
Furthermore, melons, peaches, dates, and plums from a single tree would fill several baskets;
vegetables and herbs would be measured by the swampful;
the six livestock and wild beasts would fill a carriage;
turtles, fish, and eels, separated by their seasons,
would form great schools;
birds and geese would be like clouds or the sea;
and insects and all things would grow among them.
Those that can be used for food and nourishment
are beyond count.
When Heaven and Earth produce the ten thousand things,
there is naturally a surplus
enough to feed people;
hemp, kudzu, silk, and the feathers, fur, teeth, and hides of birds and beasts
naturally have a surplus
enough to clothe people.
Abundance or insufficiency
is not a universal affliction of the world;
it is merely *Mòzǐ*'s private worry and excessive planning.
The universal affliction of the world
is that chaos damages it.
Why not try to ask together who causes the chaos?
I maintain that *Mòzǐ*'s
"*Fēi Yuè*"
causes the world to be in chaos;
*Mòzǐ*'s
"*Jié Yòng*"
causes the world to be poor.
It is not that he intends to ruin it,
but his theories cannot avoid it.
If *Mòzǐ* greatly possessed the world
or even just a single state,
he would live constrainedly, wearing coarse clothes and eating bad food,
being sorrowful and rejecting music.
If so, people would become emaciated;
if emaciated, they have no desires;
if they have no desires, rewards cannot be implemented.
If *Mòzǐ* greatly possessed the world
or even just a single state,
he would reduce the number of followers,
cut official posts,
treat labor for merit as a hardship,
share the work with the common people,
and equalize their efforts.
If so, there is no majesty;
without majesty, rewards and punishments cannot be implemented.
If rewards are not implemented,
then the worthy cannot be advanced;
if punishments are not implemented,
then the unworthy cannot be dismissed.
If the worthy cannot be advanced
and the unworthy cannot be dismissed,
then the competent and incompetent cannot be properly assigned to office.
If so,
then the ten thousand things lose their proper place,
responses to changes fail,
above, the heavenly seasons are lost,
below, the earthly advantages are lost,
and in the middle, human harmony is lost.
The world would be in turmoil,
as if parched or scorched.
Even if *Mòzǐ* wears hemp and rope belts
and eats beans and drinks water,
how can he suffice?
Having cut the root
and exhausted the source,
he has scorched the world.
Therefore, the *Xiānwáng* and *Shèngrén* did not act like this.
They knew that as a ruler,
if one is not beautiful and adorned, one cannot unify the people;
if one is not wealthy and generous, one cannot manage subordinates;
if one is not majestic and strong, one cannot prohibit violence or overcome the fierce.
Therefore, they must strike great bells,
beat sounding drums,
blow flutes and pipes,
and play zithers and harps
to fill their ears;
they must have engravings and carvings,
embroidered robes and patterns
to fill their eyes;
they must have grain-fed livestock and fine grains,
and the five fragrant flavors
to fill their mouths.
Then they increase the number of followers,
prepare official posts,
clarify rewards and celebrations,
and make punishments severe
to warn their hearts.
They ensure that all the people of the world
know that everything they desire lies in this,
so his rewards are implemented;
they know that everything they fear lies in this,
so his punishments are majestic.
When rewards are implemented and punishments inspire awe,
then the worthy can be advanced,
the unworthy can be dismissed,
and the capable and incapable can be appropriately assigned to offices.
If it is like this, then the myriad things obtain their proper places,
changes in affairs obtain their proper responses,
the timing of Heaven is gained above,
the benefits of Earth are gained below,
and the harmony of Man is gained in the middle.
Wealth and goods will gush forth like spring sources,
flow vastly like rivers and seas,
and pile up like hills and mountains.
Even if burned from time to time,
there would be no place to store them.
How then could the world suffer from insufficiency?
Therefore, if the *Rú* arts are truly practiced,
then the world will be great and wealthy;
when people are employed, they will achieve success;
and when bells and drums are struck, they will be in harmony.
The *Shījīng* says:
"Bells and drums sound grandly,
flutes and stone chimes ring clearly,
abundant blessings descend.
Great blessings descend,
and the bearing is dignified.
Once drunk and satisfied,
blessings and wealth return."
This is what is meant.
Therefore, if the *Mò* arts are truly practiced,
then the world will value frugality but become increasingly poor;
it will reject fighting but quarrel daily;
people will labor until exhausted
yet have even less success;
and they will be mournful, sorrowful, and joyless,
becoming daily more disharmonious.
The *Shījīng* says:
"Heaven is now sending down pestilence;
death and disorder are widespread.
The people have no good words;
alas, none are deterred or reformed."
This is what is meant.
To neglect affairs and merely nourish the people,
petting them
and coddling them,
providing them with thick porridge in winter
and giving them melons and parched grain in summer
to snatch a brief reputation—
this is the way of a thief.
One may obtain the acclaim of the wicked for a short time,
but it is not a long-lasting way.
Affairs will surely not be completed,
and success will surely not be established;
this is a wicked way of governing.
To rush to take advantage of the seasons and force the people,
advancing affairs and extending achievements,
while disregarding praise or blame and being indifferent to losing the people—
though affairs may advance,
the commoners will hate him.
This is again the way of a thief who is biased.
It leads to ruin and collapse,
and will inevitably end without success.
Thus, to neglect affairs to nurture a reputation
is unacceptable,
and to pursue success while forgetting the people
is also unacceptable;
both are wicked ways.
Therefore, the people of ancient times did not act this way.
They ensured the people did not suffer from heatstroke in summer
or freeze in winter.
Urgent tasks did not damage their strength,
and relaxed times did not miss the seasons.
Success was achieved and achievements were established,
and both high and low were wealthy.
The commoners all loved their superiors;
people flocked to them like flowing water
and were as joyful in their presence as with their own parents.
For their sake, they would face death and destruction without being unhappy.
There was no other reason for this
than the height of loyalty, trustworthiness, harmony, and equitable distribution.
Therefore, a ruler of a state and leader of the people
who wishes to seize the time and achieve success
will find that harmony and moderation resolve difficulties
faster than urgency;
loyalty, trustworthiness, and equitable distribution
are more persuasive than rewards and celebrations.
One must first rectify what is within oneself,
and only then gradually demand what is from others;
this is more awe-inspiring than punishments
and penalties.
If these three virtues are sincere in the superior,
then the inferiors will respond like a shadow or an echo.
Even if one wished not to be brilliant and far-reaching,
could that be achieved?
The *Shùjīng* says:
"Then the great light is submitted to,
and the people exert their strength in harmony.
Even if there is illness."
This is what is meant.
Therefore, to execute without teaching
results in frequent punishments, yet wickedness is not overcome.
To teach without executing
means the wicked people are not deterred.
To execute without rewarding
means the industrious people are not encouraged.
To execute and reward without consistency
means the inferiors will doubt, customs will be mean, and the commoners will not be unified.
Therefore, the former kings clarified ritual and righteousness to unify them,
practiced loyalty and trustworthiness to love them,
honored the worthy and employed the capable to order them,
and used ranks, robes, and rewards to reinforce them.
They timed their labor
and lightened their burdens
to harmonize them.
Like a vast canopy, they covered them;
they nurtured them
like protecting an infant.
Because of this,
wicked deeds did not arise,
thieves did not appear,
and those being transformed for the better were encouraged.
Why is this?
Because their path was easy,
their barriers were firm,
their government orders were unified,
and their signposts were clear.
Thus it is said:
If the superior is single-minded, the inferior is single-minded;
if the superior is double-minded, the inferior is double-minded.
It is like plants—the branches and leaves always resemble the root.
This is what is meant.
To benefit others when it is not beneficial to do so
is not as good as the benefit of benefiting others and then profiting from it.
To use others without loving them
is not as good as the success of loving others and then using them.
Benefiting others and then profiting from it
is not as good as the benefit of benefiting others without seeking profit.
Loving others and then using them
is not as good as the success of loving others without needing to use them.
Those who benefit others without seeking profit
and love others without needing to use them
take the world. Those who benefit others
and then profit from it,
or love others and then use them,
preserve the altars of grain and soil. Those who
do not benefit others but seek profit,
and do not love others but use them,
endanger the nation.
To observe whether a nation is ordered or chaotic, good or bad,
one can see signs even at the borders.
If the outposts are complex
and the policies at the border gates are overly scrutinizing, it is already a chaotic nation.
Upon entering its borders,
if the fields are overgrown
and the cities are exposed, it is a greedy ruler.
Observing the court,
the noble are not worthy.
Observing the offices,
the officials are not capable.
Observing the favorites,
those trusted are not sincere; this is a dim-witted ruler.
If the ruler, ministers, and officials
are meticulously scrutinizing in the accounting of goods and wealth,
in every detail,
but in the rhythms of ritual and righteousness
they are negligent and sloppy, this is a shamed nation.
If the farmers enjoy their fields,
the soldiers are at peace with hardship,
the officials love the law,
the court exalts ritual,
and the ministers deliberate in harmony, this is an ordered nation.
Observing the court,
the noble are worthy.
Observing the offices,
the officials are capable.
Observing the favorites,
those trusted are sincere; this is an enlightened ruler.
If the ruler, ministers, and officials
are generous and simple in the accounting of goods and wealth,
but in the rhythms of ritual and righteousness
they are reverent and meticulous, this is a glorious nation.
If worthiness is equal, then those who are kin are honored first;
if ability is equal, then those who are old associates are appointed first.
If the officials and underlings—
the corrupt are transformed to be cultivated,
the fierce to be honest,
and the impetuous to be sincere—this is the achievement of an enlightened ruler.
Observing the strength, weakness, poverty, or wealth of a state reveals signs:
if those above do not exalt ritual (*lǐ*), the military will be weak;
if those above do not love the people, the military will be weak;
if promises are not kept, the military will be weak;
if rewards are not properly sequenced, the military will be weak;
if the generals are incompetent, the military will be weak.
If those above are fond of pursuing merit through conquest, the state will be poor;
if those above are fond of profit, the state will be poor;
if scholar-officials are too numerous, the state will be poor;
if artisans and merchants are too numerous, the state will be poor;
if there are no regulations or measurements, the state will be poor.
If those below are poor, then those above will be poor;
if those below are wealthy, then those above will be wealthy.
Thus, the fields and the countryside
are the root of wealth;
the walls, storage pits, and granaries
are the branches of wealth.
When the common people are in seasonal harmony
and their affairs are well-ordered,
it is the source of goods;
equalized taxes and the treasuries
are the flow of goods.
Therefore, a brilliant ruler must carefully nurture that harmony,
regulate its flow,
open its source,
and from time to time adjust them,
making them so vast that the world will surely have a surplus,
and those above will not worry about insufficiency.
In this way,
those above and below are both wealthy,
and they have no need to hide anything from one another;
this is known as the ultimate point of state planning.
Thus, although Yǔ faced ten years of flood
and Tāng faced seven years of drought,
there were no famished faces in the world;
ten years later,
the annual crops ripened once again,
and the accumulated stores were in surplus.
This was for no other reason
than knowing what is meant by the root and branch, the source and the flow.
Therefore, if the fields are desolate while the granaries are full,
and the common people are destitute while the treasuries are brimming,
this is what is called the collapse of a state.
To strike at its root,
exhaust its source,
and gather everything into its branches,
yet have the ruler and ministers not know to detest this,
then its overthrow and destruction can be awaited in an instant.
Holding onto a state
but being unable to accommodate one’s own person,
this is what is called the extreme of poverty,
and it is the height of a foolish ruler.
Intending to seek wealth but losing one’s state,
intending to seek profit but endangering one’s person—
in ancient times there were ten thousand states,
but today there are only a dozen.
This is for no other reason
than that the way they lost them is one and the same.
Those who rule over men should also awaken to this.
A state of one hundred *lǐ*
is sufficient to stand independent.
Generally, those who attack others,
if not for the sake of fame,
then certainly for the sake of profit,
and if not for those, then out of anger.
When a person of humanity governs a state,
he will cultivate his will and intentions,
rectify his personal conduct,
uphold the lofty and sublime,
achieve loyalty and trustworthiness,
and aspire to refinement and order.
If a scholar wearing hemp clothes and straw sandals is truly like this,
then even if he resides in a desolate alley or a leaky house,
kings and dukes cannot compete for fame with him;
if he is supported by a state,
then no one in the world can conceal him.
If it is like this, then those seeking fame will not attack.
He will open the fields,
fill the granaries,
and make provisions convenient for use;
those above and below will be of one mind,
and the three armies will share their strength;
to launch a distant campaign and engage him in a desperate battle is impossible.
The gatherings within his borders are secure and solid;
observing the opportunity,
they cross the enemy's army
and capture their general
as easily as winnowing roasted grain.
What the enemy might gain
is not enough to heal their wounds or make up for their losses.
They love their soldiers
and fear their enemies;
if it is like this, then those seeking profit will not attack.
He will cultivate the righteousness between small and large, strong and weak,
to maintain caution;
the rituals and etiquette will be highly refined,
the ceremonial jades will be very large,
the gifts and offerings will be very generous,
and those who go to please others
will surely be refined, eloquent, and wise gentlemen.
If the enemy has any human sentiment at all,
who could be angry with them?
If it is like this,
then those seeking anger will not attack.
Since those seeking fame do not,
those seeking profit do not,
and those seeking anger do not,
the state will be as secure as a flat rock
and as long-lived as the stars of Qí and Yì.
While others are all in chaos,
I alone am well-governed;
while others are all in danger,
I alone am secure;
while others have lost everything,
I rise up to control them.
Therefore, when a person of humanity governs a state,
he does not only maintain what he has,
but will also bring others under his sway.
The *Shī* says:
“The virtuous gentleman,
his demeanor does not err.
His demeanor does not err,
he rectifies the four states.”
This is what it refers to.
Regarding the difficulty and ease of maintaining a state:
serving a violent and powerful state is difficult,
while making a violent and powerful state serve me is easy.
If you serve them with goods and treasures,
then the goods and treasures will be exhausted
but the relationship will not be bound;
if you make covenants of trust and oaths,
then once the covenant is set, it will be broken within days;
if you carve off the smallest portion of the state to bribe them,
then once the division is set, their desires will be insatiable.
The more troublesome your service,
the more severe their intrusion becomes,
inevitably reaching the point where resources are exhausted and the whole state is taken before they stop.
Even if you had Yáo on your left and Shùn on your right,
no one could escape using this path.
To use a metaphor, it is like having a maiden wear precious pearls,
carry precious jades,
and bear gold
while encountering a thief from Zhōng Shān;
even if she adopts a submissive gaze,
bends her waist and flexes her knees
like a lowly concubine,
it will still not be enough to escape.
Therefore, it is not the Way for a ruler;
simply being clever, bowing, and begging while fearfully serving them
is not enough to maintain the state or secure one's person.
Thus, an enlightened ruler does not follow this path.
He will surely cultivate rituals to unify the court,
rectify laws to unify the officials,
and level the administration to unify the people;
then, the rhythm will be unified in the court,
the many affairs will be unified among the officials,
and the masses will be unified below.
In this way,
those nearby will compete to be close,
those in distant places will offer their devotion,
those above and below will be of one mind,
and the three armies will share their strength;
his reputation will be enough to shine upon them,
his power and strength will be enough to discipline them;
with a bow and a wave of the finger,
the violent and powerful states will all hasten to follow his orders.
For instance, this is like Wū Huò wrestling with a Jiāo Liǎo pygmy.
Therefore it is said:
“Serving a violent and powerful state is difficult,
while making a violent and powerful state serve me is easy.”
This is what it refers to.
A state
is an instrument for regulating benefit in the world;
a ruler
is the position of advantage for the world's benefit.
If one holds it by attaining the Way,
then there is great peace,
great glory,
and it is the source of accumulated beauty.
If one holds it without attaining the Way,
then there is great danger,
great burden,
and having it is not as good as not having it.
When it reaches its extreme,
even seeking to be an ordinary man is impossible,
as seen with Qí Mǐn and Sòng Xiàn.
Thus, the ruler is the position of advantage for the world's benefit,
and yet he cannot secure himself;
the one who secures him must surely be the Way.
Therefore, among those who govern a state,
those whose righteousness is established will become Kings (*Wáng*),
those whose trustworthiness is established will become Hegemons (*Bà*),
and those whose schemes and plots are established will perish.
These three are what an enlightened ruler must carefully choose
and what a person of humanity must strive to make clear.
To lead a state to proclaim ritual and righteousness
and do nothing to harm them—
to perform one unrighteous act
or kill one innocent person
to gain the world,
a humane person would not do.
He firmly upholds his mind and the state,
and his resolve is as solid as this.
Those with whom he acts
are all righteous men;
the penal laws he establishes for the state
are all righteous laws;
that which the ruler decisively leads his ministers toward
is all righteous intent.
In this way, those below look up to those above with righteousness;
this is ultimate stability.
With ultimate stability, the state is settled;
with the state settled, the world is settled.
Zhòngní did not have even enough land to place a needle,
but he was sincere in his righteous will,
applied righteousness to his conduct,
expressed it in his speech,
and practiced it daily.
He was not hidden from the world,
and his name was passed down to posterity.
Now, if a prominent lord of the world
were sincere in his righteous will,
applied righteousness to his laws and measures,
expressed it in government affairs,
and reinforced it through ranks and decisions of life and death,
making it consistent from beginning to end;
if so,
then the spread of his reputation between heaven and earth
would surely be like the sun, moon, and thunder!
Therefore it is said:
By aligning the state with righteousness,
one becomes brilliant in a single day.
Tāng and Wǔ were examples of this.
Tāng used Bó,
King Wǔ used Hào;
both were lands of only a hundred lǐ,
yet the world became one,
the feudal lords became their ministers,
and all far-reaching regions
followed and submitted to them.
There was no other reason for this
than their practice of righteousness.
This is what is called establishing righteousness and becoming a King.
Even if virtue is not yet perfect
and righteousness not yet fully realized,
if the principles of the world are generally established,
punishments, rewards, promises, and agreements are trusted by the world,
and ministers clearly know what can be expected of the ruler.
Once policies are displayed,
even if profit or loss is seen,
he does not deceive his people;
once treaties are fixed,
even if profit or loss is seen,
he does not deceive his allies.
If so,
the army will be strong and the cities firm,
enemy states will fear him,
the state will be unified and extremely clear,
and allied states will trust him.
Even if located in a remote and humble state,
his prestige moves the world.
The Five Hegemons were examples of this.
They did not base themselves on government and education,
nor did they reach the heights of refinement,
nor did they perfect civil principles,
nor did they win the hearts of men.
They focused on strategies,
examined labor and rest,
were careful with stores and accumulation,
and maintained war readiness;
those above and below trusted each other firmly,
and none in the world dared oppose them.
Thus Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, Chǔ Zhuāng, Wú Hélǘ, and Yuè Gòujiàn
all ruled remote and humble states,
yet their prestige moved the world
and their strength threatened the central states.
There was no other reason for this
than their general trustworthiness.
This is what is called establishing trust and becoming a Hegemon.
To lead a state to pursue merit and profit,
not striving to expand righteousness
or align with trust,
but seeking only profit;
internally, not fearing to cheat the people
to seek small profit;
externally, not fearing to cheat allies
to seek great profit;
internally, not refining what one already possesses,
but greedily desiring what others have.
If so,
then the ministers and common people will all treat their superior with deceitful hearts.
The superior cheats the inferiors,
and the inferiors cheat the superior;
thus those above and below are divided.
If so,
then enemy states will slight them,
and allied states will doubt them.
Schemes and plots are used daily,
and the state cannot avoid danger and reduction,
reaching the extreme and perishing.
Qí Mǐn and Xuē Gōng were examples of this.
Therefore, though they used a strong Qí,
it was not to cultivate ritual and righteousness,
not to base themselves on government and education,
and not to unify the world.
They were constantly occupied with making alliances and racing abroad.
Thus their strength was enough to break Chǔ in the south,
to bend Qín in the west,
to defeat Yān in the north,
and to take Sòng in the center.
But when Yān and Zhào rose to attack it,
it was like shaking dry leaves;
the ruler died and the state perished,
becoming a great laughingstock to the world.
When later generations speak of evil,
they must cite them.
There was no other reason for this
than that they did not follow ritual and righteousness
but followed schemes and power.
These three are what a brilliant ruler carefully chooses
and what a humane person strives to make clear.
One who chooses well controls others;
one who chooses poorly is controlled by others.
A state is a great vessel of the world
and a heavy responsibility;
one must choose its placement well before setting it down.
To place it in danger is to be in peril.
One must choose the path well before leading it;
if the path is overgrown, it is blocked,
and if blocked, it perishes.
"Placing the state"
does not refer to enfeoffment,
but to what laws are followed
and what people are associated with.
Therefore, if one follows the laws of a King
and acts with the people of a King,
then one will also become a King.
If one follows the laws of a Hegemon
and acts with the people of a Hegemon,
then one will also become a Hegemon.
If one follows the laws of a perishing state
and acts with the people of a perishing state,
then one will also perish.
These three are what a brilliant ruler carefully chooses
and what a humane person strives to make clear.
Therefore, a state is a heavy responsibility;
without accumulated maintenance, it cannot stand.
Therefore, a state
is what is kept new by the age;
it may become worn,
but it does not change its nature;
it only changes its ritual jades and conduct.
A day has its morning,
and a day has its people,
yet it can have the solidity of a thousand years; why is this?
It is said:
It is upheld by the trustworthy laws of a thousand years,
and it is acted upon with the trustworthy men of a thousand years.
Humans do not have a lifespan of a hundred years,
yet there are trustworthy men of a thousand years; why is this?
It is said:
One who upholds himself with the laws of a thousand years
is himself a trustworthy man of a thousand years.
Therefore, acting with gentlemen of accumulated ritual and righteousness leads to Kingship;
acting with upright, sincere, and complete scholars leads to Hegemony;
acting with people of schemes and subversion leads to Ruin.
These three are what a brilliant ruler carefully chooses
and what a humane person strives to make clear.
One who chooses well controls others;
one who chooses poorly is controlled by others.
One who holds a state
must not do so alone;
thus, strength, stability, honor, and disgrace lie in the choice of a Prime Minister.
If the ruler himself is capable and the Prime Minister is capable,
such a one will be a King.
If the ruler is not capable
but knows enough to be fearful and seeks out the capable,
such a one will be strong.
If the ruler is not capable,
does not know fear, and does not seek the capable,
but only employs sycophants and favorites close to him,
such a one will be endangered and reduced,
and reach the extreme and perish.
A state:
if used greatly, it becomes great;
if used smallly, it becomes small.
At its greatest, it is a King;
at its smallest, it perishes.
One that balances between the great and small paths survives.
Grand employment is such that
one puts righteousness first and profit second,
and in peace, one does not worry about closeness or distance of kinship,
nor about high or low status,
but only seeks sincere ability.
This is what is meant by grand employment.
Petty employment is such that
one puts profit first and righteousness second,
and in peace, one does not worry about right or wrong,
nor manage the crooked or the straight,
but only employs those who are sycophantic or personally close to oneself.
This is what is meant by petty employment.
Grand employment is like that,
while petty employment is like this;
the distinction between the petty and the grand
is also entirely like that
or entirely like this.
Therefore it is said:
"One who is pure becomes a King (Wáng),
one who is mixed becomes a Hegemon (Bà),
and one who has neither perishes."
This is what that refers to.
If a state lacks Ritual (Lǐ), it will not be upright.
That by which Ritual (Lǐ) makes a state upright
is comparable
to a scale for light and heavy,
to a marking line for the crooked and the straight,
or to a compass and square for the round and the square.
Once these are applied, no one can deceive.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"Majestic as frost and snow,
bright as the sun and moon.
Practice it and you will survive;
do it not and you will perish."
This is what that refers to.
If the state is in danger, there is no joyful ruler;
if the state is secure, there are no sorrowful people.
Disorder means the state is in danger;
order means the state is secure.
Nowadays, those who rule over men
are urgent in pursuing pleasure but slow in governing the state;
is this not an extreme error!
This is like loving sounds and colors
while being indifferent to having no ears or eyes;
is this not lamentable!
Now, regarding human nature:
the eyes desire the ultimate in color,
the ears desire the ultimate in sound,
the mouth desires the ultimate in flavor,
the nose desires the ultimate in scent,
and the mind desires the ultimate in ease.
These five ultimates
are what human nature cannot avoid.
To nurture these five ultimates, there must be means;
without those means,
then the five ultimates cannot be attained.
A state of ten thousand chariots
can be called vast and rich;
if it also has the way of order, discrimination, strength, and solidity,
then in such a case, one will be joyful and without hardship,
and thereafter the means to nurture the five ultimates will be complete.
Therefore, all joys
are born from a well-governed state;
worries and hardships
are born from a disordered state.
Those who are urgent in pursuing pleasure but slow in governing the state
are those who do not understand pleasure.
Therefore, a bright ruler
will certainly govern his state first,
and thereafter all joys are attained within it.
A dim ruler
will certainly pursue pleasure recklessly and be slow in governing the state;
thus, his worries and hardships are beyond counting,
and he will surely reach the point of personal death and the state's destruction before he stops.
Is this not lamentable!
Intending to find pleasure,
he instead gets worry;
intending to find security,
he instead gets danger;
intending to find fortune,
he instead gets death.
Is this not lamentable!
Alas!
Those who rule over men
might well examine such words.
Thus, governing a state has a way,
and the ruler of men has a duty.
As for laboring day after day so that governance is detailed,
and in a single day distinguishing every detail,
these are things that the various officials and clerks are sent to do;
it is not worth harming the joy of leisure and peaceful rest with such things.
As for evaluating a single Chancellor (Xiàng) to lead everyone together,
making the ministers and officials all abide by the Way and turn toward the right direction in their efforts,
this is the duty of the ruler of men.
In such a case, merit will unify the world,
and fame will match that of Yáo and Yǔ.
Such a ruler
maintains the utmost essential yet is detailed in governance,
his affairs are of the utmost ease yet he has merit,
he lets his robes hang
without leaving his woven mat,
and yet none among the people within the seas do not wish to have him as their Emperor (Dìwáng).
This is what is called the utmost essential,
and no joy is greater than this.
A ruler of men
is one who considers the ability to employ others as his own ability;
an ordinary man
is one who considers his own personal ability as his ability.
A ruler of men can make others do things for him;
an ordinary man has no one to shift tasks to.
To guard a hundred mu
exhausts one's business,
for there is no one to shift tasks to.
Now, to have one person simultaneously listen to the whole world
and have time left over each day while the governance is sufficient
is because he makes others do it.
Whether grandly possessing the whole world
or small-scale possessing a single state, if one must do everything personally before it is acceptable, then the labor and exhaustion could not be more extreme; in such a case, even a slave
or a captive would not be willing to trade with the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ)
positions and duties. With this being used to encompass the world
and unify the four seas,
why must he do everything personally?
Doing it personally
is the way of a laborer
and the theory of Mòzǐ.
Assessing virtue, employing the capable, and assigning them to offices
is the way of the Sage Kings (Shèngwáng),
and what the Confucians (Ru) carefully maintain.
The Tradition (Chuán) says:
"Farmers divide the fields and plow,
merchants divide the goods and trade,
the various artisans divide the tasks and work diligently,
the scholars and officials divide the duties and listen to commands,
the rulers of the feudal states divide the land and guard it,
and the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) oversee all directions and deliberate;
then the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) can simply maintain himself in reverence."
Issuing orders thus and receiving reports thus,
there is nothing in the world that is not balanced,
and nothing that is not well-ordered and distinct.
This is what is common to all the hundred kings
and the great division of Ritual Law (Lǐfǎ).
A territory of a hundred li
can be used to take the whole world—
this is not false;
the difficulty lies in the ruler of men knowing this.
Taking the world
does not mean carrying its land along with you;
it means the Way is sufficient to unify people.
If those people are unified,
how can the land leave me and go elsewhere?
Thus, a territory of a hundred li
has ranks, positions, and ceremonial robes
sufficient to accommodate the worthy scholars (Xiánshì) of the world;
its offices and duties
are sufficient to accommodate the capable scholars (Néngshì) of the world.
Following the old laws
and selecting the good ones to use clearly
is sufficient to win the submission of those who love profit.
When the worthy scholars (Xiánshì) are unified,
the capable scholars (Néngshì) are in office,
and those who love profit are submissive,
these three being complete, the whole world is exhausted;
there is nothing that exists outside of this.
Therefore, a territory of a hundred li
is sufficient to exhaust strategic power (Shì);
manifesting loyalty and trust
and making benevolence and righteousness (Rényì) prominent
is sufficient to exhaust the people's potential.
When these two are combined, the world is taken,
and those feudal lords who are last to join will be the first to face danger.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
"From the west and from the east,
from the south and from the north,
there are none who think of not submitting."
This refers to the unification under one man.
Yì and Féng Mén
were good at mastering archery;
Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù
were good at mastering driving.
The wise and brilliant gentleman (Jūnzǐ)
is good at mastering people.
When people submit, strategic power (Shì) follows them;
when people do not submit, strategic power (Shì) leaves them.
Therefore, the King (Wángzhě) focuses his efforts on winning over people.
Thus, if a ruler of men wants good archery, hitting distant and tiny targets,
then none are equal to Yì and Féng Mén;
if he wants good driving, reaching far targets quickly,
then none are equal to Wáng Liáng and Zào Fù;
but if he wants to harmonize and unify the world
and control Qín and Chǔ,
then none are equal to the wise and brilliant gentleman (Jūnzǐ).
The use of wisdom is very simple,
and the conduct of affairs is not laborious,
yet the achievements and fame achieved are extremely great.
It is very easy to manage and provides the utmost joy.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler regards it as a treasure,
while the foolish regard it as difficult.
To be as noble as the Tiānzǐ,
as wealthy as possessing the whole world,
to be known as a Shèngwáng,
to control all people
while no one can control him—
these are the common desires of human nature,
and a King is one who possesses all of these.
To wear fine silks,
to eat rich flavors,
to manage great wealth and objects,
and to unite and rule the whole world;
to have abundant food and drink,
grand music,
high terraces and pavilions,
and vast parks and gardens;
to employ the Zhūhóu as ministers,
and to unify the world—
these are also the common desires of human nature,
and such are the ritual systems of the Tiānzǐ.
When the systems are displayed,
and the government orders are comprehensive;
if officials lose the essentials of their duties, they die;
if Gōng and Hóu lose their ritual decorum, they are confined;
if the states of the four directions
possess extravagant or deviant virtues, they must be destroyed.
When fame is like the sun and moon,
and achievements are like heaven and earth,
the people of the world respond like shadows and echoes—
these are also the common desires of human nature.
And a King is one who possesses all of these.
Therefore, regarding human nature:
the mouth likes flavors,
and no flavor is more beautiful than these;
the ears like sound,
and no music is grander than this;
the eyes like beauty,
and decorative patterns are most complex
while women are most numerous;
the physical body likes ease,
and no comfort is more pleasant than peaceful, heavy, leisure and stillness;
the heart likes profit,
and no emoluments of grain are thicker.
To possess all that the world desires together,
and to encompass the world and govern it as if governing one's own children and grandchildren—
unless a person is mad, deluded, stupid, or ignorant,
who could witness this and not be joyful?
Rulers who desire this
exist side by side,
and scholars who can establish this
have not been lacking in any generation.
Yet for a thousand years they have not met; why?
I say:
the ruler of men is not public-minded,
and the ministers of men are not loyal.
The ruler of men excludes the worthy and shows favoritism in appointments;
the ministers of men fight for positions and envy the worthy.
This is the reason they do not meet.
Why does the ruler of men not broaden his mind,
regardless of whether people are kin or distant,
regardless of whether they are noble or lowly,
and seek only those with genuine ability?
If this were so,
then the ministers of men would treat their duties lightly to yield to the worthy
and peacefully follow behind them.
If it were like this,
then Shùn and Yǔ would return,
and the Kingly enterprise would rise again.
With achievements unifying the world
and fame matching Shùn and Yǔ,
can anything else be joyful
as beautiful as this?
Alas!
Those who rule people
may also examine these words.
Yáng Zhū wept at the crossroads,
saying:
"Is this not where a single wrong step
leads to realizing one has stumbled a thousand lǐ away!"
and he wailed for it.
This is also the crossroads of glory and disgrace, safety and danger, survival and ruin;
it is even more lamentable
than the crossroads of the road.
Alas!
How sad!
Those who rule people
have not awakened to this for a thousand years.
There is no state that does not have laws for order,
and no state that does not have laws for chaos;
no state that does not have worthy scholars,
and no state that does not have useless scholars;
no state that does not have honest people,
and no state that does not have fierce people;
no state that does not have beautiful customs,
and no state that does not have evil customs.
When both paths run together, the state survives;
when the upper path predominates, the state is secure;
when the lower path predominates, the state is in danger;
when the upper path is unified, one is King;
when the lower path is unified, one perishes.
Therefore, if the laws are orderly,
the assistants are worthy,
the people are honest,
and the customs are beautiful,
and these four are aligned,
this is called "unifying the upper."
In this case, one wins without fighting
and gains without attacking;
the world submits without tiring the soldiers and weapons.
Thus, Tāng used Bó,
and Wǔwáng used Hào;
both were lands of only a hundred lǐ.
The world was unified,
the Zhūhóu became their ministers,
and among all those who could be reached,
none failed to follow and submit.
There was no other reason for this
than the alignment of those four things.
Jié and Zhòu were powerful enough to possess the world,
but even when they sought to be common men, they could not.
This was for no other reason
than that those four things were all lost.
Thus, although the laws of the hundred Kings were not the same
in this way, that to which they returned was one.
Superiors never fail to extend love to their inferiors
and regulate them with ritual;
the superiors regard the inferiors
as if they were protecting an infant.
Government orders and systems
are used to connect with the common people.
If there is anything as small as a hair that is not orderly,
then even the lonely, widowed, or orphaned will not have it imposed upon them.
Therefore, the inferiors' affection for the superiors
is as joyful as that for their parents;
they would face death but could not be made disobedient.
Ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
noble and lowly, old and young,
down to the common people,
none fail to regard this as the supreme standard.
Then all inwardly examine themselves
to be diligent in their duties.
This is what the hundred Kings have in common,
and it is the pivot of ritual and law.
Then farmers divide the fields to plow,
merchants divide goods to trade,
the various artisans divide tasks to work diligently,
scholar-officials divide duties to manage,
the rulers of the Zhūhóu who establish states divide land to guard,
and the Sāngōng oversee the various directions to deliberate.
Then the Tiānzǐ merely folds his hands and stops.
Whether going out or staying in,
nothing in the world is not balanced,
and nothing is not well-governed and distinct.
This is what the hundred Kings have in common
and is the great division of ritual and law.
As for maintaining daily order and peace,
weighing things for appropriate use,
ensuring clothes have regulations,
palaces have measures,
followers have numbers,
and that funerals, sacrifices, and implements all have their appropriate grades—
to thus encompass all things
in units of chǐ, cùn, xún, and zhàng,
such that nothing fails to follow the systems, numbers, measures, and weights before proceeding—
these are the duties of officials and subordinates
and are not worthy of being recounted before a great gentleman.
Therefore, the one who rules people,
if he establishes a supreme government in the court correctly
and those he employs to manage all affairs are truly benevolent people,
then his person is at ease and the state is well-governed,
his achievements are great and his name is beautiful;
above he can be a King,
and below he can be a Bà.
If he establishes a supreme government in the court incorrectly
and those he employs to manage all affairs are not benevolent people,
then his person is labored and the state is in chaos,
his achievements are discarded and his name is disgraced,
and the state must be in danger.
This is the pivot for the ruler of men.
Therefore, to correctly manage one person allows one to take the world;
to fail to correctly manage one person endangers the state.
To not be able to correctly manage one person
but be able to correctly manage a thousand or a hundred people—
it is said that such a thing does not exist.
Once one can correctly manage the one person,
then what labor does his person have to perform?
He merely lets his robes hang, and the world is settled.
Therefore, Tāng used Yī Yǐn;
Wén Wáng used Lǚ Shàng;
Wǔ Wáng used Zhào Gōng;
Chéng Wáng used Zhōu Gōng Dàn.
Lower than these were the Wǔ Bà;
within the inner chambers of Qí Huán Gōng, there were the practices of hanging music, extravagance, and leisurely amusements,
which in the world were not considered cultivation;
yet he convened the feudal lords nine times
and unified the world,
becoming the leader of the Wǔ Bà.
This was for no other reason
than that he knew to entrust all government affairs to Guǎn Zhòng;
this is the essential principle for one who rules others.
The wise find it easy to exert effort,
and their achievements and fame are exceedingly great;
setting this aside, what else is worth doing?
Therefore, the people of antiquity
who attained great achievements and fame
necessarily followed this way;
those who lost their states or endangered their persons
necessarily acted contrary to this.
Thus Kǒng Zǐ said:
"The knowledge of the wise
is certainly abundant,
yet they have a way to maintain the essential—
can they not be perceptive!
The knowledge of the foolish
is certainly meager,
yet they have a way to maintain a vast amount—
can they not be frantic!"
This is what it means.
For one who governs a state, once the distinctions are established,
then the ruler, chancellor, ministers, and officials
each diligently attend to what they hear,
not striving to listen to what they have not heard;
each diligently attend to what they see,
not striving to look at what they have not seen.
If what is heard and seen is truly unified,
then even in secluded and hidden places,
none of the common people would dare not to respect their roles and abide by the regulations
to transform themselves through rituals toward their superiors;
this is the sign of a well-governed state.
The way of the ruler is to govern the near rather than the far,
to govern the manifest rather than the hidden,
to govern the one rather than the many.
If the ruler can govern the near, then the far will be orderly;
if the ruler can govern the manifest, then the hidden will be transformed;
if the ruler can focus on the one, then the hundred affairs will be correct.
Indeed, for one who listens to all under heaven,
to have time to spare in a day while governance remains insufficient
is due to this;
this is the pinnacle of governance.
Having been able to govern the near,
to then strive to govern the far;
having been able to govern the manifest,
to then strive to see the hidden;
having been able to focus on the one,
to then strive to correct the hundred:
this is to go to excess.
Excess is like falling short;
it is like setting up a straight post and seeking a crooked shadow.
Being unable to govern the near,
yet striving to govern the far;
being unable to examine the manifest,
yet striving to see the hidden;
being unable to focus on the one,
yet striving to correct the hundred:
this is to be perverse;
it is like setting up a crooked post and seeking a straight shadow.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler loves the essential,
while the benighted ruler loves detail.
If the ruler loves the essential, then the hundred affairs will be detailed;
if the ruler loves detail, then the hundred affairs will be neglected.
The ruler selects one chancellor,
establishes one law,
and clarifies one purpose
to cover everything,
to illuminate everything,
and to observe the prosperity.
The chancellor
organizes and ranks the heads of all officials,
summarizes the reports of the hundred affairs,
to refine the roles of the ministers and officials of the court,
evaluates their merits,
determines their rewards,
and at the end of the year presents their achievements to report to the ruler.
If appropriate, they are approved;
if inappropriate, they are dismissed.
Therefore, the ruler of men labors in seeking them
but rests in employing them.
For one who manages a state,
gaining the strength of the common people makes him wealthy,
gaining their willingness to die for him makes him strong,
and gaining their praise makes him honored.
When these three virtues are present, the world turns to him;
when these three virtues are missing, the world leaves him.
When the world turns to someone, he is called a True King;
when the world leaves someone, it is called ruin.
Tāng and Wǔ
followed this way,
practiced its righteousness,
promoted the common interests of the world,
and eliminated the common harms of the world;
thus the world turned to them.
Therefore, they prioritized a generous reputation of virtue,
clarified ritual and righteousness to lead them,
exhibited loyalty and trustworthiness to love them,
rewarded the worthy and employed the capable to order them,
used ranks, robes, and rewards to show respect for them,
timed their labors,
and managed their tasks
to harmonize them;
they extensively covered them,
nurtured and raised them,
as if protecting an infant.
In sustaining the people, they were extremely generous;
in employing the people, they were extremely orderly;
they distinguished government orders and systems
as the means of interacting with the common people of the world.
If there was anything unreasonable even as small as the tip of a hair,
then even for the orphaned, the widowed, or the childless,
it would certainly not be imposed upon them.
For this reason, the common people valued them like a Supreme Deity,
loved them like their own parents,
and would face death or destruction for them without hesitation;
there was no other reason than that their virtue was truly brilliant
and their benefits were truly generous.
An age of chaos is not like this:
Defilement and plunder are prioritized,
schemes and subversion are demonstrated,
and petitions from actors, dwarves, and women cause confusion;
the foolish are made to command the wise,
and the unworthy are made to oversee the worthy.
In sustaining the people, they cause extreme poverty and hardship;
in employing the people, they cause extreme toil and suffering.
For this reason,
the common people despise them like a madman,
hate them like a ghost,
daily wishing to find an opportunity to strike them down
and drive them away.
If suddenly there is an invasion or difficulty,
to then hope the common people will die for one's sake
is impossible,
as there is no way for them to have earned it.
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Examine how I treat others,
and you will see why others come to me."
This is what it means.
As for those things that harm a state,
what are they?
It is said:
Using petty men to dominate the people with authority
and using cleverness to take from the people what should not be taken; these are the great disasters that harm a state.
For the ruler of a great state
to be fond of pursuing small gains
harms the state. As for his pursuit of music and women, terraces and towers, parks and gardens,
the more he tires of them, the more he seeks new ones;
this harms the state.
Not being fond of maintaining and regulating what he has,
but always greedily desiring what others have,
harms the state.
When these three evils are in his breast,
and he is further fond of using people who are schemers and subversives
to decide matters externally,
if it is like this, then his power will be light and his reputation disgraced,
the state altars will surely be in danger;
these are what harm a state.
For the ruler of a great state
not to exalt fundamental conduct
and not to respect old laws,
but to be fond of deception and artifice;
if it is like this, then the various ministers of the court
will also follow suit and form a custom of not exalting ritual and righteousness but loving subversion.
If the custom of the ministers of the court is like this,
then the common people will also follow suit and form a custom of not exalting ritual and righteousness but loving greed and profit.
When the customs of the ruler, ministers, superiors, and inferiors are all like this,
then even if the land is broad,
power will certainly be light;
even if the people are numerous,
the military will certainly be weak;
even if punishments are frequent,
orders will not be followed below.
This is what is called a state in peril;
this is what harms a state.
The scholar-officials do not act in this way;
they will certainly make detailed distinctions:
the court will certainly exalt ritual and righteousness and examine the noble and the lowly;
if it is like this, then none of the scholar-officials will not strive for integrity and die for the regulations.
The hundred officials will then unify their systems
and value their ranks;
if it is like this, then none of the officials will not fear the law and follow the guidelines.
The passes and markets are inspected but not taxed;
contracts and laws are enforced without partiality;
if it is like this, then none of the merchants will not be sincere and free from deception.
The various artisans will cut and fell timber according to the season,
extending their scheduled dates
to benefit from their skill and responsibility;
if it is like this,
then among the various artisans, none will not be loyal and trustworthy and their work will not be shoddy.
Districts and villages will lighten the taxes on fields,
reduce the collection of money,
seldom raise corvée labor,
and not snatch away the farming seasons;
if it is like this, then among the farmers, none will not be simple, hardworking, and focused.
Scholar-officials strive for integrity and die for the regulations;
thus the troops are strong.
The various officials fear the law and follow the line;
then the state is constantly free from disorder.
If merchants are honest and without deceit,
then traveling merchants are at ease,
goods and wealth circulate,
and the state’s needs are supplied.
If the various artisans are loyal and trustworthy and their work is not shoddy,
then tools and implements are skillful and convenient, and wealth is not exhausted.
If the farmers are simple, hardworking, and focused,
then above they do not miss the seasons of Heaven,
below they do not miss the benefits of the Earth,
in the middle they obtain harmony among people,
and the hundred affairs are not neglected.
This is called government orders being carried out
and customs being beautiful;
in defense one is solid,
in campaigns one is strong,
in residence one has a good name,
and in action one has merit.
This is what the Ru scholars call thorough discrimination.
There are chaotic rulers,
but no chaotic states;
there are people who govern,
but no laws that govern.
The methods of Yì have not perished,
but Yì does not hit the mark in every generation;
the laws of Yǔ still exist,
but Xià does not rule as kings in every generation.
Therefore, laws cannot stand alone,
and categories cannot carry themselves out;
if they obtain the right person, they exist;
if they lose the right person, they perish.
Law is the beginning of governance;
the Jūnzǐ is the source of the law.
Therefore, if there is a Jūnzǐ,
then although the laws are brief,
they are sufficient to be comprehensive;
if there is no Jūnzǐ,
then although the laws are complete,
one loses the proper order of application,
cannot respond to the changes of affairs,
and they are sufficient to cause chaos.
One who does not understand the meaning of the law
yet regulates the technical details of the law,
even if they are broadly learned, they will certainly cause chaos when facing affairs.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler is urgent to obtain the right person,
while a dark ruler is urgent to obtain power.
Being urgent to obtain the right person,
then the ruler is at ease and the state is governed,
merit is great and the name is beautiful;
above one can be a King,
below one can be a Hegemon.
Not being urgent to obtain the right person
but being urgent to obtain power,
then the ruler is toiled and the state is chaotic,
merit is discarded and the name is disgraced,
and the altars of soil and grain will surely be in danger.
Therefore, one who rules people
toils in searching for the right person
and rests in employing them.
The Shū says:
“Only Wén Wáng was reverent and cautious;
as a single person, he made selections.”
This is what it means.
Matching tallies
and distinguishing contracts
are the means to ensure trustworthiness;
if the superior loves schemes,
then the boastful and deceitful people among the subordinates and various officials will take advantage of this to deceive.
Drawing tallies and tossing hooks
are the means to ensure impartiality;
if the superior loves partiality,
then the subordinates and various officials will take advantage of this to be biased.
Weights, measures, and scales
are the means to ensure fairness;
if the superior loves subversion,
then the subordinates and various officials will take advantage of this to be treacherous.
Pecks, bushels, vessels, and level-sticks
are the means to ensure precision;
if the superior loves greed,
then the subordinates and various officials will take advantage of this to take bountifully and give stingily,
taking from the people without measure.
Therefore, instruments and techniques
are the downstream flow of governance;
they are not the source of governance.
The Jūnzǐ
is the source of governance.
Petty officials maintain the techniques,
while the Jūnzǐ nurtures the source;
if the source is clear, the flow is clear;
if the source is muddy, the flow is muddy.
Therefore, if the superior loves ritual and righteousness,
honors the worthy and employs the capable,
and has no heart of greed,
then the subordinates will also hold yielding in high regard,
attain loyalty and trustworthiness,
and be careful in their roles as ministers and sons.
In this way, even among the common people,
they do not wait for the matching of tallies
or the distinguishing of contracts to be trustworthy;
they do not wait for drawing tallies or tossing hooks to be impartial;
they do not wait for weights and scales to be fair;
they do not wait for pecks and bushels to be precise.
Therefore, rewards are not used yet the people are encouraged;
punishments are not used yet the people submit;
officials do not toil yet affairs are governed;
government orders are not vexatious yet customs are beautiful;
none of the common people dare not follow the laws of the superior,
emulate the will of the superior,
be encouraged in the affairs of the superior,
and find peace and joy in them.
Therefore, in land taxes and collection they forget the expense,
in their tasks and business they forget the toil,
in disasters they forget death;
city walls do not wait for repairs yet are solid,
weapons do not wait for sharpening yet are strong,
enemy states do not wait for submission yet are humbled,
and the people within the four seas do not wait for orders yet are unified.
This is called the utmost peace.
The Shī says:
“The King’s plans are truly grand;
the region of Xú has already come.”
This is what it means.
May I ask about being a ruler?
Answer:
To use ritual to distribute and dispense,
even and comprehensive without partiality.
May I ask about being a minister?
Answer:
To use ritual to serve the ruler,
loyal and obedient without slackness.
May I ask about being a father?
Answer:
Kind and generous yet possessing ritual.
May I ask about being a son?
Answer:
Respectful and loving, reaching the height of refinement.
May I ask about being an elder brother?
Answer:
Compassionate and loving, showing friendliness.
May I ask about being a younger brother?
Answer:
Respectful and yielding without being careless.
May I ask about being a husband?
Answer:
Achieving merit without being dissolute,
achieving presence with clear distinctions.
May I ask about being a wife?
Answer:
If the husband has ritual, then be gentle, following, listening, and serving;
if the husband has no ritual, then be apprehensive and maintain self-respect.
This is the Way;
if established partially, there is chaos;
if established together, there is order;
it is sufficient for examination.
May I ask how to be capable of all these?
Answer:
Examine it through ritual.
In ancient times, the Former Kings examined ritual to roam grandly and reach everywhere in the world,
and in their actions, nothing was inappropriate.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ is courteous but not strained,
reverent but not fearful,
impoverished but not distressed,
wealthy and noble but not arrogant,
encountering changes and responding to them without being exhausted;
this is examining it through ritual.
Therefore, as for the Jūnzǐ’s relationship to ritual,
he is reverent and at ease with it;
as for his relationship to affairs,
he is direct but does not fail;
as for his relationship to people,
he has few resentments, is broad-minded, and is not sycophantic;
as for what he does for his own person,
he is careful in cultivation and refinement and is not in danger;
as for his response to changing incidents,
he is quick and efficient and not confused;
as for his relationship to Heaven and Earth and the myriad things,
he does not strive to explain why they are so
but attains the skillful use of their materials.
Regarding the affairs of the various officials and the work of craftsmen,
he does not compete with their abilities
but ensures the successful employment of their efforts.
In serving his superiors,
he is loyal, obedient, and never remiss.
In commanding his subordinates,
he is impartial and universal, showing no favoritism.
In his social interactions,
he follows righteousness and associates with those of his kind.
In dwelling within his local community,
he is accommodating and does not cause disorder.
Therefore, if he is in poverty, he will certainly have a good reputation;
if he is prominent, he will certainly achieve great deeds.
His benevolence and generosity cover the whole world without weariness.
His wisdom and understanding encompass Heaven and Earth and manage all myriad changes without doubt.
His physical energy is harmonious and peaceful,
and his will is vast.
His righteous conduct fills the space between Heaven and Earth;
he is the pinnacle of benevolence and wisdom.
Such a person is called a Shèng Rén;
this is the careful examination of Lǐ.
Someone asked about governing a state.
The reply was: I have heard of Xiū Shēn,
but I have never heard of governing a state as something separate.
The ruler is the gnomon;
the people are the shadow.
When the gnomon is upright, the shadow is upright.
The ruler is the basin;
the people are the water.
When the basin is round, the water is round.
The ruler is the bowl; when the bowl is square, the water is square. When the ruler shoots, the ministers adjust their finger-guards.
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng loved slender waists,
and thus there were starving people in his court.
Therefore it is said:
I have heard of Xiū Shēn,
but I have never heard of governing a state as something separate.
The ruler is
the source of the people;
if the source is clear, the stream is clear;
if the source is turbid, the stream is turbid.
Thus, if one who possesses the Shè Jì cannot love the people
or benefit the people,
yet seeks to have the people feel affection and love for him,
it is impossible.
If the people do not feel affection or love,
yet he seeks to have them serve him
and die for him,
it is impossible.
If the people do not serve him
or die for him,
yet he seeks to have strong armies
and solid fortifications,
it is impossible.
If the armies are not strong
and the fortifications are not solid,
yet he seeks to prevent the enemy from arriving,
it is impossible.
If the enemy arrives and he seeks to avoid danger, loss, or
destruction,
it is impossible.
The actual conditions for danger, loss, and destruction
are all accumulated here;
yet to seek safety and joy
in such a state—
is that not difficult?
Such a person is a Kuáng Shēng.
A Kuáng Shēng
will fall before long.
Therefore, if a lord of men desires strength, security, and joy,
nothing is better than returning to the people;
if he desires to attach his subordinates and unify the people,
nothing is better than returning to governance;
if he desires to cultivate governance and beautify customs,
nothing is better than seeking the right person.
There are those whose accumulation of merit ensures their lineage does not end for generations.
Such a person
lives in the present age
but sets his will upon the Gǔ Zhī Dào.
Although the kings and dukes of the world may not like it,
yet this person alone likes it;
although the people of the world may not do it,
yet this person alone does it.
Those who like it are poor;
those who do it are in straits;
yet this person still continues to do it,
never stopping for even a moment.
He is clearly and uniquely enlightened regarding how the Xiān Wáng gained
or lost the world;
he knows the security or peril, the goodness or badness of the state
as clearly as distinguishing white from black.
Such a person
if used in a great capacity,
then the world will be unified
and the Zhū Hóu will become his ministers;
if used in a small capacity,
then his authority will prevail over neighboring enemies;
even if he cannot be employed,
as long as he is not allowed to leave the territory,
the state will remain free from trouble for his entire life.
Thus, he who rules over men
will be secure if he loves the people
and will be honored if he loves the Shì;
if he lacks both of these, he will perish.
The Shī says:
"The great man is the fence;
the Tài Shī is the wall."
This is what it refers to.
What is the Dào?
I say:
It is that which the ruler follows as his path.
What
is a ruler?
I say:
One who is capable of Qún.
What does it mean to be
"capable of Qún"?
I say:
He is one who is good at Shēng Yǎng the people,
good at Bān Zhì the people,
good at Xiǎn Shè the people,
and good at Fān Shì the people.
When one is good at Shēng Yǎng, the people feel close to him;
when one is good at Bān Zhì, the people feel secure with him;
when one is good at Xiǎn Shè, the people rejoice in him;
when one is good at Fān Shì, the people feel honored by him.
When these four principles are all present,
the whole world gravitates toward him;
this is what is called being "capable of Qún."
One who cannot Shēng Yǎng
will not be loved by the people;
one who cannot Bān Zhì
will not have people who feel secure;
one who cannot Xiǎn Shè
will not have people who rejoice;
one who cannot Fān Shì
will not have people who feel honored.
When these four principles are lost,
the world abandons him;
this is what is called a Pǐ Fū.
Therefore it is said:
When the Dào exists, the state exists;
when the Dào is lost, the state is lost.
Reducing the number of artisans and merchants,
increasing the number of farmers,
prohibiting thieves and robbers,
and eliminating the wicked and depraved—
these are the means by which he nurtures the people. The Tiān Zǐ has the Sān Gōng;
the Zhū Hóu have one Xiàng;
the Dà Fū take charge of their offices;
the Shì maintain their duties;
and none act without regulation and public-mindedness—
these are the means by which he orders and governs them.
Assessing virtue to determine rank,
measuring ability to assign office,
ensuring each person carries out their tasks
and each obtains what is appropriate—
making the most worthy into Sān Gōng,
the next most worthy into Zhū Hóu,
and the least worthy into Shì and Dà Fū—
these are the means by which he promotes and establishes them.
Regulating caps and hats, robes and skirts,
patterns of axes and symbols,
carvings and engravings,
all having hierarchical grades—
these are the means by which he adorns and refines them.
Thus, from the Tiān Zǐ down to the commoners,
there is no one who does not exert their ability,
achieve their will,
and find joy and security in their work;
this is what they have in common.
