Having warm clothes and sufficient food,
living in peace and wandering in joy,
with work occurring at the proper times, regulations being clear, and resources being sufficient—
this is also what they have in common.
As for the layering of colors to form complex patterns
and the layering of flavors to provide
rare and exotic delicacies, these are the surpluses.
The Shèng Wáng regulates these surpluses
to clearly distinguish differences,
above, to adorn the worthy and good and clarify the noble and the base;
below, to distinguish the elder and the younger and clarify the near and the distant.
Above in the court of kings and dukes,
and below in the homes of the common people,
the whole world clearly knows that these are not for the purpose of being eccentric,
but are used to clarify distinctions, achieve order, and preserve the state for ten thousand generations.
Thus, the Tiān Zǐ and Zhū Hóu have no wasteful expenses,
the Shì and Dà Fū have no licentious conduct,
the various officials have no negligent duties,
and the common people have no wicked customs
or crimes of theft;
their abilities can be said to match righteousness universally.
Therefore it is said:
"When there is order, the surplus reaches the common people;
when there is chaos, there is not enough even for kings and dukes."
This is what it refers to.
The Great Manifestation of the Perfect Way:
when rituals are exalted and supreme laws are established, the state has constancy;
when the worthy are honored and the capable are employed, the people know their direction;
when opinions are gathered and public examinations conducted, the people have no doubts;
when rewards go to the diligent and punishments to the negligent, the people do not become idle;
when the ruler listens to all and achieves equal clarity, the world turns to him.
Then, after clarifying roles and duties,
ordering affairs and tasks,
and assigning offices based on talents and skills,
there is nothing that is not well-ordered.
Thus, the public way prevails while the gates of private interest are blocked;
public righteousness is clear while private affairs cease.
In this way,
those of great virtue advance while those of glib speech are stopped;
those greedy for profit retreat while those of integrity and restraint arise.
The *Shū* says:
“Those who are ahead of their time shall be executed without pardon;
those who fail to reach their time shall be executed without pardon.”
When people become practiced in their tasks, they become steadfast.
The hundred affairs of men
are like the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth—one cannot borrow the function of another.
Therefore, when duties are divided, the people are not negligent;
when ranks are fixed, the order is not chaotic;
when the ruler listens to all with equal clarity, the hundred affairs do not linger.
In this way,
from the various officials and ministers down to the common people,
there is no one who does not cultivate himself before daring to feel secure and upright,
or ensure his own competence before daring to accept a post.
The common people change their customs;
petty men change their hearts;
even those of a treacherous or strange sort return to sincerity.
This is called the pinnacle of governance and instruction.
Therefore, the *Tiānzǐ* sees without looking,
hears without listening,
knows without reflecting,
and achieves without acting.
He sits alone like a block of stone, yet the world follows him as if it were a single body,
like the four limbs following the mind.
This is called the Great Manifestation.
The *Shī* says:
“Mild and respectful are the people;
this is the foundation of virtue.”
This is what it means.
Among those who are rulers of men,
there is none who does not desire strength and detest weakness,
desire security and detest danger,
desire honor and detest disgrace.
This is what Yǔ and Jié both had in common.
To obtain these three desires
and avoid these three dislikes,
what path is indeed most convenient?
I say:
It lies in being cautious in choosing a Prime Minister;
there is no path more direct than this.
Therefore, to be wise but not benevolent
is unacceptable;
to be benevolent but not wise
is unacceptable.
Being both wise and benevolent,
such a person is a treasure to the ruler
and an assistant for kingship or hegemony.
Not to be urgent in finding such a person
is unwise;
to find him and not use him
is unbenevolent.
To hope for success without having such a person
is the greatest of follies.
Nowadays, rulers of men have six afflictions:
They have the worthy do the work,
but plan it together with the unworthy;
they have the wise deliberate on it,
but discuss it with the foolish;
they have the cultivated man perform it,
but doubt him together with the corrupt and depraved.
Though they wish to succeed,
can they!
To use a metaphor,
this is like standing a straight piece of wood but fearing its shadow will be crooked;
there is no greater delusion.
The saying goes:
“The beauty of a fine lady
is the bane of the ugly;
the upright and just gentleman
is the tumor of the masses;
the person who follows the Way
is the enemy of the corrupt and depraved.”
Now, if you have the corrupt and depraved
judge their resented enemy
and ask them to be without bias,
can it be done!
To use a metaphor,
this is like standing a crooked piece of wood and seeking a straight shadow;
there is no greater disorder.
Therefore, the people of old did not act this way.
They had a Way for selecting people,
and they had a method for employing people.
The Way for selecting people
was to examine them through ritual;
the method for employing people
was to restrain them by rank.
Whether acting with righteousness or remaining still,
they were measured by ritual;
whether in wisdom, deliberation, acceptance, or rejection,
they were scrutinized by their accomplishments;
as days and months accumulated over a long time,
they were compared by their merits.
Thus, the lowly could not oversee the honorable,
the light could not outweigh the heavy,
and the foolish could not plot against the wise.
Because of this, among ten thousand actions, not one was an error.
Therefore, compare them through ritual
and observe whether they can be at peace and respectful;
give them various tasks and changes of position
and observe whether they can respond to changes;
grant them leisure and ease
and observe whether they can avoid dissipation and indulgence;
expose them to music and women, power and profit, anger and resentment, danger and hardship,
and observe whether they can avoid abandoning their post.
Between those who truly possess these qualities
and those who truly do not,
the difference is like white and black;
can they be distorted!
Just as Bólè could not be deceived about horses,
a *Jūnzǐ* cannot be deceived about people;
this is the Way of the enlightened king.
If a ruler of men desires to obtain those who are good at archery, who shoot far and hit the smallest targets,
he will offer noble ranks and heavy rewards to attract them.
Domestically, he cannot show favoritism to his own sons and brothers;
externally, he cannot exclude distant people.
Whoever can hit the target is selected.
Is this not the way to certainly obtain them!
Even a Sage could not change this.
If he desires to obtain those who are good at driving and can reach distant places quickly, covering a thousand *lǐ* in a single day,
he will offer noble ranks and heavy rewards to attract them.
Domestically, he cannot show favoritism to his own sons and brothers;
externally, he cannot exclude distant people.
Whoever can reach the goal is selected.
Is this not the way to certainly obtain them!
Even a Sage could not change this.
One who desires to govern the state and lead the people,
to harmonize and unify those above and below,
to use them internally to solidify the cities
and externally to resist difficulties—
if the state is well-governed, he will control others,
and others will not be able to control him;
if the state is in chaos, then danger, disgrace, and destruction
can be expected to arrive immediately.
Yet, when seeking ministers and assistants,
he is uniquely not public-minded in this way.
He simply employs those who are favorites, sycophants, and kin who side with him.
Is this not an extreme error!
Therefore, among those who possess a state,
there is none who does not desire to be strong,
yet suddenly they become weak;
none who does not desire to be secure,
yet suddenly they are in danger;
none who does not desire to survive,
yet suddenly they perish.
In ancient times, there were ten thousand states;
today, there are only a few thousand.
There is no other reason for this;
none of them failed to lose it because of this.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler may be partial to individuals with gold, stone, pearls, and jade,
but he is never partial to individuals with official posts and duties.
Why is this?
I say:
Because it is fundamentally not beneficial to the one being favored.
If the person is incapable and the ruler employs him,
then the ruler is deluded;
if the minister is incapable but falsely claims to be capable,
then the minister is deceitful.
When the ruler is deluded above
and the minister is deceitful below,
destruction will come in no time.
This is a path of mutual harm.
Therefore, only an enlightened ruler can truly love those he loves;
a deluded ruler will surely endanger those he loves.
Now, Wén Wáng did not lack noble relatives,
he did not lack sons and brothers,
and he did not lack favorites and sycophants.
Yet he reached far and raised Tài Gōng from among the commoners to employ him.
Could this have been out of favoritism!
Was it because he was a relative?
But the house of Zhōu was of the Jī surname,
while the other was of the Jiāng surname.
Was it because of an old acquaintance?
But they had never known each other.
Was it because he was handsome and beautiful?
But the man was seventy-two years old,
and his remaining teeth were falling out.
However, in the way they were used,
Wén Wáng desired to establish the noble Way
and desired to clarify a noble reputation
in order to benefit the world,
but he could not do so alone;
without this man, there was no one sufficient to raise it up,
so he raised up this man and used him.
Thereupon, the noble Way was indeed established,
the noble reputation was indeed clarified,
and he unified and governed the world.
He established seventy-one states, of which fifty-three were occupied by members of the Jī clan alone.
Among the descendants of Zhōu,
if they were not mad or deluded,
none failed to become illustrious feudal lords of the world.
One such as this is able to love others.
Therefore, he raised up the Great Way of the world
and established the great achievements of the world,
and only then did he bestow his pity and love upon his relatives;
those below them were still sufficient to be illustrious feudal lords of the world.
Thus it is said:
"Only an enlightened ruler is able to love those he loves;
a benighted ruler will surely endanger those he loves."
This is what this means.
Outside the wall,
the eye cannot see;
beyond a lǐ,
the ear cannot hear;
yet what the ruler of men oversees and manages
is as far as the whole world
and as near as the borders of his state.
He must have a general knowledge of them.
Transformations in the world
and matters within the borders
may include instances of laxity, change, or irregularity,
and if the ruler of men has no means of knowing them,
then this is the beginning of being constrained, threatened, and obscured.
The clarity of the ears and eyes
is narrow like this;
what the ruler of men oversees and manages
is broad like this;
that he cannot fail to know what is within it
is a danger like this.
That being so, how then shall the ruler of men know it?
It is said:
Favored attendants and close associates
are the doors, windows, and openings through which the ruler of men observes the distant and gathers the masses;
they must be prepared early.
Therefore, the ruler of men must have favored attendants and close associates who are worthy of trust
before it is acceptable;
their wisdom and intelligence must be sufficient to allow them to plan matters,
and their uprightness and sincerity must be sufficient to allow them to settle matters
before it is acceptable.
This is called the "tools of the state."
The ruler of men cannot avoid having times of leisure and rest,
nor can he avoid the changes brought by illness or death.
In such a case,
in the state,
the arrival of affairs and matters is like a bubbling spring;
if a single matter is not responded to,
it is the beginning of chaos.
Thus it is said:
The ruler of men cannot act alone.
High ministers and assisting counselors
are the foundation and the staff of the ruler of men;
they must be prepared early.
The ruler of men must have high ministers and assisting counselors who are worthy of their responsibilities
before it is acceptable;
their virtuous reputation must be sufficient to soothe and pacify the common people,
and their wisdom and deliberation must be sufficient to respond to and deal with ten thousand changes
before it is acceptable.
This is called the "tools of the state."
In the interactions between the feudal lords of the four neighbors,
they cannot fail to have contact with one another,
yet they are not necessarily close to one another.
Therefore, the ruler of men must have those who are capable of conveying his will and resolving doubts in distant places
before it is acceptable.
Their eloquence must be sufficient to untangle complications;
their wisdom and deliberation must be sufficient to resolve doubts;
their decisiveness must be sufficient to repel difficulties;
they must not return to private interests
nor turn against the lord;
and yet in responding to aggression and warding off disasters,
they must be sufficient to maintain the altars of soil and grain
before it is acceptable.
This is called the "tools of the state."
Therefore, for a ruler of men to lack favored attendants and close associates worthy of trust
is called "benightedness."
To lack high ministers and assisting counselors worthy of their responsibilities
is called "solitariness."
For those sent to the feudal lords of the four neighbors to not be the right men
is called "isolation."
To be isolated, solitary, and benighted
is called "peril."
Although the state may seem to exist,
the people of old would say it is lost.
The Shī says:
"Numerous are the many officers,
and by them Wén Wáng is at peace."
This is what this means.
As for the talents of men:
Those who are honest, cautious, and meticulous,
and who are frugal and precise in their calculations
without daring to lose or omit anything,
these are the talents for officials, scribes, and clerks.
Those who cultivate themselves and are upright,
who honor the laws and respect their duties
without having an unstable heart,
who maintain their offices and follow their professions
without daring to decrease or increase anything,
and who can be passed down through generations
without being subject to usurpation or seizure,
these are the talents for shì dà fū and heads of offices.
Those who know that exalting ritual and righteousness is how to honor the lord,
who know that loving officers is how to achieve a fine reputation,
who know that loving the people is how to stabilize the state,
who know that having constant laws is how to unify customs,
who know that honoring the worthy and employing the capable is how to grow achievements,
who know that attending to the fundamental and prohibiting the incidental is how to increase wealth,
who know that not competing with those below for small profits is beneficial to affairs,
and who know that clarifying systems
and weighing things according to their use is how to avoid being obstructed—
these are the talents for high ministers and assisting counselors,
but they have not yet reached the Way of the lord.
To be able to evaluate and appoint these three types of talents without losing their proper order
is what is called the Way of the ruler of men.
If it is like this, then the person is at ease and the state is well-governed;
achievements are great and the reputation is fine;
above, one can be a Wáng;
below, one can be a Bà;
this is the essential duty of the ruler of men.
If the ruler of men cannot evaluate these three types of talents
and does not know this Way,
he will then lower his status and exert himself,
setting aside the pleasures of the ears and eyes
to personally spend his days in detailed governance,
managing every detail in a single day,
worrying and competing with subordinates over small observations and exhausting his partial abilities;
from ancient times until now,
there has never been one like this who did not end in chaos.
This is what is meant by: "Looking for what cannot be seen,
listening for what cannot be heard,
and attempting what cannot be accomplished."
This is what this means.
As for the classification of ministers:
There are compliant ministers,
there are usurping ministers,
there are meritorious ministers,
and there are sagely ministers.
—Internally, they are insufficient to unify the people;
externally, they are insufficient to repel difficulties.
The common people are not close to them,
and the feudal lords do not trust them.
However, they are clever, quick, and flattering in speech,
and are good at winning favor from above.
These are the compliant ministers.
They are not loyal to the lord above,
but are good at gaining a reputation among the people below;
they do not care for the public Way or common justice,
they form factions and cliques,
and make it their business to surround the lord and plot for their private interests.
These are the usurping ministers.
Internally, they are sufficient to unify the people;
externally, they are sufficient to repel difficulties.
The people are close to them,
and the officers trust them.
They are loyal to the lord above
and love the common people below without wearying.
These are the meritorious ministers.
Above, they are able to honor the lord;
below, they are able to love the people.
In government orders and transformation through teaching,
they take shape below like a shadow.
In responding to the sudden and meeting with changes,
they are prompt like an echo.
Extending categories and receiving praise,
they deal with the boundless;
they complete every detail and establish the forms.
These are the sagely ministers.
Therefore, he who employs sagely ministers becomes a Wáng;
he who employs meritorious ministers becomes strong;
he who employs usurping ministers is endangered;
he who employs compliant ministers perishes.
If compliant ministers are used, there will surely be death;
if usurping ministers are used, there will surely be danger;
if meritorious ministers are used, there will surely be glory;
if sagely ministers are used, there will surely be honor.
Thus, Sū Qín of Qí,
the Zhōu Hóu of Chǔ, and
Zhāng Yí of Qín
may be called compliant ministers.
Zhāng Qùjí of Hán,
Fèngyáng of Zhào, and
Mèngcháng of Qí
may be called usurping ministers.
Guǎn Zhòng of Qí,
Jiù Fàn of Jìn,
Sūnshū Áo of Chǔ—
these may be called meritorious ministers.
Yī Yǐn of Yīn and
Tài Gōng of Zhōu
may be called sagely ministers.
This is the discourse on the ministers of men;
it is the ultimate standard for good and bad fortune, and for the worthy and the unworthy.
One must carefully record this
and cautiously select from it for oneself;
it is sufficient for examination.
Following orders and benefiting the ruler is called accordance;
following orders but not benefiting the ruler is called flattery.
Opposing orders and benefiting the ruler is called loyalty;
opposing orders and not benefiting the ruler is called usurpation.
Disregarding the ruler's honor or disgrace,
disregarding the state's success or failure,
and merely seeking to please and accommodate in order to maintain one's salary and cultivate social ties—
this is called being a traitor to the state.
When the ruler has flawed plans or flawed actions
that pose a fear of endangering the state and ruining the altars of soil and grain,
if a high official, a father, a son, or a
brother is able to offer advice to the ruler:
if it is used, he stays;
if not used, he leaves—
this is called remonstrance.
If one is able to offer advice to the ruler:
if it is used, he stays;
if not used, he dies—
this is called contention.
If one is able to unite those of like mind and collective strength,
and lead the various ministers and hundred officials to together strengthen and straighten the ruler,
though the ruler may be uneasy,
he cannot but listen,
thereby resolving the state's great calamities
and removing the state's great harms,
resulting in the honoring of the ruler and the securing of the state—
this is called assistance.
If one is able to resist the ruler's orders,
appropriate the ruler's authority,
and reverse the ruler's actions
to secure the state from danger
and remove the ruler's disgrace,
so that his achievements and merits are sufficient to accomplish the state's great benefit—
this is called rectification.
Therefore, those who provide remonstrance, contention, assistance, and rectification
are ministers of the altars of soil and grain
and treasures to the state's ruler,
whom an enlightened ruler honors and treats generously.
However, a benighted lord is confused by them, regarding them as his own enemies.
Thus, what an enlightened ruler rewards
is what a benighted ruler punishes;
what a benighted ruler rewards
is what an enlightened ruler executes.
Yī Yǐn and Jī Zǐ may be said to have remonstrated;
Bǐ Gān and
Zǐ Xū may be said to have contended;
the role of Píngyuán Jūn in Zhào may be called assistance;
the role of Xìnlíng Jūn in Wèi may be called rectification.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Follow the Way, not the ruler."
This is what is meant.
Therefore, when righteous ministers are established,
the court is not biased;
when people who provide remonstrance, contention, assistance, and rectification are trusted,
the ruler's errors do not go far;
when men of "claws and teeth" are deployed,
enemies do not arise;
when ministers of the borders are in place,
the frontiers are not lost.
Thus, an enlightened ruler loves consensus, while a benighted ruler loves solitude.
An enlightened ruler honors the worthy and employs the capable, enjoying their abundance;
a benighted ruler envies the worthy and fears the capable, destroying their achievements.
He punishes their loyalty
and rewards their traitors;
this is called supreme benightedness,
and it is the reason why Jié and Zhòu were destroyed.
When serving a sagely ruler,
there is listening and following, but no remonstrance or contention;
when serving an average ruler,
there is remonstrance and contention, but no flattery or sycophancy;
when serving a tyrannical ruler,
there is mending and trimming, but no straightening or rectification.
When coerced during times of chaos
or living in a tyrannical state
with no way to avoid it,
then exalt his beauty,
publicize his goodness,
bypass his evils,
conceal his failures,
speak of his strengths,
and do not mention his shortcomings,
making this a custom.
The *Shī* says:
"The state has a great charge,
which cannot be told to others;
protect one's own person."
This is what is meant.
Being respectful and yielding,
listening and following with agility,
not daring to make personal decisions or choices,
and not daring to personally take or give,
with the intent of according with the superior—
this is the duty of serving a sagely ruler.
Being loyal and trustworthy without sycophancy,
remonstrating and contending without flattery,
being upright and firm, with a direct will and no leaning or crooked heart,
saying what is right is right
and what is wrong is wrong—
this is the duty of serving an average ruler.
Being harmonious but not drifting,
being soft but not yielding,
being tolerant without disorder,
clearly illuminating the ultimate Way so that nothing is not harmonized,
and being able to effect transformation and change,
occasionally finding opportunity to bring him into the Way—
this is the duty of serving a tyrannical ruler.
It is like driving an unbroken horse,
like nurturing an infant,
or like feeding a starving person.
Thus, use his fear to correct his errors;
use his worry to distinguish the causes;
use his joy to lead him into the Way;
use his anger to remove his resentment;
in every turn, achieve what is intended.
The *Shū* says:
"Following orders without opposing,
subtly remonstrating without tiring;
if a superior, be enlightened;
if a subordinate, be yielding."
This is what is meant.
Those who serve others but are not accordant
are those who are not diligent;
those who are diligent but not accordant
are those who are not respectful;
those who are respectful but not accordant
are those who are not loyal;
those who are loyal but not accordant
are those without merit;
those with merit but not accordant
are those without virtue.
Thus, the way of those without virtue
harms diligence, ruins merit, and wastes toil;
therefore, the gentleman does not do it.
There is great loyalty,
there is secondary loyalty,
there is lower loyalty,
and there are traitors to the state.
Restoring the ruler with virtue and transforming him
is great loyalty;
harmonizing the ruler with virtue and supplementing him
is secondary loyalty;
using what is right to remonstrate against what is wrong and angering him
is lower loyalty;
disregarding the ruler's honor or disgrace,
disregarding the state's success or failure,
and merely seeking to please and accommodate in order to maintain one's salary and cultivate social ties—
this is being a traitor to the state.
The case of Zhōu Gōng regarding King Chéng
may be called great loyalty;
the case of Guǎn Zhòng regarding Duke Huán
may be called secondary loyalty;
the case of Zǐ Xū regarding Fū Chāi
may be called lower loyalty;
the case of Cáo Chùlóng regarding Zhòu
may be called a traitor to the state.
A humane person must respect others.
If an ordinary person is not worthy,
then they are unworthy.
To not respect a person who is worthy
is to be like a beast;
to not respect a person who is unworthy
is like playing with a tiger.
Being a beast leads to chaos;
playing with a tiger leads to danger;
calamity will befall one's person.
The *Shī* says:
"Dare not face a tiger unarmed,
dare not cross a river without a boat.
People know the one,
but no one knows the other.
Fearful and trembling, as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice."
This is what is meant.
Therefore, a humane person must respect others.
There is a way to respect others:
for the worthy, honor and respect them;
for the unworthy, fear and respect them;
for the worthy, be close to and respect them;
for the unworthy, be distant from and respect them.
Their respect is one,
their feelings are twofold.
As for loyalty, trustworthiness, uprightness, and sincerity without causing harm,
then in every encounter it is thus;
this is the substance of a person of Rén.
Taking loyalty and trustworthiness as substance,
uprightness and sincerity as the guiding principle,
ritual and righteousness as the external refinement,
moral relations and categories as the inner logic,
even a breath or a word,
a slight movement or action,
everything can serve as a model.
The Shī says:
“Neither excessive nor harmful,
few fail to take you as a model.”
This is what it refers to.
Reverence and respect are ritual;
harmony and moderation are music;
prudence is beneficial;
fighting and anger are harmful.
Therefore the Jūnzǐ finds peace in ritual and finds joy in music,
is prudent and avoids fighting and anger;
thus in a hundred actions he does not err.
The small man is the opposite of this.
The smoothness of pervasive loyalty,
the balancing of perilous contingencies,
the sounds that follow disaster and chaos—
these three, none but an enlightened ruler can know them.
To contend and only then be good,
to oppose and only then achieve merit,
to face death without selfishness,
to achieve loyalty and be public-minded—
this is called the smoothness of pervasive loyalty,
Xìnlíng Jūn was like this.
To seize and only then be righteous,
to kill and only then be benevolent,
to exchange positions of high and low and only then be upright,
with merit equal to Heaven and Earth,
and bounty covering the living people—
this is called the balancing of perilous contingencies;
Tāng and Wǔ are examples.
To err yet satisfy feelings,
to be harmonious without constant principles,
not caring about right or wrong,
not regulating the crooked or the straight,
seeking illicit agreement and improper tolerance,
living wildly in confusion and madness—
this is called the sounds that follow disaster and chaos;
Fēilián and Èlái are examples.
The Chuán says:
“To cut yet be uniform,
to be bent yet compliant,
to be different yet unified.”
The Shī says:
“Receiving the small jade and the large jade,
serving as the tassel for the states below.”
This is what it refers to.
Impartial listening,
revealing the hidden,
doubling brightness,
and the technique for dismissing the wicked and promoting the good:
praise from cliques and factions,
the Jūnzǐ does not listen to;
slander from those who are cruel and harmful,
the Jūnzǐ does not act upon;
people who are secretive, jealous, or obstructive,
the Jūnzǐ does not keep close;
requests involving goods, wealth, or bribes of livestock,
the Jūnzǐ does not grant.
All rumors,
unfounded talk,
unverified events,
floating schemes,
unfounded praise, and unfounded accusations,
that arrive without official channels yet reach the ruler directly—
the Jūnzǐ is cautious of them.
When hearing of them, he clearly evaluates them,
determining what is appropriate as appropriate,
only then does he issue punishments and rewards to return to them;
in this way,
wicked words,
wicked talk,
wicked events,
wicked schemes,
wicked praise, and wicked accusations
none will be attempted;
loyal words,
loyal talk,
loyal events,
loyal schemes,
loyal praise, and loyal accusations will all be clearly communicated,
rising from all directions and being fully expressed.
This is called impartial listening,
revealing the hidden,
doubling brightness,
and the technique for dismissing the wicked and promoting the good.
When streams and pools are deep, fish and turtles return to them;
when mountains and forests are lush, birds and beasts return to them;
when punishments and governance are fair, the hundred surnames return to them;
when ritual and righteousness are complete, gentlemen return to them.
Therefore, when ritual reaches the person, their conduct is cultivated;
when righteousness reaches the state, its governance is enlightened;
being able to hold fast to ritual, one’s noble name becomes clear;
the whole world desires them,
orders are followed and prohibitions are obeyed,
and the work of a true King is complete.
The Shī says:
“Be kind to this central state,
to bring peace to the four quarters.”
This is what it refers to.
Streams and pools are the dwelling places of dragons and fish;
mountains and forests are the dwelling places of birds and beasts;
states are the dwelling places of scholars and people.
When streams and pools dry up,
dragons and fish leave them;
when mountains and forests are desolate,
then birds and beasts leave them;
when a state loses good governance, then scholars and people leave it.
Without land, the people cannot dwell in peace;
without people, the land cannot be defended;
without the Way and the law, people will not come;
without the Jūnzǐ, the Way will not be upheld.
Therefore, land and people,
the Way and the law,
are the fundamental basis of the state.
As for the Jūnzǐ,
he is the summary essential of the Way and the law,
and cannot be absent for even a brief moment.
Having him, there is order;
losing him, there is chaos;
having him, there is security;
losing him, there is peril;
having him, there is survival;
losing him, there is ruin.
Thus, there have been cases of having good laws yet having chaos;
but having a Jūnzǐ yet having chaos,
from ancient times until now,
has never been heard of.
The Chuán says:
“Order arises from the Jūnzǐ,
chaos arises from the small man.”
This is what it refers to.
Gaining the masses moves Heaven.
Fine intentions prolong one’s years.
Sincerity and trustworthiness are like the spirits.
Boastful exaggeration chases away the soul.
The trouble for a ruler of men
is not in speaking of employing the worthy,
but in not being sincere about definitely employing the worthy.
Now, speaking of employing the worthy
is done with the mouth,
but rejecting the worthy
is done with actions.
When mouth and actions are contrary,
yet one desires the worthy to arrive
and the unworthy to withdraw,
is that not difficult!
Now, those who dazzle cicadas
must focus on making their fire bright
and shaking the tree, and that is all.
If the fire is not bright,
even if they shake the tree,
it is of no use.
Now, if a ruler of men can make his virtue bright, then the world will return to him,
just as cicadas return to a bright fire.
In approaching affairs and dealing with the people,
one uses righteousness; in responding to changes,
one is broad and tolerant;
using reverence and respect to lead them—
this is the beginning of governance.
Then, using moderation, harmony, and discerning judgment to assist it—
this is the flourishing of governance.
Then, promoting and demoting, punishing and rewarding—
this is the completion of governance.
Therefore, in the first year one gives them the beginning,
and in the third year one gives them the completion.
If one uses the completion as the beginning,
then government orders will not be carried out,
and high and low will feel resentment and hatred;
this is how chaos creates itself.
The Shū says:
“Righteous punishment and righteous execution,
do not use them to approach the people immediately;
you should only say,
‘There have not yet been compliant affairs.’”
This speaks of putting instruction first.
Standards are the yardsticks of things;
ritual is the yardstick of regulation.
Standards are used to establish quantities;
ritual is used to fix social relations;
virtue is used to order status;
and ability is used to confer office.
In all things, the rhythms should be lofty
and the common people should be treated with leniency.
When rhythms are lofty, there is refinement;
when the common people are treated with leniency, there is peace.
Refinement above and peace below
is the pinnacle of achievement and fame;
nothing can be added to it.
The ruler is the eminence of the state;
the father is the eminence of the family.
When eminence is singular, there is order;
when dual, there is chaos.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a case where two eminences vied for weight
and were able to endure for long.
There are four methods for being a teacher, and broad learning is not among them:
Being dignified and inspiring awe—
one can be a teacher;
being of advanced age and trustworthy—
one can be a teacher;
reciting and explaining without violation or offense—
one can be a teacher;
knowing the subtle and being able to discourse upon it—
one can be a teacher.
Thus, there are four methods for being a teacher, and broad learning is not among them.
When water is deep, it swirls;
when trees shed leaves, they fertilize the roots;
when disciples achieve success, they think of their teacher.
The *Shī* says:
"No word goes unanswered,
no virtue goes unrequited."
This refers to that.
Rewards should not be excessive,
and punishments should not be indiscriminate.
If rewards are excessive, the benefit reaches the *xiǎorén*;
if punishments are indiscriminate, the harm reaches the *jūnzǐ*.
If, by misfortune, one errs,
it is better to be excessive than indiscriminate;
rather than harming the good,
it is better to benefit the licentious.
*Línwǔ Jūn* and *Sūn Qīng Zǐ* discussed military affairs before King *Xiàochéng* of *Zhào*.
The King said:
"I venture to ask about the essentials of military affairs."
*Línwǔ Jūn* replied:
"Above, obtaining the seasons of heaven;
below, obtaining the advantages of the earth;
observing the movements of the enemy;
setting out after them
but arriving before them—
this is the essential art of using the military."
*Sūn Qīng Zǐ* said:
"Not so.
What I have heard of the Way of the ancients
is that the root of all military use and offensive warfare
lies in unifying the people.
If the bow and arrow are not tuned,
then *Yì* cannot hit the subtle mark;
if the six horses are not in harmony,
then *Zào Fù* cannot reach the distant goal;
if the officers and people are not close and attached,
then *Tāng* and *Wǔ* could not be certain of victory.
Therefore, one who is good at attaching the people
is one who is good at using the military.
Thus, the essential of the military lies in nothing more than attaching the people."
*Línwǔ Jūn* said:
"Not so.
What is valued in military affairs is strategic advantage and profit;
what is practiced is deception and surprise.
Those good at using the military
are sudden and obscure,
so that no one knows from where they emerge.
*Sūn* and *Wú* used this and were peerless in the world.
Why must one wait for the attachment of the people?"
*Sūn Qīng Zǐ* said:
"Not so.
What I speak of
is the military of the benevolent man
and the intent of a true king.
What you value
are schemes, power, and profit;
what you practice—
attacks, seizures, and deceptions—
are the affairs of the feudal lords.
The military of the benevolent man
cannot be deceived.
Those who can be deceived
are the negligent,
the weary,
and those among whom—between ruler and subject, superior and inferior—
virtue is dissipated and divided.
Therefore, using *Jié* to deceive *Jié*
is like a contest of skill and clumsiness where there is still luck.
Using *Jié* to deceive *Yáo*
is comparable
to throwing an egg against a rock,
to stirring boiling water with a finger,
or to jumping into water or fire—
upon entry, one is scorched or drowned.
Therefore, among the superiors and inferiors of the benevolent man,
the hundred generals have one heart
and the three armies share their strength.
The relation of subject to ruler
and inferior to superior
is like a son serving his father
or a younger brother serving his elder brother;
it is like the arms and hands protecting the head and eyes and covering the chest and abdomen.
To deceive and surprise them
or to first startle them and then attack them
is one and the same.
Furthermore, if a benevolent man employs a state of ten *lǐ*,
he will have the intelligence of a hundred *lǐ*;
if he employs a state of a hundred *lǐ*,
he will have the intelligence of a thousand *lǐ*;
if he employs a state of a thousand *lǐ*,
then he will have the intelligence of the Four Seas.
He will surely be perceptive and vigilant, and his people will be harmonious and unified.
Therefore, the military of a benevolent man,
when gathered, forms a phalanx;
when dispersed, forms ranks.
When extended, it is like the long blade of *Mòyé*—
whoever touches it is cut.
When pointed, it is like the sharp tip of *Mòyé*—
whoever faces it is shattered.
When stationed in a circle and oriented in a square,
it is like a massive boulder—
whoever strikes it will have their horns broken,
and then they will
collapse,
stumble, and retreat in disarray.
Furthermore, with whom will the ruler of a violent state
come to battle?
Those he comes with
must be his people.
But those people feel as close to me as to their parents;
their love for me is as fragrant as pepper and orchid.
When they look back at their own superiors,
it is as if looking at a brand or tattoo,
or at a mortal enemy.
In human nature,
even if one were a *Jié* or a *Zhí*,
how could they be willing to act for the sake of those they hate
and harm those they love?
This is like ordering the children and grandchildren of others to harm their own parents.
They will surely come and report it;
how then can they be deceived?
Therefore, when a benevolent man is employed, the state becomes more brilliant daily.
Among the feudal lords, those who submit first will be safe,
those who submit later will be in danger,
those who contemplate opposing him will be weakened,
and those who rebel against him will perish.
The *Shī* says:
"King *Wǔ* set forth,
reverently grasping the battle-axe;
like a blazing fire,
none dared to stop him."
This refers to that."
King *Xiàochéng* and *Línwǔ Jūn* said:
"Excellent!
We venture to ask, for the military of a true king,
what Way should be established? What conduct is appropriate?"
*Sūn Qīng Zǐ* said:
"For Your Majesty,
generals and commanders are secondary matters.
I beg to proceed to speak of the outcomes of strength and weakness, survival and ruin,
and the conditions of safety and danger for true kings and feudal lords.
When the ruler is worthy, his state is ordered;
when the ruler is incapable, his state is in chaos.
When ritual is exalted and righteousness valued, the state is ordered;
when ritual is neglected and righteousness disparaged, the state is in chaos.
The ordered are strong;
the chaotic are weak.
This is the root of strength and weakness.
When the superiors are worthy of looking up to, then the inferiors can be employed;
when the superiors are not worthy of looking up to, then the inferiors cannot be employed.
When the inferiors can be employed, there is strength;
when the inferiors cannot be employed, there is weakness.
This is the constant rule of strength and weakness.
Exalting ritual and making achievements effective
is the highest;
valuing emoluments and honoring integrity
is the next;
exalting achievement and disparaging integrity
is the lowest.
This is the general outline of strength and weakness.
Those who love scholars are strong;
those who do not love scholars are weak.
Those who love the people are strong;
those who do not love the people are weak.
Those whose government orders are trusted are strong;
those whose government orders are not trusted are weak.
Those whose people are unified are strong;
those whose people are not unified are weak.
Those whose rewards are substantial are strong;
those whose rewards are light are weak.
Those whose punishments are awesome are strong;
those whose punishments are scorned are weak.
Those whose tools, weapons, and armor are well-maintained and convenient are strong;
those whose tools, weapons, and armor are shoddy, of poor quality, and inconvenient are weak.
Those who take the use of troops seriously are strong;
those who take the use of troops lightly are weak.
Those whose authority comes from a single source are strong;
those whose authority comes from two sources are weak.
These are the constants of strength and weakness.
"The people of Qí prize the *Jìjī*;
in their skills,
those who take a single head
are granted a reward in *zī* of gold,
yet there are no fundamental rewards.
In small matters against a brittle enemy
they may be used stealthily,
but in great matters against a firm enemy
they scatter and desert.
Like flying birds,
shifting and turning back and forth without a fixed day,
these are the troops of a doomed state;
no army is weaker than this.
It is nearly equivalent to hiring laborers from the market to fight.
"The *Wǔzù* of the Wèi clan
are selected by measurement.
They wear triple-layered armor,
handle a crossbow of twelve *shí*,
carry a quiver of fifty arrows,
place a dagger-axe on their backs,
wear a helmet and carry a sword,
bring three days' rations,
and march one hundred *lǐ* by midday.
Once they pass the test, their households are exempted from labor tax,
and they are given favorable fields and residences.
Thus, their spirit and strength decline after several years,
yet their benefits cannot be taken away.
To replace them is not easy to do thoroughly.
Therefore, although the land is large,
the tax revenue is inevitably meager.
These are the troops of a state in peril.
As for the people of Qín, in their daily lives they are constrained and hard-pressed,
and their employment of the people is harsh and fierce.
They intimidate them with authority,
burden them with hardships,
habituate them with rewards,
and drive them with punishments.
They make it so that the people of the world,
in order to seek profit from the superior,
have no means other than combat.
They are constrained and then used;
only after achieving results are they credited with merit.
Merit and rewards grow together.
Taking five heads of armored soldiers earns five families as slaves.
This is the most numerous, strong, and long-lasting;
they take much land to rectify themselves.
Thus, for four generations they have had victory;
it is not luck,
it is calculated necessity.
"Therefore, the *Jìjī* of Qí
cannot face the *Wǔzù* of the Wèi clan.
The *Wǔzù* of the Wèi clan
cannot face the *Ruìshì* of Qín.
The *Ruìshì* of Qín
cannot withstand the discipline of Huán and Wén.
The discipline of Huán and Wén
cannot rival the benevolence and righteousness of Tāng and Wǔ.
If they were to encounter them,
it would be like throwing a stone at scorched grain.
Considering these several states,
all their troops seek rewards and chase profit;
they follow the way of hired laborers and selling service.
They do not yet have the principle of honoring the superior, being at peace with the system, and reaching the peak of discipline.
If a feudal lord were able to subtly refine them with discipline,
then he could rise up and annex them all.
Therefore, recruiting from nearby and selecting through muster,
exalting power and deception,
and valuing merit and profit
are ways of leading them gradually;
ritual, righteousness, and education
are ways of unifying them.
Thus, meeting deception with deception
is still a matter of skill versus clumsiness;
meeting unity with deception
is like trying to topple a great mountain with an awl or a knife;
none but the most foolish in the world would dare try.
Therefore, the army of a King does not need to be tested.
When Tāng and Wǔ executed Jié and Zhòu,
they merely folded their hands, bowed, and pointed,
and there were no violent states that did not rush to serve them.
Executing Jié and Zhòu was like executing a lone man.
Thus the *Tàishì* says,
'The lone man Zhòu';
this refers to that.
Therefore, if the army is greatly unified, it controls the world;
if slightly unified, it governs its neighbors.
As for recruiting from nearby and selecting through muster,
exalting power and deception,
and valuing merit and profit,
then victory or defeat is not constant;
they expand and contract by turns,
they survive and perish by turns,
they merely compete for dominance.
These are called 'troops of bandits,'
and a gentleman does not follow this way.
"Therefore, Tián Dān of Qí,
Zhuāng Qiǎo of Chǔ,
Wèi Yāng of Qín,
Miù Jǐ of Yān—
these are all whom the world considers good at using troops.
In their skill or clumsiness, strength or weakness,
there is nothing to distinguish them as a ruler.
Their ways are essentially one;
they have not reached harmony and unity.
Relying on deception,
stratagems and subversion,
they cannot avoid being 'troops of bandits.'
Huán of Qí, Wén of Jìn, Zhuāng of Chǔ, Hélǘ of Wú, and Gòujiàn of Yuè—these all had harmonious and unified troops.
They can be said to have entered the realm,
but they did not have the fundamental thread.
Thus they could become hegemons but not Kings.
This is the result of strength and weakness."
King Xiàochéng and the Lord of Línwǔ said:
"Excellent!
May we ask about being a general?"
Sūn Qīng Zǐ said:
"In wisdom, none is greater than discarding doubt;
in conduct, none is greater than being without fault;
in affairs, none is greater than being without regret.
When an affair reaches the point of no regret, it is enough;
success cannot be made certain.
Therefore, in issuing titles and government orders, one wishes to be strict and awe-inspiring;
in rewards and punishments, one wishes to be certain and trustworthy;
in encampment and storage, one wishes to be thorough and secure;
in movements and advances or retreats, one wishes to be stable and heavy,
yet also swift and fast.
In spying on the enemy and observing changes, one wishes to be hidden and deep,
and to use various methods of observation.
In meeting the enemy and deciding battle, one must follow what is clear to oneself,
and not follow what is doubtful to oneself.
These are called the 'Six Arts.'
Do not desire to be a general and yet loathe being dismissed;
do not be hasty for victory and forget about defeat;
do not overawe the internal and slight the external;
do not see the benefit and ignore the harm.
In all considerations, one wishes for thoroughness; in the use of wealth, one wishes for abundance.
These are called the 'Five Weights.'
There are three cases where a general does not receive orders from the ruler:
he may be killed but cannot be made to occupy an unsecure position;
he may be killed but cannot be made to attack without victory;
he may be killed but cannot be made to deceive the common people.
These are called the 'Three Ultimates.'
Whenever one receives orders from the ruler and leads the three armies,
once the three armies are settled,
the officials are in order,
and all things are rectified,
then the ruler cannot make him happy,
and the enemy cannot make him angry.
This is called the 'Ultimate Minister.'
One must deliberate before the event
and reinforce it with respect.
Be as cautious at the end as at the beginning,
and let end and beginning be as one.
This is called 'Great Good Fortune.'
In all the successes of a hundred affairs,
they must lie in respect;
in their failures,
they must lie in negligence.
Therefore, when respect overcomes indolence, there is good fortune;
when indolence overcomes respect, there is destruction.
When planning overcomes desire, things follow;
when desire overcomes planning, there is disaster.
Fight as if defending;
march as if fighting;
treat success as if it were luck.
Be respectful in planning without neglect.
Be respectful in affairs without neglect;
be respectful of the end without neglect;
be respectful of the masses without neglect;
be respectful of the enemy without neglect.
These are called the 'Five Non-Neglects.'
If one carefully practices these six arts, five weights, and three ultimates,
and handles them with reverence, respect, and non-neglect,
then he is called a 'General of the World,'
and he communicates with the divine brilliance."
Línwǔ Jūn said:
“Excellent!
May I ask about the military system of a true king?”
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
“The general dies by his drum,
the driver dies by his reins,
the many officials die by their duties,
and the officers and men die in their ranks.
At the sound of the drum, they advance;
at the sound of the gong, they retreat.
Obeying orders is paramount;
achieving merit is secondary.
To advance when ordered not to advance
is like retreating when ordered not to retreat;
their crimes are equal.
They do not kill the old or the weak,
nor do they trample the crops;
those who submit are not taken captive,
those who resist are not spared,
and those who flee for their lives are not pursued.
All executions
are not of the common people,
but of those who bring chaos to the common people.
If the common people defend their oppressors,
then they too are oppressors.
For this reason, those who follow the blade survive,
those who oppose the blade die,
and those who flee for their lives are allowed to submit.
Wēizi was enfeoffed in Sòng,
and Cáo Chùlóng was executed in the army;
the submissive people of Yīn
were provided with the means of livelihood
no differently from the people of Zhōu.
Thus, those nearby sing and rejoice in them,
while those far away stumble and rush toward them.
No matter how secluded or remote a state may be,
none fail to hasten to serve and find peace and joy in them.
Within the Four Seas, it is like one family;
all who can be reached follow and submit.
This is called being a teacher of men.
The *Shī* says:
‘From the west and from the east,
from the south and from the north,
there was not a thought but of submission.’
This is what it refers to.
A true king carries out punitive executions but does not wage war;
city walls are held but not attacked,
and soldiers resist but are not struck.
If superiors and subordinates are pleased with each other, he congratulates them.
He does not massacre cities,
does not use a hidden army,
does not detain the masses,
and the army does not exceed its season.
Therefore, those in chaos delight in his governance,
find no peace under their own superiors,
and desire his arrival.”
Línwǔ Jūn said:
“Excellent!”
Chén Xiāo asked Sūnqīng Zǐ, saying:
“Master, in your discussions on military affairs,
you always take benevolence and righteousness as the foundation.
One who is benevolent loves others;
one who is righteous follows principle;
why then use an army at all?
All reasons for having an army
are for contention and seizure.”
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
“It is not as you understand it.
The benevolent man loves others;
because he loves others, he hates those who harm them.
The righteous man follows principle;
because he follows principle, he hates those who bring chaos to it.
An army is the means to prohibit violence and eliminate harm,
not for contention and seizure.
Therefore, when the army of a benevolent man
stays, it is divine;
where it passes, it transforms;
like the falling of timely rain,
none fail to be delighted and joyful.
Thus, Yáo attacked Huāndōu,
Shùn attacked Yǒumiáo,
Yǔ attacked Gònggōng,
Tāng attacked Yǒuxià,
Wén Wáng attacked Chóng,
and Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu.
These four emperors and two kings
all used the army of benevolence and righteousness
to act throughout the world.
Therefore, those nearby were close to their goodness,
and those far away longed for their righteousness.
Their weapons did not have to be bloodied,
yet those far and near came to submit.
Virtue reached its peak here,
extending to the four poles.
The *Shī* says:
‘The virtuous and gentlemanly man,
his demeanour is without flaw.’
This is what it refers to.”
Lǐ Sī asked Sūnqīng Zǐ, saying:
“Qín has been victorious for four generations;
its army is the strongest within the seas,
and its majesty prevails among the feudal lords.
This was not done through benevolence and righteousness,
but merely by acting according to expediency.”
Sūnqīng Zǐ said:
“It is not as you understand it.
What you call expediency
is the expediency of the inexpedient;
what I call benevolence and righteousness
is the expediency of the great expediency.
Now, benevolence and righteousness
are the means to cultivate governance.
When governance is cultivated, the people are close to their superiors,
delight in their ruler,
and think lightly of dying for him.
Therefore it is said:
‘In all matters of the army,
generals and commanders are secondary matters.’
Qín has been victorious for four generations,
yet it is constantly fearful and anxious that the world will unite and crush it.
This is what is called the army of a degenerate age,
which has no fundamental thread of unity.
Thus, when Tāng banished Jié,
it was not only at the time he pursued him to Míngtiáo;
when Wǔ Wáng executed Zhòu,
it was not only after the victory on the morning of Jiǎzǐ.
Both were the result of previous conduct and constant cultivation.
This is what is called the army of benevolence and righteousness.
Now you do not seek it in the root
but search for it in the branches;
this is why the world is in chaos.”
Ritual is the ultimate standard for governance and distinction,
the foundation of a strong state,
the way for majesty to prevail,
and the summation of merit and fame.
Kings and dukes who follow it are the ones who gain the world;
those who do not follow it are the ones who lose their altars of soil and grain.
Therefore, strong armor and sharp weapons are not enough to be considered martial;
high walls and deep moats are not enough to be considered secure;
strict orders and numerous punishments are not enough to be considered majestic.
If one follows the proper Way, one will succeed;
if one does not follow the proper Way, one will fail.
The people of Chǔ used shark skin and rhinoceros hide for armor,
as hard as metal or stone.
Their iron spear-heads from Wǎn and Jù
were as painful as the stings of bees or scorpions.
Light, sharp, agile, and swift,
their soldiers were like a whirlwind.
Yet their army was endangered at Chuíshā,
and Táng Miè died.
Zhuāng Qiǎo rose in rebellion,
and Chǔ was divided into three or four.
Was this because they lacked strong armor or sharp weapons?
It was because the means by which they were unified was not the proper Way.
They took the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers as their defenses,
and the Jiāng and Hàn rivers as their moats;
they bounded themselves with the forests of Dèng
and enclosed themselves with the Fāngchéng walls.
Yet when the Qín army arrived,
Yān and Yǐng were taken
as easily as shaking down dry leaves.
Was this because they lacked secure passes and narrow obstacles?
It was because the means by which they were unified was not the proper Way.
Zhòu disemboweled Bǐ Gān
and imprisoned Jīzi;
he created the punishment of the roasting pillar
and carried out killings at all times.
His ministers lived in terror, none certain of their lives.
Yet when the Zhōu army arrived,
his orders were not followed by those below,
and he could not make use of his people.
Was this because his orders were not strict
or his punishments not numerous?
It was because the means by which they were unified was not the proper Way.
In the armies of old,
there were only halberds, spears, bows, and arrows,
yet enemy states submitted without waiting for a trial of strength.
City walls were not maintained,
moats and ponds were not reinforced,
fortifications were not established,
and mechanical stratagems were not deployed.
Yet the state was peaceful, not fearing external threats, and remained secure.
There was no other reason for this:
they clarified the Way and distributed shares equitably;
they employed the people at the proper times and loved them with sincerity.
Thus, the harmony of those below with those above was like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound.
If there were any who did not follow orders,
only then were they dealt with through punishment.
Therefore, by punishing one person, the whole world submits;
the criminal does not blame his superior,
as he knows the guilt lies within himself.
For this reason, punishments are few yet authority flows like a current;
there is no other reason for this
but that it follows the proper Way.
In ancient times, when Dì Yáo governed the world,
he perhaps killed one person
and punished two others,
and the world was well-ordered.
The *Chuán* says:
"His majesty was severe but not put to the test;
punishments were set aside and not used."
This is what that means.
Generally, when people act,
if they do so only for the sake of rewards and celebrations,
then they will stop when they see harm or injury.
Therefore, rewards, celebrations, punishments, power, and deception
are insufficient to exhaust the people's strength
or lead them to face death.
As for those who are lords and superiors,
if the way they treat their subordinates and the common people
is devoid of ritual, righteousness, loyalty, and trust,
and they only think of leading them through rewards,
punishments,
power, and deception,
or by putting them in dangerous and narrow straits
just to obtain their labor and service,
then when a great enemy arrives,
and they are made to hold a city in peril, they will surely rebel;
if they encounter the enemy in battle, they will surely flee in defeat;
if they face toil, suffering, and vexation, they will surely desert.
Suddenly they will disperse,
and the subordinates will in turn turn against their superiors.
Therefore, using rewards, celebrations, punishments, power, and deception as one's Way
is the way of hired laborers and petty merchants;
it is insufficient to unite the masses
or to make the state and family beautiful.
Thus, the people of old were ashamed of it and did not follow it.
Instead, they prioritized the sound of thick virtue to lead them,
clarified ritual and righteousness to guide them,
attained loyalty and trust to love them,
honored the worthy and employed the capable to rank them,
and used noble ranks, robes, and rewards to encourage them.
They timed their labor,
lightened their burdens
to harmonize and regulate them,
and nurtured them long
as if protecting an infant.
Once government orders were fixed
and customs were unified,
if there were those who deviated from customs and did not follow their superiors,
then the common people would all deeply loathe them
and view them as a poisonous curse,
as if exorcising something inauspicious.
Only then would punishments arise.
When such a great punishment is applied,
what disgrace could be greater?
If one seeks benefit,
yet a great punishment is added to him,
unless the person is truly insane, deluded, stupid, or ignorant,
who could witness this and not reform?
Thereafter, the common people will clearly all know to follow the laws of the superior,
emulate the will of the superior,
and find peace and joy in it.
At that point, if there are those able to be transformed for the better, cultivate themselves, rectify their conduct, accumulate ritual and righteousness, and honor the Way and virtue,
then among the common people there is none who does not value and respect them,
and none who does not feel close to and praise them.
Only then would rewards arise.
When such high rank and abundant emolument are granted,
what glory could be greater?
If one thinks it a harm,
yet high rank and abundant emolument are used to sustain and nurture him,
among the living people,
who would not desire it?
Grandly, noble ranks and heavy rewards are suspended before them,
while clear punishments and great disgrace are suspended behind them.
Even if they did not wish to be transformed,
could they do otherwise?
Therefore, the people return to him like flowing water.
What resides within him is divine,
what he brings about is transformation,
and they follow.
Those of a violent, fierce, and brave nature are transformed to be honest and sincere;
those of a biased, crooked, and selfish nature are transformed to be public-minded;
those of a boastful, contentious, and entangled nature are transformed to be harmonious.
This is called the "Great Transformation and Ultimate Unity."
The *Shī* says:
"The King's plans were truly profound,
and the Xú fāng came to submit."
This is what that means.
Generally, there are three methods for those who would annex others:
there is annexing others through virtue,
there is annexing others through force,
and there is annexing others through wealth.
When they value my reputation
and admire my virtuous conduct,
and desire to be my people,
they open their gates and clear the roads
to welcome my entry.
I then rely on their people
and occupy their places,
and the common people are all at peace.
When laws are established and orders issued,
none fail to follow and comply.
For this reason, as land is gained, power becomes even heavier;
as people are annexed, the military becomes even stronger.
This is annexing others through virtue.
If they do not value my reputation
and do not admire my virtuous conduct,
but instead fear my majesty
and are coerced by my power,
then although the people have hearts for leaving,
they do not dare to have thoughts of rebellion.
If it is like this,
then armor and weapons must be more numerous,
and the costs of maintenance must be high.
For this reason, as land is gained, power becomes even lighter;
as people are annexed, the military becomes even weaker.
This is annexing others through force.
If they do not value my reputation
and do not admire my virtuous conduct,
but use their poverty to seek my wealth,
and use their hunger to seek my fullness,
with empty bellies and open mouths
coming to return to me for food;
if it is like this,
then one must issue grain from the granaries to feed them,
and bestow wealth and goods to enrich them,
and appoint good officials to manage them.
Only after three years
can the people be trusted.
For this reason, as land is gained, power becomes even lighter;
as people are annexed, the state becomes even poorer.
This is annexing others through wealth.
Therefore it is said:
He who annexes others through virtue becomes a King;
he who annexes others through force becomes weak;
he who annexes others through wealth becomes poor.
This is true now as it was in the past.
Annexation is easy to achieve;
it is only consolidation that is difficult.
Qí was able to annex Sòng
but could not consolidate it,
so Wèi took it away.
Yàn was able to annex Qí
but could not consolidate it,
so Tián Dān took it away.
The upper lands of Hàn
were several hundred lǐ square,
complete and prosperous, yet they turned to Zhào.
Zhào could not consolidate them,
so Qín took them away.
Therefore, if one can annex them
but cannot consolidate them,
they will surely be taken away.
If one cannot annex them
and further cannot consolidate what one has,
then one will surely perish.
If one can consolidate them,
then one will surely be able to annex others.
If you obtain something and consolidate it,
no military power can be stronger.
In ancient times, Tāng started with Bó,
and Wǔ wáng started with Hào,
both being lands of a mere hundred lǐ,
yet the world became one,
and the feudal lords became their subjects.
There was no other reason
but that they were able to consolidate them.
Therefore, consolidate the gentlemen through ritual,
and consolidate the people through governance.
When ritual is cultivated, the gentlemen submit;
when governance is fair, the people are at peace.
When the gentlemen submit and the people are at peace,
this is called the "Great Consolidation."
Using this to defend, you will be firm;
using this to campaign, you will be strong.
Orders will be carried out and prohibitions respected;
the affairs of a King will be complete.
When the mold is correct,
the copper and tin are fine,
the craftsman and smith are skillful,
and the firing and alloying are properly attained,
then upon opening the mold, the Mòyé sword is finished.
However, if it is not stripped and cleaned,
and if it is not whetted and sharpened,
then it cannot even cut a rope.
But if it is stripped and cleaned,
and if it is whetted and sharpened,
then it will slice through bronze basins and bowls
or decapitate oxen and horses
in an instant.
As for the state,
it is the fundamental structure of a powerful nation.
However, if it is not taught and instructed,
and if it is not coordinated and unified,
then internally it cannot be defended,
and externally it cannot engage in battle.
If one teaches and instructs it,
and coordinates and unifies it,
then the troops will be strong and the cities firm,
and enemy states will not dare to confront it.
The state also has its means of refinement,
which are ritual, righteousness, and measure.
Therefore, the fate of a person lies in Heaven;
the fate of a state lies in Ritual.
As for the ruler of men:
if he exalts Ritual and honors the worthy, he becomes a King;
if he emphasizes law and loves the people, he becomes a Hegemon;
if he loves profit and is full of deceit, he is in danger;
if he relies on schemes, subversion, and dark treachery, he perishes.
Prestige has three types:
the prestige of Way and Virtue,
the prestige of violence and scrutiny,
and the prestige of madness and arrogance.
These three types of prestige
must be examined carefully.
If ritual and music are cultivated,
if roles and righteousness are clear,
if actions and omissions are timely,
and if love and benefit are manifest:
in this case,
the common people will value him like a Supreme Deity,
exalt him like Heaven,
feel close to him like parents,
and stand in awe of him like the gods.
Therefore, even without the use of rewards, the people are encouraged;
even without the use of punishments, prestige is exercised.
This is what is called the prestige of Way and Virtue.
If ritual and music are not cultivated,
if roles and righteousness are not clear,
if actions and omissions are not timely,
and if love and benefit are not manifest;
however, his prohibition of violence is scrutinizing,
his execution of the disobedient is thorough,
his punishments are heavy and reliable,
and his executions are fierce and certain,
striking suddenly like a thunderclap,
or crushing like a collapsing wall:
in this case,
the common people will be fearful when coerced,
but arrogant toward the superior when relaxed;
they will be submissive when detained,
but scatter when given the chance;
they will be snatched away when the enemy strikes.
Unless one coerces them with power and circumstances,
or shakes them with executions,
there is no way to hold onto the subjects.
This is what is called the prestige of violence and scrutiny.
If there is no heart for loving people,
and no deeds for benefiting people,
but instead daily practices of a way that brings chaos to people,
and when the common people cry out in resentment,
he responds by arresting and binding them,
or punishing and branding them,
failing to harmonize with the hearts of the people:
in this case,
those below will form cliques and flee in panic to distance themselves from the superior;
collapse and destruction
can be expected momentarily.
This is what is called the prestige of madness and arrogance.
These three types of prestige
must be examined carefully.
The prestige of Way and Virtue results in peace and strength;
the prestige of violence and scrutiny results in peril and weakness;
the prestige of madness and arrogance results in destruction.
Gōngsūn Zǐ said:
"Zǐfā led a generalship to attack Cài,
conquered Cài,
and captured the Marquis of Cài.
Upon returning, he reported his mission, saying:
'The Marquis of Cài has offered up his altars of soil and grain
to submit to Chǔ,
and I have assigned various officers to govern its land.'
Afterwards,
when Chǔ issued rewards,
Zǐfā declined, saying:
'Issuing warnings and spreading orders such that the enemy retreats
is the prestige of the Ruler;
mobilizing forces and attacking such that the enemy retreats
is the prestige of the General;
joining battle and exerting effort such that the enemy retreats
is the prestige of the Masses.
I, Shè, should not receive a reward based on the prestige of the masses.'"
Someone criticized this, saying:
"Zǐfā was respectful in reporting his mission,
but obstinate in declining the reward.
Now, exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
rewarding the meritorious,
and punishing the guilty—
this is not done by one person alone.
It is the Way of the Former Kings,
the root of every individual,
the response to liking the good and hating the evil.
Governance must follow this;
it has been the same from ancient times to the present.
When the enlightened kings of old undertook great affairs
and established great merit,
once the affairs were comprehensive
and the merit was established,
then the ruler enjoyed the completion,
and the various ministers enjoyed the merit.
The scholar-officials received higher rank,
the officers received higher grades,
and the common people received higher stipends.
Thus, those who did good were encouraged,
and those who did not were deterred.
Superior and inferior were of one heart,
and the three armies used their combined strength.
Therefore, all matters were completed,
and merit and fame became great.
Now Zǐfā alone acts otherwise,
going against the Way of the Former Kings,
disrupting the laws of the state of Chǔ,
demoralizing ministers who achieve merit,
and shaming those who should receive rewards.
Even if he is not executed along with his clan,
he will be looked down upon by later generations.
To act alone for the sake of personal integrity—
is this not excessive!
Therefore it is said:
Zǐfā was respectful in reporting his mission,
but obstinate in declining the reward."
Xún Qīng Zǐ addressed the Prime Minister of Qí, saying:
"To occupy a position of power over others
and practice the Way of surpassing others,
such that none in the world are resentful—
Tāng and Wǔ were examples of this.
To occupy a position of power over others
but not practice the Way of surpassing others—
though one possesses the greatest power in the world,
if he seeks even to be an ordinary man, it cannot be granted—
Jié and Zhòu were examples of this.
Thus, possessing the power to overcome others
is far inferior to possessing the Way to overcome others.
Now, rulers and ministers
overcome others through power.
To treat 'right' as right,
'wrong' as wrong,
'capable' as capable,
and 'incapable' as incapable,
setting aside one's private desires
and following the Way—
that is, the public way and universal righteousness where all can coexist—
this is the Way to overcome others.
Now, Prime Minister, above you have the exclusive ear of the ruler,
and below you have exclusive control of the state.
As for the power to overcome others,
you certainly possess it.
Why then do you not drive this power to overcome others
toward the Way to overcome others,
seeking out benevolent, generous, enlightened, and wise gentlemen to entrust to the King,
participating in the state's administration with them,
and rectifying right and wrong?
If this were done,
then who in the state would dare not to act with righteousness?
If ruler and minister, superior and inferior,
noble and base, old and young,
down to the common people,
all acted with righteousness,
then who in the world would not wish to join in that righteousness?
Worthy scholars would long for the Prime Minister's court,
capable men would long for the Prime Minister's offices,
and even people who love profit would all wish to return to Qí.
This is how the world is unified.
If the Prime Minister abandons this and does not do it,
but simply follows what the vulgar world does,
then the female ruler will cause chaos in the palace,
deceitful ministers will cause chaos in the court,
greedy officials will cause chaos in the government offices,
and the common people will all adopt a custom of greed and struggle for profit.
How can the state be maintained under such conditions?
Now, the giant Chǔ hangs before us,
the great Yàn presses behind us,
the strong Wèi hooks us on the right,
and the western border is as thin as a thread,
while the people of Chǔ possess Xiāngbèn and Kāiyáng to loom over us on the left.
If any one of these states forms a plan,
then the other three will surely rise up and take advantage of us.
In this case,
Qí will surely be cut into three or four pieces;
the state will be like a borrowed city,
and will certainly be a great laughingstock to the world. (
Which of) these two paths is worth following?"
Now Jié and Zhòu
were the descendants of Shèng Wáng,
belonging to the generations that possessed the world.
In them resided the records of power,
and they were the ruling house of the world.
Their lands were vast,
reaching a thousand lǐ within their borders.
Their people were numerous, counted by hundreds of millions.
Yet, in an instant, the world distantly abandoned Jié and
Zhòu to run toward Tāng and Wǔ.
Abruptly, everyone grew to hate Jié and
Zhòu, while honoring Tāng and Wǔ as emperors.
Why was this?
What did Jié and Zhòu lose?
And what did Tāng and Wǔ gain?
There is no other reason for this:
Jié and Zhòu were good at doing what people hate,
while Tāng and Wǔ were good at doing what people like.
What is it that people hate?
I say:
filth and corruption,
contention and plunder, and greed for profit.
What is it that people like?
I say:
ritual and righteousness, deference and yielding, and loyalty and trustworthiness.
Nowadays, those who rule others,
in their metaphors and comparisons, wish to rank themselves alongside Tāng and Wǔ.
However, in the methods they use to govern,
they are no different from Jié and Zhòu.
Yet they seek the achievements and fame of Tāng and Wǔ—
is this possible?
Therefore, all those who achieve victory
must be aligned with people;
and all those who win over people
must be aligned with the Way.
As for the Way,
what is it?
I say: ritual and righteousness, deference and yielding, and loyalty and trustworthiness.
Thus, for those who govern from forty or fifty thousand people upward,
to be strong and victorious is not due to the power of the masses;
it resides primarily in trustworthiness.
For those who govern from several hundred lǐ upward,
to be secure and stable is not due to the power of size;
it resides primarily in cultivating governance.
Nowadays, those who already have masses of tens of thousands
practice deception and form cliques to compete for followers.
Those who already have states of several hundred lǐ
practice corruption and sudden pillaging to compete for land.
If this is so, then they are discarding that which makes them secure and strong,
and competing for that which makes them endangered and weak.
They diminish that in which they are deficient
to increase that in which they have a surplus.
Being as perverse and erroneous as this,
yet seeking the achievements and fame of Tāng and Wǔ—
is this possible?
To use a metaphor:
this is like lying face down to lick the sky,
or trying to save someone from hanging by pulling their feet.
Such a theory will certainly not work;
the more one exerts effort, the further one gets from the goal.
Those who act as ministers
do not worry about whether their own conduct is viable,
but only seek wealth and profit.
This is like taking a battering ram into a cave to seek profit;
it is something a benevolent person would be ashamed of and would not do.
Thus, for humans, nothing is more precious than life,
and nothing more joyful than security.
That which nourishes life and provides the joy of security
is nothing greater than ritual and righteousness.
If a person knows to value life and enjoy security but discards ritual and righteousness,
to use a metaphor:
this is like wanting a long life while cutting one's own throat.
No ignorance is greater than this.
Therefore, a ruler of men
who loves the people will be secure,
and who likes worthies will be honored;
if he has neither of these, he will perish.
The Shī says:
"The great man is the fence;
the great multitude is the wall."
This is what it means.
The technique of force stops;
the technique of righteousness proceeds.
What does this mean?
I say:
It refers to Qín.
Its might and strength exceed those of Tāng,
Wǔ,
and Yǔ;
its vastness exceeds that of Shùn, yet its worries and troubles are beyond counting.
It is constantly apprehensive, fearing that the world will unite and crush it.
This is what is meant by "the technique of force stops."
Tāng?
Tāng and
Wǔ? What does it mean to say its might and strength exceed those of Tāng and Wǔ?
It means being able to make even those who hate it serve it.
Now, a father of Chǔ died there,
the state was seized,
and carrying the ancestral tablets of the Three Kings,
they fled to the area between Chén and Cài.
They watch for an opening and wait for a chance,
wishing they could sharpen their shins to trample Qín's belly.
Yet Qín makes the left side settle on the left,
and the right side settle on the right.
This is being able to make one's enemies serve as underlings.
This is what is meant by "might and strength exceeding Tāng and Wǔ."
What does it mean to say its vastness exceeds Shùn and Yǔ?
I say:
In ancient times, when the hundred kings unified the world
and made the feudal lords their ministers,
none ever exceeded a thousand lǐ within their borders.
Now Qín to the south even has Shāxiàn together with it,
which is in Jiāngnán.
To the north, it is a neighbor to the Hú and Mò tribes.
To the west, it has the Róng and
Bā tribes. In the east, what was in Chǔ now borders on Qí.
In Hán, it crossed Chángshān and now has Línlǜ.
In Wèi, it occupies Wéijīn, which is only one hundred and twenty lǐ from Dàliáng.
In Zhào, it sharply possesses Líng and occupies the passes of Sōngbǎi.
Backed by the Western Sea, it secures Chángshān.
Thus, its land spreads across the whole world.
