Its might moves all within the seas,
and its strength threatens the central states.
This is what is meant by "vastness exceeding Shùn and Yǔ."
Yet its worries and troubles are beyond counting,
and it is constantly apprehensive, fearing that the world will unite and crush it.
If that is the case, then what should be done?
I say: Restrain might and return to civil refinement.
Simply employ gentlemen of integrity, sincerity, and trustworthiness to govern the world.
Consequently, let them participate in the state's administration,
correct right and wrong,
and manage the crooked and the straight.
While listening to the administration at Xiányáng,
set those who are compliant in their places,
and only after that punish those who are not compliant. If it acts like this,
then troops will no longer need to go beyond the borders
and orders will be carried out throughout the world.
If it acts like this,
then even if a Míngtáng were built for it
beyond the borders to receive the feudal lords in audience,
it would surely be possible.
In today's world,
increasing one's land is not as urgent as increasing one's trustworthiness.
Yìng Hóu asked Sūn Qīngzǐ:
"What did you see upon entering Qín?"
Sūn Qīngzǐ replied:
"Its borders are naturally fortified and difficult,
its terrain is advantageous,
its mountains, forests, rivers, and valleys are beautiful,
and its natural resources are abundant.
This is a geographical victory.
Upon entering its borders
and observing its customs,
its common people are simple and honest,
their music is not decadent or foul,
and their clothing is not ostentatious.
They greatly fear the officials and are compliant;
they are like the people of antiquity.
Coming to the capital cities and government offices,
the many officials are solemn;
none are not respectful and frugal,
sincere and reverent, loyal and trustworthy without being sloppy.
They are like the officials of antiquity.
Entering its capital
and observing its high officers and gentlemen,
when they leave their gates,
they enter the public gates;
when they leave the public gates,
they return to their homes,
and they have no private business.
They do not form cliques,
they do not join factions;
they are aloof and none are not bright, well-informed, and impartial.
They are like the high officers and gentlemen of antiquity.
Observing its court,
when the court is in session,
they hear and decide on the hundred matters without delay,
appearing so calm as if there were no governance being conducted at all.
It is like the courts of antiquity.
Therefore, having achieved victories for four generations
is not a matter of luck,
but of certain principle.
This is what I saw.
Thus it is said:
'To be at ease yet well-governed,
to be concise yet detailed,
to be without vexation yet successful—
this is the height of governance.'
Qín resembles this.
Even so,
there is that which causes it apprehension.
Although it possesses all these various instruments and has them in full,
yet if one weighs it against the achievements and fame of a true King,
it falls vastly and distantly short."
Why is this?
It is because they probably have no Rú!
Therefore it is said: “One who is pure becomes a King,
one who is mixed becomes a Hegemon,
and one who has neither perishes.”
This was also the shortcoming of Qín.
Accumulating the minute:
A month does not overcome a day,
a season does not overcome a month,
and a year does not overcome a season.
Generally, people like to neglect and be careless with small matters;
and only when a great matter arrives do they start to work on it and attend to it.
In such a case,
they will always be unable to overcome those who are diligent and attentive in small matters.
Why is this?
It is because small matters arrive frequently,
their span of days is extensive,
and their accumulation is great;
great matters arrive rarely,
their span of days is shallow,
and their accumulation is small.
Therefore, one who is good with days becomes a King,
one who is good with seasons becomes a Hegemon,
one who merely mends leaks is in danger,
and one who is greatly negligent perishes.
Therefore, the King respects the day,
the Hegemon respects the season,
and the state that barely survives grieves only after danger arrives.
A perishing state only knows it is perishing when it has reached ruin,
and only knows it is dying when it has reached death;
the calamities and defeats of a perishing state
cannot be fully regretted.
The excellence of a Hegemon is manifest
and can be recorded by the season;
the achievements and fame of a King
cannot be fully counted and can be recorded by the day.
With wealth, goods, and treasures, magnitude is valued;
with government, education, achievement, and fame, it is the opposite—the one able to accumulate the minute achieves success quickly.
The *Shī* says:
“Virtue is as light as a hair,
but few among the people are able to lift it.”
This is what is meant.
Generally, the reason why wicked people arise
is because those above do not value Righteousness
and do not respect Righteousness.
Now, Righteousness
is that which limits and forbids people from doing evil and wickedness.
Now, if those above do not value Righteousness
and do not respect Righteousness,
if it is so,
then the people and commoners below
will all have the intent to abandon Righteousness
and have a heart to pursue wickedness;
this is the reason why wicked people arise.
Furthermore, the superior is the teacher of the inferior;
the subordinates' harmonizing with the superior
is like an echo responding to a sound
or a shadow resembling a form.
Therefore, one who is a superior to others
must not fail to be aligned.
Now, Righteousness
is what provides regulation within to humans
and provides regulation without to the myriad things,
providing peace for the ruler above
and providing harmony for the people below.
Internal and external, superior and inferior being regulated—
this is the essence of Righteousness.
Thus, in the essentials of governing the world,
Righteousness is the root,
and Trustworthiness comes next.
In antiquity, Yǔ and Tāng rooted themselves in Righteousness and strived for Trustworthiness, and the world was well-governed;
Jié and Zhòu abandoned Righteousness and turned their backs on Trustworthiness, and the world was in chaos.
Therefore, those who are superiors to others
must be cautious regarding Ritual and Righteousness
and strive for Loyalty and Trustworthiness
before it is acceptable.
This is the great foundation for those who rule over people.
If the hall is not swept,
then the grass in the outskirts is not (
weeded;
looking afar) when a naked blade presses against the chest,
then the eyes do not see stray arrows;
when a drawn halberd is placed upon the head,
then the ten fingers do not refuse to be severed.
It is not that these are not matters of concern,
but that in pain and care, urgency and leisure, some things must take precedence over others.
The movements of Heaven are constant;
they do not exist for the sake of Yáo,
nor do they perish for the sake of Jié.
Respond to them with order, and there is good fortune;
respond to them with chaos, and there is calamity.
Strengthen the root and regulate expenditures,
then Heaven cannot make one poor;
provide complete nourishment and move according to the seasons,
then Heaven cannot make one ill;
follow the Way and do not deviate,
then Heaven cannot bring disaster.
Therefore, floods and droughts cannot cause hunger (thirst),
cold and heat cannot cause sickness,
and strange omens cannot cause calamity.
If the root is neglected and expenditures are extravagant,
then Heaven cannot make one wealthy;
if nourishment is sparse and movement is infrequent,
then Heaven cannot make one whole;
if one turns their back on the Way and acts recklessly,
then Heaven cannot make one have good fortune.
Therefore, before floods and droughts arrive, there is hunger;
before cold and heat press in, there is sickness;
and before strange omens arise, there is calamity.
They receive the same seasons as a well-governed age,
yet their misfortunes and disasters differ from a well-governed age;
one cannot blame Heaven,
for it is their way that makes it so.
Therefore, one who is clear about the distinction between Heaven and man
can be called a Perfect Person.
To accomplish without acting,
to obtain without seeking—
this is what is called the celestial office.
In such matters,
though they be deep, the person does not apply additional thought to them;
though they be great, one does not apply additional ability to them;
though they be subtle, one does not apply additional scrutiny to them.
This is what is called not competing with Heaven for its office.
Heaven has its seasons,
Earth has its resources,
and Man has his governance.
This is what is called being able to form a triad.
To abandon that by which one forms the triad
and instead desire that which one forms the triad with
is to be confused.
The arrayed stars revolve in sequence,
the sun and moon shine in alternation,
the four seasons succeed one another,
the Yīn and Yáng undergo great transformations,
the wind and rain are widely bestowed,
and the myriad things each obtain their harmony to be born
and each obtain their nourishment to be completed.
One does not see the workings
but sees the results;
this is what is called the divine.
All know that by which things are completed,
but none know their formless nature;
this is what is called the work of Heaven.
Only the Sage does not seek to know Heaven.
Once the celestial office is established
and the work of Heaven is completed,
the physical form is prepared and the spirit is born;
likes and dislikes, joy and anger, sorrow and pleasure are stored therein.
This is what is called the celestial emotions.
The ears, eyes, nose, mouth, and physical abilities each have their own contact but cannot perform each other's functions;
this is what is called the celestial organs.
The heart resides in the center as an empty vessel
to govern the five organs;
this is what is called the celestial lord.
To use things not of its kind to nourish its kind—
this is what is called celestial nourishment.
To follow what accords with its kind is called blessing,
to go against what accords with its kind is called calamity;
this is what is called celestial governance.
To darken one's celestial lord,
disorder one's celestial organs,
abandon one's celestial nourishment,
go against one's celestial governance,
and turn one's back on one's celestial emotions,
thereby destroying the work of Heaven—
this is what is called great disaster.
The Sage purifies his celestial lord,
rectifies his celestial organs,
provides for his celestial nourishment,
accords with his celestial governance,
and nourishes his celestial emotions,
thereby making whole the work of Heaven.
In such a case,
he knows what he should do
and knows what he should not do;
then Heaven and Earth will be his officials and the myriad things his servants.
His actions are completely orderly,
his nourishment is completely appropriate,
and his life remains unharmed.
This is what is called knowing Heaven.
Therefore, great skill lies in what one does not do,
and great wisdom lies in what one does not think about.
That which is observed concerning Heaven
is limited to its visible manifestations that can be relied upon for timing;
that which is observed concerning Earth
is limited to its visible suitabilities that can be used for productivity;
that which is observed concerning the four seasons
is limited to their visible sequences that can be used for labor;
that which is observed concerning Yīn and Yáng
is limited to their visible harmony that can be used for governance.
The officials keep to Heaven,
while the ruler himself keeps to the Way.
"Are order and disorder
caused by Heaven?"
It is said:
"The sun, moon, stars, and the auspicious calendar
were the same for Yǔ and Jié;
Yǔ created order with them,
while Jié caused disorder with them.
Thus, order and disorder are not caused by Heaven."
"Is it the seasons?"
It is said:
"Luxuriant sprouting and flourishing growth in spring and summer,
and the harvesting and storing in autumn and winter,
these too were the same for Yǔ and Jié;
Yǔ created order with them,
while Jié caused disorder with them.
Thus, order and disorder are not caused by the seasons."
"Is it the land?"
It is said:
"If one gains the land, one lives;
if one loses the land, one dies.
This too was the same for Yǔ and Jié;
Yǔ created order with it,
while Jié caused disorder with it.
Thus, order and disorder are not caused by the land.
The *Shī* says:
'Heaven created the high mountain;
Dàwáng cultivated it.
He established it;
Wénwáng brought peace to it.'
This is what is meant."
Heaven does not stop winter because humans dislike the cold;
Earth does not stop being vast because humans dislike the distances;
the Jūnzǐ does not stop his conduct because of the clamor of petty people.
Heaven has its constant Way;
Earth has its constant principles;
the Jūnzǐ has his constant form.
The Jūnzǐ follows the constant Way,
while the petty person calculates his achievements.
The *Shī* says:
"If there is no error in ritual and righteousness,
why worry about what people say?"
This is what is meant.
That the King of Chǔ has a following of a thousand chariots
is not because of his wisdom;
that the Jūnzǐ sips bean soup and drinks water
is not because of his folly:
these are due to the circumstances of the times.
As for having a refined will and intent,
profound virtue and conduct,
and clear wisdom and deliberation,
being born in the present but setting one's heart on antiquity,
these are the things within one's own power.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ admires what is within himself
and does not admire what is from Heaven;
the petty person discards what is within himself
and admires what is from Heaven.
Because the Jūnzǐ respects what is within himself
and does not admire what is from Heaven,
he progresses daily;
because the petty person discards what is within himself
and admires what is from Heaven,
he regresses daily.
Thus, the reason the Jūnzǐ progresses daily
and the reason the petty person regresses daily
are one and the same.
The reason why the Jūnzǐ and the petty person are so far apart
lies right here.
When stars fall or trees groan,
the people of the state are all terrified.
They ask:
"What is this?"
I say:
"It is nothing.
These are changes in Heaven and Earth,
transformations of Yīn and Yáng,
and rare occurrences among things.
To marvel at them
is acceptable;
but to fear them
is wrong.
Now, eclipses of the sun and moon,
unseasonable wind and rain,
and the appearance of strange stars—
there has never been an age where these did not occasionally occur.
If the ruler is enlightened and the government is equitable,
then even if they all occur together,
they cause no harm.
If the ruler is benighted and the government is hazardous,
then even if not a single one occurs,
it is of no benefit.
The falling of stars
and the groaning of trees
are changes in Heaven and Earth,
transformations of Yīn and Yáng,
and rare occurrences among things.
To marvel at them
is acceptable;
but to fear them is wrong.
"Of things that have occurred,
it is human portents that should be feared:
poor plowing that damages the crops,
failure to weed that lets weeds grow,
hazardous government that loses the people,
weed-filled fields and bad harvests,
high grain prices and starving people,
and the dead lying on the roads—
these are what are called human portents.
When government orders are not clear,
when actions are unseasonable,
and when fundamental tasks are not managed—
these are what are called human portents. When effort is unseasonable,
then cattle and horses breed abnormally,
and bandits and calamities arrive together—
these are what are called human portents.
These portents are born of disorder;
if these three types of disorder occur together,
no state can be at peace.
The explanation is very close at hand,
but the disaster is very miserable.
These may be marveled at,
but should not be feared.
The *Zhuàn* says:
'Strange occurrences among the myriad things are not discussed in the books.
Useless debates
and non-urgent investigations
should be cast aside and not pursued
As for the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
and the distinction between husband and wife,
these should be refined daily and never abandoned."
"If one performs the rain sacrifice and it rains,
what does it mean?"
I say:
"It means nothing.
It is just like it raining when one does not perform the rain sacrifice.
Performing rituals to save the sun or moon during an eclipse,
performing the rain sacrifice during a drought,
or deciding great matters only after divination—
these are not done because one expects to get what one seeks,
but to provide a cultural ornament for them.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ regards them as cultural ornament,
but the common people regard them as supernatural.
To regard them as cultural ornament is auspicious;
to regard them as supernatural is inauspicious."
Among things in Heaven, none is brighter than the sun and moon;
among things on Earth, none is brighter than water and fire;
among objects, none is brighter than pearls and jade;
among human things, none is brighter than ritual and righteousness.
Therefore, if the sun and moon are not high,
their brilliance will not be glorious;
if water and fire are not accumulated,
their light and moisture will not be broad;
if pearls and jade do not shine on the outside,
then kings and dukes will not prize them as treasures;
if ritual and righteousness are not applied to the state,
then achievements and fame will not be clear.
Therefore, the fate of a person lies with Heaven;
the fate of a state lies with ritual.
Those who rule people:
if they exalt ritual and honor the worthy, they will be kings;
if they prioritize law and love the people, they will be hegemons;
if they love profit and are full of deceit, they will be in danger;
if they use schemes, subversion, and dark treachery, they will be completely destroyed.
Rather than glorifying Heaven and contemplating it,
why not treat it as a resource and regulate it?
Rather than following Heaven and singing its praises,
why not control the mandate of Heaven and use it?
Rather than looking toward the seasons and waiting for them,
why not respond to the seasons and make use of them?
Rather than following along with things and increasing them,
why not exercise one's ability and transform them?
Rather than contemplating things and treating them as mere things,
why not manage things so as not to lose them?
Rather than longing for the source from which things are born,
why not possess the means by which things are brought to completion?
Therefore, to set aside human effort and contemplate Heaven
is to lose the true nature of the myriad things.
That which has remained unchanged through the hundred kings
is sufficient to be the thread of the Way.
As one dynasty falls and another rises,
respond to them with this thread;
if the principles are threaded together, there is no disorder.
If one does not know the thread,
one does not know how to respond to changes.
The substance of the thread has never perished.
Disorder arises from deviation from it;
order is achieved through its thoroughness.
Therefore, what is valued in the Way is that
if it is moderate, it can be followed;
if it is eccentric, it cannot be practiced;
if it is concealed, it leads to great delusion.
Those who navigate waters mark the depths;
if the markers are not clear, people will sink.
Those who govern the people mark the Way;
if the markers are not clear, there will be chaos.
Lǐ (Ritual Propriety) is
the marker.
To discard Lǐ is
to darken the world;
a darkened world
is in great chaos.
Therefore, the Way is never without clarity;
there are different markers for the internal and external,
and there are constants for the hidden and the manifest,
so that the people’s falling into traps is eliminated.
All things are but one side of the Way;
a single thing is but one side of all things;
a foolish person is but one side of a single thing,
yet thinks themselves to know the Way;
they are without knowledge.
Shèn Zǐ had insight into what follows,
but no insight into what leads;
Lǎo Zǐ had insight into yielding,
but no insight into expanding;
Mò Zǐ had insight into uniformity,
but no insight into distinctiveness;
Sòng Zǐ had insight into fewness,
but no insight into plurality.
Having what follows but not what leads,
then the masses have no gate to enter.
Having yielding but not expanding,
then the noble and the base are not distinguished.
Having uniformity but not distinctiveness,
then government orders cannot be implemented.
Having fewness but not plurality,
then the masses cannot be transformed.
The Shū says:
"Have no private likes,
follow the Way of the King;
have no private dislikes,
follow the Path of the King."
This is what it means.
Secular theorists say:
"The Way of the ruler benefits from secrecy."
This is not so.
The ruler is the one who leads the song for the people;
the superior is the model for the inferior.
They will listen to the lead and respond,
observe the model and act.
If the lead is silent, the people have nothing to respond to;
if the model is hidden, the inferiors have nothing to move by.
With no response and no movement,
then the superior and inferior have no way to assist each other.
If it is like this,
then it is the same as having no superior,
and no misfortune is greater than this.
Therefore, the superior is the root of the inferior;
if the superior is open and clear,
then the inferiors will be orderly and discerning;
if the superior is upright and sincere,
then the inferiors will be honest and guileless;
if the superior is fair and just,
then the inferiors will be simple and straightforward.
Orderly and discerning, they are easy to unify;
honest and guileless, they are easy to employ;
simple and straightforward, they are easy to understand.
Easy to unify, the state is strong;
easy to employ, there is achievement;
easy to understand, there is clarity;
this is how order arises.
If the superior is secretive and meticulous,
then the inferiors will be suspicious and bewildered;
if the superior is obscure and treacherous,
then the inferiors will be deceptive and fraudulent;
if the superior is biased and crooked,
then the inferiors will form factions and cliques.
Suspicious and bewildered, they are difficult to unify;
deceptive and fraudulent, they are difficult to employ;
factional and cliquish, they are difficult to understand.
Difficult to unify, the state is not strong;
difficult to employ, there is no achievement;
difficult to understand, there is no clarity;
this is how chaos is produced.
Therefore, the ruler’s Way benefits from clarity, not obscurity,
benefits from openness, not secrecy.
Thus, when the ruler's Way is clear, the inferiors are at peace;
when the ruler's Way is obscure, the inferiors are in danger.
When the inferiors are at peace, they honor the superior;
when the inferiors are in danger, they despise the superior.
When the superior is easy to understand,
then the inferiors feel close to the superior;
when the superior is difficult to understand,
then the inferiors fear the superior.
When the inferiors feel close to the superior, the superior is secure;
when the inferiors fear the superior, the superior is in danger.
Therefore, in the ruler's Way, nothing is worse than being difficult to understand,
and nothing is more dangerous than making the inferiors fear him.
The Zhuàn says:
"When those who hate him are many, he is in danger."
The Shū says:
"He was able to make illustrious his bright virtue."
The Shī says:
"Illustrious and bright below."
Therefore, the Former Kings made things clear;
they certainly did not merely make them mysterious!
Secular theorists say:
"Jié and Zhòu possessed the world,
and Tāng and Wǔ usurped and seized it from them."
This is not so.
If one means that Jié and Zhòu held the registries of possessing the world as a matter of course, then it is so;
if one means they personally held the registries of possessing the world, then it is (not) so;
and if one says the world belonged to Jié and Zhòu, it is not so.
In antiquity, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials,
and the feudal lords had a hundred officials.
With these thousand officials,
orders were carried out throughout the states of Zhūxià;
this is called being a King;
with these hundred officials,
orders were carried out within the borders;
even if the state was not at peace,
as long as it did not reach the point of being abolished, changed, or destroyed,
this is called being a Lord.
The son of a Sage King,
the descendant of one who possessed the world,
where the records of power reside,
and the ancestral house of the world;
yet if he is untalented and not moderate,
then internally the common people hate him,
and externally the feudal lords rebel against him.
Close at hand, the territory within the borders is not unified;
far away, the feudal lords do not obey;
and orders are not carried out within his own borders.
In extreme cases, the feudal lords encroach upon and diminish him,
and attack and strike him.
If it is like this,
then even if he has not yet perished,
I say he does not possess the world.
When a Sage King dies,
the one who holds the records of power might be so weak as to be unable to hold the world together,
and the world has no lord.
If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is illustrious and whose majesty is accumulated,
and none of the people within the seas do not wish to have him as their lord and teacher,
yet if a tyrannical state alone is arrogant,
how can he punish them?
He must avoid harming innocent people,
punishing the lord of the tyrannical state
as if punishing a solitary fellow.
If it is like this,
then he can be said to be able to employ the world.
To be able to employ the world is called being a King.
Tāng and Wǔ did not take the world;
they cultivated their Way,
practiced their Yì (Righteousness),
promoted the common benefits of the world,
and eliminated the common harms of the world,
and so the world turned to them.
Jié and Zhòu did not leave the world;
they turned against the virtue of Yǔ and Tāng,
threw the distinctions of Lǐ and Yì into chaos,
acted like birds and beasts,
accumulated their misfortune,
and completed their evil,
and so the world left them.
When the world turns to someone,
it is called being a King;
when the world leaves someone, it is called perishing.
Therefore, Jié
and Zhòu did not possess the world,
and so that Tāng and Wǔ did not assassinate their lords is proven by this.
Tāng and Wǔ
were the father and mother of the people;
Jié and Zhòu were the enemies and thieves of the people.
Now, the secular theorists of today
consider Jié and Zhòu to be lords
and Tāng and Wǔ to be regicides;
but this is the same as condemning the father and mother of the people
and taking as masters the enemies and thieves of the people;
no misfortune is greater than this.
If one considers the union of the world as defining a lord,
then the world never united under Jié or Zhòu.
Thus, to say Tāng and Wǔ committed regicide
is a statement for which (the world) has never had a valid explanation;
it is merely a baseless fabrication.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven is only a matter of the right person.
The world
is a matter of the utmost gravity;
none but the most powerful can sustain it.
It is of the utmost magnitude;
none but the most discerning can differentiate its parts.
It is of the utmost populousness;
none but the most enlightened can harmonize it.
These three extremities
cannot be fully realized by anyone but a Shèngrén.
Therefore, none but a Shèngrén can truly be a King.
A Shèngrén is one who is complete in the Way and perfect in beauty;
he is the scale and the weight by which the world is balanced.
As for Jié and Zhòu, their wisdom and deliberations were extremely treacherous,
their fundamental intentions were extremely dark,
and their conduct was extremely chaotic.
Their kin became distant from them,
the worthy despised them,
and the common people resented them.
Although they were the descendants of Yǔ and Tāng,
they could not find a single person to side with them.
They disemboweled Bǐ Gān
and imprisoned Jīzǐ.
Their persons died and their states perished,
and they became the objects of the greatest execution and humiliation in the world.
Whenever later generations speak of evil, they must cite them as evidence.
This is the outcome of a situation where they could not even be tolerated by their own wives and children.
Thus, those of supreme worthiness encompass the four seas;
Tāng and Wǔ were such men.
Those of supreme incompetence are not tolerated by their own wives and children;
Jié and Zhòu were such men.
Now, those who follow the common talk of the world today
claim that Jié and Zhòu possessed the world
and made Tāng and Wǔ their subjects—
is this not an extreme error!
To use a comparison,
this is like a hunchbacked shaman or a lame exorcist considering themselves great and wise.
Thus, one may seize a state,
but one cannot seize the world from the people;
one may steal a state,
but one cannot steal the world.
One who seizes may possess a state,
but he cannot possess the world;
one who steals may gain a state,
but he cannot gain the world.
Why is this?
I say:
A state is a small instrument;
it can be possessed by a petty man,
it can be gained by petty ways,
and it can be maintained with petty strength.
The world is a great instrument;
it cannot be possessed by a petty man,
it cannot be gained by petty ways,
and it cannot be maintained with petty strength.
As for a state, a petty man can possess it,
yet it will not necessarily escape destruction.
The world
is of the utmost magnitude;
none but a Shèngrén can possess it.
Common talkers say:
“In well-ordered antiquity there were no physical punishments,
but only symbolic punishments:
branding with black ink;
wearing a grass collar instead of cutting off the nose;
wearing a ceremonial knee-pad instead of castration;
wearing hemp and straw sandals instead of cutting off the feet;
and for execution, wearing red ochre clothing without a border.
Well-ordered antiquity was like this.”
This is not so.
If it was considered well-ordered,
then people surely did not commit crimes;
not only were physical punishments not used,
but symbolic punishments were also not used.
If it is considered that people did commit crimes
but their punishments were simply made light,
then it would mean that those who killed did not die,
and those who injured were not punished.
When crimes are extremely heavy but punishments are extremely light,
ordinary people will not know that such things are evil,
and no chaos could be greater than this.
Generally, the root of punishing people
is to prohibit violence and hate evil,
and furthermore, to warn against what has not yet happened.
If those who kill do not die
and those who injure are not punished,
this is called showing favor to the violent and being lenient toward the treacherous;
it is not hating evil.
Thus, symbolic punishments almost certainly did not originate in well-ordered antiquity,
but rather arose together with the chaos of the present age.
Well-ordered antiquity was not like that.
In general, noble ranks, official posts, rewards, and punishments
are all forms of retribution, following their own kind.
If even one thing loses its proper proportion,
it is the beginning of chaos.
Now, if virtue does not match one's position,
ability does not match one's office,
rewards do not correspond to merit,
and punishments do not correspond to crimes,
no misfortune could be greater than this.
In the past, Wǔ Wáng attacked the Shāng,
executed Zhòu,
cut off his head,
and hung it from a red banner.
Now, campaigning against the violent and executing the fierce
is the height of good order.
That those who kill shall die
and those who injure shall be punished
is common to all the hundred kings;
none has ever known when this began.
When punishment matches the crime
there is order;
when it does not match the crime
there is chaos.
Therefore, when there is order, punishments are seen as heavy;
when there is chaos, punishments are seen as light.
A crime committed against order is inherently heavy;
a crime committed in a state of chaos is inherently light.
The Shū says:
“Punishments change with the age, being sometimes light and sometimes heavy.”
This is what it means.
Common talkers say:
“Tāng and Wǔ could not enforce their prohibitions and commands;
why was this?”
They say:
“Chǔ and Yuè did not submit to their control.”
This is not so.
Tāng and Wǔ were the best in the world at enforcing prohibitions and commands.
Tāng resided in Bó,
and Wǔ Wáng resided in Hào;
both were territories of only a hundred lǐ.
The world became one,
the feudal lords became their subjects,
and among all those within the reach of communication,
none did not tremble, follow, and submit so as to be transformed and comply with them;
why would Chǔ and Yuè alone not submit to control?
The system of a King
observes the geographical situation to determine tools and implements,
and balances distance to grade the tribute and offerings;
how could they all be the same!
Thus, the people of Lǔ used the táng pole,
the people of Wèi
used the kē axe-handle,
and the people of Qí used a single leather strap.
Where the land and natural conditions are different,
the tools, implements, and decorations must also be different.
Therefore, the states of the Zhūxià have the same dress and the same rituals,
while the states of the Mán, Yí, Róng, and Dí have the same dress but different systems.
Within the domain was the Diànfú;
outside the domain was the Hóufú;
beyond that were the Bīnfú;
the Mán and Yí regions were the Yàofú;
the Róng and Dí regions were the Huāngfú.
Those in the Diànfú provided daily offerings;
those in the Hóufú provided monthly sacrifices;
those in the Bīnfú provided seasonal offerings;
those in the Yàofú provided annual tribute;
those in the Huāngfú paid homage once per reign.
Daily offerings, monthly sacrifices, seasonal offerings, and annual tribute—
this is what is meant by observing the geographical situation to determine tools and implements,
and balancing distance to grade the tribute and offerings;
this is the system of a King.
Those people of Chǔ and Yuè
were of the class that provided seasonal offerings, annual tribute,
or homage once per reign.
Must they be identical to the class that provided daily offerings and monthly sacrifices
before they are said to be under control?
These are the arguments of those who haggle over trifles,
the emaciated ones in the ditches;
they are not worthy of discussing the system of a King.
As the saying goes:
“The shallow cannot be used to measure the deep;
the foolish are not sufficient to plan with the wise;
the frog in the shallow well cannot be spoken to about the joy of the Eastern Sea.”
This is what it means.
Common talkers say:
“Yáo and Shùn abdicated and transferred the throne.”
This is not so.
The Tiānzǐ
holds a position of supreme status
and is without a peer in the world—
to whom would he abdicate?
When his Way and virtue are pure and complete,
and his wisdom is extremely enlightened,
he sits facing south and listens to the world,
and among all the common people, none do not tremble, follow, and submit so as to be transformed and comply with him.
In the world, there are no reclusive scholars
and no overlooked virtues.
Those who are the same as him are right;
those who are different from him are wrong.
How could there be such a thing as abdicating the world?
It is said:
"He abdicates upon death."
This is also not so.
When a Sage King is on high,
he evaluates virtue to determine rank,
measures ability to grant office,
and causes all people to carry out their tasks, each obtaining what is appropriate;
those who cannot use righteousness to control profit,
or use artifice to refine their nature,
are all made into the common people.
When a Sage King has passed away,
if there is no Sage in the world,
then indeed no one is sufficient to take possession of the world.
If there is a Sage in the world
among the successors,
then the world will not fall apart;
the court will not change its positions,
the state will not alter its systems,
and the world will be satisfied,
no different from how it was before;
with a Yáo succeeding a Yáo,
what change could there be?
If the Sage is not in the succeeding son but among the Sāngōng,
then the world will turn to him as if returning home,
as if being restored and revitalized;
the world will be satisfied,
no different from how it was before;
with a Yáo succeeding a Yáo,
what change could there be?
It is only shifting the court and changing the system that is difficult.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven lives, the world is unified,
achieving compliance and order,
and virtue is appraised to determine rank;
when he dies, there will certainly be someone capable of taking charge of the world.
Since the divisions of ritual and righteousness are complete,
what use would there be for abdication?
It is said:
"He abdicates due to old age and decline."
This is also not so.
Blood, qi, sinews, and strength may decline,
but as for wisdom, deliberation, selection, and rejection, these do not decline.
It is said:
"The elderly cannot endure the labor and so they retire."
This is the argument of those who fear work.
For the Son of Heaven, his power is supreme and his physical form is most at ease;
his mind is most joyful and his will is never frustrated;
his body does not perform labor,
and his honor is without peer.
For clothing, he wears the five colors,
mixed with intermediate hues,
layered with patterns and embroidery,
and further decorated with pearls and jade;
for food and drink, he emphasizes the Dàláo sacrifice and prepares rare delicacies,
according to the desired fragrances and flavors;
food is served with grace,
while music is played in shifts during the meal;
the Yōng ode is performed while removing the vessels for the five sacrifices;
a hundred attendants holding offerings
wait in the western chamber.
At home, screens are set up,
and he sits leaning against a stool,
while the regional lords scurry about below the hall;
when he steps out of the door, shamans and priests have their tasks;
when he exits the gate, the ancestral sacrifices have their tasks.
He rides in the Dàlù carriage, using the fine reed mats to maintain his comfort;
at the sides are carried Gǎoběn and angelica to nurture his nose;
in front is the carved crossbar to nurture his eyes;
the sounds of the bells
match the rhythms of the Wǔ and Xiàng dances in his steps,
and match the Sháo and Hù music when the carriage moves, all to nurture his ears.
The Sāngōng hold the yoke and guide the carriage;
the regional lords hold the wheels, flank the carriage, and lead the horses;
the Dàhóu follows behind,
the Grand Officers follow him,
and the Small Marquises and Yuánshì follow them;
the common officers wear armor and line the road;
the common people hide away
and dare not look.
In residence he is like a Great God,
in motion he is like the Celestial Emperor;
in sustaining old age and nurturing decline,
is there anything better than this?
To the elderly, "retirement" means rest;
but could rest ever be as peaceful, joyful, and serene as this?
Therefore it is said:
regional lords have old age,
but the Son of Heaven has no old age.
There is abdication of a state,
but no abdication of the world;
this is the same from ancient times to the present.
To say "Yáo and Shùn abdicated"
is empty talk;
it is a tradition of the shallow
and a theory of the ignorant.
They do not understand the principles of order and chaos,
the variations of the small and large, or the supreme and the non-supreme;
they are not yet capable of reaching the Great Principles of the world.
Those who spread common theories say:
"Yáo and Shùn were unable to transform people through education."
Why is this?
They say:
"Zhū and Xiàng were not transformed."
This is not so.
Yáo and Shùn were the best in the world at education and transformation;
when they sat facing south to hear the world,
none among the living people failed to be moved to follow and obey, thus being transformed and compliant.
However, that Zhū and Xiàng alone were not transformed
was not the fault of Yáo and Shùn,
but the crime of Zhū and Xiàng.
Yáo and Shùn were the heroes of the world;
Zhū and Xiàng were the dregs of the world
and the trifles of their time.
Now those who spread common theories
do not find fault with Zhū and Xiàng
but instead criticize Yáo and Shùn;
is this not an extreme error?
This is what is called an eccentric theory.
Yì and Féng Mén were the best archers in the world,
but they could not hit a tiny target with a broken bow or a crooked arrow;
Wáng Liáng
and Zào Fù were the best drivers in the world,
but they could not travel far with a lame horse or a ruined carriage;
Yáo and Shùn were the best at education and transformation in the world,
but they could not transform the wicked and the trifling.
What generation is without the wicked?
What time is without the trifling?
From the time of Tàihào and Suìrén, none were without them.
Therefore, the originators of such stories are inauspicious,
those who learn them suffer calamity,
and those who reject them find blessing.
The Shījīng says:
"The calamities of the people
do not descend from Heaven;
gossip and backstabbing
are entirely the work of men."
This is what it refers to.
Those who spread common theories say:
"In high antiquity, burials were simple:
the coffin was three inches thick,
there were three layers of burial clothes,
and the burial did not interfere with the fields;
therefore, they were not dug up.
In the chaos of today, burials are lavish and coffins are decorated,
therefore they are dug up."
This is failing to know the Way of Governance
and not examining the reasons why graves are dug up or not.
Whenever a person steals,
it is always for a purpose;
if not to provide for a deficiency,
then it is to add to an excess.
But when a Sage King provides for the people,
he makes them all wealthy and prosperous,
leisurely and satisfied,
yet not allowed to exceed proper measures with their surplus.
Therefore, thieves do not steal,
robbers do not stab,
dogs and pigs vomit up beans and grain,
and farmers and merchants are all able to yield their goods and wealth.
Due to the beauty of the customs,
men and women do not pick up things for themselves on the road,
and the common people are ashamed to pick up what has been dropped.
Therefore Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Way prevails in the world,
would not the thieves be the first to change?"
Even if pearls and jade covered the body,
and embroidery filled the coffin,
and gold filled the outer coffin,
with cinnabar added,
and azurite layered upon it,
with rhinoceros horn and ivory used for decorations,
and Lánggān, Lóngzī, and Huájìn used for fruits,
people still would not dig it up.
Why is this?
Because the pursuit of profit is slow and hesitant,
while the shame of violating one's duty is great.
It is only in the chaos of today that things are the opposite:
those above use no laws in their commands,
and those below use no standards in their conduct;
the wise are not allowed to plan,
the capable are not allowed to govern,
and the worthy are not allowed to be employed.
If it is like this,
then those above lose the nature of Heaven,
those below lose the benefits of the Earth,
and in the middle, they lose human harmony;
thus all tasks are abandoned,
resources are exhausted,
and disaster and chaos arise.
The kings and dukes then suffer from insufficiency above,
and the common people then freeze, starve, and become emaciated below;
thus people like Jié and Zhòu gather together,
and thieves and robbers strike and plunder to endanger their superiors;
they must act like beasts
and be greedy as tigers and wolves.
Therefore, they would make dried meat of giants and roast infants.
If it is like this, then why blame those who dig up people’s graves
and pry open people’s mouths to seek profit?
Even if they are buried naked,
they will still definitely be dug up;
how can there be any proper burial?
They will even eat their flesh and gnaw their bones.
Now it is said:
“In high antiquity, burials were meager,
therefore they were not dug up;
in the chaotic present, burials are lavish,
therefore they are dug up.”
This is merely the error of treacherous people using chaotic theories
to deceive the foolish and entrap them
to steal and take profit thereby;
this is what is called great treachery.
The *Zhuàn* says:
“To endanger others to secure oneself,
to harm others to benefit oneself.”
This refers to that.
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
“By making it clear that being insulted is not a disgrace,
one causes people not to fight.
People all take being insulted as a disgrace,
therefore they fight;
if they know that being insulted is not a disgrace,
then they will not fight.”
I respond to him:
“In that case, do you also take it that human nature does not loathe insults?”
He says:
“They loathe them but do not find them disgraceful.”
I say:
“If it is like this,
then you will certainly not obtain what you seek.
Whenever people fight,
it must be because they loathe something;
it is not because they consider it a disgrace.
Now, when entertainers, dwarfs, and buffoons insult and revile each other without fighting,
is it because they have great knowledge that being insulted is not a disgrace?
The reason they do not fight
is that they do not loathe it.
Now, if someone enters another’s drainage ditch
and steals their pigs,
then they will grab swords and halberds and pursue them,
not avoiding death or injury.
Is this because they take losing a pig as a disgrace?
The reason they do not fear fighting
is because they loathe it.
Even if one takes being insulted as a disgrace,
if one does not loathe it, one will not fight;
even if one knows being insulted is not a disgrace,
if one loathes it, one will definitely fight.
Therefore, whether one fights or not
does not depend on disgrace or no disgrace,
but rather depends on loathing or not loathing.
Now, since Zǐ Sòngzǐ cannot remove people’s loathing of insults,
but devotes himself to persuading people that it is not a disgrace,
is this not an extreme error!
Even with a golden tongue and a worn-out mouth,
it will still be of no benefit.
If he does not know it is of no benefit,
then he is not wise;
if he knows it is of no benefit
yet simply uses it to deceive people,
then he is not benevolent.
Being neither benevolent nor wise,
there is no greater disgrace.
Intending to be of benefit to others,
yet being of no benefit to others,
he only receives great disgrace and retreats.
No theory is more defective than this.”
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
“To be insulted is not a disgrace.”
I respond to him:
“In every discussion, one must establish a Lóngzhèng
before it is acceptable.
Without a Lóngzhèng, right and wrong are not distinguished
and disputes are not resolved.
Therefore, what has been heard says:
‘The great supreme of the world,
the boundary of right and wrong,
the origin of distinct duties, names, and forms,
is the King’s Regulations.’
Therefore, in all speeches, discussions, and mandates, none should
not take the Sage King as a teacher,
and the Sage King’s distinctions
are honor and disgrace.
These have two aspects:
there is moral honor,
there is circumstantial honor;
there is moral disgrace,
there is circumstantial disgrace.
One’s will and purpose are cultivated,
virtue and conduct are deep,
wisdom and reflection are clear;
this is honor that comes from within,
and this is what is called moral honor.
Rank and order are noble,
tribute and salary are generous,
power and position are superior,
above being the Tiānzǐ or Zhūhóu,
below being Qīng, Xiàng, Shì, or Dàfū;
this is honor that comes from without,
and this is what is called circumstantial honor.
Dissolute and licentious, filthy and neglectful,
violating roles and disrupting principles,
arrogant, violent, and greedy for profit;
this is disgrace that comes from within,
and this is what is called moral disgrace.
Being reviled, insulted, seized, and struck,
beaten with whips, having kneecaps removed or feet cut off,
beheaded, dismembered, or displayed,
trampled, crushed, having the tongue cut or nose sliced off;
this is disgrace that comes from without,
and this is what is called circumstantial disgrace.
These are the two aspects of honor and disgrace.
Therefore, a gentleman may have circumstantial disgrace,
but he cannot have moral disgrace;
a petty person may have circumstantial honor,
but he cannot have moral honor.
Having circumstantial disgrace does not prevent one from being a Yáo;
having circumstantial honor does not prevent one from being a Jié.
Moral honor and circumstantial honor,
only a gentleman can possess both;
moral disgrace and circumstantial disgrace,
only a petty person will possess both.
This is the distinction of honor and disgrace.
The Sage Kings take it as the law,
the Shì and Dàfū take it as the Way,
the officers take it as their duty,
the common people take it to form their customs,
and ten thousand generations cannot change it.”
“Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ holds otherwise:
he alone bends his countenance to suit himself,
thinking to change it in a single morning;
his theory will certainly not work.
To use an analogy:
it is like trying to block the rivers or the sea with a handful of earth,
or having a dwarf carry Tài Shān on his head;
stumbling and being crushed to pieces
will happen in less than an instant.
You gentlemen who are friendly with Zǐ Sòngzǐ,
it would be best to stop him,
lest I fear he will end up harming his own body.”
Zǐ Sòngzǐ said:
“Human nature
desires little,
but everyone takes their own nature
as desiring much;
this is an error.”
Therefore, he leads his group of followers,
elaborates on his discussions,
clarifies his analogies and examples,
intending to make people know that nature desires little.
I respond to him:
“In that case, do you also take it that human nature desires: the eyes do not desire the ultimate colors,
the ears do not desire the ultimate sounds,
the mouth does not desire the ultimate tastes,
the nose does not desire the ultimate smells,
the body does not desire the ultimate ease?
— As for these five ultimate things,
do you also take it that human nature does not desire them?”
He says:
“Human nature
desires these indeed.”
I say:
“If it is like this,
then your theory will certainly not work.
To take human nature as desiring
these five ultimate things but not desiring much
is like
taking human nature as desiring wealth and noble status but not desiring commodities,
or loving beauty but loathing Xī Shī.
“The people of old did not do it this way.
Taking human nature as desiring much and not desiring little,
they therefore rewarded with wealth and abundance and punished with reduction and loss;
this is what the hundred kings all shared in common.
Therefore, the highest worthies were rewarded with the world,
the next worthies were rewarded with a state,
the lower worthies were rewarded with fields and towns,
and the honest and sincere commoners were provided with full clothing and food.
Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ takes human nature as desiring little and not desiring much.
In that case, did the Former Kings use what people do not desire as rewards,
and what people desire as punishments?
There could be no greater chaos.
Now Zǐ Sòngzǐ is solemn and fond of persuasion,
gathering followers,
establishing schools for teachers,
and producing written canons;
yet his theory cannot avoid taking supreme order to be supreme chaos;
is this not an extreme error!”
“Where does ritual arise from?”
He said:
“Humans are born with desires;
when they have desires but do not obtain their objects,
then they cannot but seek them.
If this seeking is without measure or boundary,
then they cannot but contend.
Contention leads to disorder,
and disorder leads to destitution.
The Former Kings loathed such disorder,
so they established ritual and righteousness to create distinctions,
in order to nourish people’s desires
and satisfy people’s seeking.
They ensured that desires would not be exhausted by things,
and that things would not be depleted by desires.
The two sustain each other and grow together;
this is how ritual arose.
Therefore, ritual is nourishment.
Grass-fed and grain-fed livestock, rice and millet,
and the blending of the five flavors,
are what nourish the mouth.
The fragrance of Sichuan pepper and orchids
is what nourishes the nose.
Carving, polishing, engraving, and incising,
along with patterned embroidery and decorative designs,
are what nourish the eyes.
Bells, drums, pipes, and stone chimes,
zithers, lutes, reed pipes, and mouth organs,
are what nourish the ears.
Spacious rooms, secluded chambers, and side apartments,
fine mats, beds, couches, and bamboo mats,
are what nourish the body.
Therefore, ritual is nourishment.”
“Once the gentleman has received this nourishment,
he also takes delight in its distinctions.
What are these distinctions?”
He said:
“The noble and the base have their grades,
the elder and the younger have their differences,
and poverty, wealth, lightness, and weight all have their appropriate counterparts.
Thus, the Tiānzǐ uses the Great Carriage and fine mats
to nourish the body;
carrying fragrant herbs at his side
to nourish the nose;
with an inlaid crossbar in front
to nourish the eyes;
the sound of the Hé and Luán bells,
with the slow pace matching the Wǔ and Xiàng dances,
and the brisk pace matching the Sháo and Hù dances,
to nourish the ears;
dragon banners with nine streamers
to nourish his trustworthiness;
coverings of resting rhinoceroses and solitary tigers,
dragon-skin belly-straps, silk tassels, and dragon patterns,
to nourish his majesty.
Therefore, the horses of the Great Carriage
must be truly well-trained and submissive
before he mounts it,
to nourish his security.
Who knows that risking death to maintain integrity is the way to nourish life!
Who knows that spending wealth is the way to nourish riches!
Who knows that respect, reverence, and yielding are the way to nourish security!
Who knows that ritual, righteousness, and cultural refinement are the way to nourish the emotions!
Therefore, if a person sees only biological life,
such a person will surely die;
if they see only profit,
such a person will surely be harmed;
if they see only laziness and cowardice as security,
such a person will surely be in danger;
if they see only sensual pleasure as joy,
such a person will surely perish.
Therefore, if a person focuses solely on ritual and righteousness,
then they will attain both;
but if they focus solely on their innate nature and emotions,
then they will lose both.
Thus, the Rú are those who enable people to attain both,
whereas the Mò are those who cause people to lose both;
this is the distinction between the Rú and the Mò.”
Ritual has three bases:
Heaven and Earth are
the basis of life;
the ancestors are
the basis of the lineage;
the ruler and the teacher are
the basis of order.
Without Heaven and Earth,
how could there be life?
Without ancestors,
how could one have come forth?
Without a ruler and teacher,
how could there be order?
If even one of these three is missing,
there is no security for people.
Therefore, through ritual, one serves Heaven above,
Earth below,
honors the ancestors,
and exalts the ruler and teacher;
these are the three bases of ritual.
Therefore, the King treats the Great Ancestor as Heaven,
the feudal lords do not dare destroy their ancestral shrines,
and the grandees and officers have regular lineage heads,
all to distinguish and honor the origin.
To honor the origin is the basis of attainment.
The Jiāo sacrifice is limited to the Tiānzǐ,
the Shè sacrifice is limited to the feudal lords,
and the principles extend to the officers and grandees;
this is to distinguish the noble and the humble, so the noble serve the noble,
and the humble serve the humble,
letting what should be large be great
and what should be small be small.
Thus, he who possesses the world serves seven generations of ancestors,
he who possesses a state serves five generations,
he who has land for five chariots serves three generations,
he who has land for three chariots serves two generations,
and those who live hand-to-mouth are not permitted to establish ancestral temples;
this is to distinguish the depth of accumulated merit: for those with deep accumulation, the stream of grace is broad,
and for those with shallow accumulation, the stream of grace is narrow.
In the Great Sacrifice,
one honors the dark water vessel,
and on the sacrificial stand, one prizes raw fish;
the Great Soup is served first,
to honor the origin of food and drink.
In the Great Sacrifice,
one honors the dark water vessel but uses wines and sweet spirits;
for food, one prioritizes millet and sorghum but eats rice and fine grains;
for offerings,
one first presents the Great Soup but satisfies the appetite with many delicacies;
this is to honor the origin while drawing near to practical use.
To honor the origin is called cultural form,
to draw near to use is called structural order;
when these two combine, they form a pattern
that returns to the Tàiyī;
this is what is called the Great Exaltation.
Thus, honoring the dark water in the vessel,
prizing raw fish on the sacrificial stand,
and prioritizing the Great Soup in the serving bowls,
is all for one and the same purpose.
The fact that the cup of fortune is not drained,
that the sacrificial meat at the completion of the rite is not tasted,
and that the three scented meats are not eaten,
is all for one and the same purpose.
The fact that during the Great Marriage the robes are not yet donned,
that the Impersonator of the Dead has not yet entered the Great Temple,
and that the minor dressing of the corpse has not occurred immediately after death,
is all for one and the same purpose.
The plainness of the Great Carriage not being fully decorated,
the hempen crown worn at the Jiāo sacrifice,
and the loose hemp worn first in mourning dress,
is all for one and the same purpose.
In the three-year mourning period,
the weeping is not repeated;
in the singing of the Qīngmiào,
one singer leads and three sigh in response;
one bell is suspended,
the drum is struck on its frame,
and red lute strings are used with holes through the bottom,
which is all for one and the same purpose.
In general, all ritual
begins with simplicity,
reaches completion in cultural form,
and ends in joyful refinement.
Therefore, at its most complete,
both emotion and cultural form are fully expressed;
at the next level,
emotion and form take turns prevailing;
at the lowest level, one returns to emotion and goes back to the Tàiyī.
Through ritual, Heaven and Earth harmonize,
the sun and moon shine,
the four seasons follow their order,
the stars and planets move,
the rivers flow,
and the myriad things flourish;
through it, likes and dislikes are moderated,
and joy and anger are made appropriate;
as a subordinate, one is obedient,
as a superior, one is enlightened;
the myriad things may change without falling into disorder,
but to deviate from it is to meet with ruin.
Is ritual not perfect indeed!
It establishes the peak as the ultimate standard,
and no one in the world can add to or subtract from it.
The root and the branches are in accord,
the end and the beginning correspond,
perfect cultural form provides distinctions,
and perfect discernment provides explanations.
Those in the world who follow it achieve order,
those who do not follow it fall into disorder;
those who follow it find security,
those who do not follow it face danger;
those who follow it survive,
those who do not follow it perish.
The petty person cannot fathom this.
The principles of *Lǐ* are truly deep.
If the examinations of "Hard and White" or "Identity and Difference" enter into them, they will be drowned;
its principles are truly great;
if arbitrary innovations of institutions or narrow and vulgar theories enter into them, they will be lost;
its principles are truly high;
if those who consider violence, arrogance, license, or lighthearted vulgarity to be "high" enter into them, they will fall.
Therefore, when the marking line is truly laid out,
then one cannot be deceived regarding crookedness or straightness;
when the balance is truly suspended,
then one cannot be deceived regarding lightness or weight;
when the compass and square are truly set,
then one cannot be deceived regarding squares or circles;
when the *Jūnzǐ* is discerning in *Lǐ*,
then he cannot be deceived by fraud and artifice.
Thus, the marking line is
the ultimate of straightness;
the balance is
the ultimate of equilibrium;
the compass and square are
the ultimate of squares and circles;
and *Lǐ* is
the pinnacle of the Human Way.
However, those who do not model themselves on *Lǐ*
and do not approve of *Lǐ*
are called "people without direction";
those who model themselves on *Lǐ*
and approve of *Lǐ*
are called "scholars with direction."
To be able to search and ponder within *Lǐ*
is called being able to deliberate;
to be able to remain unchanged within *Lǐ*
is called being able to be steadfast.
To be able to deliberate and be steadfast,
and to add to these a love for it,
is to be a *Shèng Rén*.
Therefore, Heaven is
the ultimate of height;
Earth is
the ultimate of depth;
the infinite is
the ultimate of breadth;
and the *Shèng Rén* is
the ultimate of the *Dào*.
Thus, the learner
must certainly learn to be a *Shèng Rén*,
and not merely learn to be a "person without direction."
*Lǐ*
uses material goods for its utility,
uses the distinction between the noble and the base for its pattern,
uses quantity for its application,
and uses the degree of emphasis or reduction for its essential point.
When the refined pattern is elaborate
and the emotional utility is sparse,
this is the height of *Lǐ*;
when the refined pattern is sparse
and the emotional utility is elaborate,
this is the reduction of *Lǐ*;
when the refined pattern and emotional utility serve as each other's inner and outer, or surface and lining,
proceeding together in a mixture,
this is the middle course of *Lǐ*.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* reaches the height of emphasis above,
exhausts the limit of reduction below,
and dwells in the middle in between.
Pacing,
galloping, or rushing—none go beyond this;
this is the courtyard, palace, and hall of the *Jūnzǐ*.
One who possesses this
is a *Shì Jūnzǐ*;
one who is outside this
is one of the common people;
one who, within its midst,
wanders and moves freely
and attains its proper order in every detail,
is a *Shèng Rén*.
Thus, thickness is
the accumulation of *Lǐ*;
greatness is
the breadth of *Lǐ*;
height is
the elevation of *Lǐ*;
and brilliance is
the complete fulfillment of *Lǐ*.
The *Shī* says:
"The rituals and ceremonies are perfectly measured;
the laughter and speech are perfectly appropriate."
This is what is meant.
*Lǐ*
is careful in the management of life and death.
Life is the beginning of a person;
death is the end of a person.
When the beginning and the end are both good,
the Human Way is complete.
Therefore, the *Jūnzǐ* respects the beginning and is cautious at the end.
To have the end and the beginning be as one
is the way of the *Jūnzǐ*
and the refined pattern of ritual and righteousness.
Now, to treat one’s life generously but one’s death meagerly
is to respect the person when they have consciousness
but to be neglectful when they are without consciousness;
this is the way of a wicked person and the heart of a traitor.
If a *Jūnzǐ* were to treat even a *Zāng* or a *Gǔ* with the heart of a traitor,
he would still be ashamed of it,
how much more so when serving those he highly honors and is close to!
Therefore, as for the way of death,
it happens once and cannot be repeated;
this is where the minister reaches the peak of honoring his lord,
and the son reaches the peak of honoring his parents;
here it is exhausted.
Therefore, to serve the living without loyalty and generosity
or without respect and refinement
is called being uncultured;
to send off the dead without loyalty and generosity
or without respect and refinement
is called being shabby.
The *Jūnzǐ* despises the uncultured and is ashamed of the shabby.
Thus, the coffin of the *Tiān Zǐ* has seven layers,
that of the *Zhū Hóu* has five layers,
that of the *Dà Fū* has three layers,
and that of the *Shì* has two layers;
furthermore, each has fixed amounts for the generosity or meagerness of clothing and food,
and each has ranks for the patterns and colors of the funeral fans and ornaments
to respectfully adorn them,
making the living and dead, the beginning and the end, as one.
This oneness is sufficient to fulfill human wishes;
this is the way of the former kings
and the ultimate of loyal ministers and filial sons.
The funeral of a *Tiān Zǐ* moves the four seas
and brings the *Zhū Hóu* together;
the funeral of a *Zhū Hóu* moves the entire state
and brings the *Dà Fū* together;
the funeral of a *Dà Fū* moves the whole capital
and brings the *Xiū Shì* together;
the funeral of a *Xiū Shì* moves the whole village
and brings friends together;
the funeral of a *Shù Rén* brings together the clan and relatives
and moves the local neighborhood.
The funeral of a criminal who has undergone corporal punishment
is not permitted to bring together the clan and relatives;
it only concerns the wife and children.
The coffin is only three inches thick,
the burial clothes are only three layers,
the coffin may not be decorated,
and the procession may not take place during the day,
as they are buried at dusk.
They simply follow the path to bury him,
and upon returning, there are no intervals for weeping,
no mourning garments of hemp or sackcloth,
and no ranks based on the number of months for close or distant relatives.
Each person returns to their normal state,
each person restores their beginning;
once the burial is over,
they stop as if there were no funeral at all.
This is called the ultimate disgrace.
*Lǐ*
is careful to ensure that the auspicious and the inauspicious do not interfere with one another.
At the time of placing the silk floss to listen for the breath,
the loyal minister or filial son surely knows that the person is afflicted,
yet the preparations for the laying-in and shrouding have not yet been sought;
they shed tears and are filled with dread,
yet the hope for life has not yet ceased,
and the tasks of sustaining life have not yet stopped.
Only when death has finally occurred
do they then begin
and prepare these things.
Therefore, even for a well-provided family,
it is necessary to pass a day before they can perform the *bìn*;
on the third day, the mourning garments are completed,
and then the announcements to those far away are sent out,
and the preparation of objects begins.
Thus, the *bìn*
lasts no longer than seventy days
and is not shorter than fifty days.
Why is this?
I say: So that those far away can arrive,
the hundred things sought can be obtained,
and the hundred tasks can be completed.
Their loyalty reaches its peak,
their discipline is great,
and their refined pattern is complete.
Then, on the first morning of the month, they divine for the grave site,
and on the last evening of the month, they divine for the date,
and then they perform the burial.
At such a time,
if its righteousness dictates stopping,
who could carry it out?
If its righteousness dictates carrying it out,
who could stop it?
Therefore, the burial after three months
is to enclose the appearance and use the settings of the living to adorn the dead;
it is certainly not simply keeping the dead in order to comfort the living;
it is the righteousness of expressing the height of longing and devotion.
The general principles of the funeral rites:
transform and ornament the deceased,
move them and distance them,
and as time passes, return to tranquility.
Therefore, the Way of death is this:
if there is no ornament, there is repulsiveness;
if there is repulsiveness, there is no grief.
If the deceased is kept close, there is familiarity;
familiarity leads to weariness;
weariness leads to forgetting;
forgetting leads to a lack of respect.
To lose one's revered parent in a single morning,
and yet the means by which one sends them to burial
are without grief or respect—
this is to be nearly like the birds and beasts;
the *Jūnzǐ* is ashamed of it.
Therefore, transforming and ornamenting
is the means to eliminate repulsiveness;
moving them and distancing them
is the means to fulfill respect;
time passing and returning to tranquility
is the means to preserve the living.
Ritual is that which cuts off what is too long and extends what is too short;
it diminishes the superfluous
and increases the insufficient;
it expresses the refined forms of love and respect
and nurtures the beauty of practicing righteousness.
Thus, refined ornament and coarse crudeness,
music and weeping,
joy and sorrow—
these are opposites;
yet Ritual employs them both,
raising each at the proper time to govern in turn.
Therefore, refined ornament, music, and joy
are what maintain tranquility and serve auspicious occasions;
coarse crudeness, weeping, and sorrow
are what maintain the perilous and serve inauspicious occasions.
Therefore, in establishing refined ornament,
it does not reach the point of being flirtatious or seductive;
in establishing coarse mourning garments,
it does not reach the point of emaciation or self-neglect;
in establishing music and joy,
it does not reach the point of licentiousness or indolence;
in establishing weeping and sorrow,
it does not reach the point of despondency that harms life:
this is the middle course of Ritual.
Therefore, changes in feelings and appearance
are sufficient to distinguish the auspicious from the inauspicious,
and to clarify the degrees of honor and humble, and of kinship and distance;
let these be the limit.
To go beyond this
is perverse;
even if it were difficult to do,
the *Jūnzǐ* disdains it.
Therefore, one eats according to measure,
and wears a belt according to the measure of one's waist.
To compete with one another in emaciation and self-harm
is the way of the perverse person
and is not the refined form of Ritual and Righteousness,
nor is it the feeling of a filial son;
it is something done with an ulterior motive.
Thus, joy, ease, and a smooth complexion
vs. sorrow, grief, and a haggard look—
these are the feelings of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, sorrow, or joy as expressed in the countenance.
Songs, chants, and laughter
vs. weeping, wailing, and sobbing—
these are the feelings of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, sorrow, or joy as expressed in the voice.
Grain-fed animals,
rice and millet,
wine and sweet spirits,
and fish and meat
vs. thick and thin gruel,
beans and greens,
and water—
these are the feelings of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, sorrow, or joy as expressed in food and drink.
Ceremonial caps,
embroidered robes,
and patterned silks
vs. coarse hemp,
mourning garments and headbands,
hempen clothes,
and grass sandals—
these are the feelings of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, sorrow, or joy as expressed in clothing.
Spacious rooms,
carved patterns,
fine mats,
beds and couches, tables and mats
vs. thatched huts,
lean-to shelters,
straw mats and earthen pillows—
these are the feelings of auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, sorrow, or joy as expressed in dwellings.
These two types of feelings
have their origins inherent in human life.
As for cutting them short or extending them,
broadening them or shallowing them,
increasing them or diminishing them,
categorizing them or exhausting them,
making them grand and making them beautiful,
so that the root and branch, the end and the beginning,
are all in harmony and accord,
pure and complete, sufficient to serve as a model for ten thousand generations—
this is Ritual.
None but a *Jūnzǐ* who follows it and cultivates it
can understand it.
Therefore it is said:
Nature is the original beginning and raw material;
deliberate effort is the refinement and patterns that are grand and flourishing.
Without nature, deliberate effort would have nothing to be applied to;
without deliberate effort, nature could not make itself beautiful.
When nature and deliberate effort combine,
only then is the name of the *Shèng Rén* established,
and the work of unifying the world is thus accomplished.
Therefore it is said:
*Tiān* and *Dì* combine and the myriad things are born;
*Yīn* and *Yáng* interact and transformations arise;
nature and deliberate effort combine and the world is governed.
*Tiān* can give birth to things
but cannot distinguish between things;
*Dì* can support humans
but cannot govern humans.
Among the myriad things in the universe and the category of living humans,
it is only after the *Shèng Rén* acts that distinctions are made.
The *Shī* says:
"He gathered in and harmonized the hundred spirits,
down to the *Hé* and the high peaks."
This is what it means.
The funeral rites
are the use of the living to ornament the dead;
they greatly resemble the living to send off the dead.
Therefore, one treats them as dead yet as alive,
as existing yet as gone;
the end and the beginning are one.
When death first occurs,
washing the hair and body, binding the hair, and placing rice and shells in the mouth
resemble the acts of the living.
If the hair is not washed, the comb is moistened and passed through three times and that is all;
if the body is not washed, the cloth is moistened and rubbed over it three times and that is all.
Ear-plugs are placed in the ears,
the rice in the mouth is raw,
the shells in the mouth are dry bone—
this reverses the ways of the living.
Inner garments are provided,
three layers of burial clothes are used,
but while there is a sash, there are no hooks or belts.
The face is covered and the eyes are shaded;
the hair is bound but no cap or pin is used.
One writes the name
and places it on the spirit tablet;
then the name is not seen, yet the coffin is clearly identified.
Regarding the offerings:
the cap has a chin strap but no tassels;
the jars and pots are empty and not filled;
there are mats but no beds or couches;
wooden vessels are not fully carved;
pottery is not fully finished;
and the thin vessels are not fit for use.
The reed pipes and organs are provided but not in harmony;
the zithers are strung but not tuned.
The carriages are buried but the horses are returned,
showing they will not be used.
One prepares the utensils of the living to go to the tomb,
resembling the way of moving house.
But they are incomplete and not fully functional,
having the form but not the utility.
One hastens with the carriage and buries it,
but the metal, leather, bridles, and traces do not enter,
making it clear they are not to be used.
It resembles moving house,
yet also makes clear they are not to be used—
these are all ways to deepen the expression of grief.
Thus, the utensils for the living are ornamented but not functional;
the *míngqì* have the form but are not used.
In all ritual:
serving the living
is to ornament joy;
sending off the dead
is to ornament grief;
sacrifices
are to ornament respect;
military campaigns
are to ornament majesty:
these are what the hundred kings have in common,
what has been unified from ancient times to the present;
no one knows where they originally came from.
Therefore, the tomb and its mound resemble a house in their form;
the inner and outer coffins resemble the sideboards and covers of a carriage in their form;
the funeral banners, silken hangings, and fan-shaped screens
resemble the curtains, canopies, and hangings of the living in their form;
the frame and the covers for the coffin
resemble the plastering, thatching, and fences of a house in their form.
Thus, the funeral rites
are nothing else
than to clarify the meaning of death and life,
to send off the dead with grief and respect,
and to bring the burial to a complete and thorough conclusion.
Therefore, interment,
is the respectful burial of the physical form;
sacrifices
are the respectful service to the spirit;
the inscriptions, eulogies, and genealogies
are the respectful transmission of the name.
Serving the living
is to ornament the beginning;
seeing off the dead
is to ornament the end.
When the end and the beginning are complete,
then the service of the filial son is finished and
the Way of the Sage is perfected.
To stint the dead while enriching the living is called Mò;
to stint the living while enriching the dead is called delusion;
to kill the living to see off the dead is called murder.
To grandly emulate life in order to see off the dead,
so that death and life, beginning and end, are all appropriate and good—
this is the model of ritual and righteousness,
and the Rú are this.
The three-year mourning period—why is this?
I say:
it establishes a formal pattern based on emotions,
and thereby ornaments the community,
distinguishing the measures for kin and strangers, the noble and the lowly,
and cannot be increased or decreased.
Therefore it is said:
it is a method that cannot be changed in any application.
One whose wound is deep takes a long time;
one whose pain is extreme recovers slowly.
The three-year mourning,
establishing a formal pattern based on emotions,
is designed as the ultimate expression for extreme pain;
the mourning garments of coarse hemp, the unpeeled staff, living in a hut, eating congee, sleeping on straw, and pillowing on a clod—these are the ornaments of extreme pain.
The three-year mourning period
concludes in twenty-five months;
sorrow and pain have not ended,
and longing has not been forgotten.
Yet the reason ritual cuts it off at this point
is surely because seeing off the dead must have an end,
and returning to the living must have a regulation!
Of all things born between Heaven and Earth,
those with blood and breath must have awareness;
of those with awareness, none fail to love their own kind.
Now, when large birds or beasts lose their mates,
after months or seasons have passed,
they surely return to the former place.
When they pass their old home,
they surely pace back and forth,
cry out,
stamp their feet,
and hesitate,
only then being able to leave it.
Even small creatures like swallows and sparrows
have a moment of chirping and crying
before they can leave.
Therefore, among those with blood and breath, none are as aware as humans.
Thus, for a person's feelings toward their parents,
they are limitless until death.
Should we follow the ignorant, base, or deviant person?
They forget on the evening what died in the morning.
If we allowed this,
then they would not even be equal to birds and beasts.
How could such people live together in a community without chaos?
Should we follow the cultivated Jūnzǐ?
Then the three-year mourning,
which ends in twenty-five months,
passes like a team of horses glimpsed through a crack.
If we let them follow their feelings,
it would go on forever.
Therefore, the ancient kings and Sages established a middle path and regulated the measures,
making them just enough to complete the formal pattern,
and then discontinued it.
How then are the distinctions made?
I say:
for the closest kin, the one-year period is the limit.
Why is this?
I say:
Heaven and Earth have already changed,
the four seasons have already passed through,
and all things in the universe have begun anew.
Therefore, the ancient kings modeled it after this.
Then why is it three years?
I say: to add further exaltation,
they doubled it.
Thus it is two one-year periods.
Why are there periods of nine months and below?
I say: to make them less than the full period.
Thus, three years is the exalted peak;
Sī and
Xiǎogōng are the reductions;
one year and nine months are the intermediate levels.
Above, it takes its image from Heaven;
below, it takes its image from Earth;
in the middle, it takes its rule from humanity.
