The principle by which humans live together in harmony and unity is thus exhausted.
Therefore, the three-year mourning
is the supreme formal pattern of the human way.
This is called the ultimate exaltation;
it is what the hundred kings have shared and what has been unified from ancient times to the present.
The mourning for a ruler
also takes three years—
why?
I say:
the ruler is the master of order and discernment,
the source of formal patterns and principles,
and the perfection of emotion and appearance.
If all follow each other in exalting him,
is that not appropriate?
The Shī says:
"The joyful and easy-going Jūnzǐ,
is the father and mother of the people."
Regarding that Jūnzǐ,
there is indeed the saying that he acts as the father and mother of the people.
A father can give life,
but cannot feed;
a mother can feed,
but cannot instruct.
The ruler
can both feed the people
and is good at instructing them;
three years is truly the completion!
A wet nurse feeds a child,
and the mourning is three months;
a foster mother clothes a child,
and it is nine months;
the ruler provides for all needs in every detail;
how could three years be anything but appropriate!
With him there is order,
without him there is chaos—
this is the height of formal patterns;
with him there is safety,
without him there is danger—
this is the height of emotion.
Both heights are accumulated there;
serving him for three years
is still not enough.
It is simply that there is no way to extend it further.
Therefore, the Shè
is the sacrifice to the Shè;
the Jì is the sacrifice to the Jì;
the Jiāo
is the sacrifice to the hundred kings together with High Heaven.
The three-month period of keeping the coffin in the hall
—why is this?
I say:
it is to magnify him
and treat him with gravity;
it is the ultimate exaltation
and the ultimate intimacy.
When he is about to be moved,
transferred,
and leave his chambers to return to the hills,
the ancient kings feared it would be lacking in formal pattern.
Therefore they extended the period,
and filled the days.
Thus, for the Tiānzǐ it is seven months,
for the Zhūhóu five months,
for the Dàfū three months,
all allowing the delay to accommodate the business,
the business to accommodate the completion,
the completion to accommodate the formal pattern,
and the formal pattern to accommodate the preparedness.
To accommodate all details and prepare all things is called the Way.
Sacrifices are the accumulation of the will, thoughts, and longing.
Feelings of transformation, grief, and melancholy cannot fail to arrive at certain times.
Thus, when others are in a time of joy and harmonious gathering,
the loyal minister and the filial son will also have feelings of transformation and arrival.
That which arrives in them
is a very great stirring.
If they were just suppressed and ended,
then for the accumulation of their will and thoughts, they would feel disappointed and unsatisfied.
For their ritual regulations, there would be a gap and incompleteness.
Therefore, the ancient kings established a formal pattern for them,
and the righteousness of honoring the honorable and loving the kin reached its peak.
Thus it is said:
sacrifice is the accumulation of the will, thoughts, and longing;
it is the peak of loyalty, trust, love, and respect;
and the height of ritual regulations and formal appearances.
If one is not a Sage,
no one can truly understand this.
The Sage clearly understands it,
the Shì and Jūnzǐ peacefully practice it,
the officials maintain it as their duty,
and the common people form their customs by it.
Among the Jūnzǐ, it is considered the human way;
among the common people, it is considered a matter of ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, bells and drums, flutes and stone chimes,
zithers and lutes, mouth organs and pipes,
the *Sháo*, the *Xià*, the *Hù*,
the *Wǔ*, the *Zhuó*, the *Huán*, the *Shuò*, and the *Xiàng*—
these are the cultural forms by which the gentleman manifests and alters his expressions of joy.
The *zī cuī* mourning garments, the hempen staff, living in a mourning hut, eating congee, sleeping on straw, and pillowing on a clod—
these are the cultural forms by which the gentleman manifests and alters his expressions of grief and pain.
Military expeditions have their regulations,
punishments and laws have their gradations,
none of which fail to correspond to the crime—
these are the cultural forms by which the gentleman manifests and alters his expressions of intense dislike.
Divining by turtle shell and milfoil, selecting auspicious days, fasting and purifying,
sweeping the paths, arranging the small tables and mats,
offering food, presenting sacrifices, and delivering prayers and invocations,
as if someone were there to partake of them;
taking various items and sacrificing them all,
as if someone were there to taste them;
not being hasty in raising the wine cup,
the host having the ritual vessels,
as if someone were there to receive the toast;
when the guest departs,
the host bows in farewell,
returns to change his clothes,
and takes his place to wail,
as if someone had just left.
How sorrowful!
How reverent!
Serving the dead as one serves the living,
serving the departed as one serves those who remain,
giving shape to what has no form
or shadow, and thus completing the cultural form.
Now, music is joy,
an inescapable part of human emotion,
therefore humans cannot be without music.
When there is joy, it must be expressed in sounds and tones,
and take form in movement and stillness;
this is the Way of humanity.
In sounds, tones, movement, and stillness,
the transformations of the arts of life are fully contained.
Therefore, humans cannot but feel joy,
and when there is joy, it cannot but take form;
if it takes form but is not guided by the Way,
then there cannot but be disorder.
The former kings loathed such disorder,
so they established the sounds of the *Yǎ* and the *Sòng* to guide it,
making the sounds sufficient to provide joy without becoming licentious,
making the patterns sufficient to be distinct without being obscure,
making their inflections, complexity, texture, and rhythm
sufficient to move the good hearts of people,
and preventing perverse and filthy influences from having any way to connect with them.
This is the method by which the former kings established music,
yet *Mòzǐ* criticizes it—how can this be!
Therefore, when music is performed in the ancestral temple,
and the ruler and ministers, high and low, listen to it together,
there are none who are not harmonious and reverent;
within the inner gates of the household,
when fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers, listen to it together,
there are none who are not harmonious and affectionate;
among the elders and leaders of the villages,
when old and young listen to it together,
there are none who are not harmonious and cooperative.
Thus, music is that which examines unity to determine harmony,
and compares things to adorn the rhythm;
rhythms combine to form patterns,
sufficient to lead people along one Way,
and sufficient to govern ten thousand changes.
This is the art by which the former kings established music,
yet *Mòzǐ* criticizes it—how can this be!
Therefore, when one listens to the sounds of the *Yǎ* and the *Sòng*,
one's will and intentions become broad;
when one grasps the shields and axes,
and practices the postures of bending, lifting, curling, and stretching,
one's appearance and demeanor become solemn;
when one moves through the formations and positions,
and keeps time with the rhythm,
the ranks and files become straight,
and the advances and retreats become orderly.
Thus, music, when going out, is used for military expeditions and executions,
and when coming in, is used for bowing and yielding.
Expeditions and executions, bowing and yielding—
their principle is one and the same.
In going out for expeditions and executions,
none fail to listen and obey;
in coming in for bowing and yielding,
none fail to follow and submit.
Thus, music is the great equalizer of the world,
the standard of central harmony,
and an inescapable part of human emotion.
This is the art by which the former kings established music,
yet *Mòzǐ* criticizes it—how can this be!
Furthermore, music is that which the former kings used to adorn joy;
military forces, axes, and halberds are
that which the former kings used to adorn anger.
The joy and anger of the former kings both attained their proper regulation.
Therefore, when they were joyful, the world harmonized with them,
and when they were angry, the violent and chaotic feared them.
In the Way of the former kings,
ritual and music are the most flourishing parts,
yet *Mòzǐ* criticizes them.
Therefore it is said: *Mòzǐ*’s relationship to the Way
is like a blind man's relationship to white and black,
or a deaf man's relationship to clear and muddy sounds,
or like wanting to go to *Chǔ* but seeking it by heading north.
Now, the way music enters into people is deep,
and its transformation of people is rapid;
therefore the former kings were careful in crafting its cultural forms.
When music is balanced and moderate, the people are harmonious and do not drift;
when music is solemn and grave, the people are orderly and not chaotic.
When the people are harmonious and orderly, then the troops are strong and the cities are secure,
and enemy states dare not infringe upon them.
In such a case,
none of the common people fail to be at peace in their dwellings
and find joy in their villages,
thereby being fully satisfied with their superiors.
Then their reputation becomes clear,
and their glory becomes great;
the people within the four seas all desire to have them as their leaders.
This is the beginning of true kingship.
If music is seductive and dangerous,
then the people will be drifting, slothful, base, and low.
Being drifting and slothful, they will be chaotic;
being base and low, they will be contentious.
When there is chaos and contention, then the troops are weak and the cities are invaded,
and enemy states will endanger them.
In such a case,
the common people will not be at peace in their dwellings,
will not find joy in their villages,
and will not be satisfied with their superiors.
Therefore, the discarding of ritual and music and the arising of corrupt sounds
are the roots of danger, diminishment, insult, and disgrace.
Thus, the former kings valued ritual and music and despised corrupt sounds.
As it is stated in the *Xù Guān*:
It says:
"Cultivating laws and mandates,
carefully examining punishments and rewards,
prohibiting licentious sounds,
following and cultivating them in accordance with the seasons,
ensuring that barbarian customs and corrupt sounds do not dare to disrupt the *Yǎ*—
these are the duties of the *Dàshī*."
*Mòzǐ* said:
"Music is something that the sage kings condemned,
yet the Ru practice it—this is an error."
The gentleman believes this is not so.
Music is what the sage finds joy in,
and it can improve the hearts of the people;
its influence on people is deep,
and it transforms customs and changes habits;
therefore the former kings guided them with ritual and music,
and the people were harmonious and friendly.
Now, the people have emotions of like and dislike,
but if there is no proper response to joy and anger, then there is disorder.
The former kings loathed such disorder,
so they cultivated their conduct
and corrected their music,
and the world followed them.
Therefore, the *zī cuī* mourning garments
and the sounds of wailing and weeping
make the human heart feel sorrow;
wearing armor and donning helmets, singing
in the ranks of the army,
make the human heart feel stern;
seductive appearances
and the sounds of *Zhèng* and *Wèi*
make the human heart feel licentious;
wearing formal robes and the *zhāng fǔ* ceremonial cap,
dancing the *Sháo* and singing the *Wǔ*,
make the human heart feel solemn.
Thus, the gentleman's ears do not listen to licentious sounds,
his eyes do not look at seductive women,
and his mouth does not utter evil words.
These three things—
the gentleman is careful about them.
Whenever wicked sounds affect a person, a perverse *qì* responds to them;
when perverse *qì* takes form, disorder is born there.
When correct sounds affect a person, a compliant *qì* responds to them;
when compliant *qì* takes form, order is born there.
Singing and harmonizing have their responses,
good and evil take after their own kind;
therefore the gentleman is careful about what he rejects and what he pursues.
The gentleman uses bells and drums to guide his will,
uses zithers and lutes to gladden his heart,
moves with the shield and axe,
adorns himself with feathers and tassels,
and is accompanied by stone chimes and flutes.
Thus, their purity and clarity resemble Heaven,
their breadth and greatness resemble Earth,
and their movements of bending, lifting, and circling are like the four seasons.
Therefore, when music is practiced, the will becomes pure;
when ritual is cultivated, conduct is perfected;
the ears and eyes become keen and clear;
the blood and *qì* become harmonious and balanced;
customs are transformed and traditions are changed;
the whole world becomes peaceful,
and beauty and goodness are mutually enjoyed.
Therefore it is said:
"Music is joy."
The *jūnzǐ* finds joy in attaining the *Dào*,
while the petty person finds joy in attaining their desires.
When the *Dào* is used to restrain desires,
then there is joy without disorder;
when desires are used to forget the *Dào*,
then there is delusion without joy.
Therefore, music
is that which guides joy,
and the metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments
are that which guide virtue.
When music is practiced, the people turn toward the proper direction.
Therefore, music
is the height of governing people,
yet *Mòzǐ* condemned it.
Furthermore, music
is the unchangeable aspect of harmony;
ritual
is the immutable aspect of principle.
Music brings together in unity,
and ritual distinguishes differences.
The unification of ritual and music
holds sway over the human heart.
Exhausting the source and reaching the limits of transformation
is the essence of music;
manifesting sincerity and removing falsehood
is the constant of ritual.
*Mòzǐ* condemned it,
nearly encountering punishment.
Since the enlightened kings have passed away,
no one has corrected it.
The foolish study him,
endangering their own persons.
The *jūnzǐ* understands music;
this is indeed their virtue.
A chaotic age hates goodness
and will not listen to this.
How lamentable!
It cannot be brought to completion.
Let the disciples strive in their studies,
and not be led astray.
The symbolism of sound and music:
The drums are as grand as the heavens;
the bells unify the substance;
the sounding stones are sharp and regulated;
the *yú* and *shēng* pipes are solemn and harmonious;
the *guǎn* and *yuè* flutes are stirring and vigorous;
the *xūn* and *chí* ocarinas are resonant and broad;
the *sè* zither is easy and fine;
the *qín* zither is like the affection of a wife;
the singing is clear and exhaustive;
and the intent of the dance encompasses the *Tiāndào*.
The drum—is it not the sovereign of music?
Thus, the drum resembles Heaven;
the bells resemble Earth;
the sounding stones resemble Water;
the *yú*, *shēng* (*xiāo* in harmony), *guǎn*, and *yuè*
resemble the stars, the sun, and the moon;
and the *táo*, *zhù*, *fǔ*, *gé*, *qiāng*, and *jié* resemble the myriad things.
How do we know the intent of the dance?
It is said:
The eyes do not see themselves;
the ears do not hear themselves;
yet the control of bowing and looking up, bending and stretching, advancing and retreating, slowness and speed,
is all strictly regulated;
they exert the strength of their sinews and bones
to match the rhythms of the bells and drums as they bow and gather,
and there is not one who is contrary to the rhythm;
how the gathered intent of the multitude flows smoothly!
*Kǒngzǐ* said: "I observe the village rituals,
and I know how easy and simple the *Wángdào* is."
The host personally invites the guest and the assistant guest,
and the other guests all follow them;
arriving outside the gate,
the host bows to the guest and the assistant guest,
and then the other guests all enter;
thus the distinction between the noble and the lowly is established.
Making three bows as they reach the steps,
and yielding three times as the guest ascends,
bowing upon arrival, the presentation, and the reciprocation of wine—
the rhythms of declining and yielding are numerous.
When it comes to the assistant guest, the ritual is simplified.
When it comes to the other guests,
they ascend and receive, sit to offer a sacrifice, and stand to drink;
they descend without returning a cup;
thus the distinctions of degree and reduction are clarified.
The musicians enter;
they ascend and sing three sections;
the host presents them with wine.
The *shēng* players enter and play three sections;
the host presents them with wine.
Alternating songs are performed for three sections;
combined music is performed for three sections;
the musicians announce that the music is complete,
and then they exit.
Two men raise their goblets,
and the *Sīzhèng* is established there;
thus it is known they can be harmonious and joyful without becoming dissolute.
The guest toasts the host,
the host toasts the assistant guest,
the assistant guest toasts the other guests,
the younger and older toast according to their age,
ending with the one who pours the water for washing.
Thus it is known they can respect the elders and the young without omitting anyone.
They descend,
remove their sandals, and ascend to sit;
they offer cups without limit.
In the rhythm of drinking wine,
the morning session does not neglect the morning duties,
and the evening session does not neglect the evening duties.
The guests depart,
the host bows as they leave,
and the rhythmic protocols are brought to their final conclusion.
Thus it is known they can be at ease in feasting without falling into disorder.
When noble and lowly are clear,
degrees and reductions are distinguished,
harmony and joy exist without dissolution,
elders and young are respected without omission,
and feasting is peaceful without disorder—
these five practices
are sufficient to rectify the self and bring peace to the state.
When the state is at peace, the world is at peace.
Therefore it is said:
"I observe the village rituals,
and I know how easy and simple the *Wángdào* is."
The signs of a chaotic age:
their clothing is overly ornate;
their demeanor is effeminate;
their customs are licentious;
their intent is on profit;
their conduct is mixed;
their music is depraved;
their writings are deceptive yet colorful;
their nourishment of life is without measure;
their burials are parsimonious and dismal;
they slight ritual and righteousness while valuing bravery and force;
when poor, they become thieves;
when wealthy, they become villains.
An age of order is the opposite of this.
The common affliction of people
is to be obscured by a single corner
and be ignorant of the great principles.
If there is order, then the constants are restored;
if there are two doubts, then there is confusion.
In the world, there are not two *Dào*;
in the sage, there are not two hearts.
Now the feudal lords have different governments,
and the hundred schools have different theories;
thus people must be confused about what is right and wrong,
and confused about order and chaos.
The ruler of a chaotic state
and the person of a chaotic family—
none of their sincere hearts
fails to seek correctness for themselves,
yet they are confused and stray from the *Dào*,
and others entice them toward what they can reach.
They are partial to what they have accumulated,
fearing only to hear of its faults;
they rely on their partialities
to observe other arts,
fearing only to hear of their merits.
Thus, they run away from order
while never ceasing to justify themselves.
Are they not indeed obscured by a single corner
and thus lose the pursuit of correctness?
If the heart is not applied,
then even if white and black are before one, the eyes will not see;
even if thunderous drums are at one's side, the ears will not hear.
How much more so for those things to which the mind is applied!
A person of virtue and the *Dào*
is condemned from above by the ruler of a chaotic state,
and condemned from below by the people of a chaotic family.
Is this not truly lamentable!
Therefore, causes of blindness are:
desire causes blindness,
hate causes blindness,
the beginning causes blindness,
the end causes blindness,
distance causes blindness,
proximity causes blindness,
breadth causes blindness,
shallowness causes blindness,
the past causes blindness,
and the present causes blindness.
Whenever myriad things differ, they all inevitably blind one another;
this is a common malady of the mind’s operations.
Among rulers of the past who were blinded,
Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu were such men.
Jié was blinded by Mò Xǐ and Sī Guān,
and thus did not know Guān Lóngpáng;
thereby his mind was deluded
and his conduct fell into disorder.
Zhòu was blinded by Dá Jǐ and Fēi Lián,
and thus did not know Wēizǐ Qǐ;
thereby his mind was deluded
and his conduct fell into disorder.
Thus the various ministers abandoned loyalty to serve private interests,
the common people harbored resentment and would not be employed,
and the worthy and good retired to live in seclusion and flight.
This is why they lost the lands of the nine provinces
and emptied the state of the ancestral temples.
Jié died at Géshān,
and Zhòu was hung from a red banner;
they themselves did not realize beforehand,
and no one would remonstrate with them.
This is the calamity of being blinded and obstructed.
Chéng Tāng took Xià Jié as a warning;
therefore he mastered his mind and was cautious in his governance.
Consequently, he was able to employ Yī Yǐn for a long time
and never lost the Way himself.
This is why he replaced the Xià king and received the nine divisions of the world.
Wén Wáng took Yīn Zhòu as a warning;
therefore he mastered his mind and was cautious in his governance.
Consequently, he was able to employ Lǚ Wàng for a long time
and never lost the Way himself.
This is why he replaced the Yīn king and received the nine provinces.
There was no distant region that did not present its treasures;
thus his eyes saw the full range of colors,
his ears heard the full range of sounds,
his mouth ate the full range of flavors,
his person resided in the most complete palaces,
and his name was bestowed with the most complete titles.
While he lived, the world sang of him;
when he died, all within the four seas wept for him.
This is what is called supreme flourishing.
The Shì says:
“The phoenixes dance,
their wings like shields,
their voices like flutes.
There are female phoenixes,
there are male phoenixes, delighting the heart of the Emperor.”
This is the blessing of not being blinded.
Among ministers of the past who were blinded,
Táng Yǎng and Xī Qí were such men.
Táng Yǎng was blinded by the desire for power and expelled Zài Zǐ;
Xī Qí was blinded by the desire for the state and incriminated Shēn Shēng.
Táng Yǎng was executed in Sòng,
and Xī Qí was executed in Jìn.
They expelled a worthy minister and incriminated a filial brother;
they themselves suffered execution,
and yet they did not realize it.
This is the calamity of being blinded and obstructed.
Therefore, by means of greed and meanness,
betrayal,
and struggling for power, there have never been any from ancient times to the present who did not face danger, disgrace, or destruction.
Bǎo Shū, Nìng Qī, and Xī Péng were benevolent and wise and were not blinded;
thus they were able to support Guǎn Zhòng, and their fame, profit, fortune, and emoluments were equal to those of Guǎn Zhòng.
Zhào Gōng and Lǚ Wàng were benevolent and wise and were not blinded;
thus they were able to support Zhōu Gōng, and their fame, profit, fortune, and emoluments were equal to those of Zhōu Gōng.
The Zhuàn says:
“To know the worthy is called brilliance;
to assist the worthy is called ability.
If one strives and exerts oneself in this,
one’s blessings will surely be long-lasting.”
This is what it refers to.
This is the blessing of not being blinded.
Among the guest-disciples of the past who were blinded,
the leaders of various schools were such men.
Mòzǐ was blinded by utility and did not know cultural refinement.
Sòngzǐ was blinded by the desire to reduce desires and did not know how to obtain what is truly beneficial.
Shènzǐ was blinded by law and did not know worthiness.
Shēnzǐ was blinded by authority and did not know wisdom.
Huìzǐ was blinded by rhetoric and did not know reality.
Zhuāngzǐ was blinded by Heaven and did not know man.
Therefore, if one speaks of it from the perspective of utility, the Way
consists entirely of benefit.
If one speaks of it from the perspective of common satisfaction, the Way
consists entirely of contentment.
If one speaks of it from the perspective of law, the Way
consists entirely of technique.
If one speaks of it from the perspective of authority, the Way
consists entirely of convenience.
If one speaks of it from the perspective of rhetoric, the Way
consists entirely of argumentation.
If one speaks of it from the perspective of Heaven, the Way
consists entirely of following nature.
These various perspectives
are each but a single corner of the Way.
As for the Way, it embodies the constant and exhausts all transformations;
a single corner is insufficient to characterize it.
People of partial knowledge
look at a single corner of the Way and are unable to recognize it.
Therefore, they think it sufficient and embellish it;
internally, they confuse themselves,
and externally, they delude others.
Superiors use it to blind subordinates,
and subordinates use it to blind superiors.
This is the calamity of being blinded and obstructed.
Kǒngzǐ was benevolent and wise and was not blinded;
therefore, his study of various methods was sufficient to make him a master of the Former Kings.
His school alone attained the Way of Zhōu;
he took it up and employed it,
not being blinded by accumulated habits.
Thus his virtue was equal to that of Zhōu Gōng,
and his name was ranked with the Three Kings.
This is the blessing of not being blinded.
The Sage knows the maladies of the mind’s operations
and sees the calamities of being blinded and obstructed.
Therefore, he is without fixed desire or hate, without fixed beginning or end, without fixed proximity or distance, without fixed breadth or shallowness, and without fixed past or present.
He lays out all the myriad things together and suspends the balance in their midst.
Thus the various differences cannot blind each other and throw their proper order into confusion.
What is called the “balance”?
I say: it is the Way.
Therefore, the mind cannot afford not to know the Way.
If the mind does not know the Way,
then it will disapprove of the Way
and approve of what is not the Way.
Who would wish to give free rein to their desires
yet hold to what they disapprove of
to prohibit what they approve of?
If one selects people with a mind that does not approve of the Way,
then one will surely harmonize with those who do not follow the Way
and not harmonize with those who follow the Way.
Using a mind that does not approve of the Way
and joining with those who do not follow the Way to discuss those who follow the Way—
this is the root of disorder.
How does one know this?
(I say) :
When the mind knows the Way,
then it can approve of the Way;
when it approves of the Way,
then it can hold to the Way to prohibit what is not the Way.
If one selects people with a mind that approves of the Way,
then one will harmonize with those who follow the Way
and not harmonize with those who do not follow the Way.
Using a mind that approves of the Way
and joining with those who follow the Way to discuss what is not the Way—
this is the essential for good order. Why worry about being ignorant?
Therefore, the essential for good order lies in knowing the Way.
How does a person know the Way?
I say: it is through the mind.
How does the mind know it?
I say: through emptiness, unity, and stillness.
The mind is never without storage;
yet it has what is called emptiness.
The mind is never without fullness;
yet it has what is called unity.
The mind is never without movement;
yet it has what is called stillness.
From birth, humans have knowledge;
with knowledge, there is memory.
Memory
is storage;
yet there is what is called emptiness.
Not allowing what is already stored to harm what is about to be received is called emptiness.
From birth, the mind has knowledge;
with knowledge, there are differences.
Differences mean
knowing several things simultaneously.
To know several things simultaneously
is duality;
yet there is what is called unity.
Not allowing that one thing to harm this one thing is called unity.
The mind,
when one sleeps, it dreams;
when it is at ease, it wanders on its own;
when it is put to use, it plans.
Therefore, the mind is never without movement;
yet there is what is called stillness.
Not allowing dreams and fancies to throw knowledge into disorder is called stillness.
For those who have not yet attained the Dào but seek it,
it is called emptiness, unity, and stillness.
In practicing these,
the one who awaits the Dào will require emptiness; if empty, one can enter.
The one who serves the Dào will require unity; if unified, one can reach the limit.
The one who ponders the Dào will require stillness; if still, one can perceive clearly.
Knowing the Dào and perceiving clearly,
knowing the Dào and acting upon it,
is what it means to embody the Dào.
Emptiness, unity, and stillness
are called the Great Clarity and Brightness.
Among the myriad things, none has form without being seen,
none is seen without being discussed,
and none is discussed while losing its proper place.
Sitting in a room, one sees the four seas;
dwelling in the present, one discusses the distant past and future;
surveying the myriad things broadly, one knows their true essence;
comparing and examining order and chaos, one understands their measure;
weaving together heaven and earth, one utilizes and manages the myriad things;
determining and dividing the Great Principles, the whole universe is contained within.
Vast and expansive—
who knows its limits!
Lofty and broad—
who knows its virtue!
Swirling and profuse—
who knows its form!
Its brightness equals the sun and moon;
its greatness fills the eight extremities;
this is what is called the Great Person.
How could such a person suffer from obsession?
The heart-mind is
the lord of the physical form
and the master of the spirit-like intelligence.
It issues commands but receives none.
It restrains itself,
employs itself,
deprives itself,
takes for itself,
acts by itself,
and stops by itself.
Thus, the mouth can be forced to remain silent or speak,
and the physical form can be forced to bend or stretch,
but the heart-mind cannot be forced to change its will.
What it considers right, it accepts;
what it considers wrong, it rejects.
Therefore it is said:
The heart-mind is capacious; in its selections,
it is unconstrained and must manifest itself.
Its objects are
diverse and vast,
but the height of its essence is
to be without duplicity.
The Shī says:
“Gathering, gathering the Juǎn’ěr,
they do not fill a shallow basket.
Alas, I sigh for my beloved,
and place them on the Zhōu road.”
A shallow basket is easy to fill,
and Juǎn’ěr are easy to find,
yet one cannot fill the basket if the mind is divided by the Zhōu road.
Therefore it is said:
If the heart-mind branches out, it lacks knowledge;
if it leans to one side, it is not pure;
if it is divided, it is filled with doubt.
If one uses the Dào to assist in investigating things,
the myriad things can all be known.
To personally fulfill the reasons for this is excellence.
Different categories of things cannot be mastered simultaneously;
therefore, the wise person chooses one and unifies upon it.
A farmer may be skilled in the fields,
but cannot be a Master of Agriculture;
a merchant may be skilled in the market,
but cannot be a Master of Commerce;
an artisan may be skilled with tools,
but cannot be a Master of Crafts.
There are those
who possess none of these three skills,
yet can be employed to manage the three offices.
They are said to be skilled in the Dào,
not skilled in specific things.
Those skilled in things use one thing to treat another thing as a thing;
those skilled in the Dào treat all things as things comprehensively.
Therefore, the Jūnzǐ unifies on the Dào and uses it to assist in investigating things.
Being unified on the Dào, he is upright;
using it to assist in investigating things, he is perceptive;
with an upright will and perceptive discourse,
then the myriad things are properly managed.
In the past, when Shùn governed the world,
he did not issue orders for every matter, yet the myriad things were accomplished.
Dwelling in the precariousness of oneness,
its glory fills his side;
nurturing the subtlety of oneness,
it is glorious, yet unnoticed.
Thus, the Dàojīng says:
“The human heart-mind is precarious;
the heart-mind of the Dào is subtle.”
The subtle signs of the precarious and the minute—
only an enlightened Jūnzǐ can understand them.
Therefore, the human heart-mind is like water in a basin:
if placed upright and not disturbed,
then the heavy sediment settles at the bottom and the clear brightness stays on top;
then it is sufficient to see one’s beard and eyebrows and examine the lines of the skin.
If a slight breeze passes over it,
the heavy sediment is stirred from below,
and the clear brightness is disturbed on top;
then one cannot even get a correct view of a large form.
The heart-mind is just like this.
Therefore, if one guides it with principle
and nurtures it with clarity,
so that no thing can tip it,
then it is sufficient to determine right and wrong and resolve doubts and suspicions.
If small things pull at it,
then its outward rectitude is changed
and its heart-mind within is tipped;
then it is insufficient to decide on the various principles.
Thus, many have loved writing,
but Cāngjié alone is passed down because
he was unified;
many have loved farming,
but Hòujì alone is passed down because
he was unified;
many have loved music,
but Kuí alone is passed down because
he was unified;
many have loved righteousness,
but Shùn alone is passed down because
he was unified.
Chuí made bows,
Fúyóu made arrows,
but Yì was the master of archery;
Xīzhòng made carriages,
Sāngdù mastered the harnessing of horses,
but Zàofù was the master of driving.
From ancient times until today,
there has never been one who could be a master while having a divided mind.
Zēngzǐ said:
“His courtyard is fit for catching rats;
how could he sing along with me!”
Inside a hollow rock there was a man
named Jí;
as a person,
he was good at archery and fond of pondering.
When the desires of his ears and eyes were engaged,
they ruined his pondering;
when the sound of mosquitoes and gadflies was heard,
it disrupted his concentration.
Therefore, he shut out the desires of his ears and eyes
and distanced himself from the sound of mosquitoes and gadflies;
living in solitude and pondering in stillness, he achieved understanding.
If pondering benevolence is like this,
can it be called “subtle”?
Mèngzǐ disliked bad behavior and divorced his wife—
this can be called being able to exert oneself;
Yǒuzǐ disliked sleeping and burned his palm—
this can be called being able to endure;
but neither had reached the stage of loving it.
Shutting out the desires of the ears and eyes
can be called being able to exert oneself,
but it is not yet reaching the stage of pondering.
The sound of mosquitoes and gadflies,
which disrupts one’s concentration when heard, can be called “precarious,”
but cannot be called “subtle.”
Now, the subtle one
is the Ultimate Person.
For the Ultimate Person,
what need is there for exertion?
What need for endurance?
What is precarious?
Thus, turbid light illuminates external sights;
clear light illuminates internal sights.
The Sage gives rein to his desires
and encompasses his emotions,
yet that which regulates them is principle.
What need for exertion?
What need for endurance?
What is precarious?
Therefore, when the Benevolent One practices the Dào,
there is no contrived action;
when the Sage practices the Dào,
there is no forced effort.
The pondering of the Benevolent One is respectful;
the pondering of the Sage is joyful.
This is the Way of governing the heart-mind.
Whenever there is doubt in observing things
and the heart-mind within is not settled,
then external things will not be clear.
If our deliberations are not clear,
then we cannot determine what is so and what is not.
One who walks in the dark
sees a fallen log and takes it for a crouching tiger,
or sees a stand of trees and takes them for people following behind.
The darkness has obscured his clear vision.
A drunk person crossing a hundred-pace ditch
thinks it is a step-wide drainage channel,
and bowing his head to exit the city gate,
thinks it is a small side-door.
The wine has confused his spirit.
One who presses on their eyes to look
sees one thing as two;
one who covers their ears to listen
hears a faint sound and thinks it is a loud clamor:
the physical state has confused their senses.
Therefore, looking at oxen from a mountain, they seem like sheep,
but one seeking sheep does not go down to lead them away,
for distance obscures their size;
looking at trees from the foot of a mountain,
an eighty-foot tree looks like a chopstick,
but one seeking a chopstick does not go up to break it off,
for height obscures its length.
When water moves, the reflection wavers,
and people do not use it to determine beauty or ugliness;
the condition of the water is unstable.
A blind person looks up and does not see the stars,
and people do not use this to determine existence or non-existence;
the functioning of the essence is deluded.
If there is someone who determines the nature of things at such times,
then they are the fools of the world.
When those fools determine the nature of things,
they resolve doubts with doubts,
and their resolution is bound to be incorrect.
If it is incorrect,
how can they avoid error?
South of Xiàshǒu there was a man
named Juān Shǔliáng;
as for his character,
he was foolish and easily frightened.
While walking at night under a bright moon,
he looked down and saw his shadow,
and thought it was a crouching ghost;
he looked up at his hair
and thought it was a standing demon.
He turned and ran,
and by the time he reached his home,
he lost his breath and died.
Is this not lamentable!
Whenever people believe in ghosts,
they surely determine it in moments of confusion or times of doubt and obscurity.
This is when people mistake non-existence for existence and vice-versa.
And if they apply this to proper affairs—
for instance, being afflicted by dampness
and beating a drum to cure numbness—
then they surely have the expense of wearing out a drum and losing a pig,
without the blessing of curing the illness.
Therefore, even if one is not south of Xiàshǒu,
there is no difference.
Generally, that which can know
is the nature of man;
that which can be known
is the principle of things.
Using the nature of man, which can know,
to seek the principles of things, which can be known,
without any point where doubt stops,
then one could not exhaust them even if one lived to the end of one's days.
Though the principles one masters number in the hundreds of millions,
it is still not enough to encompass the transformations of the myriad things,
and one is the same as a fool.
If one studies until old and having grown children
and is still the same as a fool,
yet still does not know his error,
that is what is called a reckless man.
Therefore, learning
is essentially learning where to stop.
Where should one stop?
I say:
Stop at ultimate sufficiency.
What is meant by ultimate sufficiency?
I say:
Sagehood.
Sagehood
is the exhaustion of human relationships;
Kingship
is the exhaustion of regulations.
Exhausting both
is sufficient to be the ultimate standard for the world.
Therefore, the learner takes the Sage Kings as teachers
and takes the regulations of the Sage Kings as the law,
following their laws to seek their unifying principles,
and striving to emulate their person.
One who turns toward this and strives
is a scholar-official;
one who categorizes this and comes close
is a Jūnzǐ;
one who knows it
is a Sage.
Therefore, having knowledge but not using it to consider this standard
is called seizing;
having courage but not using it to uphold this
is called banditry;
having keen observation but not using it to distinguish this
is called usurpation;
having many abilities but not using them to cultivate and extend this
is called craftiness;
having eloquence but not using it to speak of this
is called garrulousness.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"The world has two things:
the wrong scrutinizing the right,
and the right scrutinizing the wrong."
This refers to matching or not matching the regulations of the Kings.
If the world does not take this as the highest standard of correctness,
could there still be any who can distinguish right from wrong or manage the crooked and the straight?
As for those who do not distinguish right from wrong,
do not manage the crooked and the straight,
do not discriminate between order and disorder,
and do not manage the human Way,
even if they have ability, it is of no benefit to people
and cannot help but be harmful to people.
Instead, they will simply manage strange theories,
play with eccentric phrases,
and confuse one another;
they use forceful constraint and a sharp tongue,
are thick-faced and endure insults,
lack correctness and act willfully,
argue recklessly to seek profit,
do not like courtesy or yielding,
do not respect ritual and decorum,
and like to push and shove one another:
these are the theories of wicked men in a chaotic age,
yet those in the world who manage theories
are now mostly like this.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Analyzing words to appear discerning
and talking about things to appear eloquent—
the Jūnzǐ despises this;
having broad knowledge and a strong memory
but not matching the regulations of the Kings—
the Jūnzǐ despises this."
This is what is meant.
If acting does not benefit accomplishment,
if seeking does not benefit attainment,
if worrying does not benefit approaching the goal,
then the broad-minded can abandon it.
They do not allow it to hinder themselves,
nor does it disturb their hearts for even a moment.
They do not long for the past,
they do not fret over the future,
they have no heart of distressed self-pity,
they act according to the time,
they respond as things arrive,
they distinguish as affairs arise,
and order and disorder, right and wrong,
are clearly understood.
Thoroughness leads to success,
leakage leads to failure;
the enlightened ruler does not have the latter.
Openness leads to success,
concealment leads to failure;
the dim-witted ruler does not have the former.
Therefore, if a ruler of men is secretive, then slanderous talk will arrive,
honest speech will be turned away,
and petty people will be near while the Jūnzǐ is far.
The *Shī* says:
"Taking darkness for light,
the foxes are gray."
This means the superior is obscure and the subordinates are treacherous.
If a ruler of men is open, then honest speech will arrive,
slanderous talk will be turned away,
and the Jūnzǐ will be near while petty people are far.
The *Shī* says:
"Brilliance is below,
splendor is above."
This means the superior is enlightened and the subordinates are transformed.
The established names of the later Kings:
names of punishments follow Shāng,
names of ranks follow Zhōu,
names of ritual forms follow the *Lǐ*.
Miscellaneous names applied to the myriad things
follow the established customs of the Zhūxià;
for the various remote regions with different customs,
one follows their local agreements to communicate.
Miscellaneous names concerning humans:
that which is so by birth is called nature,
and that which is produced by the harmony of nature,
where the essence joins with stimulus and response
naturally without effort, is called nature.
The likes, dislikes, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure of nature are called the emotions.
When the emotions are such and the mind makes a choice among them, it is called deliberation.
When the mind deliberates and the abilities act upon it, it is called conscious activity.
When deliberations accumulate
and abilities are practiced
and it is then completed,
it is called conscious activity.
Acting to gain profit
is called work.
Acting to fulfill righteousness
is called conduct.
That by which the capacity to know resides in humans
is called "knowing."
When knowing encounters an object and matches it, it is called "wisdom."
That by which the capacity for action resides in humans
is called "capacity."
When capacity encounters an object and matches it, it is called "ability."
Injury to one's nature is called "illness."
Meeting with circumstances is called "fate."
These are the scattered names of what resides in humans,
and these are the established names of the Hòu Wáng.
Therefore, when a Wáng zhě institutes names,
names are fixed and realities are distinguished,
the Dào is practiced and intentions are communicated,
then he carefully leads the people and unifies them.
Therefore, splitting phrases and arbitrarily creating names to disorder the rectified names,
causing the people to be confused and doubtful,
and causing much argument and litigation,
is called "great wickedness";
this crime is of the same kind as forging tallies and measures.
Thus his people dare not rely on strange phrases to disorder the rectified names.
Thus his people are honest;
being honest, they are easy to employ;
being easy to employ, they achieve success.
Since his people dare not rely on strange phrases to disorder the rectified names,
they are unified in the Dào and laws and are careful in following orders.
In this way, their legacy lasts long.
A long legacy and completed success
are the ultimate of order;
this is the result of being careful in maintaining the agreement of names.
Now that the Shèng Wáng have passed away,
the maintenance of names has become lax,
strange phrases have arisen,
names and realities are confused,
and the form of right and wrong is not clear,
so that even officials who uphold the law and scholars who recite texts
are all in disorder.
If a Wáng zhě were to arise,
he would surely follow old names
and create new names.
This being so, the purpose for which names exist,
the basis by which similarity and difference are determined,
and the essential pivot of instituting names
must be examined.
When different forms have divided hearts, and they communicate about
different things, names and realities are obscurely entangled,
noble and base are unclear,
and similarity and difference are not distinguished;
in such a case, intentions will surely suffer the misfortune of not being understood,
and affairs will surely suffer the calamity of being hindered and abandoned.
Therefore, the wise person makes distinctions and institutes names to point to realities,
upwardly to clarify noble and base,
downwardly to distinguish similarity and difference.
When noble and base are clear
and similarity and difference are distinguished;
in such a case, intentions will not suffer the misfortune of not being understood,
and affairs will not suffer the calamity of being hindered and abandoned;
this is the purpose for which names exist.
Then, on what basis are similarity and difference determined?
It is said:
based on the Tiān Guān.
For all of the same class and same nature,
the way their Tiān Guān perceive things is the same;
therefore, things are compared and contrasted as being similar or likely, and thus communicated;
this is how they share their agreed names to signify things to one another.
Shape, body, color, and pattern are differentiated by the eye;
sound, high and low pitch, the tuning of the yú, and strange sounds are differentiated by the ear;
sweet, bitter, salty, bland, pungent, and sour and strange tastes are differentiated by the mouth;
fragrance, stench, perfume, floral scent, rankness, muskiness, and strange odors are differentiated by the nose;
pain, itching, cold, heat, smoothness, sharpness, lightness, and heaviness are differentiated by the body;
explanations, causes, joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, love, hate, and desire are differentiated by the heart.
The heart has the capacity for verifying knowledge.
With verifying knowledge, one can then rely on the ear to know sound
and rely on the eye to know shape;
however, verifying knowledge must surely wait for the Tiān Guān to register their respective categories
before it is possible;
if the five organs register something but do not know it,
and the heart verifies it but has no explanation,
then everyone will invariably say they do not know it.
This is the basis by which similarity and difference are determined.
Thereafter, one follows by naming them:
if they are the same, name them the same; if they are different, name them different.
If a single name is sufficient to communicate, use a single name;
if a single name is not sufficient, use a combined name.
If single and combined names do not conflict, they can be shared;
even if shared,
it does no harm.
Knowing that different realities have different names,
therefore one ensures that different realities never lack different names,
so they cannot be confused,
just as one ensures that the same realities never lack the same names.
Therefore, although the myriad things are numerous,
there are times when one wishes to refer to them all-enclusively,
and so one calls them "things."
"Things"
is the Great General Name.
Pushing further to generalize,
within the general there is the general,
until one reaches the point where there is nothing more general, and then one stops.
There are times when one wishes to refer to them specifically,
and so one calls them "birds and beasts."
"Birds and beasts"
is the Great Specific Name.
Pushing further to specify,
within the specific there is the specific,
until one reaches the point where there is nothing more specific, and then one stops.
Names have no inherent appropriateness;
they are agreed upon to name things.
When the agreement is fixed and the custom is established, it is called "appropriate";
what differs from the agreement is called "inappropriate."
Names have no inherent reality;
they are agreed upon to name realities;
when the agreement is fixed and the custom is established,
it is called a "real name."
Names have an inherent goodness;
if they are direct, easy, and not conflicting,
they are called "good names."
Things may have the same shape but different locations,
or different shapes but the same location;
these can be distinguished.
When shapes are the same but the locations are different,
although they can be grouped together,
they are called two realities.
When the shape changes but the reality is not different and yet becomes different,
it is called "transformation."
When there is transformation but no difference in reality,
it is called one reality.
This is how affairs are examined for reality and numbers are fixed;
this is the essential pivot of instituting names.
The established names of the Hòu Wáng
must be examined.
"Being insulted is not a disgrace,"
"The Shèng Rén does not love himself,"
"Killing a thief is not killing a person"—
these are examples of being confused about using names and thereby disordering names.
Testing them against the purpose for which names exist and observing how they operate
will allow one to prohibit them.
"Mountains and abysses are level,"
"Human nature's desires are few,"
"Grass-fed and grain-fed animals do not add sweetness,
and great bells do not add joy"—
these are examples of being confused about using realities and thereby disordering names.
Testing them against the basis by which similarity and difference are determined and observing how they harmonize
will allow one to prohibit them.
"To negate while leaning on a pillar,"
"To have oxen and horses is not to have horses"—
these are examples of being confused about using names and thereby disordering realities.
Testing them against the agreement of names
and using what they accept to contradict what they reject
will allow one to prohibit them.
In general, all perverse sayings and deviant words that depart from the Zhèng Dào and are arbitrarily created
are all similar to these three types of confusion.
Therefore, an enlightened Míng Jūn knows their distinctions and does not argue with them.
The people are easily unified by the Dào
but they cannot be reasoned with concerning its causes;
therefore, an enlightened Míng Jūn presides over them with power,
guides them with the Dào,
declares to them with orders,
makes things clear to them with discourse,
and prohibits them with punishments.
Thus, his people's transformation by the Dào is like that of a spirit;
what use would there be for arguments?
Now that the Shèng Rén are gone,
the world is in disorder,
and wicked words have arisen;
a Jūnzǐ has no power to preside over them
and no punishments to prohibit them;
therefore, there are arguments and explanations.
If realities are not understood, one then names them;
if names are not understood, one then designates them;
if designations are not understood, one then explains them;
if explanations are not understood, one then argues about them.
Therefore, designations, naming, arguing, and explaining
are the great outward patterns of use
and the beginning of the Wáng zhě's work.
When the name is heard and the reality is understood,
that is the use of a name.
When names are accumulated to form a pattern,
that is the beauty of names.
When use and beauty are both attained,
it is called knowing names.
Names
are that by which one designates and accumulates realities.
Phrases
combine names of different realities to communicate a single idea.
Arguments and explanations
do not differentiate the names of realities in order to communicate the Dào of movement and stillness.
Designations and names
are the application of argument and explanation.
Argument and explanation
are the heart's representation of the Dào.
The heart
is the master craftsman of the Dào;
the Dào
is the guiding principle of order.
When the mind accords with the Dào,
speech accords with the mind,
and words accord with speech.
One rectifies names (Zhèng Míng) to set expectations,
and requests substance to ensure understanding.
One distinguishes differences without error,
and makes categorical inferences without contradiction.
When listening, one aligns with cultural patterns;
when distinguishing, one exhausts all causes.
Using the Correct Way (Zhèng Dào) to distinguish craftiness
is like pulling a string to determine straightness or crookedness.
For this reason, perverse theories cannot cause confusion,
and the Hundred Schools (Bǎi Jiā) have no place to hide.
One possesses the clarity of comprehensive listening
without an air of arrogance;
one possesses the depth of comprehensive coverage
without a look of boasting of virtue.
If one’s theories are practiced, the world is rectified;
if they are not practiced, one clarifies the Way and does not fall into obscure destitution.
This is the discernment and speech of the Sage (Shèng Rén).
The Shī says:
"Majestic and grand,
like ritual jades Guī and Zhāng,
with a fine reputation and high esteem.
The joyful and easy-going Jūnzǐ
is the model for the four directions."
This is what it refers to.
The moderation of yielding is attained, and
the logic of seniority is followed.
Taboos are not mentioned,
and ominous words are not uttered.
Speak with a benevolent mind,
listen with a learned mind,
and distinguish with an impartial mind.
Do not be moved by the criticism or praise of the masses,
do not cater to the eyes and ears of observers,
do not be bribed by the power and influence of the noble,
and do not find advantage in the words of those who spread partiality.
Thus, one can dwell in the Dào without duality,
rebuke without seizing,
and benefit without drifting.
Value justice and impartiality while scorning petty contention;
this is the discernment and speech of the scholar-gentleman (Shì Jūnzǐ).
The Shī says:
"The long night is vast,
forever thinking of the lack.
The Great Antiquity (Dà Gǔ) was not negligent,
Ritual and Righteousness (Lǐ Yì) were not in error,
why worry about the words of others!"
This is what it refers to.
The Jūnzǐ’s words
are smooth and refined,
humble and categorized,
and though seemingly uneven, they are uniform.
He rectifies his names
and fits his words
in order to clarify his intent and righteousness.
These names and words
are the servants of intent and righteousness.
If they suffice for mutual understanding,
then he stops;
to be careless with them
is craftiness.
Therefore, if a name suffices to point to a reality
and words suffice to show the limit,
then he stops.
Anything beyond this is called Rèn;
it is what the Jūnzǐ discards,
but the fool picks up as his own substance.
Thus the fool's words
are vague and coarse,
clamorous and uncategorized,
and babbling like a boiling pot.
He lures with names
and dazzles with words,
but has no depth regarding intent or righteousness.
Thus he relies on borrowing without limit,
works hard without merit,
and is greedy without a reputation.
Therefore, regarding the wise person's words:
when considered, they are easy to understand;
when practiced, they are easy to be at peace with;
when maintained, they are easy to establish.
When successful, one surely attains what they like and avoids what they hate.
The fool is the opposite of this.
The Shī says:
"To be a ghost or a water-demon
is impossible to achieve;
having a bashful face,
one looks at people without end.
I made this good song
to exhaust his fickleness."
This is what it refers to.
All those who talk of governance and wait for the removal of desires
are those who lack the means to guide desires and are trapped by the existence of desires.
All those who talk of governance and wait for the lessening of desires
are those who lack the means to moderate desires and are trapped by the abundance of desires.
Having desires or having no desires
are of different categories;
they belong to life and death and are the equipment of human nature (Xìng),
not the cause of order or chaos.
The abundance or scarcity of desires
are of different categories;
they are the quantity of emotions (Qíng),
not the cause of order or chaos.
Desires do not wait for the possibility of attainment,
but the seeker follows what is permissible.
That desires do not wait for the possibility of attainment
is what is received from Heaven (Tiān);
that the seeker follows what is permissible
is what is received from the mind (Xīn).
The single desire received from Tiān
is controlled by the many seekings received from the Xīn;
it is indeed difficult to categorize it with what is received from Tiān.
Among the things people desire, life is the greatest;
among the things people hate, death is the greatest.
However, there are people who leave life and go toward death;
it is not that they do not desire life and instead desire death,
but that it is unacceptable to live and acceptable to die.
Therefore, if desires exceed but action does not reach them,
it is the Xīn that stops it.
If what the Xīn permits accords with principle (Lǐ),
then even if desires are many,
how could it harm governance?
If desires do not reach but action exceeds them,
it is the Xīn that commands it.
If what the Xīn permits loses principle,
then even if desires are few,
how could it stop chaos?
Thus order and chaos lie in what the Xīn permits,
and not in what the Qíng desire.
If one does not seek it where it is
but seeks it where it is not,
though they say "I have attained it,"
they have lost it.
Nature (Xìng)
is the completion of Tiān;
emotions (Qíng)
are the substance of Xìng;
desires (Yù)
are the responses of Qíng.
Seeking what one desires because it is considered attainable
is what Qíng surely cannot avoid.
Considering something permissible and thus guiding it
is what wisdom surely must produce.
Therefore, even for a gatekeeper,
desires cannot be removed;
even for the Son of Heaven (Tiān Zǐ),
desires cannot be exhausted.
Although desires cannot be exhausted,
one can approach exhausting them;
although desires cannot be removed,
the seeking can be moderated.
Although what is desired cannot be exhausted,
the seeker still approaches exhausting them;
although desires cannot be removed,
if what is sought is not obtained,
the deliberator wishes to moderate the seeking.
Regarding the Way (Dào): moving forward, it approaches exhausting desires;
pulling back, it moderates the seeking;
nothing in the world is like it.
All people follow what they permit
and reject what they do not permit.
To know that nothing is like the Dào
and yet not follow the Dào—
such a thing does not exist.
Suppose there is a person who desires the South
regardless of how much,
and hates the North
regardless of how much;
would they, because the South cannot be fully reached,
leave the South and run toward the North?
Now, what people desire
is without limit,
and what they hate
is without limit;
would they, because what is desired cannot be fully reached,
leave the path of obtaining desires and take up what is hated?
Therefore, if it is the Dào that can be followed, follow it;
how could diminishing it cause chaos?
If it is not the Dào that can be followed, leave it;
how could increasing it lead to order?
Therefore the wise discuss the Dào and that is all;
the precious theories of the small schools
will all have their wishes wither away.
Whenever people take something,
what they desire never comes in a pure form;
whenever they discard something,
what they dislike never leaves in a pure form.
Therefore, in no action can a person afford not to employ the *quán* (standard) together with it.
If the balance is not level,
then the heavy will be suspended high
and people will think it is light,
while the light will be suspended low
and people will think it is heavy;
this is how people are confused about weight.
If the *quán* is not correct,
then misfortune will be lodged within what is desired
and people will think it is a blessing,
while a blessing will be lodged within what is disliked
and people will think it is misfortune;
this is also how people are confused about misfortune and blessing.
The *Dào*
is the correct *quán* of both past and present.
If one departs from the *Dào* and makes internal choices for oneself,
then one will not know where misfortune and blessing reside.
Regarding those who exchange:
if they exchange one for one,
people say
there is neither gain nor loss;
if they exchange one for two,
people say
there is no loss but there is gain;
if they exchange two for one,
people say
there is no gain but there is loss.
A calculator takes what is more;
a planner follows what is permissible.
To exchange two for one,
no one would do it,
for the calculation is clear.
To proceed from the *Dào* and go forth
is like exchanging one for two;
what loss could there be?
To depart from the *Dào* and make internal choices for oneself
is like exchanging two for one;
what gain could there be?
To use a hundred years' worth of accumulated desires
to exchange for a single moment's worth of resentment,
and yet still do so—
this is because the calculation is not clear.
Should there be anyone who tries to look deeply into what is hidden and difficult to observe,
yet whose mind treats *lǐ* (principles) lightly while not regarding external objects as heavy,
such a person does not exist;
one who regards external objects as heavy but does not suffer internal anxiety,
such a person does not exist.
One whose conduct departs from *lǐ* but is not externally in danger,
such a person does not exist;
one who is externally in danger but does not feel internal fear,
such a person does not exist.
When the heart is anxious and fearful,
then even with fine meat in the mouth, one does not know its flavor;
with ears listening to bells and drums, one does not know their sound;
with eyes looking at embroidered robes, one does not know their pattern;
with a light and warm robe on a smooth mat, the body does not know its comfort.
Therefore, even facing the beauty of the myriad things, one cannot be satisfied;
even if one happens to find leisure and is satisfied,
one cannot let go of it.
Thus, even facing the beauty of the myriad things, one has great anxiety;
even while possessing the benefits of the myriad things, one has great harm.
For one like this,
is he seeking objects?
Is he nourishing life? Or is he trading away longevity?
Thus, wanting to nourish one's desires but indulging one's passions,
wanting to nourish one's nature but endangering one's form,
wanting to nourish one's joy but attacking one's mind,
wanting to nourish one's reputation but disordering one's conduct—
for one like this,
though he may be enfeoffed as a *Hóu* (marquis) and called a *Jūn* (lord),
he is no different from a common thief;
though he may ride in a carriage and wear a ceremonial cap,
he is no different from a person with no feet.
This is what is called making oneself a slave to objects.
When the mind is calm and joyful,
then even if colors are less than ordinary, they can nourish the eyes;
even if sounds are less than ordinary, they can nourish the ears;
coarse rice and vegetable soup can nourish the mouth;
clothes of coarse cloth and shoes of coarse hemp can nourish the body;
a cramped room, reed screens, straw mats, and a simple table can nourish the form.
Therefore, without the beauty of the myriad things, one can nourish joy;
without the status of rank and position, one can nourish a reputation.
If, in this state, the world were added to him,
then what he does for the world would be much,
but his own private joy would be little increased;
this is what is called valuing oneself and making objects one's servants.
Unfounded words,
unseen conduct,
and unheard-of plans—
the *Jūnzǐ* (exemplary person) is cautious of them.
Human nature is bad;
its goodness is *wèi* (artifice).
Now, human nature
is born with a fondness for profit;
if this is followed,
then strife and robbery arise
and deference and yielding perish;
it is born with envy and hatred;
if this is followed,
then violence and villainy arise
and loyalty and good faith perish;
it is born with the desires of the ears and eyes,
and a fondness for sounds and beauty;
if this is followed,
then licentiousness and chaos arise
and *lǐ yì* (ritual and righteousness) and the patterns of civilization perish.
Thus, to follow human nature
and indulge human passions
will inevitably result in strife and robbery,
conform to the violation of duty and the disordering of principles,
and culminate in tyranny.
Therefore, there must be the transformation of teachers and laws
and the guidance of *lǐ yì*,
and only then will there be deference and yielding,
conformity to civilization and principles,
and a culmination in order.
Observing it from this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is bad
and its goodness is *wèi*.
Therefore, crooked wood must await the press-frame and the application of steam and bending
before it can be made straight;
blunt metal must await the whetstone and grinding
before it can be made sharp.
Now, human nature is bad
and must await teachers and laws before it can be corrected,
and obtain *lǐ yì* before it can be ordered.
If people today lack teachers and laws,
then they are biased, dangerous, and incorrect;
if they lack *lǐ yì*,
then they are rebellious, chaotic, and unordered.
In ancient times, the *Shèng Wáng* (Sage Kings) considered human nature to be bad,
regarding it as biased, dangerous, and incorrect,
as well as rebellious, chaotic, and unordered.
For this reason, they created *lǐ yì*
and established laws and measures
to rectify and adorn human passions and nature
so as to correct them,
and to discipline and transform human passions and nature
so as to guide them.
They caused all people to proceed toward order
and conform to the *Dào*.
Today, those who are transformed by teachers and laws, accumulate learning, and follow *lǐ yì*
are *Jūnzǐ*;
those who indulge their passions and nature,
find comfort in wantonness, and violate *lǐ yì*
are *Xiǎorén* (petty persons).
Observing it from this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is bad
and its goodness is *wèi*.
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"When people learn,
it is because their nature is good."
I say:
This is not so.
This shows a failure to understand human nature
and a lack of scrutiny regarding the distinction between human nature and *wèi*.
In all cases, nature
is what is completed by *Tiān* (Heaven);
it cannot be learned
and it cannot be worked at.
*Lǐ yì*
are what are produced by the sages;
they are what people become capable of through learning
and what they complete through effort.
What is in a person but cannot be learned or worked at
is called nature;
what is in a person and can be learned and made capable, or worked at and completed,
is called *wèi*.
This is the distinction between nature and *wèi*.
Now, as for human nature,
the eyes can see
and the ears can hear.
The clarity by which one can see does not depart from the eye,
and the sharpness by which one can hear does not depart from the ear;
that the eyes are clear and the ears are sharp
is clearly not something that can be learned.
*Mèngzǐ* said:
"Human nature is good,
and if it is not, it is because people have all lost and abandoned their nature."
I say:
If this were so, it would be an error.
Now, as for human nature,
from birth it departs from its original simplicity and departs from its natural endowment,
so that it must be lost and abandoned.
Observing it from this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is bad
and its goodness is *wèi*.
What is called "nature is good"
refers to not departing from original simplicity yet finding it beautiful,
and not departing from innate resources yet finding them beneficial.
If innate resources and original simplicity are to beauty,
and the mind's intent is to goodness,
as if the clarity that allows for sight does not depart from the eye,
and the keenness that allows for hearing does not depart from the ear,
therefore it is said:
"the eye is clear and the ear is keen."
Now, the nature of man:
when hungry, he desires to be full;
when cold, he desires to be warm;
when weary, he desires to rest;
this is the emotional nature of man.
Now, when a man is hungry,
and seeing an elder he does not dare to eat first,
it is because he intends to yield;
if he is weary and does not dare to seek rest,
it is because he intends to take over the labor of another.
A son's yielding to his father,
or a younger brother's yielding to his elder brother;
a son's taking over labor for his father,
or a younger brother's taking over labor for his elder brother—
these two behaviors are both contrary to nature and go against emotions.
However, the way of a filial son
is the refined pattern of ritual and rightness.
Therefore, to follow emotional nature
results in no yielding;
to yield is to go against emotional nature.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it is then clear that human nature is evil,
and that its goodness is conscious activity.
An inquirer asks:
"If human nature is evil,
then from where do ritual and rightness arise?"
The response to this is:
All ritual and rightness
are born from the conscious activity of the Shèng Rén,
they are not originally born from human nature.
Thus, a potter molds clay to make a vessel;
so the vessel is born from the conscious activity of the potter,
not originally born from human nature.
Thus, a carpenter carves wood to complete a vessel;
so the vessel is born from the conscious activity of the carpenter,
not originally born from human nature.
The Shèng Rén accumulated thoughts and reflections and practiced conscious habits
to produce ritual and rightness and establish laws and standards;
so ritual, rightness, laws, and standards
are born from the conscious activity of the Shèng Rén,
they are not originally born from human nature.
As for the eye liking colors,
the ear liking sounds,
the mouth liking flavors,
the heart liking profit,
and the body and skin liking pleasure and ease—
these are all born from the emotional nature of man;
they are spontaneous upon being stimulated,
and do not wait for deliberate effort before being produced.
That which cannot be spontaneous upon stimulation,
but must certainly wait for deliberate effort before being so,
is called conscious activity.
This is where nature and conscious activity are born,
and is the evidence of their difference.
Therefore, the Shèng Rén transformed nature and initiated conscious activity;
conscious activity being initiated, ritual and rightness were born;
ritual and rightness being born, laws and standards were instituted.
So ritual, rightness, laws, and standards
are what the Shèng Rén produced.
Thus, that by which the Shèng Rén are the same as the masses,
and not different from the masses,
is nature;
that by which they are different from and surpass the masses
is conscious activity.
To like profit and desire gain
is the emotional nature of man.
Suppose there are brothers with wealth and property to divide;
if they follow their emotional nature,
liking profit and desiring gain;
if it were like this, then the brothers would clash and snatch from each other;
but if they are transformed by the refined patterns of ritual and rightness,
if it were like this, then they would yield even to fellow countrymen.
Therefore, following emotional nature leads brothers to contend,
while transformation by ritual and rightness leads to yielding to fellow countrymen.
Generally, when people desire to do good,
it is because their nature is evil.
The shallow desires to be deep,
the ugly desires to be beautiful,
the narrow desires to be wide,
the poor desire to be rich,
the lowly desire to be noble—
if one truly does not have something within,
one will certainly seek it from without.
Therefore, the rich do not desire wealth,
and the noble do not desire power—
if one truly has something within,
one will certainly not reach for it from without.
Looking at it from this perspective,
people's desire to do good
is because their nature is evil.
Now, human nature
originally lacks ritual and rightness,
therefore one strives in learning to seek to have them;
nature does not know ritual and rightness,
therefore one thinks and reflects to seek to know them.
So, if it were just birth alone,
then man would have no ritual or rightness,
and not know ritual or rightness.
If man has no ritual or rightness, there is chaos;
if he does not know ritual or rightness, there is rebellion.
So, if it were just birth alone,
then rebellion and chaos would be within himself.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and that its goodness is conscious activity.
Mèngzǐ says:
"Human nature is good."
I say:
This is not so.
Generally, what has been called "good" by the world from ancient times to today
is correctness, order, peace, and stable governance;
what is called "evil"
is being biased, dangerous, rebellious, and chaotic;
this is the distinction between good and evil.
Now, if we truly believe that human nature is inherently correct, orderly, peaceful, and well-governed,
then what use would there be for Shèng Wáng?
What use would there be for ritual and rightness?
Even if there were Shèng Wáng and ritual and rightness,
what could they possibly add to correctness, order, peace, and stable governance?
But now it is not so;
human nature is evil.
Therefore, the Shèng Rén of ancient times, because human nature is evil,
considered it biased, dangerous, and not correct,
rebellious, chaotic, and not well-governed.
Thus, they established for them the authority of lords and superiors
to oversee them,
clarified ritual and rightness to transform them,
established laws and regulations to govern them,
and weighted punishments to restrain them,
so that all under heaven would emerge into order
and conform to goodness.
This is the governance of the Shèng Wáng
and the transformation through ritual and rightness.
Now, suppose we try to remove the authority of lords and superiors,
dispense with the transformation of ritual and rightness,
remove the governance of laws and regulations,
and dispense with the restraint of punishments;
stand by and watch the interactions of the people of the world—
if it were like this, then the strong would harm the weak and rob them,
the many would tyrannize the few and shout them down,
and the world would fall into rebellion, chaos, and mutual destruction
in less than a moment.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it is clear that human nature is evil,
and that its goodness is conscious activity.
Therefore, those who are good at speaking of the past
must find proof in the present;
those who are good at speaking of Heaven
must find evidence in man.
In all arguments, what is valued is having logical consistency
and verifiable evidence.
Therefore, if one sits and speaks of it,
once one stands up, it should be possible to establish it,
and once extended, it should be possible to put it into practice.
Now Mèngzǐ says,
"Human nature is good,"
but there is no logical consistency or verifiable evidence;
when he sits and speaks of it,
once he stands up, it cannot be established,
and once extended, it cannot be put into practice—
is this not an extreme error?
Therefore, if nature were good,
then one could dispense with Shèng Wáng
and put an end to ritual and rightness;
because nature is evil,
one follows Shèng Wáng
and values ritual and rightness.
Thus, the straightening board is produced
because of crooked wood;
the ink-line is initiated
because of what is not straight;
lords and superiors are established and ritual and rightness are clarified
because nature is evil.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it is then clear that human nature is evil,
and that its goodness is conscious activity.
Straight wood does not wait for the straightening board to be straight,
for its nature is straight;
crooked wood must wait for the straightening board, steaming, and forcing
before it becomes straight,
because its nature is not straight.
The nature of man today is evil;
it must await the governance of Sage Kings
and the transformation of ritual and righteousness
before it can issue forth in order and conform to goodness.
Viewing it from this perspective,
then it is clear that man's nature is evil,
and that his goodness is conscious activity.
A questioner says:
"If ritual and righteousness are accumulated conscious activity,
then they are man's nature,
which is why the Sages could produce them."
One responds:
This is not so.
A potter molds clay and produces tiles;
are tiles and clay then the nature of the potter?
A carpenter carves wood and produces vessels;
are vessels and wood then the nature of the carpenter?
The Sages' relation to ritual and righteousness
is just like the potter molding and producing them.
Since ritual and righteousness are accumulated conscious activity,
how could they be man's original nature?
As for the nature of all men,
Yáo and Shùn versus Jié and Dào Zhí,
their nature is one and the same;
the Jūnzǐ versus the Xiǎorén,
their nature is one and the same.
Now if we were to take ritual, righteousness, and accumulated conscious activity to be man's nature,
then why honor Yáo and Yǔ?
Why honor the Jūnzǐ?
The reason Yáo, Yǔ, and the Jūnzǐ are honored
is because they can transform nature,
initiate conscious activity,
and from that conscious activity produce ritual and righteousness.
Thus the Sages' relation to ritual, righteousness, and accumulated conscious activity
is just like the potter molding and producing them.
Viewing it from this perspective,
