then as for ritual, righteousness, and accumulated conscious activity,
how could they be man's nature?
What is despised in Jié, Dào Zhí, and the Xiǎorén
is that they follow their nature,
obey their emotions,
and are content with arrogance and unrestrained behavior,
which results in greed, profit-seeking, and contention.
Thus man's nature is clearly evil,
and his goodness is conscious activity.
Heaven did not favor Zēng, Qiān, or Xiào Jǐ
and exclude the common people.
Yet Zēng, Qiān, and Xiào Jǐ alone were rich in the reality of filial piety
and perfected the reputation of filial piety.
Why is this?
Because they reached the ultimate in ritual and righteousness.
Heaven did not favor the people of Qí and Lǔ
and exclude the people of Qín.
Yet as for the righteousness between father and son or the distinction between husband and wife, the people of Qín
do not equal the filial, reverent, respectful, and cultured people of Qí and Lǔ.
Why is this?
Because the people of Qín follow their emotions and nature, are content with arrogance and unrestrained behavior, and are negligent toward ritual and righteousness.
Is it that their nature is different?
"The man in the street can become Yǔ."
What does this mean?
I say:
What made Yǔ to be Yǔ
was his practice of benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards.
Thus benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards
have principles that can be known and can be practiced.
Moreover, the man in the street
possesses the faculty to know benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards,
and possesses the capacity to practice benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards;
thus it is clear that he can become Yǔ.
Suppose that benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards essentially had no principles that could be known or practiced?
Then even Yǔ would not have known benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards,
nor could he have practiced benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards.
Or suppose the man in the street essentially lacked the faculty to know benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards,
and essentially lacked the capacity to practice benevolence, righteousness, laws, and standards?
Then the man in the street
would internally be unable to know the righteousness of father and son,
and externally be unable to know the standards of ruler and minister.
(Not so). Today this is not the case;
the man in the street
can internally know the righteousness of father and son,
and externally know the standards of ruler and minister.
Thus the faculty by which he can know
and the capacity by which he can practice
are clearly within the man in the street.
Now, if we take the man in the street
with his faculty to know
and capacity to practice,
and base them on the principles of benevolence and righteousness which can be known and the capacity by which they can be practiced,
then it is clear that he can become Yǔ.
If the man in the street applies himself to the arts and engages in learning,
concentrating his mind and focusing his will,
thinking, searching, and examining closely,
adding day to day over a long period,
accumulating goodness without ceasing,
then he will attain the level of the divine and enlightened
and form a triad with Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, the Sage
is one who has reached that state through accumulation.
It is asked:
"If Sagehood can be achieved through accumulation,
yet most people cannot accumulate it,
why is this?"
I say:
They can, but they cannot be made to do so.
Thus the Xiǎorén can become a Jūnzǐ
but is unwilling to become a Jūnzǐ;
the Jūnzǐ can become a Xiǎorén
but is unwilling to become a Xiǎorén.
The Xiǎorén and Jūnzǐ
are never such that they cannot become each other;
yet the reason they do not do so
is that they can, but cannot be made to do so.
Thus the man in the street can become Yǔ—
that is true;
but that the man in the street will actually become Yǔ—
that is not necessarily so.
Even if he does not become Yǔ,
it does not detract from the fact that he can become Yǔ.
One's feet can walk everywhere under heaven,
yet there has never been anyone who could walk everywhere under heaven.
Artisans, farmers, and merchants
are never such that they cannot do each other's work,
yet they never actually do each other's work.
Viewing it from this perspective,
although something can be done,
it may not necessarily be done;
although it is not done,
it does not detract from the fact that it can be done.
Thus the difference between the actual "doing" or "not doing" and the potential "can" or "cannot"
is vast indeed;
it is clear that they cannot be equated.
Yáo asked Shùn:
"What are human emotions like?"
Shùn replied:
"Human emotions are very unlovely;
why ask further?
Once a man has a wife and children, his filial piety toward his parents declines;
once his desires are satisfied, his faithfulness to his friends declines;
once his rank and salary are full, his loyalty to his lord declines.
Such are human emotions!
Such are human emotions!
They are very unlovely;
why ask further?"
Only the worthy are not like this.
There is the knowledge of the Sage,
the knowledge of the Shì and Jūnzǐ,
the knowledge of the Xiǎorén,
and the knowledge of the menial laborer.
To speak much, yet with pattern and categorization,
discussing the reasons for things all day long,
though the words undergo a thousand shifts and ten thousand changes,
their unifying principle remains one:
this is the knowledge of the Sage.
To speak little, yet be direct and concise,
being orderly and lawful
as if following a marking line:
this is the knowledge of the Shì and Jūnzǐ.
To speak with flattery
and act with perversity,
having many regrets in one's undertakings:
this is the knowledge of the Xiǎorén.
To be glib and quick-witted yet without principle,
possessing various minor talents and wide-ranging but useless skills,
making rapid but fine distinctions that are not urgent,
not caring about right or wrong,
not discussing the crooked or the straight,
but only intent on defeating others:
this is the knowledge of the menial laborer.
There is the highest courage,
the middle courage,
and the lower courage.
When the world is upright,
one dares to hold oneself straight;
when the former kings' Way is present,
one dares to carry out its purpose.
Above, one does not follow the lords of a chaotic age;
below, one does not follow the customs of the people of a chaotic age.
Where benevolence resides, one does not fear poverty;
where benevolence is absent, one does not value wealth or status.
If the world knows of him,
he wishes to share enjoyment with the world;
if the world does not know of him,
he stands alone and towering between Heaven and Earth without fear:
this is the highest courage.
To be respectful in ritual and frugal in intent,
greatly valuing good faith and lightly valuing goods and wealth,
daring to promote and honor the worthy,
and daring to pull down and discard the unworthy:
this is the middle courage.
To value oneself lightly and value goods heavily,
to be comfortable with disaster while seeking broad excuses,
to escape through any means,
not caring about right or wrong
or the reality of whether a thing is so or not,
but only intent on defeating others:
this is the lower courage.
*Fánruò* and *Jùshǔ*
are the fine bows of antiquity;
however, if they do not receive the straightening frame,
then they cannot correct themselves.
The *Cōng* of *Huán Gōng*,
the *Quē* of *Tài Gōng*,
the *Lù* of *Wén Wáng*,
the *Hù* of *Zhuāng Jūn*,
and the *Gānjiàng*, *Mòyé*, *Jùquē*, and *Bìlǘ* of *Hélǘ*—
these are all the fine swords of antiquity;
however, if they are not applied to the grindstone, they cannot be sharp,
and if they do not receive human effort, they cannot cut.
*Huáliú*, *Qíjì*, *Xiānlí*, and *Lù’ěr*
are all the fine horses of antiquity;
however, there must be the constraint of the bit and bridle in front,
the majesty of the whip and crop behind,
and the addition of *Zàofù*’s driving,
and only then can they cover a thousand *lǐ* in a single day.
Now, although a person may have a beautiful nature and a discerning and wise mind,
they must seek a worthy teacher to serve
and select worthy friends to befriend.
If they find a worthy teacher to serve,
then what they hear are the Ways of *Yáo*, *Shùn*, *Yǔ*, and *Tāng*;
if they find good friends to befriend,
then what they see are the actions of loyalty, trustworthiness, respect, and deference.
That one's person daily advances toward benevolence and righteousness without being aware of it
is because of the influence upon them.
Now, if one dwells with those who are not good,
then what they hear are deceptions, slanders, frauds, and falsehoods,
and what they see are the actions of filth, excess, depravity, and greed for profit.
That one's person is about to be subjected to punishment and execution without being aware of it
is because of the influence upon them.
The *Chuán* says:
"If you do not know the son,
look at his friends;
if you do not know the ruler,
look at his attendants."
It is influence and nothing more,
it is influence and nothing more.
The Son of Heaven has no wife,
which tells people he has no equal.
Within the four seas, there is no ritual for guests,
which tells people there is no place where he does not belong.
His feet are able to walk,
but he waits for assistants before advancing;
his mouth is able to speak,
but he waits for officials before issuing edicts.
To see without looking,
to be keen of hearing without listening,
to be trusted without speaking,
to know without deliberating,
and to achieve merit without moving
tells of the utmost perfection.
As for the Son of Heaven,
his power is most weighty,
his form is most at ease,
his mind is most satisfied,
his will is nowhere frustrated,
his form is nowhere labored,
and his honor is unsurpassed.
The *Shī* says:
"Everywhere under Heaven,
there is no land that is not the King's;
to the very shores of the land,
there are none who are not the King's subjects."
This is what is meant.
When a sage king is on high
and social distinctions and righteousness are carried out below,
then the scholar-officials have no dissolute behavior,
the various clerks and officials have no negligent tasks,
the common people have no wicked or strange customs,
there are no crimes of theft or robbery,
and no one dares to violate the prohibitions of the superior.
All the world clearly knows that theft and robbery cannot bring wealth,
all know that harming others cannot bring longevity,
and all know that violating the prohibitions of the superior cannot bring safety.
By following the Way,
people obtain what they like;
by not following the Way,
they inevitably encounter what they hate:
for this reason, punishments and crimes are extremely few, while majesty flows everywhere like a stream.
All the world clearly knows that if they act wickedly, even the means of hiding or fleeing are insufficient to escape,
so none fail to admit their guilt and plead.
The *Shū* says:
"All people bring guilt upon themselves."
This is what is meant.
Therefore, when punishment matches the crime, there is majesty;
when it does not match the crime, there is contempt.
When rank matches worthiness, it is honored;
when it does not match worthiness, it is debased.
In antiquity, punishment did not exceed the crime,
and rank did not surpass virtue;
thus, one might execute the father yet make the son a minister,
or execute the elder brother yet make the younger brother a minister.
Punishments and penalties were not directed in anger at the crime,
and rank and rewards did not surpass virtue,
and thus distinctions were clearly communicated through sincerity.
Because of this, those who did good were encouraged,
those who did bad were discouraged,
punishments and penalties were extremely few while majesty flowed like a stream,
and government orders were perfectly clear while transformation was as effortless as if by a god.
The *Chuán* says:
"One man has reason for celebration,
and the millions rely on it."
This is what is meant.
In a chaotic age, it is not so;
punishments and penalties are directed in anger at crimes,
rank and rewards surpass virtue,
crimes are judged by clan,
and worthiness is promoted by lineage.
Thus, one person commits a crime and the three branches of the clan are all exterminated;
even if one's virtue is like that of *Shùn*,
they cannot escape shared punishment,
which is judging crime by clan.
If the ancestors were worthy,
then the descendants must be prominent;
even if their conduct is like that of *Jié* or
*Zhòu*, their rank must be honored,
which is promoting worthiness by lineage.
Judging crime by clan
and promoting worthiness by lineage—
though one may wish for no chaos,
can it be achieved?
The *Shī* says:
"The hundred rivers bubble and boil,
the mountain peaks crumble and collapse;
the high banks become valleys,
the deep valleys become hills.
Alas for the people of today,
why do they not take warning?"
This is what is meant.
If one evaluates laws based on the sage kings,
then one knows what to value;
if one regulates affairs based on righteousness,
then one knows what is beneficial.
Evaluating so as to know what to value,
one then knows what to nourish;
regulating affairs so as to know what is beneficial,
one's actions then know where to proceed from.
These two
are the root of right and wrong
and the source of gain and loss.
Thus, in King *Chéng*’s relationship with the Duke of *Zhōu*,
there was nowhere he went where he did not listen to him,
for he knew what to value.
In Duke *Huán*’s relationship with *Guǎn Zhòng*,
in state affairs, there was nowhere he went where he did not employ him,
for he knew what was beneficial.
*Wú* had *Wǔ Zǐxū* but could not employ him,
and the state even came to ruin,
for they turned their backs on the Way and lost the worthy.
Therefore, one who honors sages becomes a King,
one who values the worthy becomes a Hegemon,
one who respects the worthy survives,
and one who is negligent toward the worthy perishes—
this has been the same from antiquity to the present.
Therefore, exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
grading the noble and the base,
distinguishing the close and the distant,
and ordering the elder and the younger—
this is the Way of the former kings.
Therefore, by exalting the worthy and employing the capable,
the ruler is honored and those below are at peace;
by having grades for the noble and the base, orders are carried out and do not go astray;
by having distinctions for the close and the distant,
then implementation is carried out without contradiction;
by having an order for the elder and the younger,
then tasks and duties are quickly completed and there is time for rest.
Therefore, the benevolent
are benevolent toward this;
the righteous
distinguish this;
the temperate
treat life and death according to this;
the loyal
are sincere and cautious regarding this.
One who combines these and is capable in them
is complete.
To be complete yet not boastful,
and to be single-minded in self-goodness,
is called being a Sage.
Because they are not boastful,
for this reason, the world does not compete with them in ability, and they achieve the good use of their merit.
Having merit yet not possessing it as one's own,
for this reason, they are valued by the world.
The *Shī* says:
"The virtuous person and gentleman,
his demeanor is without error;
his demeanor is without error,
he corrects the four states."
This is what is meant.
Please perform the *Chéng Xiàng*,
the calamity of the age:
ignorance and darkness ruin the worthy and good.
If a ruler has no worthy men,
it is like a blind man having no guide—
how wandering and lost!
Please lay the foundation,
be cautious about the Sage.
If the ignorant are self-willed, affairs will not be governed;
if the ruler is jealous and insists on winning,
and the ministers do not remonstrate,
disaster is certain.
Discussing the faults of ministers,
reverse their practices.
Honor the ruler, stabilize the state, and value worthiness and righteousness.
Rejecting advice and glossing over faults,
or being ignorant and blindly conforming,
the state will surely meet with misfortune.
What is meant by "useless"?
The state is full of selfishness;
cliques surround the ruler and factions are employed.
Keeping the worthy distant and the slanderers close,
loyal ministers are blocked and the ruler’s power shifts.
What is meant by "worthy"?
To clarify ruler and minister:
above, able to honor the ruler; below, to love the people.
If the ruler truly listens to them,
the world will be united and all within the seas will be his guests.
The curse of a ruler:
slanderers achieve their ends.
When the worthy and capable flee, the state falls;
ignorance compounded by ignorance,
darkness by darkness,
he becomes a *Jié*.
The disaster of an age:
envying the worthy and capable.
*Fēi Lián* managed the government and *È Lái* was employed;
debasing his will and intent,
enlarging his parks and gardens,
and raising high his terraces and pavilions.
*Wǔ Wáng* was angry and led the army to *Mù Yě*;
*Zhòu*’s soldiers turned their positions and *Qǐ* surrendered.
*Wǔ Wáng* treated him well,
enfeoffed him in *Sòng* and established his ancestors.
The decline of an age:
slanderers are welcomed.
*Bǐ Gān* was cut open and *Jī Zǐ* was imprisoned;
*Wǔ Wáng* executed the tyrant,
and *Lǚ Shàng* signaled with his banner so that the *Yīn* people were won over.
The misfortune of an age:
hating worthy scholars.
*Zǐ Xū* was killed and *Bǎi Lǐ* was moved;
*Mù Gōng* obtained him,
and through his strength matched the Five Hegemons (*Wǔ Bà*) and employed the Six Ministers (*Liù Qīng*).
The ignorance of an age:
hating great *Ru* scholars.
Rejecting and excluding them, *Kǒng Zǐ* was detained;
*Zhǎn Qín* was dismissed three times,
and *Chūn Shēn*’s way was cut short,
the foundation completely lost.
Please manage the foundation,
think of the worthy.
*Yáo* remains throughout ten thousand generations as if seen today.
Slanderers are boundless;
crookedness and bias are what to doubt.
The foundation must be applied:
distinguish the worthy from the useless.
The Way of *Wén* and *Wǔ* is the same as that of *Fú Xì*.
Those who follow it achieve order;
those who do not follow it have chaos—
why should there be doubt?
In all *Chéng Xiàng*,
distinguish laws and methods.
The pinnacle of perfect governance returns to the Later Kings.
*Shèn*, *Mò*, *Jì*, and *Huì*—
the theories of the Hundred Schools are truly imprecise.
Governance returns to unity,
and cultivating it brings good fortune.
The gentleman holds it in his heart as if tied;
the common people are of two minds,
and slanderers reject it;
their outward conduct is investigated.
Water is perfectly level,
upright and not tilting;
if the methods of the heart are thus, one resembles a Sage.
When a person has power,
and is upright and uses it to guide, they will surely equal Heaven.
When the world has no king,
the worthy and good are impoverished.
Tyrants eat fine meat
while benevolent people eat chaff.
Ritual and music are extinguished
and cease; Sages go into hiding
and the methods of *Mò* are practiced.
The constant thread of governance:
ritual and punishment.
The gentleman cultivates them and the common people are at peace.
Clarify virtue and be cautious with punishments;
the state is then governed and all within the four seas are peaceful.
The intent of governance:
put power and wealth last.
The gentleman is sincere and waits with fondness;
he dwells in firm integrity,
has deep reserves,
and is capable of long-term thought.
Thought then becomes refined,
the glory of the will.
Liking and unifying it, the spirit is completed.
When spirit and essence meet,
unified and not divided,
one becomes a Sage.
The Way of governance:
beauty that does not age.
The gentleman follows it and is handsome and good.
Below, he teaches the younger generation;
above, he serves the ancestors.
The *Chéng Xiàng* concludes;
its words do not stumble.
The gentleman speaks of it to be smooth and reaching,
honoring the worthy and good,
and distinguishing the calamities and curses.
Please perform the *Chéng Xiàng*,
speak of the Sage Kings.
*Yáo* and *Shùn* valued the worthy and personally yielded;
*Xǔ Yóu* and *Shàn Juǎn*
valued righteousness and lightened profit, their conduct manifest.
*Yáo* yielded to the worthy
for the sake of the people.
Broadly benefiting and universal love, his virtue was applied equally.
Distinguishing and governing those above and below,
there are ranks for the noble and lowly, clarifying ruler and minister.
*Yáo* handed over to the capable;
*Shùn* met his time.
Valuing the worthy and promoting virtue, the world was governed.
Even if there are worthy
Sages, if they happen not to meet their time,
who would know them?
*Yáo* did not claim virtue for himself;
*Shùn* did not decline.
*Yáo* gave his two daughters as wives and entrusted him with affairs.
Great indeed was *Shùn*!
Standing facing south, all things were prepared.
*Shùn* handed over to *Yǔ*
the world.
He still promoted the worthy without losing order.
Externally not avoiding enemies,
internally not favoring relatives,
he gave to the worthy.
*Yǔ* labored with mind and strength;
*Yáo* had virtue.
Without using shields and spears, the *Sān Miáo* submitted.
Raising *Shùn* from the fields,
he entrusted the world to him
and he himself took rest.
Obtaining *Hòu Jì*,
the five grains flourished.
*Kuí* became Music Director and birds and beasts submitted.
*Xiè* became Minister of Education,
and the people knew filial piety and fraternal respect, honoring the virtuous.
*Yǔ* had merit:
he suppressed the great flood.
He removed harm from the people and drove out *Gòng Gōng*.
In the north he cleared the Nine Rivers,
opened the Twelve Islets,
and dredged the Three Rivers.
*Yǔ* expanded the land
and pacified the world.
He personally labored for the people.
He obtained *Yì*, *Gāo Yáo*, *Héng Gé*, and *Zhí Chéng* as assistants.
*Xiè* was the Dark King;
he sired *Zhāo Míng*.
They lived in *Dǐ Shí* and moved to *Shāng*.
Fourteen generations later,
there was *Tiān Yǐ*, who was *Chéng Tāng*.
*Tiān Yǐ Tāng*
discussed and raised the appropriate.
He personally yielded to *Biàn Suí* and raised *Móu Guāng*.
Following the ancient Sages, the foundation will surely expand.
Wishing to set forth words:
in a chaotic age, the good are hated and it is not governed.
Hiding faults and envying the worthy,
long following villainy and deceit, rarely is there no disaster.
How troublesome!
Perversity causes it.
Sagely wisdom is not used; the ignorant plan.
The front carriage has overturned,
but the one behind does not know to change—
when will they wake?
Not waking up,
not knowing suffering.
Confused and losing the goal, switching high and low.
Loyalty does not reach the top;
ears and eyes are covered, gates and doors are blocked.
Gates and doors are blocked—
great confusion.
Perversity, chaos, and darkness never end.
Right and wrong are reversed.
Forming cliques and deceiving those above, they hate the upright and honest.
Uprightness is hated,
the heart has no restraint,
and crooked, perverse deviance causes one to lose the way.
Do not blame others for your own faults;
how could my self-proclaimed beauty be without cause!
If one does not know to be cautious,
there will certainly be consequences later;
to resent yet persist in error without repentance
leads to many sycophants being advanced,
and fickle words giving rise to deceitful behavior.
The disposition of people
is such that one must be prepared;
they compete for favor, envy the worthy, and harbor mutual hatred.
They are jealous of merit and disparage the virtuous;
below, they gather factions, and above, they obscure the truth.
When the superior is obstructed and blinded,
he loses his supporting power;
he employs sycophants and cannot control them—
like the disaster caused by Shú Gōng Zhǎngfù,
which led to Lì Wáng being exiled to Zhì.
Zhōu Yōu and Lì,
the reasons they failed
were that they did not listen to warnings and harmed the loyal.
Alas, what kind of person am I,
that I alone should meet such times in a chaotic age!
Desiring to speak from the heart,
my words are not followed;
I fear suffering a violent end like Zǐxū,
whose advice was ignored,
and who was beheaded, placed in a leather vessel, and thrown into the Jiāng.
Observe past events
to caution oneself;
order and chaos, right and wrong, can thus be understood.
I entrust my meaning to this Chéng Xiāng song.
Let us complete the Chéng Xiāng,
and speak of the methods of governance.
The ruler's deliberations have five constraints to make them clear:
if the ruler strictly observes them,
those below will be fair and upright,
and the state will flourish.
Let ministers fulfill their offices
and none live in idleness;
attend to the fundamentals, practice frugality, and wealth will be limitless.
Let all affairs follow the superior,
none being allowed to command one another
so that the people's strength is unified.
When they keep to their duties,
food and clothing will be sufficient.
Generosity and parsimony should have grades, and ranks and garments should be clear.
Benefits must only look to the superior;
none may grant favors arbitrarily;
who then could gain privately?
When the ruler’s laws are clear,
and his deliberations follow a constant standard,
once the models are set, the people will know the right direction.
Advancing and retreating follow regulations;
no matter high or low rank,
who could act for private gain?
When the ruler models the law
and prohibits what should not be done,
none will fail to find the teachings pleasing and reputations will not shift.
Those who cultivate them will find glory;
those who depart from them will find disgrace;
who would seek any other teacher?
When punishments are appropriate and displayed,
and one guards the boundaries,
those below cannot use their influence to favor private houses.
Crimes and calamities have regulations;
none may vary the weight of punishment, so authority is not divided.
Let us speak of the basis of leadership:
clarity brings good fortune.
If the lord loves deliberation, he will certainly plan well.
Let the five ways of listening be cultivated and guided;
then all will be ordered and successful—who could take control for themselves?
Listen according to constant principles,
and clarify the actual petitions.
Use the "three and five" methods to examine carefully and apply rewards and punishments.
Those who are prominent will certainly get what they deserve,
and those hidden will become prominent;
the people will return to sincerity.
Let speech be measured
and checked against reality.
Distinguish truth from falsehood so that rewards and punishments are certain.
Those below will not deceive those above;
all will speak according to the facts,
as clear as the sun.
When communication from above flows freely,
even the hidden and distant will be reached.
Observe those who follow the law and those who do not; see even what is not visible.
Once ears and eyes are enlightened,
officials will respect the laws and none will dare to be unrestrained.
When the ruler’s commands are issued,
their execution follows regulations;
officials should carefully carry them out without confusion or deceit.
Those below should not make private requests;
each should receive what is appropriate
and set aside cleverness or clumsiness.
If ministers carefully follow,
and the ruler controls changes,
and the public examines and thinks well so that deliberations are not chaotic,
in this way the world is governed;
future generations will take this as a model, forming a consistent thread of law.
Here is a great thing:
it is neither silk nor fabric,
yet its patterns form a beautiful composition.
It is neither the sun nor the moon,
yet it brings light to the world.
Through it, the living obtain longevity;
through it, the dead are buried;
through it, city walls are made secure;
through it, the three armies are made strong.
Pure, it makes one a King;
mixed, it makes one a Hegemon;
without any part of it, one perishes.
Your servant is ignorant and does not recognize it;
I venture to ask the King.
The King says:
Is it not that which is refined but not ornate?
Is it not that which is simple and easy to understand, yet reaches the highest principles?
Is it not that which the gentleman respects but the petty person does not?
If one's nature does not attain it, one is like a beast;
if one's nature attains it, is one not very refined and elegant?
If a common man exalts it, he becomes a Sage;
if a feudal lord exalts it, does he not unify the Four Seas?
Reaching the utmost clarity yet concise,
most compliant yet having a distinct form—
please return this to Lǐ. Lǐ.
August Heaven sent down great things
to bestow upon the people below;
some are thick and some are thin,
they are never uniform or equal.
Jié and Zhòu brought chaos with them;
Tāng and Wǔ showed worthiness with them.
Whether confused or clear,
whether brilliant or solemn,
they circulate throughout the Four Seas
in less than a single day.
The gentleman use it for cultivation;
Zhí used it to break into houses.
It is as vast as Heaven
and as subtle as to be formless.
Through it, righteous conduct is corrected;
through it, undertakings are completed.
It can prohibit violence and provide for the destitute;
the common people depend on it to find peace and tranquility.
Your servant is ignorant and does not recognize it;
I wish to ask its name.
It is said:
Is it not that which finds safety in the broad and level
and danger in the steep and narrow?
Is it not that which treats the pure as kin
and the defiled as enemies?
Is it not that which is hidden deep within
yet conquers enemies without?
Is it not that which models itself after Yǔ and Shùn
and can cover their tracks?
Conduct, movement, and stillness depend on it
before they can be appropriate.
It is the essence of blood and breath,
and the glory of will and intent.
The common people depend on it to find peace;
the world depends on it to find order.
It is clear, reaching, pure, and without blemish;
this is called the Knowledge of the gentleman. Zhì.
There is a thing here:
at rest, it is all-encompassing and quiet, reaching to the lowest;
in motion, it is supremely high and great.
What is round in it matches the compass;
what is square in it matches the T-square.
It is as vast as Heaven and Earth;
its virtue is as thick as that of Yáo and Yǔ.
It is as subtle as a fine hair
yet it fills the great universe.
Suddenly, it reaches the furthest distance;
swiftly, it chases itself and returns.
Looming high, it is the remedy for the world's difficulties.
Its virtue is thick and never discarded;
the five colors are complete in its pattern.
It goes and comes through the confused and weary;
it connects to the Great Spirit.
Its exits and entries are extreme;
none know its gate.
If the world loses it, it perishes;
if the world gains it, it survives.
This disciple is not clever,
but wishes to present this;
the gentleman has set forth these words,
and I ask to fathom their meaning.
It says:
Is this that which is vast and yet does not obstruct?
It fills the Great Universe (Dà Yǔ) without being cramped,
yet it enters the smallest crevices without being crowded.
It travels far and moves swiftly, yet cannot be used to send a message.
It comes and goes in a daze, yet cannot be firmly blocked.
It arrives violently, killing and wounding, yet is not subject to calculation or dread.
Its merit covers the world, yet it does not claim its placement for itself.
It relies on the earth and roams the universe,
befriending the wind and fathering the rain.
In winter it produces cold,
in summer it produces heat.
Vast is its spirit;
let us attribute it to the Cloud (Yún). The Cloud.
There is a thing here:
naked is its form,
it transforms repeatedly like a spirit.
Its merit covers the world,
providing the patterns for ten thousand generations.
Rites (Lǐ) and music are established by it,
nobility and meanness are distinguished by it.
It nourishes the aged and grows the young;
they depend on it to exist.
Its name and title are not beautiful,
for it is a neighbor to the violent.
When its merit is established, its body is discarded;
when the work is done, its home is destroyed.
It casts off its elderly
and gathers its later generations.
It is a benefit to mankind,
but a victim of birds.
Your servant is ignorant and does not recognize it;
I ask the Five Greats (Wǔ Tài) to divine it.
The Five Greats (Wǔ Tài) divine it, saying:
Is this that which has the body of a beautiful woman
but the head of a horse?
It transforms repeatedly but does not live long?
It is good at being strong but clumsy at being old?
It has parents but no male or female mate?
It hides in winter and roams in summer,
eating mulberry leaves and spitting silk,
first in chaos and later in order?
It is born in summer yet hates the heat;
it likes moisture yet hates the rain.
It takes the pupa as its mother
and the moth as its father.
Three times it bows and three times it rises,
then its work is complete.
This is called the principle of the Silkworm (Cán). The Silkworm.
There is a thing here:
it is born on mountain slopes
and dwells in halls and rooms.
It has no knowledge and no skill,
yet is good at tailoring robes.
It does not thieve or steal,
yet it travels by boring through holes.
Day and night it joins and separates
to create patterns;
it is able to form vertical alliances
and is also good at connecting horizontal ones.
Below it covers the common people,
above it adorns emperors and kings.
Its achievements are very broad,
but it is not seen as worthy or good.
When used in season, it survives;
when not used, it perishes.
Your servant is ignorant and does not recognize it;
I dare to ask the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) says:
Is this that which is large when it begins to live,
but small when its work is done?
It has a long tail and a sharp point?
Its head is sharp and penetrating, while its tail is winding and trailing?
Going once and coming once,
it uses its tail to complete its work.
It has no feathers and no wings,
yet it moves back and forth with extreme speed.
When the tail is born, the work begins;
when the tail is wound around, the work ends.
It takes the Hairpin (Zān) as its father
and the Case (Guǎn) as its mother.
Having sewn the outer garments,
it then joins the inner linings.
This is called the principle of the Needle (Zhēn). The Needle.
When the world is not well-ordered,
please allow me to present a Strange Song (Guì Shī):
Heaven and Earth change places,
the four seasons shift their directions.
The stars fall and plummet,
morning and evening are dark and blind.
The dim and dark ascend to brightness,
the sun and moon are hidden below.
Fairness and impartiality
are called opportunistic;
one whose will is for the public benefit,
dwelling in many-storied towers and spacious halls,
without private grudges against people,
or sounding the alarm to prepare weapons.
When Way (Dào) and Virtue (Dé) are pure and complete,
slanderous mouths clamor loudly.
Humane people are rejected and constrained,
while the arrogant and violent dominate.
The world is dark and perilous,
fearing the loss of the era's heroes.
Chī dragons act as lizards,
owls act as Phoenixes (Fènghuáng).
Bǐ Gān was disemboweled,
Kǒngzǐ was detained in Kuāng.
How clear is their bright knowledge!
How sorrowful is their encounter with unlucky times!
How they strive for the great practice of rites and righteousness!
How dark is the blindness of the world!
Bright Heaven does not return to order,
the sorrow is boundless.
After a thousand years, there must be a reversal;
this is the constant of antiquity.
Disciples, exert yourselves in learning;
Heaven will not forget you.
The Sages (Shèng Rén) fold their hands,
for the time is almost at hand.
When faced with the doubt of the foolish,
I wish to hear words of reversal.
The Small Song (Xiǎo Gē) says:
"I think of those distant lands,
how they are obstructed!
Humane people are bent and constrained,
violent people are prosperous.
Loyal ministers are in danger,
slanderers are in favor."
Xuán jade and Yáo pearls,
people know not to wear them.
Coarse cloth and fine brocade,
people know not the difference.
Lǘ Jū and Zǐ Shē—
no one acts as a matchmaker for them.
Mómo and Diāofù—
these are the ones who bring joy.
Taking the blind for the seeing,
taking the deaf for the hearing.
Taking peril for safety,
taking good fortune for calamity.
Alas!
O High Heaven (Shàng Tiān)!
How can they be the same!
A Great Summary (Dàlüè). He who rules men:
if he exalts Rites (Lǐ) and honors the worthy, he will be a King (Wáng);
if he values the law and loves the people, he will be a Hegemon (Bà);
if he loves profit and practices much deceit, he will be in peril.
To be near to all four sides,
nothing is better than the center.
Therefore, the King (Wáng) must reside in the center of the world;
this is Rites (Lǐ).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) has an outer screen;
the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) have an inner screen;
this is Rites (Lǐ).
An outer screen—
he does not wish to be seen from the outside;
an inner screen—
he does not wish to see inside.
When a Feudal Lord (Zhūhóu) summons his minister,
the minister does not wait for the carriage to be harnessed
but runs while pulling on his robes in reverse;
this is Rites (Lǐ).
The Book of Poetry (Shī) says:
"Topsy-turvy, topsy-turvy,
from the lord comes the summons."
When the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) summons the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu),
he provides the carriage and prepares the horses;
this is Rites (Lǐ).
The Book of Poetry (Shī) says:
"I go out with my carriage,
to those pasture lands.
From the place of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),
it is said I have come."
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) wears the Mountain Crown (Shān Miǎn);
the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) wear the Black Cap (Xuán Guān);
the Great Officers (Dàfū) wear the Ceremonial Crown (Bì Miǎn);
the Scholars (Shì) wear the Leather Cap (Wéi Biàn);
this is Rites (Lǐ).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) holds the Tǐng tablet;
the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) hold the Tú tablet;
the Great Officers (Dàfū) carry the Hù tablet;
this is Rites (Lǐ).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) uses the carved bow (Diāo Gōng);
the Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) use the red bow (Tóng Gōng);
the Great Officers (Dàfū) use the black bow (Hēi Gōng);
this is Rites (Lǐ).
When Feudal Lords (Zhūhóu) visit each other,
a Minister (Qīng) acts as the intermediary;
he brings all the trained scholars to follow,
while leaving humane men to guard the state.
Use a *guī* to engage a person,
a *bì* to inquire after a scholar,
a *yuàn* to summon a person,
a *jué* to sever ties with a person,
and a *huán* to recall one who was severed.
The ruler’s benevolent heart is established therein;
wisdom is its servant,
and ritual is its full expression.
Therefore, a King puts benevolence first and ritual second;
such is the bestowal of Heaven.
The records of the *Pìnglǐ* say:
“If the ritual gifts are too lavish, they harm virtue;
if wealth is extravagant, it destroys ritual.”
“Ritual, ritual,” they say;
is it merely about jade and silk?
The *Shī* says:
“The things are fine,
provided they are accompanied by sincerity.”
If the time is not appropriate,
if the interaction is not respectful,
and if there is no joy,
then even if the things are fine,
it is not ritual.
Those who travel by water mark the depths
so that people do not fall in;
those who govern the people mark the sources of disorder
so that people do not go astray.
Ritual
is the marker;
the former Kings used ritual to mark the disorder of the world.
Nowadays, those who abolish ritual
are removing the markers.
Therefore, the people are confused
and fall into calamity and disaster;
this is why punishments and penalties are so numerous.
Shùn said:
“Only when I follow rightful desires is there order.”
Thus, the emergence of ritual
is for those from the Worthies down to the common people;
it is not for the purpose of becoming a Sage,
yet it is also the means by which one becomes a Sage.
Without learning, one does not achieve it:
Yáo learned from Jūn Chóu,
Shùn learned from Wù Chéng Zhāo,
and Yǔ learned from Xī Wáng Guó.
At fifty, one does not complete the physical rigors of mourning;
at seventy, only the mourning garment is kept.
In the ritual of the groom meeting the bride in person,
the father stands facing south
and the son kneels facing north.
The father pours wine for him and commands him:
“Go and meet your helpmate,
to complete the affairs of our ancestral lineage.
Lead with reverence to continue the line of our late mothers;
may you have constancy.”
The son says:
“Yes.
My only fear is that I will be incapable;
how could I dare forget your command!”
Now, as for “action,”
it refers to the practice of ritual.
As for ritual:
the noble are respected,
the elderly are treated with filial piety,
the elder brothers are treated with fraternal respect,
the young are treated with kindness,
and the lowly are treated with benevolence.
Bestowing gifts upon one's household
is like using rewards and honors in the state;
expressing anger toward one's servants and concubines
is like using punishments on the myriad people.
The Jūnzǐ toward his son:
loves him but does not show it on his face,
employs him without an overbearing appearance,
and guides him with the Way without coercion.
Ritual takes following the human heart as its basis;
therefore, even if something is absent from the *Lǐjīng*,
if it follows the human heart,
it is all ritual.
The general principles of ritual:
in serving the living,
it is the adornment of joy;
in seeing off the dead,
it is the adornment of grief;
in military affairs,
it is the adornment of majesty.
Loving kin, being faithful to old friends, employing the meritorious, and rewarding the laborious are the gradations of benevolence.
Honoring the noble, respecting the honorable, exalting the worthy, venerating the elderly, and respecting the elders are the categories of righteousness.
When their practice attains its proper measure,
it is the order of ritual.
Benevolence is love,
therefore it is affectionate.
Righteousness
is principle,
therefore it is practiced.
Ritual
is regulation,
therefore it completes.
Benevolence has its neighborhood;
righteousness has its gate.
If one dwells where it is not the neighborhood of benevolence,
it is not benevolence.
If one exits through what is not the gate of righteousness,
it is not righteousness.
Extending kindness without principle
does not complete benevolence;
pursuing principle without courage
does not complete righteousness;
examining regulation without harmony
does not complete ritual;
harmony that is not expressed
does not complete music.
Therefore it is said:
benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music—
their ultimate purpose is one.
The Jūnzǐ dwells in benevolence by means of righteousness,
only then is it benevolence.
He practices righteousness by means of ritual,
only then is it righteousness.
He establishes ritual by returning to the root and completing the branches,
only then is it ritual.
When these three are all mastered,
only then is it the Way.
Gifts of money and goods are called *fù*;
carriages and horses are called *fèng*;
clothes and garments are called *suì*;
curios and favorites are called *zèng*;
jade and shells for the mouth are called *hán*.
*Fù* and *fèng* are used to assist the living;
*zèng* and *suì* are used to see off the dead.
If seeing off the dead does not reach the coffin or the corpse,
or if condoling the living does not reach their sorrow,
it is not ritual.
Therefore, for auspicious matters one travels fifty *lǐ*;
in rushing to a funeral one travels a hundred *lǐ*,
so that the *fèng* and *zèng* arrive in time for the ceremony;
this is a great principle of ritual.
Ritual
is the pulling-rope of governance.
If one governs without ritual,
governance will not proceed.
When the Tiānzǐ ascends the throne,
the Shàngqīng comes forward and says:
“How long is this sorrow!
To be able to remove hardship is a blessing;
to be unable to remove hardship is to be a thief.”
He presents the Tiānzǐ with one tablet.
The Zhōngqīng comes forward and says:
“He who matches Heaven and possesses the land below
thinks of matters before they occur
and thinks of hardships before they occur.
Thinking of matters before they occur is called ‘connection’;
with connection, matters are easily accomplished.
Thinking of hardships before they occur is called ‘prevention’;
with prevention, calamity does not arise.
Thinking of matters only after they occur is called ‘lateness’;
with lateness, matters do not succeed.
Thinking of hardships only after they occur is called ‘distress’;
with distress, calamity cannot be warded off.”
He presents the Tiānzǐ with two tablets.
The Xiàqīng comes forward and says:
“Be reverent and cautious, and do not be idle.
Those who celebrate are in the hall;
those who condole are at the gate.
Calamity and blessing are neighbors;
none know through which door they enter.
Be prepared!
Be prepared!
The myriad people look up to you!”
He presents the Tiānzǐ with three tablets.
Yǔ, upon seeing farmers working in pairs, would lean on the crossbar of his carriage in respect;
when passing a settlement of ten households, he would certainly dismount.
To execute too early,
or to hold court too late,
is not ritual.
Governing the people without ritual—
any movement will lead to their falling.
Bending until level is called *bài*,
bending below the level is called *qǐshǒu*,
and bending until the forehead touches the ground is called *qǐsǎng*.
The ministers of a *dàfū* do not perform the *qǐshǒu* when bowing;
this is not to honor the household ministers,
but is the means by which they are distinguished from the ruler’s subjects.
Those of the first commission are ranked by age in the township;
those of the second commission are ranked by age in the clan;
as for those of the third commission,
even if a clansman is seventy years old, he dares not take precedence over them.
There are upper *dàfū*,
middle *dàfū*,
and lower *dàfū*.
In auspicious matters, honor is prioritized;
in funeral matters, kinship is prioritized.
Ruler and subject must be honorable;
father and son must be intimate;
brothers must be harmonious;
and husband and wife must be joyful.
The young are led by the elder,
and the old are provided with sustenance.
Thus, Heaven and Earth give birth to them,
and the sages perfect them.
The *pìn* rite
is an inquiry;
the *xiǎng* rite
is an offering.
The *sīdí*
is a private audience.
The beauty of speech is
solemn and majestic.
The beauty of the court is
dignified and orderly.
For those who are subjects,
there is remonstrance but no slander,
there is departure but no resentment,
and there is grievance but no rage.
A ruler toward a *dàfū*
inquires about his illness three times
and attends his funeral three times;
toward a *shì*,
he inquires once
and attends once.
Unless it is to inquire about illness or offer condolences at a funeral,
a feudal lord does not go to the home of a subject.
After the burial,
if the ruler was a friend of the deceased’s father,
if he offers food, one may eat it,
not avoiding fine grain or meat,
but if there is wine or sweet liquor, one declines it.
The living quarters should not exceed the ancestral temple in grandeur,
and banquet robes should not exceed sacrificial garments;
this is ritual propriety.
The hexagram *Xián* in the *Yì*,
reveals the way of husband and wife.
The way of husband and wife
must be correct,
as it is the foundation of the relationships between ruler and subject, and father and son.
*Xián*
means resonance;
it is to use the high to place oneself below the low,
to use the male to place himself below the female,
and for the yielding to be above while the firm is below.
The significance of inviting a *shì*
and the way of personally meeting the bride
are to emphasize the beginning.
Ritual propriety
is that which people walk upon;
if they lose that which they walk upon,
they will surely trip, fall, or drown.
That which is lost may be slight, yet the chaos it causes is great:
such is ritual propriety.
is like the balance and scale to weight,
or the plumb line and ink to straightness.
Therefore, without ritual propriety, man cannot live;
without ritual propriety, affairs cannot be completed;
and without ritual propriety, the state and family cannot be at peace.
The sounds of the *hé* and *luán* bells
match the *Wǔ* and *Xiàng* dances when walking
and match the *Sháo* and *Hù* dances when hurrying.
The gentleman listens to the pitch-pipes and practices his bearing before going out.
When the frost falls, the bride is welcomed;
when the ice melts, the taking of lives ceases. Within the inner quarters,
one attends the wife once every ten days.
When sitting, look at the knees;
when standing, look at the feet;
when responding and speaking, look at the face.
When standing, look ahead six *chǐ*, and multiply this by six; six times six is thirty-six,
which is three *zhàng* and six *chǐ*.
Form and appearance, emotion and utility
are respectively internal and external, surface and substance,
within ritual propriety.
To be able to search and seek is called the ability to deliberate.
In ritual propriety,
the fundamental and the incidental follow each other,
and the end and the beginning correspond.
Ritual propriety
uses wealth and goods for utility,
uses nobility and lowliness for pattern,
and uses quantity for distinction.
A lower minister serves the ruler with goods;
a middle minister serves the ruler with his own person;
an upper minister serves the ruler by recommending other men.
The *Yì* says:
"Return by one's own path,
how could there be blame?"
The *Chūnqiū* considers *Mù Gōng* to be worthy
because it considers him able to change.
If a *shì* has envious friends,
then worthy associates will not be close;
if a ruler has envious ministers,
then worthy men will not arrive.
One who obscures the public interest is called deluded;
one who hides the virtuous is called envious;
one who supports the envious and deluded is called craftily treacherous.
Craftily treacherous people
and envious, deluded ministers
are the weeds and plagues of the state.
One whose mouth can speak of it
and whose person can practice it
is a treasure of the state.
One whose mouth cannot speak of it
but whose person can practice it
is a vessel of the state.
One whose mouth can speak of it
but whose person cannot practice it
is a utility of the state.
One whose mouth speaks good
but whose person practices evil
is an omen of disaster for the state.
Those who govern a state respect its treasures,
love its vessels,
employ its utilities,
and remove its omens of disaster.
Without wealth, there is no way to nourish the people's feelings;
without education, there is no way to order the people's nature.
Therefore, every family has a five-*mǔ* homestead
and a hundred-*mǔ* field;
they attend to their labor and their time is not taken away;
this is the means to enrich them.
Establishing the *Tàixué*,
setting up the *xiāng* and *xù* schools,
cultivating the six rites,
and clarifying the seven teachings:
these are the means to guide them.
The *Shī* says:
"Give them drink and food,
teach them and instruct them."
Then the king's business is complete.
When *Wǔ Wáng* first entered *Yīn*,
he honored the village gate of *Shāng Róng*,
he bowed to the prison of *Jīzǐ*,
and he wept at the grave of *Bǐgān*;
thus the whole world turned toward goodness.
In the world and the state, there are outstanding *shì*;
in every age, there are worthy men.
The lost do not ask the way;
the drowning do not ask for a ford;
and a man destined for ruin loves to be alone.
The *Shī* says:
"My words are but for use,
do not treat them as a joke.
The people of old had a saying:
'Consult the grass and firewood cutters.'"
This means one should inquire widely.
Those who have laws act according to the laws;
those who do not have laws proceed by analogy.
By means of the root,
one knows the branch;
by means of the left,
one knows the right;
for all the hundred matters have different
principles yet maintain a mutual coherence.
Rewards and punishments
are applied only after universal categories are understood.
In extending education and practice of customs,
they proceed only after mutual compliance is achieved.
For those eighty years of age, one son is exempt from service;
for those ninety, the entire family is exempt;
for the disabled who cannot be cared for except by others, one person is exempt from service.
During mourning for parents,
one is exempt from service for three years.
For the zīcuī and dàgōng mourning grades,
one is exempt from service for three months.
Those following the feudal lords do not
participate; those newly married
are exempt from service for one year.
Kǒngzǐ said that Zǐjiā Jū was a continuous Great Officer,
but not equal to Yànzǐ;
Yànzǐ
was a minister of achievement and utility,
but not equal to Zǐchǎn;
Zǐchǎn
was a man of benevolence,
but not equal to Guǎn Zhòng.
As for Guǎn Zhòng’s character,
he exerted effort for achievement but not for righteousness;
he exerted effort for wisdom but not for humaneness;
he was a rustic man
and cannot be considered a Great Officer of the Son of Heaven.
Mèngzǐ saw Wáng Xuān three times
without speaking of affairs.
His disciples asked:
“Why have you met the King of Qí three times and not spoken of affairs?”
Mèngzǐ said:
“I first attack his corrupt heart.”
Gōngxíng Zǐzhī went to Yān
and met Zéng Yuán on the road;
he asked:
“What is the Lord of Yān like?”
Zéng Yuán said:
“His will is lowly.
One whose will is lowly treats things lightly;
one who treats things lightly does not seek help.
If he does not seek help,
how can he succeed?
He is like a captive of the Dī or Qiāng tribes:
he does not worry about being bound in a fortress,
but worries that he will not be cremated.
To profit by a hair’s breadth in autumn
while the harm exhausts the state—
yet he still does it.
How can this be considered a wise plan?”
Now, as for one who has lost a needle,
he seeks it all day and does not find it;
when he does find it,
it is not because his eyes have become brighter,
but because he focused his gaze and saw it.
The mind’s relationship to deliberation is just like this.
Righteousness and profit
are things that all people possess.
Even Yáo and Shùn could not remove the people’s desire for profit;
however, they could make it so their desire for profit did not overcome their love of righteousness.
Even Jié and Zhòu could not remove the people’s love of righteousness;
however, they could make it so their love of righteousness did not surpass their desire for profit.
Therefore, when righteousness overcomes profit, it is an age of order;
when profit overcomes righteousness, it is an age of chaos.
If those above value righteousness, then righteousness overcomes profit;
if those above value profit, then profit overcomes righteousness.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven does not speak of quantity;
the feudal lords do not speak of profit and harm;
the Great Officers do not speak of gain and loss;
the scholars do not speak of the circulation of goods and wealth.
The ruler of a state does not breed cattle and sheep for profit;
ministers who have offered their pledges do not breed chickens and pigs for profit;
the High Ministers do not manage gifts and distributions;
the Great Officers do not cultivate orchards and gardens.
From the ranked scholars upwards, all are ashamed of profit and do not compete with the people for business;
they take pleasure in sharing and giving, and are ashamed of accumulating and hoarding.
Thus, the people are not distressed by a lack of wealth,
and the poor have a place to occupy their hands.
Wén Wáng executed four;
Wǔ Wáng executed two;
Zhōugōng completed the task;
by the time of Chéng and Kāng, there were no executions at all.
Accumulating great wealth while being ashamed of having nothing,
and placing heavy burdens on the people while punishing those who are unable to bear them—
this is why corrupt conduct arises
and why punishments are so numerous.
If those above love righteousness,
then the people will quietly
cultivate themselves; if those above love wealth,
then the people will die for profit.
These two
are the crossroads of order and chaos.
A proverb of the people says:
“Do you wish to be wealthy?
Then endure shame,
be duplicitous,
cut off old friends,
and turn your back on righteousness.”
If those above love wealth,
then the conduct of the people will be like this;
how could there not be chaos?
Tāng, during a drought, prayed saying:
“Is my government immoderate?
Have I caused the people suffering?
Why has the lack of rain reached such an extreme!
Are the palaces too magnificent?
Is the influence of women too great?
Why has the lack of rain reached such an extreme!
Is bribery practiced?
Are slanderous men flourishing?
Why has the lack of rain reached such an extreme!”
Heaven’s creation of the people
was not for the sake of the ruler.
Heaven’s establishment of the ruler
was for the sake of the people.
Therefore, in ancient times, the dividing of land and establishing of states
was not merely to ennoble the feudal lords;
the arranging of offices
and the grading of ranks and salaries
was not merely to honor the Great Officers.
The Way of the ruler is to know people;
the Way of the minister is to know affairs.
Therefore, in Shùn’s governing of the world,
he did not issue commands regarding specific affairs, yet all things were accomplished.
A farmer is skilled in the fields but cannot be made an overseer of farming;
the same is true for artisans and merchants.
Replacing the unworthy with the worthy—
one does not wait for divination to know it is auspicious.
Using order to attack chaos—
one does not wait for battle to know of victory.
The people of Qí wished to attack Lǔ,
but they feared Biàn Zhuāngzǐ
and did not dare to pass through Biàn.
The people of Jìn wished to attack Wèi,
but they feared Zǐlù
and did not dare to pass through Pú.
To not know and yet ask of Yáo and Shùn;
to have nothing and yet seek from the Treasury of Heaven.
It is said:
As for the Way of the former kings,
that is Yáo and Shùn;
as for the vastness of the Six Duplicates,
that is the Treasury of Heaven.
The learning of a gentleman is like the shedding of a skin;
he changes completely and moves on.
Therefore, his walking is an example;
his standing is an example;
his sitting is an example;
his facial expressions and the tone of his voice are examples.
He does not delay in doing good;
he does not let questions remain overnight.
One who is good at learning exhausts its principles;
one who is good at acting investigates its difficulties.
A gentleman establishes his will as if in extremity;
even if the Son of Heaven or the Three Ducal Ministers ask what is correct,
he answers according to right and wrong.
A gentleman is in straits and extremity but does not lose his way;
he is weary and tired but does not become careless;
he faces disaster and hardship but does not forget the words spoken on the mats.
If the year is not cold, there is no way to know the pine and cypress;
if matters are not difficult, there is no way to know that the gentleman is never for a day without these qualities.
When the rain is light,
the Hàn River thus remains hidden.
For those who perfect the small become great;
those who accumulate the minute become prominent;
those whose virtue is supreme have a harmonious radiance in their appearance;
when their conduct is perfected, their reputation spreads far.
The petty person is not sincere within yet seeks reputation without.
To speak without citing a teacher is called rebellion;
to teach without citing a teacher is called betrayal.
Such rebellious and betraying people
are not admitted by a wise ruler,
and when the scholars and Great Officers of the court meet them on the road, they do not speak with them.
Those whose actions are insufficient
make many excuses;
those whose trustworthiness is insufficient
speak with excessive claims of sincerity.
Therefore, the *Chūnqiū* approves of the *Xūmìng* agreements,
while the *Shī* criticizes frequent oaths of alliance;
their underlying intent is the same.
Those who are good at the *Shī* do not over-explain;
those who are good at the *Yì* do not perform divination;
those who are good at the *Lǐ* do not require assistants;
their underlying intent is the same.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The words of a filial son are worthy of being heard,
and his actions are worthy of being seen.
That his words are worthy of being heard
is how he pleases those far away;
that his actions are worthy of being seen
is how he pleases those nearby.
When those nearby are pleased, they become intimate;
when those far away are pleased, they follow him.
To be intimate with those nearby and to have those far away follow him
is the way of a filial son."
When Zēngzǐ was departing,
Yànzǐ accompanied him to the outskirts
and said:
"I, Yīng, have heard
that a gentleman gives words as a parting gift,
while a commoner gives wealth.
I, Yīng, am poor and have no wealth;
I ask to borrow the role of a gentleman
to give you words as a gift: The wheels of a carriage
are made from the wood of Tàishān;
when placed in a shaping frame
for three or five months,
they become curved;
even when worn out, they do not return to their original straightness.
A gentleman's shaping frame
must be chosen with care;
be cautious of it.
Fragrant herbs like Lánchǎi and Gǎoběn,
when soaked in honeyed wine,
their scent is changed once they are worn as a pendant.
Even an upright ruler, if influenced by sweet wine,
can be won over by slander;
that which a gentleman is influenced by
must be chosen with caution."
A person's relationship to learning
is like jade's relationship to carving and polishing.
The *Shī* says:
"As if cut, as if filed,
as if carved, as if polished."
This refers to the pursuit of learning.
The Jade of Héshì
and the rough jade of Jǐnglǐ,
once the jade-worker carves them,
they become treasures of the world.
Zǐgòng and Jìlù
were originally rustic men,
but through exposure to learning
and practicing ritual and righteousness,
they became renowned scholars of the world.
To learn without satiety
and to love scholars without weariness
is to be a storehouse of Heaven.
If a gentleman has doubts, he does not speak;
if not asked, he does not speak;
thus his way reaches far and increases daily.
One who has much knowledge but no intimacy with others,
who is broadly learned but has no guiding principle,
who loves many things but has no fixed purpose—
the gentleman does not associate with such a person.
If one does not recite and chant when young,
and does not engage in discussion and debate when mature,
although such a person may be acceptable,
they are not yet accomplished.
When the gentleman is single-minded in teaching
and the disciple is single-minded in learning,
accomplishment is swift.
When a gentleman advances in office, he can increase the reputation of his superior and decrease the worries of those below.
To occupy a position without ability
is deception;
to receive a large salary without being of benefit
is theft.
A scholar does not necessarily have to serve in office,
but one who serves in office must engage in learning.
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I, Cì, am weary of learning
and wish to rest by serving a ruler."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'Gentle and respectful morning and night,
performing duties with reverence.'
Serving a ruler is difficult;
how can one find rest in serving a ruler?"
"In that case, I, Cì, wish to rest by serving my parents."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'The filial son's devotion is never exhausted,
and forever will blessings be granted to your kind.'
Serving parents is difficult;
how can one find rest in serving parents?"
"In that case, I, Cì, wish to rest with my wife and children."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'An example to his wife,
extending to his brothers,
and so governing the family and the state.'
Managing a wife and children is difficult;
how can one find rest with a wife and children?"
"In that case, I, Cì, wish to rest with friends."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'Friends assist one another,
assisting with dignified demeanor.'
Dealing with friends is difficult;
how can one find rest with friends?"
"In that case, I, Cì, wish to rest by farming."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The *Shī* says:
'By day go gather the reeds,
by night twist them into ropes.
Quickly mount the roof,
for then it is time to sow the hundred grains.'
Farming is difficult;
how can one find rest in farming?"
"In that case, is there no rest for me, Cì?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Look at that grave:
so solitary,
so high,
so secluded.
In this, you will know where rest is found."
Zǐgòng said:
"How great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
and the petty man finds his end there."
Regarding the love of beauty in the *Guófēng*,
the *Zhuàn* says:
"It fulfills one's desires yet does not transgress the proper limits.
Its sincerity can be compared to metal and stone;
its sounds can be performed in the ancestral temple."
The *Xiǎoyǎ* does not comply with corrupt superiors;
its authors withdraw themselves to reside in lowly positions.
Hating the government of the present
and longing for the past,
their words are refined
and their sounds are mournful.
When a state is about to flourish,
it must value teachers and honor mentors;
when teachers are valued and mentors are honored, the laws and standards are preserved.
When a state is about to decline,
it must despise teachers and slight mentors;
when teachers are despised and mentors are slighted, then people seek their own gratification;
when people seek their own gratification, the laws and standards are destroyed.
In ancient times, a common man became an officer at the age of fifty.
The sons of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords underwent the capping ceremony at nineteen;
after being capped, they presided over governance,
for their education was complete.
If someone is a gentleman and loves learning,
he is the right person;
if such a person is not taught,
it is ill-omened.
If someone is not a gentleman but loves learning,
he is not the right person;
if such a person is taught,
it is like providing provisions to a bandit
or lending weapons to a thief.
Those who are not confident in their own conduct
speak with excessive and overflowing words.
The worthy men of old
were as lowly as commoners in hempen clothes
and as poor as ordinary men.
For food, they did not have enough congee;
for clothing, their coarse garments were not whole.
Yet, they would not advance if it were not in accordance with ritual,
and they would not accept anything if it were not in accordance with righteousness.
From where did they derive this?
Zǐ Xià's family was poor,
and his clothes were like hanging quail feathers.
Someone said:
"Why do you not take office?"
He said:
"Among the feudal lords, those who are arrogant toward me,
I do not serve as a minister;
among the grandees, those who are arrogant toward me,
I do not see them again."
Liǔ Xià Huì shared clothes with a gatekeeper and was not suspected;
this has been heard of for a long time.
To contend for profit as small as a fingernail
yet lose one's palm.
One who rules others cannot but be cautious in choosing ministers;
a commoner cannot but be cautious in choosing friends.
Friends are
those through whom one mutually possesses something.
If ways are different,
how can they mutually possess anything?
Spread firewood equally and apply fire,
the fire approaches the dry;
pour water on level ground,
the water flows to the damp.
The following of categories for each other
is as clear as this;
by observing people through their friends,
where could there be doubt?
In choosing friends from among the good,
one cannot but be cautious;
this is the foundation of virtue.
The *Shī* says:
"Do not help forward a great carriage;
the dust will only blind you."
This says not to dwell with petty men.
Lán jǔ and lù zuò,
appearing wise but being otherwise.
Weak and easily coerced,
appearing benevolent but being otherwise.
Fierce, obstinate, and fond of fighting,
appearing brave but being otherwise.
Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and goodness to a person
are like goods, wealth, grain, and rice to a household;
those who have much are rich,
those who have little are poor,
and those who have none are destitute.
Therefore, if one cannot do the great things
and does not do the small things,
this is the way to abandon the state and discard one's life.
All things have that which they ride upon to come;
that which rides upon their emergence
is that which returns to them.
Rumors destroy it;
goods and sexual beauty distance one from it.
That from which disaster arises
arises from the minute;
therefore, the Jūnzǐ cuts it off early.
The trustworthiness of speech
lies between the qū and the gài vessels.
If in doubt, do not speak;
if not asked, do not speak.
The wise are clear about affairs
and understand calculations;
they cannot be served without sincerity.
Thus it is said:
"A Jūnzǐ is hard to please;
if you try to please him not in accordance with the Dào,
he is not pleased."
The saying goes:
"A rolling marble stops at a bowl or pot;
a rumor stops at the wise."
This is why the words of various schools and heterodox studies dislike the Ru.
If right and wrong are in doubt,
then measure them by distant matters,
test them by near objects,
and examine them with a calm heart;
rumors will then stop,
and evil words will die.
Zēng Zǐ was eating fish;
there was some left over.
He said:
"Add soup to it."
The disciples said:
"Adding soup spoils it;
it is better to braise it."
Zēng Zǐ wept and said:
"Is there a different intent!
I am saddened that I heard of this so late."
Do not use your own shortcomings to encounter others' strengths.
Therefore, block and avoid your shortcomings,
move and follow what you serve.
To be clever in knowledge but not follow the law,
to be observant and discerning but practice deviance,
to be brave and decisive but lack ritual:
these are what the Jūnzǐ detests.
One who speaks much but is systematic
is a Sage;
one who speaks little but follows the law
is a Jūnzǐ.
One who speaks much without law and flows volubly,
although eloquent,
is a petty man.
The law of the state forbids picking up what is lost on the road,
detesting the common people's habit of gaining without proper allotment.
If there is a sense of sharing and duty,
then the world can be accommodated and governed;
if there is no sense of sharing and duty,
then even one wife and one concubine will cause chaos.
As for the people of the world,
each has their own distinct intent;
yet there are things they commonly grant.
Those who speak of flavor grant it to Yì Yá;
those who speak of sound grant it to Shī Kuàng;
those who speak of governance grant it to the Sān Wáng.
After the Sān Wáng had fixed the laws and measures
and established rituals and music to pass them down,
if one does not use them but changes and creates on their own,
how is that different from altering the harmony of Yì Yá
or changing the pitch-pipes of Shī Kuàng?
Without the laws of the Sān Wáng,
the world would not wait to perish,
and the state would not wait to die.
One that drinks but does not eat
is the cicada;
one that neither drinks nor eats
is the ephemera.
Yú Shùn and Xiào Jǐ were filial yet their parents did not love them;
Bǐ Gān and Zǐ Xū were loyal yet their rulers did not use them;
Zhòng Ní and Yán Yuān were wise yet were destitute in the world.
If one is coerced in a violent state and has no way to avoid it,
then exalt their goodness,
publicize their beauty,
speak of their strengths, and do not mention their shortcomings.
One who is compliant yet perishes
is slandered;
one who is broad yet destitute
is criticized;
one who purifies himself yet becomes more turbid
is harmed by mouths.
A Jūnzǐ can make himself worthy of honor
but cannot make others necessarily honor him;
he can make himself worthy of use
but cannot make others necessarily use him.
Proclamations and oaths did not reach the level of the Wǔ Dì;
covenants and curses did not reach the level of the Sān Wáng;
exchanging hostage sons did not reach the level of the Wǔ Bà.
Kǒngzǐ visited the temple of Lǔ Huán Gōng;
there was a leaning vessel.
Kǒngzǐ asked the temple keeper:
"What vessel is this?"
The temple keeper said:
"This is likely the vessel for the right side of the seat."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have heard that for the vessel of the right side of the seat,
when empty it leans,
when half-full it stands straight,
and when full it overturns."
Kǒngzǐ looked back and said to his disciples:
"Pour water into it!"
The disciples ladled water and poured it in;
half-full, it stood straight;
full, it overturned;
empty, it leaned. Kǒngzǐ sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
How can there be anything full that does not overturn?"
Zǐ Lù said:
"May I venture to ask if there is a way to maintain fullness?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"With intelligence and sagely wisdom,
maintain them with stupidity;
with merit covering the world,
maintain it with yielding;
with courage and strength that soothe the age,
maintain them with timidity;
with wealth possessing the four seas,
maintain it with humility.
This is what is called the way of ladling out and reducing."
Kǒngzǐ served as the acting Chancellor for Lǔ;
after attending court for seven days, he executed Shǎozhèng Mǎo.
His disciples came forward to ask him, saying:
"Now, Shǎozhèng Mǎo
is a famous man of Lǔ.
When the Master took up the government, he began by executing him;
could this not be a mistake?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Sit down!
I will tell you the reason.
There are five types of evil in people,
and theft and robbery are not among them:
the first is having a mind that is discerning yet treacherous;
the second is conduct that is perverse yet persistent;
the third is speech that is false yet eloquent;
the fourth is a memory for the vulgar that is extensive;
the fifth is following what is wrong and making it appear glossy.
If a person has even one of these five,
they cannot escape execution by a gentleman,
and Shǎozhèng Mǎo possessed all of them.
Therefore, his dwelling was enough to gather followers and form a faction;
his talk was enough to disguise heterodoxy and confuse the masses;
his strength was enough to oppose the right and stand alone.
This is the hero of the petty men,
and he could not but be executed.
For this reason, Tāng executed Yīn Xié;
Wén Wáng executed Pān Zhǐ;
Zhōu Gōng executed Guǎn Shú;
Tài Gōng executed Huá Shì;
Guǎn Zhòng executed Fù Lǐ Yǐ;
Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī and Shǐ Fù.
These seven individuals
belonged to different eras but shared the same mind;
they could not but be executed.
The *Shī* says:
'The anxious heart is troubled,
hated by the crowd of petty men.'
When petty men form a crowd,
that is enough to cause anxiety."
Kǒngzǐ served as the Sīkòu of Lǔ.
There was a father and son who were litigating against each other;
Kǒngzǐ detained them
and did not resolve the matter for three months.
The father requested to stop the suit,
and Kǒngzǐ released them.
Jì Sūn heard of this
and was displeased,
saying:
"This old man is deceiving me.
He told me:
'In governing a state, one must use filial piety.'
Now he should have killed one person to punish unfilial conduct,
yet he released them."
Rǎn Zǐ reported this.
Kǒngzǐ sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
When those above lose the Way,
and those below are killed for it—
how can that be right?
To fail to teach the people
yet to listen to their litigation
is to kill the innocent.
When the three armies suffer a great defeat,
one cannot behead them;
when the prisons are not well-ordered,
one cannot use punishment;
this is because the blame does not lie with the people.
Now, to be lax in commands yet strict in executions
is to be predatory.
To have times for growth
but no set times for collection
is to be violent.
Not to teach yet to demand success
is to be oppressive.
Only after these three are eliminated
can punishments then be applied.
The *Shū* says:
'Let punishments be righteous and executions be righteous;
do not use them to achieve your ends;
I will only say there has been no compliant service.'
This means teaching first."
Therefore, the former kings first displayed the Way,
and those above first practiced it.
If this did not work,
they honored the worthy to bring it to a peak.
If this did not work,
they discarded the incompetent to simplify things.
After reaching the peak for three years, the common people followed like the wind.
If personal practice is not followed,
then they waited and applied punishment;
then the people knew their crime.
The *Shī* says:
"Grand Master Yǐn Shì,
is the foundation of Zhōu;
holding the scales of the state,
maintaining the four quarters,
screening the Son of Heaven,
so that the common people are not misled." Because of this, majesty was stern yet not put to the test,
and punishments were laid aside and not used;
this is what is meant.
The present age is not so:
they throw teaching into chaos
and multiply punishments,
so the people are confused and fall into them;
then they follow up by controlling them.
Thus, punishments become more numerous while evil is not overcome.
A bank three feet high cannot be climbed by an empty carriage,
yet a mountain a hundred fathoms high can be climbed by a carriage with a heavy load.
Why?
Because of the gradual slope.
People do not climb over a wall several fathoms high,
but a boy will frolic upon a mountain a hundred fathoms high.
Because of the gradual slope.
Now, the gradual decline of the world has lasted for a long time,
can one then make the people not overstep?
The *Shī* says:
"The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
its straightness like an arrow.
It is what the gentleman treads,
and what the petty man looks upon.
Looking back with yearning,
the tears fall in streams!"
Is it not sorrowful!
The *Shī* says:
"Look at that sun and moon,
long, long are my thoughts.
The road is said to be far,
how can it be said they can come?"
The Master said:
"If one bows their head like Yī,
will they not come?"
Kǒngzǐ was observing the water flowing to the east.
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Why is it that the gentleman, when seeing great water, must observe it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Now, water universally provides for all living things without acting for itself;
it resembles Virtue.
Its flow seeks the lower ground,
winding and turning but always following its principle;
it resembles Righteousness.
Its vast surging never exhausts its source;
it resembles the Way.
If there is a breach and it flows forth,
its response is swift like an echo.
Its rushing into a valley a hundred fathoms deep without fear
resembles Courage.
When filling a container, it is always level;
it resembles Law.
When full, it does not seek to be leveled off;
it resembles Uprightness.
It is soft and yielding yet reaches into the minute;
it resembles Discernment.
In going out and coming in,
it makes things fresh and clean;
it resembles Good Transformation.
Though it makes ten thousand turns, it must flow East;
it resembles Will.
This is why the gentleman, when seeing great water, must observe it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have things that I find shameful,
I have things that I find vulgar, and
I have things that I find dangerous.
Being young and unable to study hard,
and being old with nothing to teach;
I find this shameful.
Leaving one's hometown,
serving a ruler and achieving success,
then meeting an old friend
and having no words of old times for them;
I find this vulgar.
Dwelling with petty men
is what I find dangerous."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If someone advances like an anthill,
I am with them.
If someone stops like a hill,
I am done with them."
Nowadays, those whose learning is not even like a wart or a cyst
yet arrogantly wish to be teachers of others.
Kǒngzǐ went south to Chǔ.
He was trapped between Chén and Cài;
for seven days he had no cooked food.
The goosefoot soup had no grain in it,
and the disciples all had the look of hunger.
Zǐlù came forward to ask him, saying:
"I, Yóu, have heard:
For those who do good, Heaven rewards them with blessings;
