for those who do not do good, Heaven rewards them with calamity.
Now the Master has accumulated Virtue, amassed Righteousness, and cherished beauty,
practicing these for a long time;
why then do you dwell in such hardship?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu does not understand;
I will tell you.
Do you think that those who are wise must necessarily be employed?
Has Wángzǐ Bǐgān not had his heart cut open?
Do you think that those who are loyal must necessarily be employed?
Has Guān Lóngpáng not been executed?
Do you think that those who give remonstrance must necessarily be employed?
Was Wú Zǐxū not dismembered outside the East Gate of Gūsū?
Encountering or not encountering the right time
is a matter of timing;
being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent.
There have been many gentlemen of broad learning and deep strategy
who did not encounter their time.
Looking at it from this perspective,
those who do not encounter their age are numerous;
why should it be only Qiū?
Furthermore, the zhǐ and lán orchids grow in the deep forest;
it is not because there are no people that they lack fragrance.
The learning of a gentleman
is not for the sake of success;
it is so that when in poverty he is not distressed,
and when in sorrow his will does not falter,
and knowing the beginning and end of misfortune and fortune, his heart is not confused.
Being worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent;
acting or not acting
is a matter of the person;
encountering or not encountering the right time
is a matter of timing;
life and death
are a matter of fate.
Now, if there is a person
who does not encounter his time,
even if he is worthy,
can he put his principles into practice?
If he encounters his time,
what difficulty would there be?
Therefore, the gentleman gains broad learning and makes deep plans,
cultivates his person and rectifies his conduct
to wait for his time."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu!
Sit down!
I will tell you.
In the past, Jìn Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr's ambition for hegemony was born in Cáo;
Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn's ambition for hegemony was born in Huìjī;
Qí Huán Gōng Xiǎobái's ambition for hegemony was born in Jǔ.
Therefore, those whose dwellings are not secluded do not think far,
and those whose persons are not at ease do not have broad ambitions.
How could you know that I will not achieve my aim beneath the Sāngluò?"
Zǐgòng was observing the North Hall of the Ancestral Temple of Lǔ.
When he came out, he asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Earlier, Cì was observing the North Hall of the Great Temple.
I had not even finished
when I looked back at the northern eaves; they were all unevenly finished.
Is there a reason for those eaves?
Or was it a mistake by the craftsmen?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the hall of the Great Temple,
there once was a reason.
The officials brought in fine craftsmen,
and they followed beauty and regulated patterns;
it was not that they lacked fine materials,
but it was because they valued refinement."
Being filial at home and fraternal abroad
is the minor conduct of a person;
being obedient to superiors and sincere to subordinates
is the middle conduct of a person;
following the Way and not the ruler,
following righteousness and not the father,
is the great conduct of a person.
If the will is settled by ritual,
and speech is employed according to categories,
then the Way of the scholar is complete;
even Shùn could not add a hair's breadth to this.
There are three reasons why a filial son does not follow an order:
if following the order puts the parent in danger,
and not following the order keeps the parent safe,
then not following the order is loyalty;
if following the order brings disgrace to the parent,
and not following the order brings honor to the parent,
then for a filial son, not following the order is righteousness;
if following the order leads to animal-like behavior,
and not following the order leads to refined cultivation,
then for a filial son, not following the order is respect.
Therefore, not following an order when it should be followed
is not being a son;
following an order when it should not be followed
is not being loyal.
One who is clear on the meaning of when to follow and when not to follow,
and is able to achieve reverence,
loyalty, trust, uprightness, and sincerity in order to act with caution,
can then be called greatly filial.
The Chuán says:
"Follow the Way and not the ruler,
follow righteousness and not the father."
This is what it means.
Therefore, being able to remain respectful despite toil and exhaustion,
being able to maintain righteousness despite disaster and hardship,
and being able to maintain love despite misfortune, adversity, and being hated
without losing one's affection,
no one but a person of benevolence can do this.
The Shī says:
"The filial son's bounty is never exhausted."
This is what it means.
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"If a son follows his father's orders,
is he filial?
If a minister follows his ruler's orders,
is he loyal?"
He asked three times,
and Kǒngzǐ did not reply.
Kǒngzǐ hurried out
and told Zǐgòng:
"Earlier, the ruler asked Qiū,
saying:
'If a son follows his father's orders,
is he filial?
If a minister follows his ruler's orders,
is he loyal?'
He asked three times and Qiū did not reply.
What do you, Cì, think of this?"
Zǐgòng said:
"If a son follows his father's orders,
he is filial;
if a minister follows his ruler's orders,
he is loyal.
Master, what else is there to answer?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What a petty man!
Cì, you do not understand.
In the past, if a state of ten thousand chariots
had four ministers who would remonstrate,
then its borders would not be reduced;
if a state of a thousand chariots
had three ministers who would remonstrate,
then its altars of soil and grain would not be in danger;
if a household of a hundred chariots
had two ministers who would remonstrate,
then its ancestral temple would not be destroyed.
If a father has a son who remonstrates,
he will not perform acts contrary to ritual;
if a scholar has a friend who remonstrates,
he will not do what is unrighteous.
Therefore, if a son merely follows his father,
how can the son be filial?
If a minister merely follows his ruler,
how can the minister be loyal?
It is by examining the reasons for following that one can be called filial or loyal."
Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ:
"If there is a person here
who rises early and goes to sleep late,
plowing, weeding, and planting,
with calluses on hands and feet
to support his parents,
yet he does not have the reputation of being filial,
why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Is it perhaps because his person is not respectful?
Or because his words are not humble?
Or because his facial expression is not compliant?
The ancients had a saying:
'Is it the clothes?
Is it the silk?
I will not rely on you.'
Now, one rises early and goes to sleep late,
plowing, weeding, and planting,
with calluses on hands and feet
to support his parents.
If he is without those three faults,
how then could he not have the reputation of being filial?
Is it perhaps that the friends he associates with are not benevolent people?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu, remember this;
I will tell you:
Though one may have the strength of the most eminent man in the state,
he cannot lift his own body.
It is not for lack of strength,
but because the position does not allow it.
Therefore, if one remains at home and his conduct is not cultivated,
it is the fault of the person;
if one goes out and his reputation is not prominent,
it is the fault of his friends.
Therefore, the gentleman is sincere in his conduct within
and befriends the worthy when he goes out;
how then could he not have the reputation of being filial?"
Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ:
"If a Great Officer of Lǔ uses a bed during the mourning refinement ritual,
is this in accordance with ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I do not know."
Zǐlù went out
and said to Zǐgòng:
"I thought the Master knew everything,
but the Master simply does not know some things."
Zǐgòng said:
“Why do you ask?”
Zǐlù said:
“I, Yóu, asked
if it is in accordance with the rites for a Great Officer of Lǔ to use a bed after the Liàn sacrifice.
The Master said:
‘I do not know.’”
Zǐgòng said:
“I will ask him for you.”
Zǐgòng asked:
“Is it in accordance with the rites to use a bed after the Liàn sacrifice?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“It is not in accordance with the rites.”
Zǐgòng went out
and said to Zǐlù:
“Did you say the Master had something he did not know?
The Master simply knows everything;
your question was wrong.
According to the rites,
when dwelling in a state,
one does not criticize its Great Officers.”
Zǐlù went to see Kǒngzǐ dressed in formal attire.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Yóu,
why do you look so self-satisfied?
In the past, the Jiāng River flowed out from Mín Shān.
When it first emerged,
its source was small enough to overflow a goblet.
But when it reached the ferry of the Jiāng River,
unless one lashed boats together
and avoided the wind,
it could not be crossed.
Is it not simply that the water increases as it flows downstream?
Now your clothes are grand,
and your expression is full of pride;
who in the world would be willing to admonish you? Yóu!”
Zǐlù hurried out,
changed his clothes, and returned,
appearing more humble.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Mark this,
and I will tell you:
Those who are cautious in speech are not flowery;
those who are cautious in action do not boast.
One who displays knowledge and ability only in their expression
is a petty person.
Therefore, when the gentleman knows something, he says he knows it;
when he does not know, he says he does not know—
this is the essence of speech.
When he is capable of something, he says he is capable;
when he is not capable, he says he is not capable—
this is the ultimate of conduct.
When speech has essence, there is wisdom;
when conduct reaches the ultimate, there is benevolence.
If one is both wise
and benevolent, how could anything be insufficient!”
Zǐlù entered.
The Master said:
“Yóu,
what is a wise man like?
What is a benevolent man like?”
Zǐlù replied:
“A wise man makes others know him;
a benevolent man makes others love him.”
The Master said:
“You may be called a shì.”
Zǐgòng entered.
The Master said:
“Cì,
what is a wise man like?
What is a benevolent man like?”
Zǐgòng replied:
“A wise man knows others;
a benevolent man loves others.”
The Master said:
“You may be called a shì jūnzǐ.”
Yán Yuān entered.
The Master said:
“Huí,
what is a wise man like?
What is a benevolent man like?”
Yán Yuān replied:
“A wise man knows himself;
a benevolent man loves himself.”
The Master said:
“You may be called a míng jūnzǐ.”
Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ:
“Does a gentleman also have worries?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“The gentleman, before he has attained his aim,
takes joy in his intent;
once he has attained it,
he takes joy in his governance.
Therefore, he has a lifetime of joy
and not a single day of worry.
As for the petty person,
before he has attained his aim,
he worries about not getting it;
once he has attained it,
he fears losing it.
Therefore, he has a lifetime of worry
and not a single day of joy.”
Gōngshū could not improve upon the marking line and ink;
the Sage cannot improve upon the rites.
As for the rites,
the common people follow them without understanding them,
while the Sage follows them and understands them.
Zéngzǐ said:
“Do not distance those close to you while drawing close to those distant;
do not be unkind yourself and then resent others;
do not wait until punishment has arrived to cry out to Heaven.
Distancing those close while drawing close to those distant—
is that not a reversal?
Being unkind yourself and resenting others—
is that not being far off?
Waiting until punishment has arrived to cry out to Heaven—
is that not too late?
The Shī says:
‘The trickling water from the source
was not dammed or blocked.
When the wheel hub is already broken,
only then one enlarges the spokes.
When the matter has already failed,
then one heaves a great sigh.’
Will that be of any benefit!”
Zéngzǐ was ill;
Zéng Yuán was holding his feet.
Zéngzǐ said:
“Yuán, mark this!
I will tell you:
Fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and alligators still consider the deep abyss to be shallow
and dig holes within it.
Hawks and kites still consider the mountains to be low
and build nests on top of them.
When they are caught,
it must be because of bait.
Therefore, if a gentleman can refrain from letting profit harm righteousness,
then shame and disgrace will have no way to reach him.”
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
“Why is it that the gentleman values jade and despises mǐn stone?
Why is that?
Is it because jade is scarce and mǐn stone is common?”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“Hah!
Cì,
what kind of talk is this?
Would a gentleman despise something because it is common
or value it because it is scarce?
As for jade,
the gentleman compares his virtue to it.
Gentle, soft, and lustrous—
that is benevolence.
Firm and with distinct patterns—
that is wisdom.
Solid and unyielding—
that is righteousness.
Sharp-edged but not harmful—
that is conduct.
It breaks but does not bend—
that is courage.
Flaws and beauty are both visible—
that is sincerity.
When struck,
its sound is clear, resonant, and far-reaching,
ending abruptly—
that is elegance.
Therefore, even if mǐn stone has ornate carvings,
it is not as glorious as jade.
The Shī says:
‘I think of the gentleman,
gentle like jade.’
This is what it refers to.”
Zéngzǐ said:
“If I travel with others and am not loved,
I must be lacking in benevolence.
If I associate with others and am not respected,
I must be lacking in seniority.
If I handle wealth and am not trusted,
I must be lacking in trustworthiness.
If these three are found in oneself,
how can one resent others?
Those who resent others are at a dead end;
those who resent Heaven have no understanding.
To fail in oneself and then turn to blame others—
is that not also convoluted!”
Nánguǒ Huìzǐ asked Zǐgòng:
“Why is the Master’s gate
so mixed with different kinds of people?”
Zǐgòng said:
“The gentleman rectifies himself and waits;
he does not reject those who wish to come,
nor does he stop those who wish to leave.
Furthermore, at a good physician’s gate, there are many sick people;
beside a straightening board, there is much crooked wood.
This is why it is mixed.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“A Jūnzǐ has three forms of empathy.
To have a ruler and be unable to serve him,
yet to have ministers and demand their service,
is not empathy;
to have parents and be unable to repay them,
yet to have children and demand their filial piety,
is not empathy;
to have an elder brother and be unable to respect him,
yet to have a younger brother and demand his obedience to commands,
is not empathy.
If a Shì is clear about these three forms of empathy,
then he can rectify his own person.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“A Jūnzǐ has three reflections,
which he must not fail to consider.
If one is young and does not learn,
when grown up, one will lack ability;
if one is old and does not teach,
after death, there will be no remembrance;
if one has much and does not give,
when impoverished, one will have no one to help.
For this reason, in youth, the Jūnzǐ reflects on being grown
and thus learns;
in old age, he reflects on death
and thus teaches;
in times of abundance, he reflects on poverty
and thus gives.”
Lǔ Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ:
“I wish to evaluate the Shì of my state,
to govern the state with them.
May I ask how to select them?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“To be born in the present world,
while setting one’s heart on the Dào of antiquity;
to reside amidst the customs of today,
while wearing the garments of antiquity;
for one to set this aside and do wrong,
is that not rare indeed!”
Āigōng said:
“In that case, are those who wear the Zhāngfǔ, Qùjù,
Shēndài, and carry the Jìnhù,
all of them worthy men?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“Not necessarily so.
Those who wear the Duānyī, Xuánsháng,
and Miàn while riding in a Lù,
their intention is not on eating meat;
those who wear the Zhǎncuī, Jiānjù,
and carry a staff while sipping congee,
their intention is not on wine and meat.
To be born in the present world,
while setting one’s heart on the Dào of antiquity;
to reside amidst the customs of today,
while wearing the garments of antiquity;
for one to set this aside and do wrong,
even if such people exist,
are they not rare indeed!”
Āigōng said:
“Good.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“There are five types of people:
there is the Yōngrén,
there is the Shì,
there is the Jūnzǐ,
there is the Xiánrén,
and there is the Dàshèng.”
Āigōng said:
“May I ask what sort of person is called a Yōngrén?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The so-called Yōngrén is one whose
mouth cannot speak good words,
and whose heart knows no unease;
he does not know how to select Xiánrén and good Shì to rely upon as his own concern;
in action, he does not know what to strive for;
in standing still, he does not know where to settle;
daily he makes choices among material things,
yet does not know what is valuable;
he follows things like a current,
not knowing where he is returning;
his five senses are his masters,
and his heart follows them to ruin;
such a person
can be called a Yōngrén.”
Āigōng said:
“Good!
May I ask what sort of person is called a Shì?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The so-called Shì is one who,
though he cannot fully master all principles and arts,
must have a standard that he follows;
though he cannot encompass all beauty and goodness,
must have a place where he dwells.
Therefore, in knowledge, he does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be certain in what he knows;
in speech, he does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be certain in what he says;
in action, he does not strive for quantity,
but strives to be certain in the path he takes.
Thus, once knowledge is known,
once speech has been spoken,
and once action has been taken,
they are like his life, soul, and skin—they cannot be changed.
Therefore, wealth and honor are not enough to add to him,
and lowliness or poverty are not enough to diminish him;
such a person
can be called a Shì.”
Āigōng said:
“Good!
May I ask what sort of person is called a Jūnzǐ?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The so-called Jūnzǐ is one who
speaks with loyalty and trustworthiness,
yet his heart does not claim merit;
benevolence and righteousness reside in his person, yet his expression is not boastful;
his thoughts are clear and penetrating, yet his words do not contend;
thus, appearing as though he could be reached by others,
that is a Jūnzǐ.”
Āigōng said:
“Good!
May I ask what sort of person is called a Xiánrén?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The so-called Xiánrén is one whose
conduct accords with the standards,
yet does not harm his original nature;
whose words are sufficient to be a law for the world,
yet do not bring harm upon himself;
though he may possess the wealth of the world,
no one begrudges him his wealth;
though he bestows gifts to the world,
he does not suffer from poverty.
Such a person
is called a Xiánrén.”
Āigōng said:
“Good!
May I ask what sort of person is called a Dàshèng?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The so-called Dàshèng is one whose
wisdom connects to the Dà Dào,
who responds to changes without exhaustion,
and who discerns the true nature and essence of all things.
The Dà Dào
is that by which transformations occur
and all things are brought to completion;
nature and essence
are the means by which one orders right and wrong, and chooses or rejects.
Thus, his deeds are as vastly discerning as Heaven and Earth,
as clearly observant as the sun and moon;
he unites the essentials of all things like wind and rain.
Grand and earnest,
his deeds cannot be traced;
like the successor of Heaven,
his deeds cannot be fully known;
the common people are serene and do not even recognize their neighbor.
Like this,
he can be called a Dàshèng.”
Āigōng said:
“Good!”
Lǔ Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ about the cap of Shùn,
but Kǒngzǐ did not answer.
He asked three times,
and he still did not answer.
Āigōng said:
“I asked you about the cap of Shùn,
why do you not speak?”
Kǒngzǐ replied:
“The kings of old
had duties yet wore simple robes with gathered collars;
their government loved life and hated killing.
Therefore, the phoenixes dwelt in the trees,
the Qílín were in the outskirts and fields,
and the nests of crows and magpies could be peered into by stooping.
You do not ask about this, but ask about the cap of Shùn;
that is why I did not answer.”
Lǔ Āigōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
“I was born within the deep palace,
and grew up in the hands of women.
I have never known grief,
never known worry,
never known toil,
never known fear,
and never known danger.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“What you have asked,
is the question of a sagely ruler.
I, Qiū,
am a man of humble status;
how would I be sufficient to know of this?”
The Duke said:
“If not from you, I would have no one from whom to hear of it.”
Kǒngzǐ said:
“When you enter the temple gate and turn right,
ascending by the eastern steps,
you look up to see the rafters and roof-beams,
and look down to see the low tables and mats.
Their vessels remain,
but the people are gone.”
If the lord uses this to contemplate sorrow,
then how could sorrow fail to arrive?
The lord combs his hair and puts on his cap at dawn
and attends court at daybreak.
If even one matter is not responded to,
it is the beginning of disorder.
If the lord uses this to contemplate worry,
then how could worry fail to arrive?
The lord attends court at daybreak
and retires when the sun is past its zenith.
Among the descendants of the feudal lords, there must be some who are in the lower courtyard of the lord.
If the lord uses this to contemplate toil,
then how could toil fail to arrive?
When the lord goes out through the four gates of Lǔ
to look upon the four outskirts of Lǔ,
in the ruins of fallen states, there will surely be several chariot canopies there.
If the lord uses this to contemplate fear,
then how could fear fail to arrive?
Furthermore, I, Qiū, have heard it said:
The ruler is the boat;
the common people are the water.
The water can carry the boat,
and the water can overturn the boat.
If the lord uses this to contemplate peril,
then how could peril fail to arrive!"
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Do the sash, the ceremonial cap, and the zhāngfǔ cap
have any benefit to benevolence?"
Kǒngzǐ stood up respectfully and said:
"How grandly the lord speaks!
Those wearing mourning hemp and carrying a staff of mourning do not listen to music;
it is not that their ears cannot hear,
but the garments make it so.
Those in embroidered robes and patterned skirts do not eat pungent food;
it is not that their mouths cannot taste,
but the garments make it so.
Furthermore, I, Qiū, have heard it said:
one who loves a grand display of goods does not keep damaged items,
and a high official does not engage in the marketplace.
As for whether there is benefit or no benefit,
the lord surely knows it already."
Lǔ Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"May I ask about how to select people?"
Kǒngzǐ replied, saying:
"Do not select the persistent,
do not select the contentious,
and do not select the glib.
The persistent
are greedy;
the contentious
are disorderly;
the glib
are deceitful.
Therefore, only after a bow is tuned does one seek strength in it;
only after a horse is submissive does one seek excellence in it;
and only after a scholar is trustworthy and sincere does one seek wisdom and ability in him.
If a scholar is not trustworthy and sincere but has much wisdom and ability,
he is like a dhole or a wolf;
one must not approach him closely.
A saying goes:
'Huán Gōng employed his former enemy;
Wén Gōng employed his former thief.'
Thus, an enlightened ruler relies on strategy and does not trust in anger;
a dark ruler trusts in anger and does not rely on strategy.
When strategy overcomes anger, there is strength;
when anger overcomes strategy, there is ruin."
Dìng Gōng asked Yán Yuān, saying:
"Have you also heard of Dōngyě Bì’s skill in driving?"
Yán Yuān replied, saying:
"He is indeed skilled.
However,
his horses will soon fail."
Dìng Gōng was displeased
and went inside to say to his attendants:
"Does a gentleman indeed slander others?"
Three days later, the stable official came to report,
saying:
"Dōngyě Bì’s horses have failed.
The two outer horses broke away,
and the two inner horses returned to the stable."
Dìng Gōng rose from his mat and said:
"Quickly, prepare the carriage and summon Yán Yuān!"
When Yán Yuān arrived,
Dìng Gōng said:
"The other day, I asked you,
and you said:
'Dōngyě Bì’s driving,
though it is skilled,
however,
his horses will fail.'
I do not know how you knew this."
Yán Yuān replied, saying:
"I knew it by observing governance.
In the past, Shùn was skillful in employing the people,
and Zàofù was skillful in employing horses.
Shùn did not exhaust his people,
and Zàofù did not exhaust his horses.
Therefore, Shùn had no lost people,
and Zàofù had no lost horses.
Now, as for Dōngyě Bì’s driving,
he mounts the chariot and holds the reins;
his posture and the bit are perfectly aligned;
in pacing, trotting, and galloping,
the morning rituals are completed;
in crossing dangers and reaching distances,
the horses' strength is exhausted.
Yet he still demands more from the horses without ceasing.
That is how I knew it."
Dìng Gōng said:
"Good!
Could you elaborate further?"
Yán Yuān replied, saying:
"I have heard it said:
When a bird is exhausted, it pecks;
when a beast is exhausted, it claws;
when a person is exhausted, he deceives.
From ancient times until now,
there has never been one who exhausted those below him and yet avoided peril."
Yáo asked Shùn, saying:
"I wish to bring the world to submission.
What should I do?"
Shùn replied, saying:
"Hold to the One without losing it;
act on the subtle without sloth;
be loyal and trustworthy without tiring;
and the world will come to you of its own accord.
Holding to the One is like Heaven and Earth;
acting on the subtle is like the sun and the moon.
When loyalty and sincerity are abundant within,
they are manifest without
and take form across the four seas.
Is the world not just in a single corner?
What is there that would be difficult to bring about?"
Wèi Wǔ Hóu planned an affair and it was correct,
and none of his ministers could match him.
He retired from court with a joyful look.
Wú Qǐ stepped forward and said:
"Has anyone ever informed the attendants of the words of Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng?"
Wǔ Hóu said:
"What were the words of Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng?"
Wú Qǐ replied, saying:
"Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng planned an affair and it was correct,
and none of his ministers could match him.
He retired from court with a worried look.
Shēn Gōng Wū Chén stepped forward and asked:
'The King holds court and has a worried look. Why is this?'
King Zhuāng said:
'I have planned an affair and it was correct,
and none of my ministers could match me.
This is why I am worried.
It is found in the words of the Zhōng Guī,
which say:
"A feudal lord who finds a teacher for himself will become king;
he who finds a friend will become a hegemon;
he who finds someone to challenge him will survive;
but he who plans for himself and finds none equal to him will perish."
Now, even with my unworthiness, none of my ministers can match me;
my state is close to ruin!
This is why I am worried.'
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng felt worry,
yet you feel joy."
Wǔ Hóu withdrew a few steps, bowed twice, and said:
"Heaven has sent you to correct my faults."
When Bó Qín was about to return to Lǔ,
Zhōu Gōng said to Bó Qín’s tutor:
"You are about to depart.
Why not note down your young master’s fine virtues?"
The tutor replied, saying:
"He is a lenient person,
fond of relying on himself,
and is cautious.
These three are his fine virtues."
Zhōu Gōng said:
"Alas!
Are you taking human vices for fine virtues?
A gentleman loves to lead with the Way and its virtue;
thus his people return to the Way.
As for his leniency,
he goes out without making distinctions,
yet you praise it.
As for his fondness for relying on himself,
this is the reason for becoming narrow and petty.
A gentleman might have the strength of an ox,
but he does not compete with the ox in strength;
he might run like a horse,
but he does not compete with the horse in running;
he might have the knowledge of a scholar,
but he does not compete with the scholar in knowledge.
For competing
is the spirit of those who are equal."
You further praise this conduct. That caution of his
is actually due to his shallowness.
I have heard it said:
"Do not overstep and fail to see the scholars."
When seeing a scholar, ask him:
"Could it be that I have been unobservant?"
If one does not hear,
then matters will rarely arrive;
and when they rarely arrive, one becomes shallow.
That shallowness
is the way of a base person;
would you then still praise it?
I tell you:
I,
as the son of Wén Wáng,
the brother of Wǔ Wáng,
and the uncle of Chéng Wáng,
am not of low status in the world.
Yet, those whom I visited carrying ritual gifts numbered ten;
those who returned the gifts to meet with me numbered thirty;
those scholars I treated with respectful courtesy numbered over a hundred;
those who wished to speak and requested to conclude their business numbered over a thousand.
From among these, I only obtained three scholars
to correct my person
and to stabilize the world.
The reason I obtained these three scholars
was not from among the ten or the thirty people,
but rather from among the hundred and the thousand.
Therefore, to superior scholars, I showed modest courtesy;
to lower scholars, I showed generous courtesy.
Everyone considered me to be excessively fond of scholars,
and thus the scholars came.
Only after the scholars arrived could things be seen;
and only after things were seen could one know where right and wrong lay.
Be warned!
You, using the state of Lǔ to be arrogant toward others,
are close to ruin!
Scholars who depend on a salary can still be treated with arrogance,
but scholars who correct themselves cannot be treated with arrogance.
Those scholars who correct themselves
abandon nobility for lowliness,
abandon wealth for poverty,
abandon ease for toil,
and though their complexions are dark and weathered, they do not lose their integrity.
Because of this, the principles of the world do not cease,
and cultural refinement is not discarded."
A saying goes:
"The border warden of Zēngqiū
met with the Prime Minister of Chǔ, Sūn Shū Áo, and said:
'I have heard:
Those who stay in office for a long time are envied by scholars;
those whose salaries are generous are resented by the people;
those whose positions are exalted are disliked by the ruler.
Now you, Prime Minister, have all three of these
yet you have not offended the scholars and people of Chǔ.
Why is this?'
Sūn Shū Áo said:
'I have been Prime Minister of Chǔ three times, yet my heart has become even more humble;
each time my salary increased, my charity became even more widespread;
as my position became more exalted, my etiquette became even more respectful.
This is why I have not offended the scholars and people of Chǔ.'"
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ,
"I, Cì, do not yet know how to be a subordinate to others."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Being a subordinate to others?
Is it not like the earth?
Dig deep into it and sweet springs are found;
plant in it and the five grains are sown;
grasses and trees proliferate there;
birds and beasts are reared there.
When alive, things stand upon it;
when dead, they enter it.
Its achievements are many, yet it does not claim merit for its virtue.
Being a subordinate to others
is indeed like the earth."
In the past, Yú did not use Gōng Zhī Qí and Jìn annexed it;
Lái did not use Zǐ Mǎ and Qí annexed it;
Zhòu disemboweled Prince Bǐ Gān and Wǔ Wáng gained the realm.
By not drawing close to the worthy or employing the wise,
their persons died and their states perished.
Those who make arguments say:
"Sūn Qīng was not equal to Kǒngzǐ."
This is not so.
Sūn Qīng was pressed by a chaotic age,
distressed by harsh punishments;
above there was no worthy ruler,
below he encountered the tyrannical Qín.
Propriety and righteousness were not practiced,
moral transformation was not achieved;
the benevolent were constrained and restricted.
The world was in darkness,
complete conduct was criticized,
and the feudal lords were greatly leaning toward ruin.
At that time,
the wise were not permitted to plan,
the capable were not permitted to govern,
and the worthy were not permitted to be employed.
Therefore, the rulers above were deluded and saw nothing,
and the worthy were kept at a distance and not accepted.
Thus, Sūn Qīng harbored the heart of a potential sage,
put on the appearance of feigned madness,
and looked upon the world with feigned foolishness.
The Shī says:
"Being both enlightened and wise,
to preserve one's person."
This is what it refers to.
This is why his reputation was not clear,
his followers were not numerous,
and his radiance was not broad.
Scholars of today
who obtain the legacy and teachings of Sūn Qīng
find them sufficient to be the models and standards for the world.
Where he remains is divine;
where he passes, transformation occurs.
Observing his virtuous conduct,
Kǒngzǐ could not surpass him.
The world does not examine him in detail,
saying he was not a sage.
What can be done about it!
The world was not well-governed,
for Sūn Qīng did not meet his time.
His virtue was like that of Yáo and Yǔ,
yet the world little knew him.
His methods were not used,
and he was doubted by others.
His wisdom was most clear;
following the Way and correcting his conduct,
it was sufficient to be the fundamental law.
Alas!
How worthy!
He should have been a sovereign.
Heaven and Earth did not know,
favoring Jié and Zhòu,
and killing the worthy and good.
Bǐ Gān had his heart cut out;
Kǒngzǐ was detained in Kuāng;
Jiēyú withdrew from the world;
Jīzǐ feigned madness;
Tián Cháng committed rebellion;
Hélǘ usurped power.
Those who do evil gain blessings,
and those who are good meet with calamity.
Those who make arguments today
again do not examine the reality,
but instead believe in mere reputations.
The times and eras were different;
from what could his praise have arisen?
Not being allowed to govern,
how could his achievements be completed?
With his will cultivated and his virtue profound,
who could say he was not worthy?
